descs.en: He thinks her hands are broken and opens every door for her. She secretly got her surgeon’s hands back, and works nights in a basement as the family’s ghost surgeon.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Elara Lin is a final-year medical student who talks all the time, practises stitches on bananas, and on her first morning on the surgical ward tells the chief resident he's missed a leak. She's right. By the end of the day Wang Xing Yue has handed her logbook to someone else, so that he can ask her to dinner. He's been in love with her for fifteen months. The only person he's told is his brother, who sent him a paper about voles.

She's also the Lins' surgeon. When the family's people bleed somewhere a hospital can't see them, she goes, with whatever she can steal. In a supply room at three in the morning she begs him not to ask, and he promises he won't. He keeps that promise for three and a half years: through a knife at her father's door that cuts through her right wrist, a winter when she stops talking, and the year she gets her hands back in secret on a machine in a garage and goes back to work in a cellar, in a mask, as Doctor Ghost.

He's known since she mended his pillowcase at two in the morning. He never asks her to stop. He restocks her bag instead, and when she finally calls him, he comes with blood.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Elara has been in the corner of every Lin book so far: late, in scrubs, with her hair falling out of its clip, crying at weddings, stapling somebody's head on a kitchen table. I wanted to know what all that cost her, and who looks after the person who looks after everyone.

Xing Yue isn't a nice man to anyone but her. He makes residents sick on his ward rounds, he checks her location, he goes through her bag, and he lies to his own professor without blinking. I didn't want the book to tell him off for any of it. The one thing he never does is ask her to be someone else, and that felt like the most romantic thing I could give her.

There's blood, because it's a book about surgeons, but the medicine stays at story level. The love scenes are slow and mostly come after night shifts, in early light, which is how she likes them. Nobody has a baby. They get a house with a long kitchen, two pagers, a phone in a drawer that rings at half past eleven, and each other.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a 21+ medical romance, warm and funny for most of its length, but it has some hard moments:

• Love scenes throughout, heated and detailed but not explicit, from She Narrates Everything on

• An infected knife wound treated over the phone at night (Three in the Morning, on Speaker)

• A gunshot wound, sepsis and surgery on a kitchen table, with stolen hospital supplies (Zhao Zhendong Is Bleeding Out, Fifteen Days of Drips)

• A shooting in a noodle shop and a head wound closed at home (Staples on a Kitchen Table)

• A people-smuggling boat and cold, frightened survivors at a border bridge (The Seventh Guest)

• Burns after a workshop fire (Again?)

• A knife attack, heavy bleeding and a serious hand injury (The Knife at the Red Door)

• Nerve pain, withdrawal into silence, and a father's confession to a crime that killed her birth parents in a fire (The House Is Too Quiet, A Name in a Ledger, Elara Before the Lins)

• A prison visit (Her Mother's Window)

• Secret surgery outside hospitals, falsified records and lies to police and employers (A Surgeon Who Doesn't Exist, The Cellar Under the Rope Store, Doctor Ghost)

• A girl's face cut with a bottle by her father, mentioned (The Cellar Under the Rope Store)

• A gunshot to the thigh and life-threatening bleeding (Two Surgeons, One Table)

• A workplace inquiry and suspension (I Know)

• A footbridge collapse with many casualties (A Mass Casualty Night)

• A partner who tracks her phone and goes through her bag, shown without judgement (from Three in the Morning, on Speaker)

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
City Hospital — the teaching hospital at the foot of the hill. Ward 9B, general surgery, is on the ninth floor of the tower; the old 1930s block stands behind it.
Harbourside General — the big hospital by the harbour, where Elara does her intern year and goes back to training in 2027.
The Crestview — the private hospital on the hill above the old racecourse, where Dr. Meng repairs her hand and Ms. Cui makes her cry.
The hospital garden — behind the old block: a camphor tree older than the hospital, a koi pond, and the fourth window along on the first floor, which was her mother's ward.
14 Banyan Terrace — his flat, the top two floors and roof of a white 1950s building ten minutes downhill from City Hospital.
2 Camphor Hill — the old doctor's house above the hospital, with a long kitchen and a back room for the rig. Bought in both their names, without asking.
The Walled City — the old district where the Lins live, behind a red door with a brass fish knocker and eleven chairs that don't match.
The cellar under the rope store — the room Raiden builds next to the garage near the Docks, behind a steel door painted to look like wood.
Doctor Ghost — the name the docks give the masked surgeon who never speaks and always hums.
The rig — Jinx's steel training machine for Elara's hand: springs, a pinch gauge, pins and a wire that buzzes. Every knob turns a quarter.
The ghost phone — the line that rings only from her father's or Uncle Mok's numbers. From July 2027 it lives in the kitchen drawer.
The dot — her phone location, shared with him ‘for night shifts’ from 2023, and his with her from 2026.
The rules — what they wrote on the back of his suspension letter. Rule one: nobody does this alone.
Qu Xiaoyue — her birth name, ‘little moon’. Elara is a moon of Jupiter, so she kept a piece of it.
Qu Lighterage — her father's firm: four lighter boats between the ships and the old Walled City piers.
Plum Steps — the children's home at the top of a long flight of stone steps, closed in 2011.
Loupes — magnifying glasses surgeons wear to operate. Hers are dark red, made for her eyes, with E.L. inside the arm.
Registrar, consultant — a registrar is a mid-level surgeon in training; a consultant is the senior surgeon in charge.

chapters.title: The Student Who Told the Chief Resident He Was Wrong
chapters.desc: On the first morning of her surgery rotation, a final-year student tells the chief resident he’s missed a leak. She’s right, and he has seen her face before.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d rather be wrong about this one.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The ward round on 9B started at seven, and Wang Xing Yue had never once started it late.

Professor Liao was at a conference across the water until Thursday, which meant the round was his. He had been chief surgical resident for two months. He had a junior resident, Dr. Rao, two years out of medical school, whose notes were neat and who didn’t read them back. He had an intern, Dr. Weng, three weeks into his first job and still jumping every time his bleep went off. He had a second resident already scrubbed in theatre. And he had four final-year students on their first day, in clean white coats with the fold lines from the packet still in them, holding their notebooks against their chests like shields.

At bed nine he stopped and held out his hand for the drug chart.

He read it. He handed it to Dr. Weng.

“Read it to me.”

Weng read it. An antibiotic, twice a day, a normal dose.

“His kidneys are working at a third of what yours are,” said Xing Yue. “It’s on the front page of his notes. Read it again.”

Weng read it again, faster, and stopped in the same place.

“Again. Slower. You’re not tying your shoes.”

The old man in bed nine was watching all this with great interest over his breakfast tray. Weng went red from the collar up, read it a third time, saw it, and said, “Oh.”

“Change it before you go to lunch. Then go and look up what it does to kidneys, and tell me tomorrow, without notes.”

He moved on. The students moved after him in a clump, the way students always did, as if standing close together would make them smaller. Three of them were looking at the floor. The fourth was a small one at the back with her hair coming out of its clip, and she wasn’t looking at the floor. She was looking at him, with her head on one side, the way people look at weather coming in over the harbour, more interested than frightened.

He didn’t think about it. He had a ward to get round.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bed fourteen was Mr. Yin Shoucheng, seventy-one, a retired bus driver, day four after the right side of his bowel had been taken out for a cancer and the two ends joined up again. He’d had a bad night. Temperature up to thirty-eight and a half at two in the morning. Heart rate a hundred and twelve. He had been restless, the nurses said, and kept trying to get out of bed. When Xing Yue listened to the back of his chest there were crackles at the bottom on the right.

“Chest,” said Xing Yue. “He’s seventy-one, he’s had a general anaesthetic, he’s not been breathing deeply because it hurts. Sputum sample, chest X-ray this morning, start antibiotics for a chest infection, get the physio up to him before ten. Sit him out in the chair after.”

Dr. Rao wrote it down.

“Sorry,” said a voice at the back, “can I say something?”

She didn’t wait to find out if she could.

“His heart rate went up first,” said the small student with the clip. “Before the fever. It was ninety yesterday at lunch and a hundred and four at four o’clock and the temperature didn’t go up till the night. It’s on the obs chart. And he said his tummy hurts more today than yesterday, not less. I came in at six to see my patients and he was awake, so I said good morning, and I pressed on his belly when I said it.” She stopped, and then went on, because apparently she couldn’t help it. “He didn’t like it. On the right. Near where the join would be.”

Nobody on the team breathed.

The residents knew he didn’t get corrected. He never got angry about it. He was almost never wrong, that was all, and when you told him he was, you’d better be right, because he would take your argument apart in front of the patient and you’d stand there in your new white coat and watch him do it.

Xing Yue looked at her.

“The chest is the commonest cause of a fever on day four,” he said.

“I know,” she said. “I’d still want the scan. If it’s his chest and we scan him, we’ve lost an hour and some money. If it’s a leak and we wait, Mr. Yin pays for it.” She swallowed. Her face had gone pink and her voice hadn’t changed at all. “I’d rather be wrong about this one.”

Mr. Yin, from the bed, said, “So would I, young lady.”

Xing Yue put the notes down on the end of the bed.

He warmed his hands against each other and laid one flat on the old man’s belly, and pressed, gently, below the ribs on the left, and then in the middle, and then low on the right. On the right the muscles went hard under his palm before he’d pressed a centimetre. Mr. Yin sucked in his breath through his false teeth and grabbed the sheet.

Xing Yue took his hand away.

“Sorry, Mr. Yin.” He straightened up. He looked at the student. “You’re right. Book the scan.”

Then he turned to Dr. Rao.

“You saw this chart at six,” he said. “Why did a student find it?”

Rao went white. He opened his mouth.

“Don’t answer that. Book a CT with contrast. Ring theatres and tell the coordinator I may need a slot this afternoon. Then come back and read every chart on this ward again, and this time read the numbers instead of copying them.”

Rao went. He went fast, with his neat notes held against his chest.

Xing Yue picked up Mr. Yin’s chart and started writing on it. Out of the corner of his eye he could see the small student. She was standing up straight and her face had gone from pink to white, as if she’d just understood what she’d done and who she’d done it to, and she looked as though she might be sick, and under that, at the same time, as though she’d never been so happy in her life.

He looked at her properly then.

Round face. Quick dark eyes. Long dark hair, a great deal of it, trying to get away from a plastic clip. A cardigan under the white coat with a pocket full of pens and something that crinkled. He had seen that face before.

It was on the sixth floor, fifteen months ago, a little after six on a Saturday morning, at the end of a night when he’d been called down to look at a young man’s ribs after a van hit him: three cracked ribs on the left, a clear scan, not a surgical problem. He’d been on his way out when the family came up the corridor, and a girl in a T-shirt with her hair half out of a clip had stopped him by the lift and asked, all in one breath, whether anyone had checked her brother’s spleen, because it was the left ribs, wasn’t it, and the spleen sat right under the left ribs, and she’d read that it could bleed slowly and look like nothing for hours.

He’d said they’d checked. He’d said the scan was clear and they’d keep an eye. She’d said, “Oh, good, thank you, sorry,” and gone past him into the room, talking already.

He’d gone home and not slept. He’d put it down to the night. He’d been putting it down to the night for fifteen months.

He finished writing on Mr. Yin’s chart, and signed it, and moved on to bed fifteen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the round, he saw her slip the intern something from her cardigan pocket. A boiled sweet, in a twist of wrapper. Weng looked at it as if it were a medal.

✦ ✦ ✦

The CT was done at twenty to ten. Xing Yue looked at it in the dark of the reporting room with the radiologist. There was a small leak from the join, and a pocket of fluid sitting beside it that hadn’t been there on Friday.

Theatre was at one.

He found the student in the corridor outside the doctors’ room, eating a cereal bar standing up, reading Mr. Yin’s notes over somebody’s shoulder.

“You found it,” he said. “You’ll want to see it. Go and scrub.”

She stared at him with her mouth full. Then she swallowed and said, “Yes. Yes. Sorry. Yes,” and went, and came back, because she’d gone the wrong way.

✦ ✦ ✦

She talked while she scrubbed.

Not to him. To herself, mostly, about where the soap was and how hot the tap went and how the last time she’d scrubbed it had been for a toe. He stood at the next sink with his arms under the water and didn’t say anything, and she glanced across and found him watching her hands, and talked faster.

She had good hands. Small, quick and sure. She did every finger, every side of every finger, the backs, the wrists, the way you were taught and nobody did after the first year.

On the badge clipped to her scrubs it said LIN ELARA, FINAL YEAR.

Lin.

He’d known that, really, since bed fourteen. A young man hit by a van, a Lin, a room to himself on the sixth floor because someone had looked at his wallet. A grey-haired man in the corridor that morning with a face like the side of a building and two men behind him. He’d known whose family it was the way everyone in this city knew.

LIN ELARA, FINAL YEAR. He was on her rotation sheet. For the next six weeks he’d be signing her logbook: her cases, her skills, the line at the bottom that said whether she was fit to be a doctor.

He held his hands up and let the water run off his elbows. She held hers up beside him and did the same, and looked across at him, and her face went pink again above the mask she hadn’t tied yet.

He decided, there, at the sink, with his hands dripping. And then he decided what he’d have to do first.

✦ ✦ ✦

In theatre she held the retractor where he put her and didn’t move it a millimetre in two hours.

He took the join apart. He washed Mr. Yin out until the fluid ran clear. He brought the end of the bowel out onto the skin as a stoma, for a few months, until the old man was strong enough to have it put back. It was ordinary work and he’d done it many times.

She said small things under her breath the whole way through, not chatter, just “okay, okay, there, okay.” The scrub nurse looked at her over her mask, twice, the second time with her eyebrows up.

Xing Yue didn’t look at her at all. He found that he didn’t want her to stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four o’clock he went to find Dr. Fei Ran in the registrars’ office.

Fei was a senior registrar, four years older than him and in no hurry to be anything else, and she was eating noodles out of a plastic tub at her desk with her feet on the bin. She looked up.

“I need you to take over one of the students,” he said. “Assessments, logbook, all of it. Lin Elara.”

Fei put her chopsticks down.

“The one who found Mr. Yin’s leak,” she said. “I heard. The whole floor heard.” She looked at him. “Why?”

He didn’t answer.

“With a student you met this morning?”

“Yes.”

Fei looked at him for another few seconds. He looked back. Then she picked up the rotation sheet off the pile beside her, crossed his name out at the top of one line, wrote hers in, initialled it, and went back to her noodles.

“I’m not going to ask,” she said, with her mouth full. “I’m going to tell everyone at Christmas.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went down to recovery at half past five.

Mr. Yin was awake, more or less, with a mask on his face and a nurse checking his drip. He opened his eyes when Xing Yue came to the end of the bed and looked at him with the deep, puzzled calm of a man still full of anaesthetic.

“Doctor,” he said, through the mask.

“It went well, Mr. Yin. You’ll be sore. You’ll be all right.”

The old man nodded slowly. Then he moved his head on the pillow and looked past him, down the ward, as if he were looking for someone.

“Where’s the little doctor?” he said. “The one who talks.”

Xing Yue looked down the ward too. She wasn’t there. She’d been sent home at five by Fei, who’d seen her eat a second cereal bar standing up and decided she’d had enough first day.

“Tomorrow,” he said. “She’ll come tomorrow.”

chapters.title: Love at First Sight Is a Sleep-Deprivation Symptom
chapters.desc: Elara finds her logbook handed to someone else and marches into the chief resident’s office to apologise for being right. He tells her why.
chapters.epigraph: “I can’t take you to dinner and sign your logbook. I picked dinner.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
On Tuesday he didn’t look at her once.

Elara noticed, because she spent the whole round trying to stand somewhere he’d have to. She stood at the end of beds. She stood by the drug trolley. At bed six she stood so close to his elbow that she could smell the soap on him, which was the plain kind in the hospital dispensers, and tea, and he turned the page of the chart and asked Dr. Rao for the potassium as if she were a coat stand.

He asked Dr. Rao for a great deal that morning. He asked him why a man on a drip had no fluid chart, and why a woman whose drain had stopped draining hadn’t been told anything, and what Rao thought “patient comfortable” meant, written at four in the morning about someone who’d been given morphine twice. He asked it all in the same flat voice, never loud. Rao answered the first one and then stopped trying. By bed twelve his ears had gone a dark painful red, and the patient in bed twelve, a big woman with a gallstone, patted his hand when Xing Yue had moved on.

At the end of the round Elara gave Rao a boiled sweet. He took it without looking and put it in his pocket, and then he looked at it and said, “Thanks,” in a voice like he’d been punched.

She went to see Mr. Yin after. He was sitting up with the stoma bag under his gown, grey and cross and alive. He told her the jelly was terrible and asked whether she was married.

“I’m a student,” said Elara.

“That’s not an answer,” said Mr. Yin, and went to sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday, Dr. Fei Ran stopped her outside the sluice and said, “I’m doing your logbook now, by the way. I’ve got your sheet. Come and find me Friday and we’ll go through it.”

“Oh,” said Elara. “Okay. Sure. Thanks.” Then: “Why?”

Dr. Fei was already halfway down the corridor with a tub of noodles. “Ask him,” she said over her shoulder, and went into the lift.

Elara stood outside the sluice.

She knew why. Obviously she knew why. She’d stood on a ward round on her first morning and told a chief resident in front of his whole team and his patient that he’d got it wrong. She’d said tummy. She’d said it twice. She’d eaten a cereal bar in the corridor in front of him with her mouth open. And now he’d handed her logbook to someone else, because he couldn’t stand the sight of her, and she’d spend six weeks on his unit being invisible, and at the end of it someone would write fine in the box, and fine was what you wrote about a student you’d forgotten.

She thought about it through a clinic. She thought about it on the bus. She thought about it in the shower, in the kitchen, through dinner, and at the long table in the Walled City afterwards, while Ah Sim scraped the pots and told her she was eating like a bird.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight she went up to Eliana’s room, because the light was on under the door.

It was always on. Her little sister was nineteen and slept from four in the morning to noon like a bat, in a nest of hoodies, with three screens on the desk and a fourth on her knees. Elara sat on the end of the bed and told her everything: the round, Mr. Yin, the leak, the scan, the sink, the logbook, Dr. Fei and the noodles, tummy.

Eliana didn’t look round from the screens. When Elara had run out, she said, “He’s thirty. From the north. No girlfriend. Nothing online. He eats beef noodles at eleven every night he’s on call, at the place across from the ambulance bay.”

Elara looked at the back of her head.

She didn’t ask how she knew. Nobody in the family asked Eliana how she knew anything. You’d only get a look.

“I didn’t ask for that,” Elara said.

“No,” said Eliana, and typed something.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday she went to apologise.

She’d written it out. Not on paper, in her head, on the bus, in three parts, the way she did with patients’ histories so she wouldn’t lose anything. One, she was sorry she’d contradicted him in front of Mr. Yin, because you didn’t do that, and it wasn’t how she’d been brought up, even if he’d been wrong. Two, she was sorry about the corridor. Three was the important one, and she’d lost three somewhere around the stop by the fish market, but it would come back to her when she got there. It always did.

His office was at the end of the surgical corridor on the ninth floor. It was a room the size of a cupboard with one window, a desk, two chairs, a computer older than she was and a shelf of journals. The door was half open. He was at the desk, writing in a set of notes, in handwriting that looked from the door like a seismograph.

It was seven in the evening. She knocked on the frame.

He looked up. He looked at her. He put the pen down.

“Dr. Wang,” said Elara. “Sorry. Have you got a minute? It’ll be one minute. It might be two. I wanted to say sorry. I’ve got three things.”

He said nothing. He took his glasses off and began to clean them on a folded handkerchief from his pocket. She took that as a yes.

She told him the first thing. It came out longer than it had been on the bus, because she explained why you didn’t contradict a senior doctor in front of a patient, which he presumably knew, and then she explained that she’d still have said it, because of Mr. Yin, which wasn’t really an apology at all, and she heard herself not apologising and went on anyway. She did the second thing. She said the cereal bar had been a mistake. She said she was normally quite tidy. This was a lie, and she could feel it on her face, so she said it again to make it more convincing. Then she stopped, because three had not come back.

“And three,” she said. “Mr. Yin’s eating jelly. He says it’s terrible. I don’t know if that’s three. I think three was something else. But I thought you’d want to know about the jelly.”

She ran out.

The office was quiet. Somewhere down the corridor a trolley went past with a bad wheel.

He put his glasses back on.

“You didn’t do anything wrong,” he said. “On the round, or in the corridor. You were right. You’ll be right again, and you should say so again, and you shouldn’t come and apologise for it.”

“Oh,” she said. “Then why did Dr. Fei—”

“I asked her to take your logbook because I’m taking you to dinner.” He said it in the same voice he’d used on the ward for potassium. “I can’t take you to dinner and sign your logbook. I picked dinner.”

Elara stood in the doorway.

She looked at him. He looked back. His face didn’t change at all. It was a serious face, a bit older than thirty, with the dark-framed glasses and the hair cut short and neat, and a tiredness round the eyes that seemed to live there. He didn’t look like he was joking. She didn’t think he knew how.

“That wasn’t a question,” she said.

“No.”

“You’re meant to ask. People ask. Would you like to have dinner, and then I say yes or no.”

“You can say no,” he said.

She waited for him to say something else. He didn’t. He sat there with his hands flat on the notes and looked at her, and she understood that he was waiting, and that if she said no he would say all right, and pick up his pen, and never mention it again, and be exactly the same on the ward tomorrow. She understood it so clearly that her stomach turned over.

She didn’t say no.

“Oh,” said Elara.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then, because she couldn’t help it, she went on.

Was it allowed? It probably wasn’t allowed. He was the chief resident and she was a student on his unit, and there were rules about that, there had to be, there were rules about everything, there was a rule about how long you could leave a cannula in. She got her phone out. She found the student handbook. It took her a while because the university had put it inside another document inside a folder called General, and she talked the whole time she was looking, about the folder, and the university, and the time they’d moved the anatomy exam and told everybody by fax.

She found it. She read it to him out loud.

Students should not enter into a personal relationship with any member of staff who has a role in their teaching assessment or supervision. Where such a relationship exists or begins, the staff member must declare it and withdraw from that role.

She read it twice. She looked up.

“You’ve withdrawn,” she said.

He said he had, on Monday, at four o’clock. She said that was before he’d asked her, and he said he still hadn’t asked her.

That was true, and she opened her mouth to say so, and shut it again.

“Friday,” he said. “After your skills session.”

“I can’t on Friday. It’s the banana night. In the skills lab. We do suturing on bananas, all the final years, it’s a sort of competition, it isn’t really a competition, it’s for practice, but everyone treats it like one, and I won last year, so I have to go, or Shu Kai will say I was scared.”

“Then after the bananas,” said Xing Yue.

She heard herself say, “Okay.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, on the way down the corridor, she noticed things. She’d always noticed things. It was the one part of being a doctor that she’d been good at before she knew anything.

He cleaned his glasses when he wanted time to think. He’d done it when she knocked, and again when she read out the handbook, slowly, getting every corner of each lens. His watch was a plain steel one with a second hand, an old-fashioned one, for pulses. He hadn’t looked at his phone once in twenty minutes, and it had buzzed on the desk three times. He walked beside her, not in front of her, and he shortened his steps without seeming to think about it, because his legs were twice the length of hers.

She talked. She talked about Mr. Yin and the jelly, and about how her brother had once been in this hospital, on the sixth floor, last year, after a van, and how her father had stood in the corridor all morning and made every nurse on the floor nervous. He didn’t say anything to that. She thought he must be bored, and looked up, and found him listening as though she were giving him a history and he’d need every word later.

They came to the lifts. He pressed the button for her.

When the doors opened, he put his hand at the small of her back to steer her in.

It was a light touch, through her cardigan. It lasted about as long as it took her to step forward. Then he took his hand away fast, as if he’d touched a hot pan, and put it in his pocket, and stood back from the doors.

She turned round in the lift and looked at him.

He was standing in the corridor in his white shirt and his dark tie with his hand in his pocket, looking at her, and his face was as serious as it had been in the office, and his ears had gone faintly pink.

She didn’t think. She reached out of the lift and took hold of his tie.

She didn’t pull it. She just held it, in her fist, the dark blue silk of it, warm from him. He went completely still. The doors started to close. She looked at her own hand on his tie as though someone else had put it there and let go, and the doors shut between them, and she was alone in the lift with her face on fire.

She rode down nine floors with her hands over her face.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the taxi on the way back to the Walled City, she worked it out.

She’d gone in there with three things to say sorry for. She’d said two, lost the third, talked for a quarter of an hour about a folder called General, and come out with a date she hadn’t been asked on and hadn’t agreed to.

Except she had agreed to it. She went over it again, the whole thing, from the knock. Somewhere between then I say yes or no and after the bananas, she’d said yes. She hadn’t decided to. She’d just said it, the way you put your hand out when something’s falling.

She’d held his tie.

She put her forehead against the cold window of the taxi and watched the harbour go past, all its lights, and laughed out loud, and the driver looked at her in the mirror.

“Good day?” he said.

“I don’t know,” said Elara. “I think so. I’ll tell you on Friday.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At home the light was still on under Eliana’s door.

Elara went past it and into her own room and lay down on the bed with her shoes on. After a minute her phone buzzed on her chest.

Eliana: the noodle place shuts at 1. fyi

She hadn’t told her. She hadn’t told anyone. She lay on her bed and looked at the ceiling and didn’t reply, and after another minute the phone buzzed again.

Eliana: you’re welcome

Three came back to her at twenty past one, when she was nearly asleep. It had never been an apology: she’d been thinking about him since the sink.

chapters.title: Suturing Practice on a Banana
chapters.desc: She beats every student in the skills lab with a needle and a banana. At dinner she talks for three hours, and on the steps outside he stops her in the middle of a story.
chapters.epigraph: “Finish the story later.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The skills lab was in the old medical building on the hill, a long room on the ground floor with tall windows and a glass panel in the door, and on Friday nights in September it smelled of bananas.

Xing Yue wasn’t teaching. He’d taught the session for three years and had handed it on to a registrar this year, and he had no reason to be there except that he had come up the hill in the car at half past six and parked outside and walked down the corridor and stopped at the glass.

Thirty final-year students sat at long benches with a banana each, taped to a board, a needle holder, forceps, scissors, and a packet of suture. Each banana had a cut down it, through the skin, a few centimetres long. The idea was to close it so neatly that you couldn’t get a fingernail into the line. The registrar at the front had a stopwatch, which wasn’t the idea at all, but there had always been a stopwatch, because they were students.

She was on the second bench, by the window.

She talked the whole time. He could see it through the glass: her mouth going, her head turning to the boy beside her, a tall boy with an expensive haircut who looked like he wanted her to stop. Her hands didn’t care what her mouth was doing. They went down the cut, in and out, the needle turning in the holder, a knot, a snip, the next one, without hurry and without a single wasted move. It was like watching someone knit while they were telling you about their holiday.

She put her instruments down and held up her hand.

The registrar looked at the stopwatch, and at the banana, and ran a fingernail down the line, and said something, and the room groaned. The boy with the haircut put his head in his arms.

Xing Yue stood at the glass with his hands in his pockets and didn’t go in.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came out at half past eight with her bag over her shoulder and her cardigan buttoned wrong, eating the banana.

She saw him and stopped dead in the corridor with her mouth full.

“You’re faster than me,” he said.

She swallowed. “You were watching?”

“Since the start.”

“Oh no.” She looked at the banana in her hand. She’d got to the stitches. “Everyone says I talk too much to be a surgeon. Dr. Mao in second year said it in front of the whole class. He said, Miss Lin, theatre is a quiet place. I said, then I’ll be quiet in it. I wasn’t. I’m not.”

“You can talk and sew at the same time,” said Xing Yue. “Most people can’t do either.”

The tall boy with the haircut came out of the lab behind her with his board under his arm. He saw who she was talking to and his whole face changed. He held the board out.

“Dr. Wang. Sorry. Would you mind looking at my knots? I’m never sure about the tension.”

Xing Yue looked at the banana without taking it.

“Your third and fifth knots will slip by morning,” he said. “In a person that’s a bleed. You’re pulling the second throw up before the first is down, because you’re watching her instead of your hands. Do fifty tonight. Don’t do them here.”

The boy went the colour of the banana. He said thank you, which was more than most of them managed, and went down the corridor fast.

Elara watched him go. Then she looked up at Xing Yue with her eyebrows high.

“That was Shu Kai,” she said. “His father’s on the hospital board.”

“Then he’ll want his knots to hold.”

She laughed, a short surprised laugh that went up the corridor, and put the end of the banana in the bin by the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her to Old Bian’s.

It was a northern place up a narrow flight of stairs above a tailor’s, eight tables and a kitchen you could see into, with a calendar from a flour company on the wall and the same plastic tablecloths it had had when he came south. Old Bian came out of the kitchen in his vest and looked at Xing Yue, and then at her, and then at Xing Yue again, and said nothing at all, which from Old Bian was a speech.

She stood at the top of the stairs and looked down at her cardigan.

“I’m in my cardigan,” she said. “I’ve got banana on it. You said dinner and I thought, he means the canteen, or noodles, or something, and I didn’t change, and you’re in a coat.”

“It’s the same coat I wear to the ward.”

“It’s a nice coat.”

“Sit down, Elara.”

She sat down. She looked at the menu, which was written on the wall in chalk, and he watched her look at it. She read it the way she’d read the obs chart: everything, top to bottom. She went back to the lamb dumplings and the cold cucumber and the noodles with the chilli oil and the braised pork with the hard-boiled eggs. When Old Bian came, Xing Yue ordered those, and the soup, and the flatbreads, and a pot of tea.

“That’s too much,” she said.

“You looked at all of them twice.”

She went pink, and then, after a minute, she forgot to be pink. He watched it happen. The food came, and she ate as though she’d been on a ward since six in the morning, which she had, and she started to talk.

She talked about Mr. Yin, who had asked for her twice and who had told her the hospital jelly tasted of shampoo. She talked about the banana night, and how bananas were the closest thing to skin you could get for the price, because the peel held a stitch and tore if you were rough, the way skin did, and how in first year they’d used pigs’ feet from the market and the whole lab had smelled of it for a week. She talked about her classmates, all of them, with a story each. She told him about the time she’d split her jeans down the back seam at a bus stop on her way to an exam, in second year, and had gone into the toilets at the station with her sewing kit and—

“Wait,” she said. “Wait, I’m not telling that one yet. That’s a long one. I’ll tell it later.”

She told him about the Walled City instead, in pieces. A big family. A tall old house with too many stairs. Her father, who was “in logistics”, and she said it with a little face that told him she knew exactly what he’d think of that. A sister with a flower shop. A brother who drew buildings. Another sister who didn’t talk. A little sister with three screens who knew everything about everyone.

“She knew you eat beef noodles at eleven on call nights,” said Elara. “She didn’t say how. I didn’t ask.”

He put his tea down.

“She’s right,” he said.

“Of course she’s right. She’s always right. It’s horrible.”

He listened to all of it.

He found he wanted every piece of it, not to use, just to have: the brother who drew buildings, the bus stop, the pigs’ feet. He’d sat in rooms with consultants and professors and his father’s board and listened to people talk for hours and felt nothing but the time going. With her he didn’t feel the time going at all. When he looked at his watch it was a quarter to eleven.

She caught him listening. She stopped with a dumpling halfway to her mouth.

“You’re doing it,” she said.

“Doing what?”

“Listening. Like it’s a history. Like you’re going to have to present me on the round tomorrow.” She put the dumpling down. “Nobody listens to me like that. My family love me, but they stopped listening when I was about four, because I never stop. It’s like having the radio on.”

“I’m not going to stop,” he said.

She looked at him across the plastic tablecloth for a few seconds. Then she ate the dumpling.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was after eleven when she remembered the thing about names.

“I was named after a moon,” she said. “Did you know that? Elara. It’s one of the moons of Jupiter. A small one. There are about eighty and nobody can name more than four of them, and I’m one of the ones nobody can name.” She was pleased about it. “My mother chose it. My father says she liked the sound.”

He said nothing.

He could see her working it out. She’d seen his name on the rota a hundred times. Wang Xing Yue. She looked up at the ceiling, at the flour-company calendar, and back at him, and her face went slowly scarlet from the neck up.

“Star,” she said. “And moon. Your name’s star and moon.”

He picked up his tea.

“Oh no,” said Elara. She put both hands over her face. “Oh no. Don’t tell anyone. If my brother finds out he’ll put it on a cake.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He paid at the counter while she was in the toilet. Old Bian took the money, and counted out his change, and looked at the door she’d gone through, and then at him.

“She talks,” said Old Bian.

“Yes.”

Old Bian nodded, as if that settled something, and went back into his kitchen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The stairs down to the street were steep and narrow, with a light at the top and a light at the bottom and nothing in between, and she went first, and stopped on the last step but one, under the bottom light, in the doorway, and turned round to finish the jeans story.

“So I’m in the toilets at the station,” she said, “in my underwear, with my jeans across my knees and the sewing kit from my bag, and it’s one of those tiny ones from a hotel, with three colours of thread and none of them blue—”

He was on the pavement, one step below her. On the step she was nearly as tall as he was. Her face was level with his.

He took his glasses off, folded them, and put them in the pocket of her cardigan.

She glanced down at the pocket and kept going.

“—and I’ve got eleven minutes till the exam and the exam is anatomy, which I’d stayed up all night for, so my hands are shaking, and I’m doing a running stitch down the whole back seam—”

He put two fingers on the side of her throat, just under the angle of her jaw, where the pulse was.

She stopped.

He felt it under his fingers. Quick and light and hard, the way a bird’s would be, if you held one. He took his time over it, as though he were going to write it down.

“Fast,” he said, and kissed her.

It started the way he’d started it, careful, his fingers still on her throat as if he were checking she was all right. It didn’t stay that way. She made a small sound against his mouth and took his shirt in both fists, right at the front, a great handful of it in each hand, and pulled him up the step towards her, hard, so that he had to put his other hand on the wall beside her head. He forgot about her pulse. He forgot about the step, and the street, and the tailor’s dark window, and Old Bian, who was certainly listening at the top of the stairs. She kissed him back as if she’d been waiting for him to stop wasting time, and she tasted of tea and chilli, and when he pulled her closer she came up onto her toes on the step and her clip came loose from her hair and fell.

He caught it in his hand without looking.

When they stopped she didn’t let go of his shirt. She stood on the step with her forehead nearly on his and her breath going fast, and her hair everywhere, all of it down now, over her shoulders, and she was laughing, without any sound, in little breaths.

“Finish the story later,” she said.

She didn’t finish it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before he could drive her home he had to take the spare pair of glasses out of the glovebox. She watched him do it and didn’t say anything, and he saw her hand go to the cardigan pocket and stay there.

She wouldn’t let him drive into the Walled City. She had him stop at the mouth of the alley by the noodle stall, under the one streetlight, and he said he’d walk her to the door, and she said no.

“Not yet,” she said. “If my father sees a car he doesn’t know at the door after midnight, he’ll have the number plate run before you’re home. He runs checks on the postman. I’m not joking. The postman’s been the same man for nine years and Baba still has him looked at every Lunar New Year.”

He didn’t like it. He didn’t say so.

“All right,” Xing Yue said.

She got out. She walked three steps up the alley. Then she came back, at a run, and bent down to his open window, with her hand on the roof of the car and her hair blowing across her face.

“I’ve got your glasses,” she said. “In my pocket.”

He said he had another pair.

“I know. I saw. But these are yours.”

“Keep them till Monday,” he said.

She looked at him through the window. Then she leaned in and kissed him again, fast, on the corner of his mouth, because she’d come back for that and not for the glasses at all, and he knew it, and she knew he knew it. She straightened up and ran up the alley, and turned the corner by a red door he couldn’t quite see, and was gone.

He sat in the car with the engine running. He found he was still holding her hair clip.

He put it in the glovebox with the spare case, and drove home.

chapters.title: She Narrates Everything
chapters.desc: A month of noodles at eleven and walks to taxis. Then she brings breakfast to his flat after his night on call, and doesn’t go home.
chapters.epigraph: “I thought it was sleep deprivation. I gave it fifteen months.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
The noodle place across from the ambulance bay had four tables, a fridge full of beer nobody was allowed to drink, and a television on a bracket that only showed horse racing. It was open till one. On the nights he was on call, he came down at eleven in his scrubs with his pager on his waistband and ate beef noodles at the table by the window, and from the second week of September, she was there first.

She’d moved to Dr. Fei’s colorectal team on the seventh floor by then, which meant they never saw each other on the wards at all. That was the point. She saw him in the noodle place instead, and on the walk from the noodle place to the taxi rank outside the main entrance, which took four minutes if you walked normally and twenty if you were her.

She talked. He ate and listened. When his pager went he read it, and finished his mouthful, and stood up.

Once, at the end of September, he answered his phone at the table, and she heard a registrar’s voice on the other end, high and fast, explaining something about a drain. Xing Yue listened for about ten seconds.

“You’ve had that drain on your list since eight,” he said. “It’s eleven. Don’t ring me to tell me it’s blocked. Ring me when you’ve been to look at it.” He put the phone down on the table and turned back to her. “Do you want more chilli?”

She stared at him.

“That was horrible,” said Elara.

“He’ll go and look at it.” He pushed the chilli oil across the table. “You were telling me about the man with the fish hook.”

She was. She went back to it. But on the walk to the taxi she took his hand, which she hadn’t done before, and held it the whole four minutes, which took twenty.

✦ ✦ ✦

He kissed her in doorways. At the taxi rank, against the pillar by the hospital’s main doors, with the security guard pointedly looking at the sky. In the porch of the old granite block, under the verandah, where nobody went at night. Once in the rain, at the bottom of the hill, when a taxi drove past them without stopping and she said a word Ah Sim would have washed her mouth out for, and he laughed, and pulled her in under his coat, and they were both soaked through anyway.

He never did anything more than that on a call night.

He’d told her on the first one. He didn’t start anything he might have to walk away from in the middle. Not on call. She’d laughed and said that sounded grand, as if he were a ship’s captain, and he’d said it wasn’t grand, it was only true, and then his pager had gone, and he’d walked away in the middle.

She found it maddening. She also found it sweet, which was worse, and she told Eliana so at one in the morning, and Eliana said, “Ew,” without looking round.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Friday in October he was on call all night.

She knew, because she knew his rota better than her own. She knew he’d come off at seven on Saturday morning and walk home down the hill, because he walked to work and only drove at night. She knew where home was. He’d told her the address the second week, plainly, in case she ever needed it, and she’d pretended not to write it down.

At half past six on Saturday morning she bought breakfast from the bakery by the hospital that opened first: two pork buns, two egg tarts, a soy milk and a hot tea. She stood outside 14 Banyan Terrace at five past seven with the bag in one hand and her heart going and thought, this is a terrible idea. You haven’t been asked. He’s been up all night. He’s going to open the door and look at you like a drain he’s been asked to look at.

It was a white building from the fifties, four floors, with curved balconies and a frangipani tree by the gate. His name was on the top buzzer. She pressed it.

Nobody answered at first. Then the door clicked.

✦ ✦ ✦

He opened the door of the flat in his scrubs and his socks, with his glasses pushed up on his forehead, grey with tiredness all the way through, the colour of the hospital walls.

He looked at her. He looked at the bag.

“You shouldn’t have come,” he said. “I’m no use to anyone. I’ve been in theatre since three.”

“I know. That’s why I came. I brought pork buns.” She held up the bag. “You can tell me to go away. I’ll go away. But I’ll leave the buns.”

He stood in the doorway for a few more seconds. Then he stood back to let her in.

She went in and looked.

It was the whole top of the building, two floors of it, with a staircase going up to a roof she could see the light coming down from. One wall of the big room was books, floor to ceiling, medical and not, in no order she could see. A shelf by the kitchen held round flat cakes of tea in paper wrappers, a dozen of them, stacked like plates. There was a long grey sofa and a low table and a good lamp, and that was nearly all. Nothing on the walls, no photographs, no plants. It was clean and quiet and so empty that her footsteps sounded.

“You live like a monk,” she said.

“I live at work,” said Xing Yue.

She put the bag down on the kitchen counter and turned round and looked at him properly. He was holding onto the back of the sofa.

“Shower,” said Elara. “Go on. You smell of theatre. I’ll make the tea. And then you’re eating, and I don’t want to hear that you’re not hungry, because you’re a surgeon who’s been up all night, and you’re always hungry, you just don’t notice.”

He looked at her as though she’d spoken in another language. Then he went upstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came down ten minutes later in a clean grey T-shirt and soft trousers with his hair wet, and she sat him on the sofa and put a pork bun in his hand and watched him eat it.

She talked while he ate. She told him about the bakery woman, who’d asked if the second bun was for her boyfriend, and how she’d said yes before she’d thought about it and then stood there in the queue going hot. She told him about Mr. Yin, who’d gone home on Thursday with his stoma bag and his daughter and a box of the hospital jelly he’d said he hated. She told him the jeans story at last, all of it, the station toilets and the hotel sewing kit and the pink thread and the exam, and that she’d passed.

He’d finished both buns and one egg tart. He was sitting back against the arm of the sofa with his tea and his eyes half shut, and he hadn’t looked away from her once.

“I saw you before,” he said. “Before the ward round.”

She stopped.

“Last June,” he said. “The sixth floor. Your brother had been hit by a van. I was called down to look at his ribs. I was leaving when your family came up the corridor, and you stopped me by the lift and asked if anyone had checked his spleen.”

Elara looked at him.

She thought back. She tried as hard as she’d ever tried at anything. She remembered that morning, the phone at six, her father’s face, the car, the corridor on the sixth floor, Raiden in the bed with his eye swollen shut, saying he was fine in his silly voice. She remembered asking about the spleen; she’d asked everyone about the spleen. She did not remember him at all. Not his face, not his glasses, nothing.

“Oh no,” she said. “Oh no. I don’t remember you. I’m so sorry. I don’t. That’s awful. You were there and you were tall and you were a doctor and you told me about my brother and I don’t remember a single thing about you.”

“I’d have worried if you did. You’d been up since six with your brother in a bed.”

“But you remembered me.”

“Yes,” he said. He drank his tea. “I thought it was sleep deprivation. I gave it fifteen months.”

She sat with her hands round her cup and stared at him. Her face was burning. She opened her mouth and nothing came out, and that, for her, was so rare that he started to smile, which for him was rarer.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him about the Lins then, because she was embarrassed, and when she was embarrassed she talked, and she’d only ever told him the funny parts.

She told him the rest in pieces. That her father was in logistics the way the tide was in water. That everyone in the Walled City over fifty still went a bit quiet when he walked down the street, though he’d got old, and grey, and was frightened of his daughters now. That she was the fourth of five and wasn’t really any of their blood.

“I’m adopted,” she said. “Baba brought me home from a children’s home when I was three. That’s all I know. I don’t know where I came from. I don’t know anything from before. I asked once, when I was about seven, and he said I was from a children’s home and he’d wanted me, and that was all there was, and he looked so sad that I never asked again.”

He didn’t say anything. She saw his jaw go tight. She hadn’t said it to make anyone angry, and he was angry anyway, on her behalf, with something he couldn’t see and couldn’t fix, and she could tell he hated that more than anything.

“My mother died a few months after I came,” she said. “Having my little sister. The house went quiet after that. Not for long. A few weeks, a month. But I remember it. All the doors shut and nobody talking at dinner and Baba sitting in the kitchen at night. I was three. I didn’t like it.” She turned her cup round in her hands. “So I talked. Somebody had to. I think I just never stopped.”

She looked up at him to see if that was too much.

“Keep talking,” said Xing Yue.

She laughed, a bit wetly, and told him about Ah Sim, who’d been with the family since before any of them were born and who called her little sparrow, and about the noodle stall at the mouth of the alley, and about her room at the top of the house, which had posters she was too old for and refused to take down. Somewhere in the middle of the posters he put his tea on the table and leaned towards her and took her chin in his fingers and tipped her face up to the window, the way you’d turn someone’s face to the light to look at their pupils.

She went on. She was in the middle of the band on the second poster. He looked at her face in the morning light, at her eyes, checking something and finding it fine, and then he kissed her in the middle of the band’s name, and she laughed into his mouth, because he’d done it again, and he’d done it on purpose.

He didn’t stop. She stopped laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’ve got a rule,” she said, a while later, with her hands in his wet hair.

He was lying back along the sofa and she was more or less on top of him, and the tea had gone cold, and the sun had come round onto the books.

“About call nights.”

“That was last night,” he said. “Now I’m off.”

“That’s cheating.”

“It’s the rule,” said Xing Yue. He looked up at her. His glasses were on the table and his eyes were dark, worn out and wide awake at the same time, and he didn’t ask her anything. He put his hand flat on her back, under her cardigan, warm through her shirt. “Don’t go home.”

She was already taking the cardigan off.

✦ ✦ ✦

His bedroom was upstairs, under the slope of the roof, with a window that looked out over the hill and the white wall of the hospital tower and the harbour beyond it, and blinds that cut the morning into stripes.

She talked. She’d known she would. She talked while he undid the buttons of her shirt one at a time, slowly, as if he were taking out stitches and didn’t want to mark the skin, and she told him so, and he said nothing and kept going. She talked while his mouth went down her throat to the place he’d put his fingers on the steps in September, and stayed there, and she told him her pulse was probably a hundred and forty and that he should write it down. She talked when his glasses were long gone and his hands were warm on her ribs, on her waist, careful and exact, learning her like anatomy. She talked when she pulled the T-shirt over his head and found him lean and pale and much stronger than she’d thought, and when she said that out loud he laughed against her shoulder, a low startled sound.

He was careful. He was so careful that she started to laugh again and told him she wasn’t going to break, that she’d seen him close an abdomen, she knew he could go faster than this. Then he wasn’t careful.

Somewhere after that she stopped narrating.

She didn’t notice when. She noticed afterwards. She remembered the stripes of light moving on the ceiling, and his breath at her ear, and her hands holding onto his back, and the sound of her own voice saying his name, his whole name, as if it were the only word she had left and she was going to make it last. She remembered him saying hers, all of it, every time. He’d never shorten it in his life. She remembered thinking, clearly, from a long way off: oh, so this is what it’s for. All that talking. It’s so you know what it means when you stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

After, he tucked her in.

She was lying in the middle of his bed in the striped light with her hair everywhere, and he got up, and she thought he was going to the bathroom, and instead he pulled the sheet and the blanket up over her shoulders and tucked them in down both sides, firmly, the way the nurses did on the ward, so that she was wrapped like a spring roll.

“What are you doing?”

“You’ve been up since six.” He picked her phone off the floor, where it had fallen out of her cardigan pocket, and held it up to her face to open it, and set an alarm. “Three o’clock. You’ll want to eat something.”

“You’re the one who’s been up all night.”

“Yes,” said Xing Yue, and lay down beside her, on top of the blanket, as though he’d been switched off.

He reached for her hand under the covers before he went. He found her wrist and turned it, and his thumb settled on the inside of it, on the pulse, and stayed there. She felt it go heavy as he fell asleep. It didn’t move.

She lay awake for a few minutes in the striped light and looked at his face. It looked younger asleep, and less certain. She thought about telling him so, and decided to keep it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke at three in the afternoon to her alarm and an empty bed.

There was a glass of water on the table by the bed, and a note on the pillow beside her, on a sheet torn from a prescription pad.

She picked it up. It looked like a heart monitor having a bad day. Pharmacists at City Hospital had been known to ring him and ask what he’d written. Nurses held his drug charts up to the window.

She read it. It didn’t take her long.

Gone to buy food. Back by half three. You don’t snore. You talk in your sleep. Don’t go home.

She lay back in his bed with the note on her chest and the sun on the wall and laughed until she had to put the pillow over her face.

chapters.title: The Lins Are Not Told
chapters.desc: For her twenty-third birthday he gives her surgical loupes made for her eyes. She goes to the family dinner alone, and gets into his car at midnight still in her dress.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re the one part of my life nobody’s ever bled on.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
He gave her the box at breakfast, because he couldn’t wait till the evening and because the evening wasn’t his.

She’d stayed the night. She stayed most nights now that weren’t call nights, and some that were, sleeping in his bed while he was at the hospital and leaving it in a state that took him ten minutes to put right when he came in at eight in the morning. She was at the kitchen counter in his T-shirt and her own socks, eating rice porridge out of the pan with a spoon, when he put the box down beside her.

It was a hard black case, the size of a pencil case, with a clasp.

She looked at it. She looked at him.

“It’s my birthday,” she said, “and you’ve bought me a pencil case.”

“Open it.”

She put the spoon in the pan and opened it.

Inside, in grey foam cut to fit them, was a pair of surgical loupes: glasses with small magnifying barrels set into the lenses, angled down, the kind surgeons wore to see fine work. The frames were dark red. She’d once said, in Old Bian’s, that every pair she’d ever borrowed in the skills lab was black and made her look like a beetle.

She didn’t touch them.

“These are through-the-lens,” she said. “These are made for someone. These are made for a person’s eyes. You can’t just buy these, you have to be measured, you have to—” She stopped. He watched her get there. “The eye test.”

“Yes.”

“In September. The staff eye test. The email from occupational health. I went to the optician on the fourth floor of the old block and a woman measured how far apart my eyes were and made me hold a needle holder over a bit of foam at the height I’d want to work at, and I thought it was strange, but I thought it was the university, they do strange things, they once made us all do a hearing test in a cupboard—”

“I booked it.”

She took them out of the foam. She turned them over. Inside the left arm, small, in plain capitals, was engraved E.L.

She put them on.

He’d known they’d fit. He’d still been worried. They sat right, on her small nose, the barrels set exactly at the angle of her eyes, and she looked down through them at the porridge pan and then at her own hands and then, without meaning to, at his, on the counter, and she started to cry.

“They cost more than my year,” she said. “My whole year. My fees and my books and my food.”

“They’re for twenty years of work,” said Xing Yue. “That isn’t expensive.”

She took them off and held them in both hands and cried on them a bit, and wiped them on his T-shirt, and put them back in the foam with great care, and shut the case. Then she put her arms round his neck from the stool and held on.

“You got me measured,” she said into his collar, “without telling me. You lied to me with an email.”

“Yes.”

“That’s not normal.”

“No,” he said. He didn’t apologise. He didn’t think she wanted him to. She held on tighter.

✦ ✦ ✦

She asked him at the door, while she was putting her shoes on, not to come to the dinner.

He’d known since the box that she would.

“Not yet,” she said. “It’s not you. It’s them. It’s my father. You know what he’s like about the postman. If I bring a man to dinner, he’ll have you looked into before the soup, and he’ll find out you’re at City Hospital and you’re the chief resident and you’re from the north, and then he’ll find out everything else, your school and your grandmother and what you had for breakfast in nineteen ninety-eight, and then he’ll sit at the end of the table and say nothing at you for three hours. I want to do it properly. When it’s a good time.”

“When’s a good time?”

“I don’t know yet,” Elara said. “Soon.”

He nodded, and kept what he thought of it to himself, and she kissed him on the chin, which was as high as she could reach without the step, and went off down the stairs with her bag and the black case held against her chest like a hymn book.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in theatre all afternoon with a perforated ulcer and a registrar who’d been told twice where the duodenum was.

“Stop,” said Xing Yue. “Take your hands out.”

The registrar took his hands out.

“What’s that?”

The registrar looked. “The—”

“Don’t guess. You’ve guessed twice. Look at it, and when you know, tell me, and until you know, keep your hands where they are.”

The scrub nurse looked at the ceiling. The registrar looked at the duodenum for a full half minute, sweating into his mask, and then told him, correctly, and Xing Yue said, “Good. Now you can put your hands back in,” and they finished the case without another word.

Afterwards Dr. Fei caught him at the lifts.

“It’s your student’s birthday,” she said. “Ex-student. Lin Elara. The whole of the seventh floor sang to her at handover. The nurses made her a card. Mr. Yin sent a box of mooncakes from home with his daughter, a month late, with a note that said, for the little doctor who talks.” She was watching his face. “I thought you’d want to know.”

“Thank you,” said Xing Yue.

Fei went on watching him until the lift came, and got in it without another word.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Lins’ dinner was at eight in the Walled City, at the house he’d never seen, behind a red door he’d seen the edge of once in the dark.

He spent the evening at his desk with a paper on bile leaks and didn’t read any of it. At half past eleven he got the car out, the dark blue saloon he only drove at night, and drove across the city with the windows down, and parked at the mouth of the alley under the one streetlight, by the noodle stall with its shutters down, and turned the engine off, and waited.

At five past twelve the passenger door opened and she got in.

She was in a dress. He’d never seen her in a dress. It was dark green and plain and came to her knees, with short sleeves, and she had a coat over it and her hair was up, properly up, with pins, for once, and some of it was already coming down. She had a box on her lap from a bakery and a bag of oranges and a paper crown from a cracker, which she took off her head when she saw him looking.

“Raiden,” she said. “He makes everyone wear them. Drive. No. Don’t drive. Wait. Let me tell you first, or I’ll forget.”

She told him the dinner.

It came out in no order at all. Ah Sim had made the long noodles and stood over her until she’d eaten the whole bowl without biting through one, for long life, because if you bit through one it was bad luck, and she’d nearly choked. Raiden had made a toast that went on for six minutes and was mostly about a crane he was drawing. Elowen had brought a chestnut cake from the good bakery on Harbour Road and her husband had stood behind her the whole time with his hands in his pockets like a wall. Eliana had given her a USB stick and said, don’t plug it into anything at the hospital, and refused to say what was on it.

“And Ev wasn’t there,” said Elara.

She stopped.

“My sister. The one who doesn’t talk. Something happened to her in October and she won’t say what and nobody will tell me, and she’s staying in the room over Elowen’s shop, and she won’t come to the house. So I took her cake. On the way. I sat with her for half an hour.” She looked down at the bakery box on her knees. “She doesn’t talk. So I talked for both of us. I told her about Mr. Yin and the jelly and the loupes. I told her about you.”

He waited.

“Not your name,” she said. “Just that there was a you. She looked at me.” Elara’s voice went odd. “She doesn’t look at people much. She looked at me and I think she was pleased. I think. You can’t always tell with Ev.”

He didn’t ask what had happened to her sister. He could see she didn’t know.

“And Baba asked if I was happy,” she said. “At the end. When everyone was getting their coats. He doesn’t ask things. He’s been learning to. Elowen made him. He came and stood beside me by the fire and asked if I was happy at the hospital, and I said yes, and he looked at me, the way he looks at people, like he’s reading the small print, and he said, good. I didn’t say why.”

She went quiet. That was so unusual that he turned in his seat to look at her.

“I’d like to be the why,” said Xing Yue. “Out loud. In front of them.”

“I know.” She was looking out through the windscreen at the alley, at the lamp on the wall, at the red door round the corner she wouldn’t let him see. “Soon. I promise. I just—” She turned the box round on her knees. “Everything in that house is everybody’s. Everybody knows everything. Everybody’s had their hands in everything. Things come home in the middle of the night that you can’t talk about, and you help, and you don’t ask, and you wash it off in the sink.” She looked at him then. “You’re the one part of my life nobody’s ever bled on. I want to keep it like that for a bit.”

He heard it twice.

He heard that she meant it as the best thing she could say about him, and he believed her. He heard, under it, the sound of a door being eased shut with him on the other side of it, and he understood that she didn’t hear that at all.

He let the second one go. For tonight.

She’d started talking again, about her father, about the time Baba had come to her school play when she was nine and sat in the front row in his coat and the whole school had gone silent, and the boy playing the king had forgotten his lines—

He reached across and took her hand off the bakery box.

He turned it over, palm up, in his, in the light from the streetlamp. Her wrist was small. He could see the blue lines under the skin. He found the pulse with his thumb, the way he’d found it on the steps, and it jumped under his thumb when she felt him do it, and her story stopped.

He bent his head and kissed the inside of her wrist, where the pulse was.

Then he kissed her mouth, hard, while she was still halfway through a word about the king.

She made a sound and grabbed his collar with her free hand. The bakery box slid off her knees into the footwell. The oranges went everywhere. She came across the car towards him as far as her seatbelt let her, which wasn’t far, and swore at the seatbelt into his mouth, and he felt her laugh, and then not laugh, and her hand went from his collar to the back of his neck and pulled him down. Her elbow hit the horn.

It went off down the alley like a ship.

They broke apart. A shutter went up somewhere above the noodle stall and a voice shouted something about the time, and she put both hands over her mouth and shook with laughter in the passenger seat with her hair coming down, and somewhere up the alley a dog started barking.

“Drive,” said Elara, through her fingers. “Drive, drive, before my father comes out in his dressing gown.”

He drove.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t let go of him all the way home. Her hand was on his leg, on his knee and then higher, and she was talking, fast, about nothing, about the oranges rolling round the footwell and the woman upstairs from the noodle stall who’d shouted at Raiden for twenty years, and he took every corner of the hill road slower than he wanted to.

The green dress came off in the hall, in the end. He’d meant to get her upstairs. She had other ideas, and the zip was at the back, and she turned round on the stairs and stood with her back to him, on the step above, with her hair falling out of its pins, and said, “Please, it’s been driving me mad all night,” and he took the zip down slowly, one tooth at a time, and kissed every bit of her back as it came out, until she stopped saying anything about the dress at all.

He took her up the rest of the stairs.

He was slow with her. He’d been slow the first time because he hadn’t wanted to get anything wrong, and he was slow now because he knew how, and because it was her birthday, and because she’d shut a door on him in the car and he wanted, without saying so, to be let back in by another one. He took her hair down, every pin, and put the pins on the table by the bed in a row. He kissed the inside of her wrist again, and the other one, and the inside of her elbow, and the hollow of her throat, and he went on until her talking slowed and broke and started again in another voice, lower, with no stories in it, and then until it wasn’t talking, only his name, said into the dark over and over, as if she were calling him back from somewhere.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on her front across the bed with her chin on her hands, in the light from the landing, and he lay on his back beside her and watched her think.

Then she got up, without a word, and went downstairs naked and came back with the black case, and got back into bed, and opened it, and put on the loupes.

She turned and looked at him through them, close up, with the little barrels pointing at his face, enormous-eyed, like a beetle in red glasses, and said in her most serious ward-round voice, “Dr. Wang, I’m going to need to examine you more closely.”

He laughed.

Not the short sound she got out of him sometimes, against her shoulder, half swallowed. He lay on his back in his own bed and laughed out loud, helplessly, with his hand over his eyes, until his ribs hurt, and she sat on the bed beside him in her loupes and nothing else and looked down at him through the barrels in total astonishment.

“I’ve never heard you do that,” she said.

He couldn’t answer her. She took the loupes off and put them carefully back in their case, and put the case on the table beside her hairpins, and lay down on top of him, and put her ear on his chest to hear it from the inside.

chapters.title: Three in the Morning, on Speaker
chapters.desc: Her silent sister rings from a strange phone about a man with an infected knife wound who can’t go to a hospital. For three weeks Elara calls back at three every morning, and Xing Yue writes things down and doesn’t ask who.
chapters.epigraph: “Go back to sleep. I’ve written it down.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
In February she was a final-year student on her surgical internship at Harbourside General, across the harbour, which meant she was a junior doctor in everything but the money.

She clerked patients and took blood and put in drips and wrote up the drug charts for a registrar to sign. She did nights. She was on the wards at three in the morning in scrubs with a list on the back of her hand, and the patients on the surgical floor loved her, because she talked to them. She knew the name of every grandchild on the ward. She knew which old man wanted the window open and which wanted the curtain shut and which one had been a dancer and would show you, if you asked, how he’d held his arms. She ate standing up at the nurses’ station, out of a paper bag, and gave her egg tarts away to whoever looked like they needed one more.

She slept wherever she was when she stopped. Mostly that was his bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third Thursday in February she was asleep in it at five in the afternoon.

She’d come off a night at nine that morning. He’d come off a night on call at noon and come home and got in beside her without waking her, and they’d both been asleep in the grey light from the blinds when her phone went on the floor by the bed.

She found it by feel. Unknown number. She answered on the fourth ring, with her eyes shut.

“Ev?” She knew it was Ev before anyone spoke. She didn’t know how. “Ev, it’s—what is it? Where are you? Whose phone is this?”

“I need you to tell me what to do,” said Evangeline.

Elara sat up.

She felt herself change. It happened on the wards sometimes, at night, when a nurse called her name in a certain voice, and it was happening now in his bed with the sheet round her waist: everything else went out of her, the sleep and the warmth and the dream she’d been having, and what was left was clear and cold and still.

“Tell me what you see,” she said.

Beside her he was awake. She didn’t see him wake. She felt the mattress move, and the lamp came on, and he sat up against the headboard and looked at her face.

She put the phone on speaker and laid it on the duvet between them, so her hands were free.

Evangeline’s voice came out of it, low and flat, the way it always was, but saying more words in a row than Elara had heard from her in a year. A fever. Shaking, all over, so the bed rattled. A wound on the left side, low, below the ribs, eight centimetres, maybe more. A knife. He had stitched it himself. Eleven stitches. Red all round them, hot, swollen in a ridge, the stitches pulling. Something yellow at the bottom end, and a smell. A red line running out from the cut towards the hip. He was talking, but not to her. He didn’t know her.

Xing Yue had put a pen in Elara’s hand. She didn’t know where he’d got it. He’d torn the back cover off a journal from the bedside table and put that in her other hand, blank side up, and she was writing on her knee.

“How long since the injury?” she said.

“Six days. I think.”

“Is he breathing fast? Is his heart going fast?”

A pause. “Yes.”

“Is he confused? Does he know where he is?”

“No. He’s talking to someone who isn’t there.”

Elara breathed out.

She told her. She told her what it was, plainly, because you didn’t lie to Ev and because Ev would know: that it was an infected wound and it was spreading, that the red line was the infection going up the lymph channels, that the fever and the racing heart and the confusion were how sepsis started, and that people died of it. Young strong people. That he needed a hospital and a surgeon and antibiotics into a vein.

“He can’t,” said Evangeline.

“Ev—”

“He can’t. If he goes to a hospital, they’ll ask. Then they’ll find out.”

There was a silence on the line. Elara looked at the phone on the duvet. She could hear a radio somewhere at the other end, and something that might have been a cat.

“Who is he?” she said.

Nothing.

She looked up. Xing Yue was looking at her, not at the phone. His face was completely calm. He didn’t say a word or ask a thing. He picked up his own phone off the table and began to look something up on it, fast, with his thumb.

“Okay,” said Elara. She heard her own voice go level. “Okay. Listen to me. I’m going to tell you exactly what to do, and you’re going to do all of it, and if any of the things I tell you to watch for happen, you put him in a car and take him to a hospital whether he can or not, and you call me from the car. Do you promise?”

“Yes.”

“Do you have something to write on?”

A pause. Paper moving.

“Go,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told her everything.

The stitches out, every one, so it could drain. Washing it out with boiled water and salt, a lot of it, more than you’d think, until what came out was clean. Leave it open. Pack it loosely. Change it twice a day. She named two antibiotics, the two she’d have wanted for him herself if she’d had him on her ward, and as she said them Xing Yue turned his phone round and held it up for her to see, and he’d found the same two, and under them the things to watch out for, and she nodded at him without stopping.

He took the journal cover back off her knee. He wrote the names of both antibiotics on it, under her notes, in square careful block capitals, each letter separate, like a child’s, so that anyone could have read them.

She could read his writing. She was the only person in the hospital who could. He did it anyway.

She told Ev about the fever and the water with sugar and salt and the cool cloths, and what to watch for: if he got more confused, if he couldn’t stay awake, if his skin went blotchy, if he stopped passing water, if the red line kept climbing.

“Mark where it is now,” Elara said. “With a pen. Then you’ll know. And if it’s any one of those things, you go. Promise me again.”

“I promise.”

Elara looked at the phone on the duvet. She had to ask. She didn’t want to, and she had to.

“Ev.” Her voice wobbled, once. She hated it. “Ev, do you love him?”

The line went quiet except for the radio and the cat.

“Call me at three,” said Evangeline, and hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat on the edge of the bed with the phone in her lap and shook.

She didn’t cry. She just shook, all over, from her shoulders down, the way you do after you’ve run for a bus. He sat behind her and put his hand flat on her back, between her shoulder blades, and left it there, and said nothing at all.

She waited for him to ask.

She knew he wanted to. She’d been on the phone for twenty minutes in his bed telling her sister how to treat a stab wound on someone who couldn’t go to a hospital, and he was a surgeon, and he’d heard every word, and he’d looked it up on his phone. She waited for him to say who is he, or what’s going on, or Elara, you can’t do this.

“Will she do it right?” he said.

She turned and looked at him.

“Ev?” Her laugh came out wrong. “She’ll do it exactly. She’ll do it more exactly than anyone at Harbourside. She’ll write it down in tiny letters and do it to the minute.”

“Then he’s got a chance.”

“I don’t know who he is.”

“No,” said Xing Yue. He put the journal cover with the block capitals on it on the table by her side of the bed, squared up with the edge, where she’d see it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She called at three.

He’d set an alarm. She didn’t know he had until it went at ten to, on his side, low, and he reached over and turned it off and put his hand on her shoulder in the dark, and she sat up.

She rang the number back. Ev answered before it had rung twice, as if she’d been standing beside it.

“Better, I think,” said Evangeline. “Yes. The line hasn’t moved. Yes. I promise.”

Elara lay back down in the dark with the phone on her chest.

“It hasn’t moved,” she said.

“Good,” he said, from the other pillow. “Go back to sleep. I’ve written it down.”

She didn’t know what he’d written down.
