In the morning she found out: a sheet from the prescription pad on the kitchen counter, under the teapot, with the time and line hasn’t moved on it, and under that, in his own unreadable hand, a list of the things she’d told Ev to watch for, as if he were keeping a chart on a patient he’d never seen.

✦ ✦ ✦

She called at three every night for three weeks.

Most nights she was at his flat. Twice she was on a night shift at Harbourside, and rang from the doctors’ room with the door shut, and the nurses wondered who she was talking to in that voice. Once she was in the Walled City, in her old room at the top of the house, whispering, with her father asleep two floors below.

The line went back. A centimetre, then three, and then there was no line at all. The fever had broken on the first night. He was awake. He was difficult. He was, Ev said, in more words than Ev used, eating.

Every morning, when she got up, there was tea on the counter. He made it before she was awake, the dark Pu’er he drank, in the small brown pot, and left it under a folded cloth to keep it hot, and he was gone to the hospital or asleep or sitting at the table with a journal, and he never mentioned it.

On the fourth morning, when Ev said the red line was gone, Elara came down the stairs in his shirt and found him at the counter reading, and climbed up onto the rung of the stool beside him so she was tall enough, and took his face in both hands, and kissed him until he put the journal down.

“What was that for?” he said, when she let him go.

“The tea,” said Elara. “Every day. You think I don’t notice.”

He looked at her. His glasses had gone crooked.

“I know you notice,” he said, and pulled her off the stool.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the second week he asked her to share her location with him.

He asked at breakfast, plainly, while she was looking for her other shoe. For night shifts, he said. She was crossing the harbour at two in the morning in taxis. She was walking from the ferry. If something happened, he wanted to know where.

She laughed. She found the shoe under the sofa. She got her phone out and did it then and there, in front of him, and held it up so he could see her name come up on his screen, a small blue dot on a map, in his kitchen.

“There,” she said. “Now you’ll know every time I go to the bakery.”

He didn’t say anything. He put his phone in his pocket.

He looked at it more than he’d ever have admitted. She knew, because he knew things. He knew when she’d been at the bakery before she said so. He knew when her taxi had gone the long way round the harbour because of roadworks, and asked about the roadworks. Once, when she was on a night shift, she went down to the hospital car park at four in the morning for some air and stood by the ambulance bay for ten minutes, and her phone buzzed in her pocket.

Xing Yue: Car park?

Elara: AIR. go to sleep

Xing Yue: I’m on call.

She stood by the ambulance bay in the cold and read that twice. Then she put the phone back in her pocket and went back upstairs, smiling, and didn’t think too hard about why she was smiling. She didn’t turn it off.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Thursday in March, at three, Ev asked if he could have a shower.

“Yes,” said Elara. “Fine. A quick one. Don’t scrub it, pat it dry, and if he’s an idiot about it I’ll know.”

She hung up. She lay back on the pillow in the dark.

Xing Yue was awake. He always was, for the calls. His pager had gone at half past two and he’d taken it in the kitchen, and she’d heard him through the floor, low and flat and terrible, telling some registrar that if he rang him about a potassium of four point one again he’d come in and give it to him intravenously himself. Then he’d come back up and got into bed and put his hand on her hip, warm, and waited with her for three.

“She’s got a man,” said Elara. “Ev. My sister who says about ten words a month. She’s got a man, and he’s alive, and he wants a shower.”

“Good for her,” said Xing Yue.

“He was dying in February. On a floor somewhere. She was the only person he had.” She was talking faster now, the way she did when she’d been frightened and wasn’t any more. “And I don’t know who he is. I don’t know his name. I don’t know what he does that means he can’t go to a hospital with a stab wound. I don’t know what she’s doing with him. She’s never had anyone. She’s never even let anyone sit next to her on the bus, and now she’s in a room with a man who’s been knifed, and she rang me—”

“Back to bed,” he said.

“I’m in bed.”

“Back to sleeping, then. It’s three in the morning. You’ve got a ward round at eight.”

He pulled the duvet up over her shoulder and tucked it in, down her back, firmly, the way he did, and she let him, and kept talking. She told him about Ev when she was little, sitting under the kitchen table with a book while everyone shouted. About Ev growing orchids on the windowsill and checking their roots without touching them. About how she’d always thought Ev would end up alone in a tall room with plants and be perfectly happy, and how she’d never once thought Ev might want—

He leaned over her in the dark and stopped her mouth with his.

She made a surprised sound. Then she stopped being surprised. She got her arms out from under the tucked-in duvet, which took some doing, and put them round his neck and pulled him down on top of her, and the duvet came untucked all down one side, and she felt him laugh against her mouth.

“You said sleep,” she said.

“I changed my mind.”

They didn’t sleep until it was light.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay with her head on his chest and watched the blinds go grey and thought about it.

He hadn’t asked. Three weeks of calls at three in the morning, a man with a knife wound and no name, her sister in a room somewhere, two antibiotics written in block capitals, and he hadn’t asked her once who it was or where or why. He’d set alarms. He’d made tea. He’d sat up in the dark with her every night and kept a chart.

She had a world that rang in the middle of the night, and she’d always gone towards it when it did, without thinking, the way you go towards a cry. She’d always thought that was the part of her nobody would put up with. That one day somebody would say: them or me.

She lifted her head and looked at him. He was asleep, with his thumb on the inside of her wrist.

She put her head back down and decided not to wonder any more whether he ever would.

chapters.title: Zhao Zhendong Is Bleeding Out
chapters.desc: Her sister’s husband crawls home with a bullet in his side, and Elara steals what she needs from the hospital. In the supply room Xing Yue finds her, and she begs him not to ask.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t ask me. If you ask, I’ll tell you.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The emergency department at City Hospital on a Saturday night sounded like a market that had caught fire.

She was a student on it for six weeks, her last rotation before finals, and she loved it more than anything she’d done in medical school except the bananas. A drunk man in cubicle four was singing. A girl in cubicle six had put her hand through a window and was being brave about it in front of her boyfriend and not brave at all about it when he went for coffee. Elara had sat with her and talked about the boyfriend, who was clearly an idiot, until the girl laughed and forgot to watch the needle.

At three in the morning she was eating a biscuit at the nurses’ station and thinking about the girl’s hand. Upstairs, Xing Yue was in theatre with an appendix. He’d texted her at half past one: Appendix. Then another one, possibly. Eat something. She’d sent back a photo of the biscuit.

At twenty past three her phone rang. A number she didn’t know.

“Miss Lin? Miss Elara?” A young man’s voice, high and shaking. “It’s Peng. From the gatehouse. At your sister’s. At the house on the hill.”

She put the biscuit down.

“It’s Mr. Zhao,” said Peng. “He came back. He crawled. From the sea road. He’s—Miss Lin said to tell you: gunshot, left side, three days, fever, he’s lost a lot of blood, he’s been in the sea. She said bring everything. She said steal it if you have to.” He took a breath that broke in the middle. “She said no hospital. She said come.”

“I’m coming,” said Elara.

She was already walking.

✦ ✦ ✦

The surgical supply room was off the corridor between the emergency department and the lifts, behind a door with a keypad that every student knew the code for, because the nurses said it out loud.

She went in and shut the door behind her and stood with her back against it.

Then she started.

She took two of the big blue bags from the stack by the door, the ones the porters used for linen, and opened them on the floor. Bags of fluid off the shelf, four, six, and she thought of three days and a fever and took eight. Giving sets. Cannulas, two sizes, a handful of each. Tape. Saline for washing, the big bottles, as many as she could carry. Gauze, a whole box, and another. Gloves. A green drape in its paper. Local anaesthetic and syringes and needles from the drawer. A suture pack, though she knew she wouldn’t close it, because you didn’t close a wound like that, not after three days in the sea; she took it anyway. On the shelf by the window were the instrument cases from theatre, sterilised and sealed in their blue wrap, and she took the top one, and put it in the bag, and looked at the shelf where the antibiotics should be, and they weren’t there.

They were in the emergency drug cupboard, two doors down. She’d have to go back out into the corridor for those. She’d have to open the cupboard in front of the nurses’ station.

She would do it. She’d smile at Sister Kuai and say she’d been sent, and Sister Kuai would believe her, because everyone did. She was already planning it, the smile, the exact words, and her hands were steady and fast and her heart was going so hard she could feel it in her teeth.

The door opened behind her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She turned round with a bag of fluid in each hand.

He was in the doorway in his theatre scrubs and cap, with his mask pulled down round his neck and his glasses on, and he’d come down for something, a drain, she found out later, for a man in resus with an abscess. He’d come in fast, the way he did everything, and he stopped.

He looked at the blue bags open on the floor. At the fluid. At the boxes of cannulas and the bottles of saline and the instrument case in its blue wrap. At her, with a bag in each hand, in her scrubs, at twenty-five past three in the morning.

The bags in her hands touched, and clinked.

She saw him understand that she was stealing. She saw him understand that it was a great deal, that it was everything you’d need to keep someone alive on a table that wasn’t in a hospital. She saw him open his mouth.

“Don’t,” she said. “Don’t ask me. Please.” Her voice shook. She couldn’t stop it. “If you ask, I’ll tell you. I’ll tell you everything, I won’t be able not to, and then it’s yours too. Then you’ll know. Then it’s yours as well as mine and you’ll have to do something about it, and you’re the chief resident, and I can’t—please. Please don’t ask me.”

He didn’t say anything.

He stood in the doorway and looked at her. It was the longest she had ever seen him not speak. Outside in the corridor somebody laughed, and a trolley went past, and the drunk man in cubicle four had started another song.

Then he came into the room and shut the door behind him.

He bent down and looked into the bag on the floor. He took out the instrument case. He turned it over and read the label on the blue wrap, the list of what was inside it, typed by the sterile services department in the basement, and he put it on the shelf.

“Take the other one,” he said. “That one’s missing a needle holder.”

He took the next case down off the shelf, read its label, and put it in her bag.

She stared at him.

“I won’t ask,” said Xing Yue.

✦ ✦ ✦

He picked up both bags. She tried to take one and he didn’t let her.

“I need antibiotics,” she said. “They’re in the drug cupboard. I have to go past the station.”

“Which?”

She told him. He put the bags down by the door again and went out, and she stood alone in the supply room with her hands over her mouth, and three minutes later he came back with two boxes from the drug cupboard and put them in the top of the second bag, under the gauze, without a word. She found out later he’d signed them out to the man with the abscess in resus.

He carried both bags down the corridor and out past the ambulance bay to the taxi rank at the main doors, at a quarter to four in the morning, in his theatre scrubs, as if he did it every night. There was one taxi. He opened the back door and put the bags in, and they clinked, and the driver looked round.

He didn’t ask her where she was going.

He took his phone charger out of the pocket of his scrubs, the cable and the plug, and put it in the outside pocket of her bag. She didn’t know why. She found out a little after six.

Then he turned round and put his hand on the back of her head, under her hair, and kissed her against the side of the taxi.

It was hard and short, nothing like the kisses at the taxi rank in the autumn, the kind of thing you do with your hands when you can’t do anything else with them. The metal of the car was cold through her scrubs. She held onto his arms.

He let her go.

“Go,” he said. “Ring me when you can.”

She got in. The taxi pulled away. When she looked back through the rear window he was standing on the kerb under the lights of the main doors in his scrubs, with his hands at his sides, and then the taxi turned onto the hill road and he was gone.

She gave the driver the address on the hill. He looked at her in the mirror and drove like he meant it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The gate was open. The taxi went straight through it and up the gravel to the front steps at eight minutes to four, because the guard at the gatehouse waved it in and then ran after it.

She went in with a bag over each shoulder.

The kitchen was at the back of the house, and every light in it was on. She came through the doorway at a run and stopped.

He was on the kitchen table.

Zhao Zhendong. Her sister’s husband. The man who stood behind Elowen like a wall. He was grey. His lips were blue. He was naked to the waist and something filthy was wound round his middle, and there was a towel over his side, and Elowen was standing at the head of the table in a nightdress with her feet bare and bleeding, holding his hand.

Elara felt her face go white. She felt it go still. Then she felt it turn into someone else’s, the way it had in his bed in February, everything warm going out of it.

“Okay,” said Elara. “Okay. Okay.”

She dropped the bags on the counter and unzipped them.

“I stole all of this,” she said fast, already pulling on gloves. “From the hospital. From the supply room. If anyone ever finds out, I will never be a doctor, and I’ll go to prison, and I don’t care, Jie, I don’t care, move his arm, I need a vein.”

She found one on the inside of his elbow on the second try. She thought, distantly, that the first try would have been fine if her hands had been warm. She taped it down and looked round for somewhere to hang the bag, and there was nowhere, and she opened the cupboard above the table and took a coat hanger off the back of the hall door, which someone was holding open, and hung the bag of fluid from the cupboard door. Then another needle in the other arm. Then the antibiotics, the two boxes from the drug cupboard, the ones he’d signed out to a stranger.

“Antibiotics,” she said. “The strongest I could find. Into the drip. He needs fluids, he needs these, and he needs—” She stopped. She looked down at the towel over his side. “Show me.”

Elowen lifted the towel.

Elara looked at the wound and didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took two hours.

Afterwards she could remember almost none of it in order. She remembered the light. The kitchen light was good, a long bright lamp over the table, and she thought, Jie chose this for cooking and now I’m doing this under it. She remembered pulling out the strips of shirt he’d packed into himself, black and stiff, one at a time, and the sound he made, and how she didn’t stop. She remembered the saline running off the edge of the table onto the floor and the guards mopping it with towels, pink and then red and then pink. She remembered cutting away what was dead, the grey and the black, in small careful snips, with the instruments from the case he’d chosen for her, and finding the needle holder in it, where it should be, and thinking of him for one second, and putting him away.

She didn’t talk. That was the thing everyone remembered afterwards, and she didn’t, because she never knew she was doing it. All she said were small words to herself, under her breath: okay, okay, there, okay.

Elowen talked. Elowen held his face between her hands and talked to him for two hours without stopping, about the flower market and the soy milk man and a lemon tree, and when he screamed she put her forehead on his and kept talking. Once he opened his eyes and told her to go upstairs, and she said no.

At some point Chen Si was standing in the kitchen doorway, soaked to the knees, in a camel coat, and Elara didn’t see him come.

At six, the sky outside the kitchen window started going grey.

She stripped off her gloves. They were red to the wrist. She dropped them on the floor and stood with her hands braced on the edge of the counter and her head down, breathing.

“That’s all I can do,” she said. “It’s clean. It’s open. The antibiotics are going in. Now it’s his body. If the fever breaks in the next two days, he lives. If it doesn’t—” She stopped. “If it doesn’t, we take him to a hospital, Jie, Red Notice or no Red Notice. I won’t let him die on a kitchen table because of a piece of paper.”

“Neither will I,” said Elowen.

Elara lifted her head and looked at her sister. At the blood on her hands, and her nightdress, and her bare cut feet. At her face, which was perfectly calm.

“You held him for two hours,” Elara said. “You didn’t look away once. You didn’t even cry.”

“I’ll cry later,” said Elowen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her phone was dead.

She found that out at ten past six, in the hall, when she took it out to ring him and the screen stayed black. She stood by the lemon tree in her bloody scrubs and stared at it. Then she remembered the outside pocket of her bag.

The charger was there. His cable and his plug. She plugged it into the wall by the stairs and sat down on the bottom step and waited for her phone to come back on, and put her face in her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

They carried him upstairs at seven, on a door Raiden had taken off its hinges. She didn’t know when Raiden had come. He was just there, in a coat over his pyjamas, white as paper, with a screwdriver, and he took the door off the cupboard under the stairs in about a minute and didn’t make a single joke.

She hung the drips from the curtain rail in the big room at the end of the corridor.

She checked the lines. She checked the dressing. She checked his breathing and his pulse and his colour, and wrote them all down on the back of an envelope she found on the dressing table, with the time, the way Xing Yue would have.

Elowen sat down on the floor beside the bed and took his hand.

Elara went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past seven she stood in the guest bathroom at the other end of the corridor and texted him.

Elara: Alive. For now.

The answer came back before she’d put the phone down on the edge of the basin. It came so fast that she knew he’d been holding his phone. She knew he’d been watching the little blue dot of her on his screen, on the hill, all night, between the appendix and the next one, in the theatre corridor, in the coffee room, wherever he’d been.

Xing Yue: Good. Eat.

She turned the tap on.

She turned it on full, so it roared in the basin, and sat down on the floor of her sister’s guest bathroom with her back against the bath and her knees up and his charger in her hand, and cried with her other hand over her mouth, so that nobody in the house would hear her over the water.

chapters.title: Fifteen Days of Drips
chapters.desc: For two weeks she changes drips and dressings on the hill, and he drives her there in the dark and waits at the bottom of the road. On the last day he asks one question.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not asking who. I only want to know if he’s alive.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
He set the alarms on his own phone.

He didn’t tell her he was doing it. On Sunday afternoon, when she came back down the hill in a taxi for two hours to shower and sleep, and slept for forty minutes on his sofa with her shoes on, he took her phone out of her hand and looked at the list she’d written on the back of her own wrist in biro: the times for the drips, every four hours, round the clock, and the dressings, morning and evening. He put them all into his phone. Then he put them into hers, with a different sound, so that if one of them didn’t wake her the other would wake him.

She woke at ten to six to his hand on her shoulder and her own alarm going and looked at him as if he’d done a magic trick.

“I put them in,” he said.

“How did you know the times?”

He turned her wrist over and showed her. She looked at the blue writing on her own skin and laughed, the first time since Saturday, a short tired sound, and put her face against his arm.

He drove her back up the hill. He stopped at the bottom of the hill road, where it left the sea road and started to climb, two kilometres below the gate, and she got out. A car came down out of the dark to meet her, one of the cars from the house, with the young guard from the gatehouse driving, and took her up.

“You can take me to the top,” she said.

“No.”

He didn’t explain it. She didn’t make him. She’d asked him not to ask, and he’d said he wouldn’t, and if he drove up to the gate of the house where it was happening, he’d see, whatever he said. He wasn’t going to see. He’d decided that in the supply room.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday at noon she rang him in clinic.

He was between patients, in the small room on the third floor with the couch and the sink and the window onto the car park, and he answered on the first ring, because he’d been holding the phone under the desk.

She didn’t say anything at first. He could hear that she was in a corridor. He could hear that she was crying, the way you cry when you’ve got your hand over your mouth so that a house full of people won’t hear you.

“Elara,” he said. “Breathe first. Then tell me.”

She breathed. He heard her do it, twice, the way she’d have told a patient to.

“It hasn’t broken,” she said. “The fever. It’s the second day. It should have started coming down. It’s thirty-nine eight.”

He didn’t ask who. He didn’t ask what she’d done or where or with what. He asked the things he’d have asked a registrar on the phone at two in the morning: when the last dose had gone in, what his heart rate was, whether he was passing water, whether the wound was any redder than at six. She told him. He listened. He told her what he’d be watching for in the next six hours, and what would make him stop watching and get the patient into a hospital whatever anyone said, and she said, “That’s what I said. That’s exactly what I said to them,” and her voice steadied.

“Then you were right,” he said. “Eat something. Ring me at six.”

He put the phone face down on the desk and sat for a few seconds with his hand flat on it.

Then he called in the next patient, a woman with a hernia, and was entirely polite to her for fifteen minutes.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning on Tuesday his phone buzzed on the pillow beside his head.

Elara: It broke

Elara: it broke at 2. he’s sweating through everything. his heart’s down to 96

He was awake. He’d been awake since one, lying on his back in the dark looking at the small blue dot of her on his screen, on the hill, where it had been since the evening. It hadn’t moved. He’d watched it not move.

Xing Yue: Sleep now. I’ll get you at four.

✦ ✦ ✦

From then on he drove her every morning.

She’d gone back to the emergency department in the daytime. She couldn’t not. Finals were in seven weeks. So she went up the hill twice a day instead: in the evening by taxi, after her shift, to change the packing, and at four in the morning, with him, to change it again before she had to be back on the floor at eight.

He picked her up at half past three outside the main doors. He drove her across the city in the dark with the windows down so she wouldn’t fall asleep. He stopped at the bottom of the hill road, under a streetlight beside a bus shelter that no bus used at that hour, and she got out with her bag and the car from the house came down for her and took her up into the dark, and he turned the engine off.

He waited.

He slept, sometimes, in the driver’s seat, with the seat pushed back and his glasses on the dashboard. He’d learned to sleep anywhere as a resident and he slept there. He woke whenever a car came down the hill, and it was never the car from the house, and he went back to sleep.

At five the car from the house brought her back down and turned and went up again, and she walked over to him in the grey light with her bag on one shoulder and a black bin bag in her other hand, knotted at the top.

The first morning he got out of the car and held his hand out for it.

She looked at him. She knew what was in it. Old dressings, old packing, gloves, the dirty things that came out of a wound you weren’t supposed to have.

“It’s clinical waste,” she said. “You can’t just—”

“I know what it is.” He took it out of her hand. “The hospital has a whole room for it.”

He put it in the boot of his car. At seven, when he went in for his day, he carried it down to the basement with his bag over his other shoulder and put it in the yellow bin in the waste room behind the boiler house, with everyone else’s, where nobody would ever look at it again. He did that every morning for two weeks.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Wednesday he went down to the theatre office on the second floor and asked for the stock book.

It was an old-fashioned ledger, because the computer system kept losing things, and it lived on the shelf behind the theatre manager’s desk. On the Saturday night page, against the appendix he’d done at two in the morning, he wrote in one instrument set opened and contaminated, returned for reprocessing, and the fluids and the dressings, and the gauze. It matched, more or less, what had gone out of the supply room in two blue bags. He initialled it.

The theatre manager, who had known him for six years, looked over his shoulder at it and said, “Busy night.”

“Yes,” said Xing Yue, and put the book back on the shelf.

He’d never written anything in a patient’s record or a hospital book that wasn’t true. He looked at his initials for a second longer than he needed to. Then he went to his ward round.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday the emergency department’s student lead, Dr. Geng, caught him at the lifts.

“Your Miss Lin,” said Dr. Geng, who was a good doctor and a kind man and wanted to know. “She’s been missing shifts. Leaving early. She looks like she hasn’t slept since Christmas. Is there something I should know?”

Xing Yue looked at him.

“It’s a family emergency,” he said. “It’s real. She’ll make up the hours.”

Dr. Geng waited for more. There wasn’t any more. After a while he nodded and said, all right, and that if she needed anything she should come and see him, and he meant it, and got in the lift.

On Friday it was Dr. Nie.

Nie was a registrar in the emergency department, two years ahead of Xing Yue in training and two years behind him in everything else, who liked to stand at the nurses’ station and talk loudly enough for the patients to hear. Xing Yue was down for a referral, a man with a gallbladder, and Nie leaned on the station beside him with a coffee and said, “Your little student friend’s gone walkabout again. Third time this week. She turned up yesterday at ten. Some of us were here at eight.”

The nurses at the station went quiet.

Xing Yue finished writing in the gallbladder man’s notes. He signed them. He put the pen in his pocket.

“Would you like to talk about your own absences instead?” he said. “The two Fridays in February when you were at a course that the course has no record of. The afternoon in January you left your list to a first-year and went to the races. I know which race. I can tell you which horse.” He looked at Nie, not loudly. “Or would you like to go and see the man in bay three, who’s been waiting for you for an hour and a half with a broken wrist?”

Nie put his coffee down on the station and went to bay three.

Nobody in the emergency department asked about Miss Lin again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He fed her.

He put food in her hand, because she didn’t eat otherwise. Rice balls from the shop by the ferry, wrapped in seaweed, that she could eat in the car. Soy milk in a carton with the straw already in. Pork buns, always, from the bakery by the hospital, which opened at six and which he went to at six and came back from before she was out of the shower. He put a box of something on the passenger seat every morning before he picked her up, and she ate it on the way across the city without seeming to notice she was eating, talking with her mouth full, and he watched the box empty out of the corner of his eye.

Between the morning dressing and her shift she slept in his bed. Between her shift and the evening dressing she slept in his bed. He came home at lunchtime twice that week, which he never did, to find her face down on top of the duvet in her scrubs with her shoes still on, and took the shoes off, and put the duvet over her.

He put her shoes by his front door. Facing out, toes to the door, side by side, so that when the alarm went at three in the morning she could step into them in the dark without bending down and without turning on a light. She noticed on the third day. She stood in the hall at three in the morning looking down at her shoes, pointing at the door like two small dogs waiting for a walk, and he heard her laugh in the dark.

She kept them that way afterwards and never said why.

✦ ✦ ✦

Halfway across the city one morning, she fell asleep mid-sentence.

She’d been telling him about a man in the department with a fish bone stuck in his throat who’d insisted on keeping the bone. She got as far as and he wanted it in a little bag and stopped. He looked across. Her head had gone against the window. Her mouth was a little open. She was breathing slowly for the first time in a week.

He looked at the clock on the dashboard. It was ten to four. She was due at the house at a quarter past.

He drove past the turning for the hill road. He drove on along the sea road to the roundabout at the end and round it and back, and past the turning again, and to the roundabout at the other end and round that, and back, slowly, in the dark, with the sea on one side and the hill on the other. He did it twice. It came to twenty minutes.

When he stopped at the bus shelter she woke up and looked at the clock and said, “Oh God, I’m late, I’m late,” and then she looked at him. “Did you drive round?”

“Twice.”

“You can’t just—”

“It’s a dressing,” he said. “It’s not a drip. It’ll keep twenty minutes. You won’t.”

She looked at him for a few seconds. Then she got out with her bag and went up the hill, and he watched her go, and he didn’t regret it at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the tenth morning she came down the hill grey.

He got out of the car and took the bin bag off her. Then he took her chin in his hand and turned her face to the streetlight and pulled her lower eyelid down gently with his thumb, the way you would in clinic to look for anaemia, and looked at the colour inside it.

“You’re pale,” he said.

“I’m not anaemic, I’m just tired, I’ve had about nine hours’ sleep in four days, you don’t need to examine me in a bus shelter—”

He kissed her. He kissed her with his thumb still on her cheekbone, in the bus shelter, against the side of the car in the grey light, slow, and she stopped arguing and put her arms inside his coat round his waist and leaned on him with her whole weight, as if her legs had just been told they could stop. He held her up. A car came down the hill road and its lights went over them and away.

“Fine,” she said into his mouth. “I’m pale.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The fifteenth day was a Sunday.

She went up the hill at five in the evening in a taxi, and he drove out at half past six and waited at the bus shelter, because she’d texted at four: Last one tonight I think. Come and get me?

She came down at seven.

It was nearly dark. The car from the house left her at the bus shelter and went back up, and she walked over slowly with her bag over her shoulder and no bin bag, and he got out of the car and stood by it and watched her come. She stopped in front of him.

“That’s the last one,” she said. “He’s on tablets. He can do his own dressings, or my sister can. I showed her. He walked to the bathroom on his own this morning and he hated every step.” She was looking at his chest. “I’m not going back up.”

He’d promised. He’d kept it for fifteen days. He’d driven her to the bottom of a hill every morning for two weeks and carried somebody’s blood to a bin and written a lie in a book, and he hadn’t asked once.

He asked one thing.

“I’m not asking who,” he said. “I only want to know if he’s alive.”

“Yes,” said Elara.

“Good.”

She looked up at him then. Her eyes filled.

“It was my sister’s husband,” she said. “Elowen’s. Zhao. He’d been shot. Three days before. He crawled up from the sea.” She swallowed. “You didn’t ask. So I’m telling you. I wanted to.”

He put his hand on the side of her face.

“I’m glad it was you up there,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got into the car. She didn’t put her seatbelt on.

He was reaching for the key when she climbed over the gearstick into his lap.

It was not graceful. Her knee hit the steering wheel and her bag fell into the footwell and her elbow knocked his glasses sideways, and she didn’t care about any of it. She took his face in both hands and kissed him as though she’d been starving for two weeks and he was the first thing she’d been given to eat. He pushed the seat back to make room for her, blind, with one hand, and she followed him down with it. Her hands were in his hair. She kissed his mouth, his jaw, his mouth again, hard, with a small desperate sound at the back of her throat, as if fifteen days were coming out of her at once.

He held her. He let her.

Then, slowly, she slowed down. Her kisses got softer and further apart. Her forehead came down against his, and stayed there, and her hands loosened in his hair, and he felt her whole weight settle on him, warm, heavy.

“Sorry,” she said, slurred. “I’m so tired. I’ve got to tell you about the gauze. Evangeline’s got this way of folding it, she folds it in thirds, she says it’s how our mother folded towels, and I love you, and it’s much neater than mine, I’m going to start doing it on the ward—”

She was asleep.

He sat in the driver’s seat at the bottom of the hill road, under the streetlight, in the dark, with her asleep on top of him, her face in his neck and her breath on his skin and his glasses crooked on his nose.

He didn’t move for an hour.

He’d keep it. He knew she hadn’t heard herself say it. He knew she wouldn’t remember. He’d keep it anyway, the way you keep a thing someone drops without noticing, and give it back to her when she knew she’d lost it.

chapters.title: Every Wrong Answer
chapters.desc: Finals, flashcards in bed and a dare he cheats on. She graduates with her family in the hall, and he waits for her on the back stairs.
chapters.epigraph: “Get it wrong and I’ll kiss you anyway.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
On the last Sunday in April she fell asleep at her father’s table with a dumpling halfway to her mouth.

She’d come straight from a night in the emergency department, in a taxi, in her scrubs under her coat, because Sunday lunch in the Walled City was Sunday lunch and you didn’t miss it for anything less than a death, and even then Ah Sim would want a note. She sat down at the long table between Raiden and Eliana. She took a dumpling from the plate with her chopsticks. She remembered lifting it.

The next thing she knew, Raiden was saying, “Leave her, leave her, it’s beautiful, it’s like a statue,” and Ah Sim was saying something about the dumpling getting cold, and the dumpling was still in her chopsticks, an inch from her mouth, and her arm was aching.

She blinked. Everyone at the table was looking at her, and nobody was laughing except Raiden, and her father was looking at her in a way she didn’t like, the way he looked at a ship that was late.

“Night shift,” she said. “Sorry. Night shift. I’m fine.”

She ate the dumpling. It was cold.

Halfway down the table, Evangeline was passing the vinegar to Elowen. Elara watched her hand go across the cloth, half asleep, and saw it. A ring. A plain silver one, on the fourth finger of her left hand, catching the light from the window when she moved.

Elara looked at it. Then she looked at her sister’s face, which was doing nothing at all, as usual. Then she looked at her own bowl.

She didn’t say anything. Ev had never once asked her about the phone calls. Elara could manage not asking about a ring.

✦ ✦ ✦

Finals started on the fifteenth of May.

She revised at his flat, because the Walled City house had too many stairs and too many people on them and Raiden kept coming in to tell her about drainage. His flat had a study nobody used, with a desk and a lamp and nothing else, and she spread out over it in a week: textbooks, flashcards in rubber bands, highlighters with the lids off, a skeleton hand she’d borrowed from the anatomy department and had to give back by the end of term. He’d come in at night from the hospital and find her asleep across the desk with her face on the brachial plexus and a highlighter in her fist, and he’d take the highlighter out of her hand, put the lid on it, and carry her upstairs.

At midnight in the second week she asked him to quiz her.

“Be horrible,” she said. She was in his bed in one of his shirts, cross-legged, with a stack of flashcards in her lap. “Be like you are on the round. Be like you are with Rao. If I get it wrong I want to feel like I’ve been run over.”

He took the flashcards. He read the first one.

“Signs of a tension pneumothorax.”

She told him. She got most of it. She forgot one.

“Nearly,” said Xing Yue.

“Nearly? Nearly? That’s not horrible. That’s what you’d say to a dog. Do the voice. Do the you’re not tying your shoes voice.”

He looked at her over the top of the card. He opened his mouth. She watched him try. She watched him get as far as the first word of something cutting and stop, and look at her sitting cross-legged in his shirt with her hair everywhere, and give up.

“I can’t,” he said.

“Why not?”

“Because it’s you.”

She stared at him. She went pink. She took the card out of his hand and hit him on the arm with it.

“That’s not helpful,” she said. “That’s lovely, and it’s not helpful. Fine. If you won’t be horrible, we’ll do it another way.” She thought about it, with her chin in her hand. “A dare. For every one I get right, you kiss me. For every one I get wrong, you have to tell me something about you. Something real. Something I don’t know. Because you never tell me anything, you just listen, and I’ve told you everything I’ve ever thought since I was three, and I know about four things about you, and one of them’s your shoe size.”

He thought about it for exactly as long as it took her to start to regret it.

“All right,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got the first one right. Causes of a raised calcium.

He leaned over and kissed her. Not long. A light warm kiss at the corner of her mouth, as if he were ticking a box.

She got the second one right. He kissed her again, longer, with his hand on her knee.

She got the third one wrong. She knew it was wrong as she said it. She mixed up two nerves in the hand, which she never did, because she’d done the hands for a week. She stopped.

“Wrong,” she said. “Go on. Something real.”

He kissed her.

“That’s cheating,” she said against his mouth. “That’s a wrong one. You don’t get to—”

“Get it wrong and I’ll kiss you anyway,” said Xing Yue. “I’ll pay later.” He kissed her again, and she forgot which nerve she’d been wrong about.

They got through about a dozen flashcards that night. She got most of them right. He kissed her for all of them. By the last one the cards were on the floor and his shirt was half off her shoulder and his glasses were on the bedside table, and she was holding his face and saying, “You owe me three, you owe me three,” and he said he knew, and didn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

He paid on Thursday.

She was on the sofa with her feet in his lap and a textbook on her chest, and he was reading a journal, and without looking up from it he said, “My father wanted me to run his hospitals.”

She put the textbook down.

“In the north,” he said. “There’s a group of them. Private. My grandfather built them. My father’s the chairman. He wanted me to train there, and then go onto the board, and then take it over. Everyone in the family assumed I would.” He turned a page. “I wanted to cut people open. Not sit in a room and talk about them. So I came south. As far as I could get. That’s one.”

She kept still. She didn’t want to frighten it off.

“Two,” he said. “I have a brother. An Yu. He’s three years younger. He started a company when he was twenty-two and he earns more before breakfast than I will in my whole life, and he rings me every Sunday to tell me I work too hard.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“What’s three?” she said.

He put the journal down on his knee. He looked at her feet in his lap, at her socks, which didn’t match.

“Three,” he said, “is that I’ve never told anyone about the first two. Not like that. Not because they asked.”

She sat up and climbed along the sofa and put her arms round his neck, and he put his hand on her back, and they stayed there until her textbook slid off the cushion onto the floor and neither of them picked it up.

She didn’t ask how many hospitals. She thought: a few. Some clinics. A family business, like hers.

She’d find out in November how wrong she was.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the third week of finals, at one in the morning, her phone rang. It was her father’s number. It was never her father.

“Little sister.” Uncle Mok, her father’s driver, who had driven her to school every day for twelve years. “Sorry. Sorry. It’s Ah Kuen. From the boats. He’s cut his hand on a cable. It’s deep. Your father says not the hospital, but only if you can. You’ve got exams. He said to say you’ve got exams.”

“I’m coming,” said Elara.

She was already up. Xing Yue was awake beside her. He watched her pull her jeans on over his shirt.

“The Walled City,” she said. “One of Baba’s men. A hand. It’s not a—it’s just a hand.” She found her bag. She’d started keeping a few things in it since March. “I’ll get a taxi.”

He was already reaching for his car keys.

He drove her. He stopped at the mouth of the alley under the one streetlight, by the shuttered noodle stall, because she still wouldn’t let him see the red door, and he didn’t ask to. She ran up the alley with her bag.

In her father’s kitchen a man called Ah Kuen, who she’d known since she was six and who used to give her sugar cane, sat at the long table with his hand wrapped in a tea towel and his face grey. Her father stood by the fire with his arms folded. Uncle Mok stood by the door.

She unwrapped the towel. She looked. A cable had gone across the palm and opened it deep, but it had missed the tendons; he could bend every finger, she made him show her. She washed it out at the sink. She numbed it. She sat at her father’s table at a quarter past one in the morning, a week before her surgical paper, and closed it, neat and fast, under the kitchen lamp, without saying a word except small ones to herself.

Her father watched her the whole time. He didn’t say anything either. When she’d finished, and dressed it, and told Ah Kuen to come and see her in a week and not to get it wet, and not to lift anything, and to come to her and not to anybody else, her father unfolded his arms.

“You’ve got exams,” he said.

She said she knew.

“I said only if you could.”

“I could,” said Elara.

He looked at her, the way he did. Then he nodded and went to put the kettle on, and that was all, and she washed her hands at the sink and went back down the alley, and Xing Yue was there, in the car, under the streetlight, with the engine running and two pork buns on the passenger seat, though it was half past one and she couldn’t think where he’d found them.

He didn’t ask about the hand. He asked if she’d been careful about her own.

“Always,” she said, and ate both buns.

✦ ✦ ✦

The results came out on the fifteenth of June, a Thursday, on a board in the old medical building and by email at the same time, and she read them standing in his kitchen at nine in the morning, on her phone, three times.

Distinction. And under it, a separate line, because they’d sent a separate email: the prize in clinical surgery for her year.

She screamed. She didn’t mean to. She screamed so loudly that the woman in the flat below banged on the ceiling with something, and she didn’t care, and she rang him at the hospital and screamed down the phone, and he was on a ward round, and she heard him say to somebody, “Give me one minute,” and then, to her, “Tell me again. Slowly.” She told him again. Slowly.

“Good,” he said. His voice was strange. “That’s—good. Elara. That’s what you are.”

She heard somebody on the ward say, “Dr. Wang? Are you all right?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Graduation was on the last Thursday in June, in the Great Hall at the top of the hill, a long grey stone building with a hammer-beam roof and windows that let in more pigeons than light.

Her whole family came. Her father in the funeral suit, because it was his only suit, with Uncle Mok two steps behind him. Elowen, in green, with Zhao Zhendong beside her, walking carefully, she was glad to see, the way you walk when you’ve been told to and have decided to listen. Raiden, in a waistcoat he had designed for the occasion, which had small embroidered scalpels on it. Evangeline, at the end of the row, in pale blue, silent, with the silver ring on her hand. Eliana with her phone.

They sat in the fourth row and cheered when she walked across the stage, so loudly that the Vice-Chancellor paused and looked at them over his glasses. Raiden whistled through his fingers. Elowen cried, which she would later deny. Her father didn’t move at all, and when she looked down from the stage with her certificate in her hand his face was wet.

Xing Yue was at the back.

She saw him as she came down the steps from the stage. He was standing by the doors in a dark grey suit, against the wall, behind the last row, where the latecomers and the photographers stood. He didn’t wave or smile. He stood with his hands folded in front of him and watched her come down the steps as if she were the only thing in the hall.

Nobody in her family knew who he was.

Except Eliana. Eliana turned round in her seat in the fourth row and looked straight down the hall at him, over all the heads, for a second. Then she lifted her phone and took a photograph, and turned back round, and said nothing to anyone.

✦ ✦ ✦

The back stairs of the Great Hall went down from behind the stage to a side door by the porters’ lodge. Nobody used them except the porters and the pigeons. She went down them at a run in her gown, holding the skirt of it up in one hand and her cap in the other, while her family was still fighting its way out of the fourth row.

He was there. He was halfway down, on the landing, by the old wooden banister with the carved knob at the turn, as though he’d known exactly where she’d come.

She didn’t stop. She came down the last steps to the landing and took hold of his tie, the way she had in the lift in September, and this time she pulled.

He came. She kissed him against the old banister with her cap in one hand and his tie in the other and her gown falling round her feet, and he put both arms round her and lifted her off the step and kissed her back, hard, as though he’d been standing at the back of that hall for two hours waiting to be allowed. The carved knob of the banister dug into her back. She didn’t care.

“Dr. Lin,” she said against his mouth. She’d never said it before. She wanted to hear how it sounded.

He said it back to her, low, into her hair, as if he were signing her name somewhere official. She started to cry.

“I’m a doctor,” she said. “I’m a real one. Oh my God.”

“You were one in September,” said Xing Yue. “Bed fourteen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They stood on the landing for a few minutes with his arms round her, listening to the sound of the hall emptying overhead. Somewhere outside, she could hear Raiden shouting her name.

“Elara,” he said.

She knew what he was going to say. She’d known it in the hall, watching him stand at the back.

“I’d like to meet them,” he said. “Your family. Properly. I’ve been standing at the back of rooms for nine months.”

She put her forehead against his chest.

“Elowen’s getting married,” she said. “Properly, this time. In September, in the shop. Everybody’s going to be there. All of us, all at once, all the friends, half the Walled City.” She looked up at him. “Come to that. Come to the wedding. If I bring you to Sunday lunch, it’ll be you and my father at one end of a table for three hours. If you come to the wedding, they’ll all see you at once and nobody can make a scene, because it’s Elowen’s day, and she’d kill them.”

He looked down at her for a few seconds.

“September,” he said.

“I promise.”

She watched him not like it, and then decide to wait anyway, the way he’d decided at the bottom of the hill road, and put it away somewhere.

He bent his head and kissed her once more, quick, on the mouth, and let her go, and she went back up the stairs holding her gown, to where her family was shouting.

chapters.title: The Flat on Banyan Terrace
chapters.desc: She starts as an intern across the harbour and is living out of a bag. He gives her a key and a floor plan with a room marked hers, and it’s already finished.
chapters.epigraph: “The study’s yours. So is the rest of it.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
On the first of July he became an associate consultant, which meant a new badge, a better office, a parking space he’d never use, and his name on the board outside Ward 9B in white letters instead of on the rota in pencil.

On the third of July she started as an intern at Harbourside General, on the surgical floor, and he didn’t see her awake for nine days.

She was on fourteen-hour days. She left before six and came back after nine, and she came back to the Walled City some nights and to his flat others, depending on which was nearer to wherever she’d fallen asleep, and she lived out of a canvas bag that went everywhere with her and held, at various times, scrubs, a toothbrush, a stethoscope, a banana, his spare glasses case, three phone chargers and a textbook on fluid balance with a rice ball squashed flat in the back of it.

He picked her up from the ferry at night when he could. She fell asleep in his car before he’d got out of the terminal car park. She did it three nights running, the second week of July, in the middle of three different sentences, and on the third night he sat outside 14 Banyan Terrace with the engine off and her asleep against the window and watched her breathe for twenty minutes before he woke her.

That was when he went to see the architect.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the same week he made an intern on his own team cry.

The intern had had a man on the ward on Tuesday night with a falling blood pressure and a belly that was getting bigger, and had written repeat in the morning and gone to sleep in the on-call room, because the registrar hadn’t answered his bleep and the intern hadn’t tried again. The man had bled into his abdomen for six hours. Xing Yue had found him on the morning round, grey and sweating, and taken him to theatre at eight, and he’d lived, just.

At the lunchtime meeting, in front of the whole surgical department, Xing Yue put the man’s observation chart up on the screen.

He didn’t raise his voice. He asked the intern to read the numbers out, one at a time, every hour, from ten at night to six in the morning. The intern read them. It took a while. Nobody in the room moved. When he got to four in the morning his voice went, and he stopped, and Xing Yue waited, and after a while he started again.

“What did you write at midnight?” said Xing Yue.

“Repeat in the morning.”

“Why?”

The intern didn’t have an answer.

“When your registrar doesn’t answer,” said Xing Yue, “you ring again. Then you ring the next one up. Then you ring me. You ring until somebody comes. If I’m asleep, I’ll wake up. If I’m in theatre, someone will hold the phone to my ear. Nobody on my team ever writes repeat in the morning next to numbers like that. Not once. Do you understand?”

The intern said yes. He was crying by then, without any sound, in front of forty people. Xing Yue thanked him for presenting and moved on to the next case.

Afterwards Dr. Fei found him in the corridor.

“That was brutal,” she said.

“The man nearly died.”

“I know. I’m not saying it was wrong. I’m saying it was brutal.” She looked at him. “You were always bad. You’ve got worse since you’ve been happy. It’s as if you’ve got more to lose.”

He didn’t answer that.

✦ ✦ ✦

He gave Elara the envelope on a Sunday in late July, the first day she’d had off in three weeks.

It was a plain brown envelope. Inside was a key on a ring, a new one, cut that week. And a floor plan. Not an estate agent’s plan; the architect’s, of the top two floors of 14 Banyan Terrace, with every room drawn in, and one of them, the small room off the big room on the lower floor, the one with the window over the frangipani tree, marked in his handwriting with a single letter. E.

She sat on his sofa and looked at it.

“What’s this?” she said.

“A key. And a plan.”

“I can see it’s a key and a plan.” She turned the plan round. “That’s the study. You’ve drawn an E on the study.”

“Come and look.”

She followed him. He opened the door.

The study had been empty since he moved in: a desk, a lamp, nothing. It wasn’t empty now. The old desk was gone. In its place was a new one, wide and pale, in plain oak, set lower than any desk he’d ever have used, because he had measured her. In May, during finals, she’d sat at the old desk with her shoulders up round her ears, and one night while she was asleep across it he’d taken a tape measure and marked, in pencil on the wall, the height of her elbows when she sat. The new desk was at that height. There was a reading lamp on it with a long arm that would reach anywhere. There was a suturing board on the desk, the good kind with a skin pad that took a hundred hours of practice, and a tray of instruments beside it. There were shelves on the wall at a height she could reach without a chair, and her textbooks were already on them, the ones she’d left here in May, and a row of empty shelves beyond them, waiting.

There was a small armchair by the window. Under the window, the frangipani was in flower.

She stood in the doorway and didn’t go in.

“When did you do this?” she said.

He told her: the last three weeks. Before he’d asked her, she said, and he said he hadn’t asked her yet.

“You’ve put my name on the post box,” said Elara. “I saw it. When I came in. Downstairs. It says WANG and under it it says LIN. I thought it was a mistake. I thought it was someone else.”

“It’s you,” said Xing Yue.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was furious for the rest of the evening.

He’d known she would be. He’d thought about it, and decided to do it anyway, because he could see her asleep in his car and he could see the room, and the one seemed to fix the other, and he hadn’t wanted to ask her until it was real. He’d wanted her to say yes or no to a thing, not to an idea.

She didn’t see it like that. She walked round the big room with the plan in her hand and told him what she saw. He’d decided for her. He’d measured her in her sleep. He’d put her name on a box before she’d said a word, as though she were a parcel. He’d gone and done the whole thing on his own and then presented it to her finished, like an operation, like a patient who’d been asleep the whole time, and what if she’d wanted to choose the desk, what if she’d hated oak, what if she didn’t want to live here at all?

“Do you?” he said.

“That’s not the point.”

He listened. He didn’t argue. He waited until she’d run down, the way he’d waited in his office in September, and then he said the only thing he had.

“If you say no, I’ll take it all down. The desk goes back. The name comes off the box. You keep the key, for when you want to come. Nothing changes.”

She stopped walking.

She looked at him across the big room. He looked back. He meant it. He’d have taken the desk down that night with a screwdriver if she’d said so, and put the old one back, and never mentioned it, and they both knew it. They both also knew that she wasn’t going to say so, and had known it since the doorway of the study, and that she’d been shouting at him for an hour because he’d known it first.

She went into the study. She looked at the desk.

Then she put both hands on it and pushed herself up and sat on it, on the edge, with her feet hanging, and it was exactly the right height for that too, which he had not measured. She put her hand out. He came.

She pulled him in by the front of his shirt until he was standing between her knees, and kissed him, hard, with her hands on his face, as if she were still angry, and she was, a bit. He put his hands flat on the desk on either side of her.

“It’s the right height,” she said, when she let him breathe. She didn’t sound pleased about it.

“I measured.”

“I know you measured. That’s what I’m angry about.” She kissed him again, more slowly. “I’ll pay rent.”

“The flat’s paid for.”

She looked at him. She’d known that, really. She’d been in the building’s post. She’d seen the letters that came, the ones from banks that weren’t asking for anything.

“Then I’ll pay for the groceries,” she said. “All of them. Every week. You’re not allowed to buy a single egg.”

He thought about it. She was a Lin, and she’d grown up in a house where money came and went in ways nobody talked about, and she’d paid for her own books since she was eighteen out of a flower shop’s profits and a scholarship and pride. He knew pride when he saw it. He’d left the north and his father’s money on pride.

“All right,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told her father she was moving closer to work.

That was true. It was nearer the ferry than the Walled City, and she had to cross the harbour every morning. She told Xing Yue that she’d told him that, and that her father had looked at her across the kitchen and said, “Good. You look tired,” and that was all.

On the morning of the twelfth of August, a Saturday, at seven, an old black Mercedes stopped outside 14 Banyan Terrace.

Xing Yue watched it from the top-floor window. A big grey-haired man got out of the driver’s seat in a short-sleeved shirt, and opened the boot, and began to carry boxes from it to the street door: one at a time, carefully, cardboard boxes from the Walled City with ELARA — BOOKS and ELARA — WINTER and ELARA — DON’T ASK written on them in marker. Elara came running down the stairs in her scrubs to meet him and took the boxes from him at the door. She didn’t let him in. He didn’t try to come in.

When he’d carried the last one, the big man stood on the pavement by the frangipani tree and looked up.

He looked straight up at the top floor windows, where Xing Yue was standing. He looked for a few seconds, with no expression at all. Then he got back in the old Mercedes, and drove away, and as far as Xing Yue ever knew, he said nothing to anyone.

“That was Uncle Mok,” said Elara, out of breath, coming up the stairs behind a box. “Baba’s driver. He’s driven me to school since I was six. He doesn’t talk.”

“He saw me.”

“Mok sees everything. He doesn’t talk,” she said again, as if that settled it, and put the box down in the hall and went to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

She worked fourteen hours that day.

He unpacked nothing. He knew better. He stacked the boxes in her study, in the order she’d want them, which he’d worked out from the writing on the sides, and he filled the fridge.

He’d been noticing what she liked for eleven months. He hadn’t meant to keep a list. He’d kept one. The peach yoghurt with the bits in, not the smooth one. The sesame paste she ate off a spoon. The green tea biscuits from the shop by the ferry. Mandarins, the small sweet ones with the loose skin. The pork buns, which he’d buy fresh, but he froze a bag of them anyway. The hot sauce from Old Bian’s, which Old Bian didn’t sell and had given him in a jam jar when he asked, with a look. Spring onion pancakes. The bad orange fizzy drink from the vending machine on the seventh floor that she drank when she was sad. Everything went in the fridge, on the shelves, in rows.

At ten past ten that night she came in through the door that was hers now, talking.

She talked in the hall, taking her shoes off. She put them by the door, facing out. She talked about a woman with a gallbladder and a man who’d tried to discharge himself in his gown and a registrar who’d made her put in a drip four times because he didn’t like how she’d taped it. She put her bag on the floor in the hall and her lanyard on the kitchen counter and her phone on the arm of the sofa and her stethoscope on the stairs, and he followed her round and picked them up and put them in a row on the counter, and she walked past the counter and moved them all into a heap, and kept talking, and neither of them mentioned it.

She opened the fridge.

She stopped talking.

She stood in front of the open fridge for a few seconds in the light from it, in her scrubs, looking at the peach yoghurt and the sesame paste and the bad orange drink in a row on the bottom shelf. Then she shut it, and leaned her forehead on the door.

“You’re having a bath,” said Xing Yue. “Doctor’s orders.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He ran it while she sat on the closed toilet lid and talked about the gallbladder. He made it hotter than he liked and checked it with his wrist. He put her in it, and she sank down until only her face and her knees were out of the water, and closed her eyes, and talked.

He washed her hair.

He knelt on the bathroom floor beside the bath and took the clip out, and wet her hair with the shower head, holding his hand over her eyes so the water wouldn’t go in them, and washed it with his shampoo, which made her smell like him, and which she complained about, and leaned her head back into his hands. Her hair was long and thick and full of fourteen hours. He took his time. He worked the shampoo through from her scalp to the ends, and rinsed it, and did it again, with his fingers slow and firm at the back of her neck where she carried everything, and she stopped talking about the gallbladder and started making small sounds instead, and then stopped making any sound at all.

He rinsed it for the last time. He squeezed the water out of the ends.

“I love you,” he said.

He said it plainly, kneeling on the floor in a wet shirt with his hands in her hair, the way he’d have told her a result. He’d been carrying it since April. He hadn’t been able to put it down.

She opened her eyes.

She turned her head on the edge of the bath and looked at him. Her face was pink from the hot water and her hair was dark and heavy over her shoulders.

“You heard that?” she said. “In the car? In April? I thought I’d dreamed that. I woke up the next day and thought I’d dreamed it, I was talking about gauze—”

“Yes,” said Xing Yue.

She sat up in the bath so fast the water went over the side onto his knees, and put both wet arms round his neck, and kissed him, soaking him to the skin, and said into his mouth, “I love you, I love you, I meant it, I was asleep but I meant it,” and he kissed her back with his hands still in her wet hair until there was nearly as much bathwater on the floor as in the bath.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her to bed with her hair still wet.

It was slow. It was the slowest it had been, slower than the first morning, because there was nowhere either of them had to be and nobody who would ring, and because for the first time there was no going home afterwards; this was home. He dried her with a towel, all of her, slowly, as if it were a job worth doing properly, and she laughed at him and let him, and then she wasn’t laughing, because he didn’t stop when she was dry. He kissed the water off her shoulders that the towel had missed. He kissed the inside of her wrist, where he always went first. She pulled him down with her onto the bed and her wet hair was cold on the pillow and on his arm and the rest of her was warm, and she didn’t talk, for once, at all, the whole time. She looked at him. She held his face in her hands and looked at him in the lamplight, as though she were the one checking something now.

Afterwards she fell asleep across him with her damp head on his chest.

He lay in the bed in the flat that had both their names on the box downstairs and listened to the frangipani tree moving outside the study window, and found he was holding her wrist, his thumb on the pulse, and he left it there.

chapters.title: The Cake
chapters.desc: Elara makes four tiers of cake for Elowen’s wedding, and the tall doctor in glasses comes and stands beside it. Nobody introduces him, and at midnight her father asks his name.
chapters.epigraph: “Sunday. One o’clock. Bring him.” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
She made the cake in his kitchen over three nights, after fourteen-hour shifts, and told him it was relaxing.

He didn’t believe her the first night. She could see him not believing her. She came in at ten, put her shoes by the door, washed her hands at the kitchen sink for a full surgical scrub, and then stood at his counter until three in the morning with a tray of pink sugar paste and a pair of tweezers and a ball tool, making camellias. One petal at a time. She rolled each one so thin you could see the lamp through it, and frilled the edge, and laid it on the flower over the last one, the way the real petals sat on the bush Elowen had grown in the shop window for ten years.

On the second night he stood at her shoulder and said, “You hum.”

“I don’t hum.”

“You’ve been humming for an hour. The same tune. It goes up at the end.”

She hadn’t known. She tried to catch herself at it and couldn’t; it only happened when she wasn’t listening. He said it went up at the end like a question. She said that was probably because she’d never known the answer, and laughed, and forgot about it, and a minute later he said she was doing it again.

He held the lamp for her. He’d worked out that she was faster if somebody moved the light to wherever she was looking, so he stood beside her and moved it. When she held out her hand without looking up, he put the next thing in it: the tweezers, the ball tool, the small brush, the water for the edges. He’d had scrub nurses do it for him since he was a student. He was good at it.

“You’d make a terrible scrub nurse,” she said, at one in the morning. “You keep looking at my face instead of my hands.”

“Your hands don’t need watching.”

She put the tweezers down.

She had pink sugar dust on her fingers and a petal stuck to the side of her thumb. She turned round on her stool and took his face in both her sugary hands, and kissed him, slowly, as though she’d been waiting all evening to do it and had made herself finish the flower first. When she let him go there were pink fingerprints on his jaw. She looked at them and started to laugh.

“Don’t wipe them,” she said. “Leave them. They suit you.”

He left them. He went to bed with them.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the third night there were four tiers in his fridge, which he’d emptied for them, and a tray of sugar camellias under a clean tea towel on the counter, and a smaller one, separate, in a box of its own, deep pink, with a wire stem.

“That’s for Zhao,” she said. “For his lapel. Mr. Wen at the flower market says the real bush has given enough this year, and Elowen’s not going to cut it for a buttonhole. So he gets mine.” She looked at it. “He won’t eat it. I told him not to eat it. He’ll probably eat it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden’s van came for the cake at nine on Saturday morning.

She went to work. She was on a day shift at Harbourside and couldn’t swap it, and she spent the whole shift checking her phone for photographs of the cake from Raiden, who sent a dozen, of the cake in the van, the cake on the counter, the cake under the arch Raiden had built out of shipyard timber, and one of himself, eating a loose petal, captioned it fell off.

She came to the shop at a quarter to eight in the evening, straight from the ferry, in a dress she’d changed into in the doctors’ room toilets, with her lanyard still round her neck because she forgot.

It was the flower shop in the Walled City, but you wouldn’t have known it. The shelves were gone. There were white roses in buckets down both sides of an aisle four metres long, and tulips over the floor Raiden had laid, and an arch of old dark timber at the far end with Zhao already standing under it, in black, with her sugar camellia in his lapel. There were thousands of tiny lights strung across the ceiling, all of them off, waiting for something Eliana wouldn’t explain. There were two dogs in ribbons. There were thirty people.

And there was her cake, on a table by the cooler, four tiers of it, covered in pink flowers, with every petal she’d made over three nights lit by the warm light from the street.

She stood in front of it. She was so pleased with it that it hurt.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the cooler, a woman was being introduced to everyone.

She was tall and quiet and broad-shouldered, in a black leather jacket, with grease under her nails, and somebody had backed her into the corner by the big glass-fronted fridge where the roses were kept, and was bringing her people one at a time, as if she were the guest of honour and nobody had asked her. Raiden’s girlfriend. The one nobody had known about. The whole shop was talking about it.

Elara was next. She stuck her hand out.

“Elara,” she said. “I’m a surgeon.” She saw the woman’s hands, and the shiny pink marks on the backs of them, old and new, and her mouth went on without her. “Are those burns from an exhaust? You should use silicone gel.”

The woman looked down at her own hands. Then she looked at Elara. She opened her mouth to say something.

Elara didn’t hear it. Across the room, through the door, past the buckets of white roses, a tall man in a dark suit and glasses had just come in off the street, a little out of breath, as though he’d walked fast from somewhere, and he was looking for someone, and he found her.

She forgot the woman at the cooler completely.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d been on a ward round. He’d told her he might be late, and he was, and she didn’t care. He came straight across the shop to her, between the buckets, past Aurelia Chen in gold, past two old men from the tea shop, past the dogs, and he didn’t stop until he was beside her and the cake, and then he stood there.

He didn’t touch her. He stood very close beside her, so close his sleeve was against her arm, and looked at the cake.

“It’s the best thing in the room,” he said.

She went red to the ears.

Nobody introduced him. Her father was across the room, talking to Elowen, with his hands clasped in front of him. Raiden was with the woman at the cooler, glowing like a lamp. Evangeline was at the back, in pale blue, with her arms folded, watching the door. Eliana was in a hoodie with her laptop and a lanky boy from next door with a medical textbook under his arm, who’d apparently come because Eliana told him to.

Nobody introduced him, and everybody noticed.

She felt them notice. Aunties she’d known all her life looked at him over their paper cups of tea. A man from the tea shop said something to another man from the tea shop. Aurelia Chen looked at him from the counter for a full minute with her head on one side, the way she’d look at a stone she was thinking of setting, and then looked at Elara, and smiled a small, interested smile, and said nothing at all.

One of the aunties, Mrs. Chau from the fish stall, came up to the cake and admired it and then looked up at him.

“And who’s this?” she said.

“A colleague,” said Elara, before she’d thought. “From the hospital.”

She felt him go still beside her.

It was only a moment. Mrs. Chau said how nice, and took a photograph of the cake, and went. He didn’t say anything. He didn’t move away. But she’d felt it, the small stillness, like a hand taken away, and she stood beside him with her face hot and wished she could take the word back and put it somewhere else.

✦ ✦ ✦

Across the shop the lanky boy with the textbook had seen him.

She watched it happen. The boy looked up from beside Eliana and saw Xing Yue by the cake and went faintly pink at the ears, and Xing Yue looked back at him over the buckets, and neither of them said a word. Neither of them nodded. They looked at each other for a second, the way you’d look at someone across a ward you hadn’t expected to see on it, and then they both looked away.

“Do you know him?” she said.

“He’s my cousin,” said Xing Yue. “Yu Chen. He lives next door to your father.”

She stared at him.

“He’s my cousin,” she said, “and he lives next door to my father, and you never—”

“You never asked if I had a cousin.”

She opened her mouth and shut it again. She thought about it. It was true.

“Later,” she said. “You’re telling me all of it later.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The lights came on at nine forty-one.

All of them at once, the thousands of them across the ceiling, gold and warm, as if the sky had come into the shop. Everyone looked up. Eliana, at the back, didn’t look up at all; she looked at her laptop, and pressed one key, and shut it.

Then her father walked Elowen down the aisle.

He did it in his funeral suit, because it was his only suit. Elowen was in a white dress with a camellia in her hair. The aisle was four metres long and it should have taken a few seconds, and her father’s arm was shaking, and halfway down, between the second row of tulips, he stopped. He looked at Zhao under the arch. He said, “Zhendong,” and then something else, too low for Elara to hear, a question, about a lemon tree. She didn’t understand it. Zhao did. Zhao Zhendong, who had crawled up a hill with a bullet through him and lain on a kitchen table for two hours under her hands without asking her once to stop, stood under the arch in his black suit and cried.

Then Elowen was crying, and her father, and then everyone.

Elara cried hardest. She always did. She cried at weddings and graduations and dogs being reunited with their owners on the news. She stood by her cake and cried with her mouth open, and without looking, beside her, he took something out of his inside pocket and put it in her hand.

A handkerchief. White, cotton, ironed into a square, with a sharp crease.

She looked at it through her tears. Then she looked at him.

“You iron your handkerchiefs,” she said, wetly.

“Yes.”

She blew her nose on it, loudly, during the vows. He didn’t flinch.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, when the shop was all noise and paper cups of champagne and cake being cut, Zhao came over.

He came over for the cake. He took a slice from Elara on a paper plate and ate it with his fingers, with the sugar camellia still in his lapel, uneaten, which she was proud of. Then he looked up from the plate at the man standing beside her.

He looked at him over the paper plate. Elara knew that look. She’d seen men in the Walled City go pale under it.

Xing Yue looked back.

“How’s the side?” he said, low.

Zhao didn’t say anything. He went on looking. Elara held her breath. She didn’t know what Zhao knew. She didn’t know what Zhao had worked out, from the bags she’d brought up the hill in March, and the hospital labels on them, and the instrument case with the needle holder in it.

“Hm,” said Zhao.

He took another slice of cake and went back to his wife, and that was the end of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody else came near them, the whole evening.

The family was busy. The whole family was busy, all night, with Raiden and the woman in the leather jacket, whose name was Jinx, and who had built someone’s motorbike and apparently given Lin Jian a look across the shop that had made him go and stand outside. Everyone was talking about Raiden. Raiden was talking about Raiden. Elowen went and talked to Jinx at the cooler with a face like a closed door, and came away with a different face. The party moved to a restaurant down the street and back to the shop and out onto the pavement, and somebody had a guitar, and Elara and the tall man in glasses went everywhere it went, side by side, and nobody stopped them.

She slid by underneath it. She’d never been so grateful to her brother.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight he said he had to be on the ward at seven.

They went out by the front door, because the back lane was busy; she’d seen Eliana go out that way with the boy from next door an hour before and not come back, and she wasn’t going to think about that. They walked down the street to the taxi rank at the end, past the shut shops and the tea merchant’s dark windows, under the awning of the old pharmacy where the taxis stopped. There were no taxis. There was a sign saying TAXI and a bench and the smell of rain coming.

“I said colleague,” she said.

He didn’t answer.

“To Mrs. Chau. I said colleague. I didn’t mean it. It just came out. It’s what I say at work when people ask, and my mouth said it before I—”

“I know,” he said.

“It’s not what you are.”

He took his glasses off. He folded them and held them out to her, and she took them, because he seemed to want her to, and she stood there holding his glasses in one hand and his handkerchief in the other under the awning of the old pharmacy, and he took the hand with his glasses in it by the wrist and pressed it flat against his own chest, under his jacket, over his shirt, so she could feel his heart going.

It was going as fast as hers had on the steps.

He kissed her.

He kissed her as though he’d been standing beside her all evening without touching her and had used up every bit of patience he had. She leaned back against the pharmacy’s shutter and it rattled, and she didn’t care, and she put her arms up round his neck with his glasses still in her fist and kissed him back until her lips hurt, until her knees went, until a taxi came round the corner and stopped right beside them and the driver leaned on his horn.

They broke apart. The driver was grinning.

“Next Sunday,” Elara said, breathless, with her hand flat on his chest. “Lunch. My father’s house. Everyone. I’ll tell them tomorrow. I promise. I’m not saying colleague ever again.”

He put his glasses back on and looked down at her.

“Your bag,” he said. “You left it on the counter.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked back up the street for her bag.

Her father was standing in the doorway of the shop.

He was alone. Everyone else was inside, or on the pavement further up with the guitar. He was standing in the lit doorway with his hands in his pockets and the gold light behind him, enormous and grey, in his funeral suit, and he’d seen them come up the street together.
