She could tell from his face that he’d seen a good deal more than that. The taxi rank was in plain view of the shop door. It always had been. She hadn’t thought.

They stopped in front of him.

He didn’t look at her. He looked at the man beside her.

“Who is he?” he said.

She felt Xing Yue not move. She felt herself want to say something, anything, colleague, a friend, a doctor from the hospital, Baba this is, and she didn’t. She looked at her father.

“Ask him,” said Elara.

Her father looked at her for a second. Then he looked back up at Xing Yue, who was taller than him, which hardly any men were.

“What’s your name?” said Lin Jian.

“Wang Xing Yue.”

Her father looked at him for a few seconds more, in the doorway, with his hands in his pockets, reading the small print.

Then he turned to Elara.

“Sunday,” he said. “One o’clock. Bring him.”

He went back inside, and fetched her bag off the counter, and came back out, and put it into her hands without another word.

chapters.title: Sunday Lunch in the Walled City
chapters.desc: The red door, eleven chairs and a father who has learned to ask things. Xing Yue tells the whole table he means to marry her.
chapters.epigraph: “Does she eat when she’s on nights?” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
It took two Sundays, because he was on call for the first one.

Elara rang her father to tell him. Xing Yue heard her side of it from the kitchen: the explanation, which went on for some time and took in the rota, the hospital, the ward, the patients and the general unfairness of surgery, and then a silence, and then, “Yes, Baba. The next one. I’ll tell him.” She came out of the study with the phone in her hand and a strange look on her face.

“He said the next one,” she said. “He said, a surgeon on call is a surgeon on call. He said, I don’t mind waiting. He’s never said I don’t mind waiting in his life. Elowen’s taught him things. It’s frightening.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The red door was at the top of the alley, past the noodle stall, round the corner he’d never been allowed to turn.

It was a narrow old door, painted the deep red of a lacquer box, with a brass knocker in the shape of a fish that had been rubbed gold in the middle by sixty years of hands. Elara didn’t knock. She opened it, because it was her house, and went in ahead of him talking, and he followed her into a hall that went straight up into the dark, all stairs, and smelled of soup and woodsmoke.

The kitchen was at the back. It was long and low, with a fire at the far end, and a long table down the middle with eleven chairs round it, none of them the same: a carved one at the head, some plain ones, a bentwood one, a child’s high chair that nobody had sat in for years and nobody had moved. The whole family was at the table already. They all looked up.

An old woman the size of a child came out of a door at the end of the kitchen with a ladle in her hand. She looked at him from his shoes to his hair and back down again.

“Too thin,” she said. “Sit.”

He sat where she pointed the ladle.

✦ ✦ ✦

He knew who they all were. Elara had told him a hundred times, and he’d listened every time.

Lin Jian at the head, in the carved chair, grey and enormous, in a cardigan, with his hands flat on the table on either side of his bowl. Elowen on his right, cool and sharp, in green, and beside her Zhao, in black, who looked at Xing Yue across the table and didn’t stop. Raiden opposite them, with a plaster on his thumb and his chair tipped back, delighted with everything. Eliana halfway down with her laptop open beside her soup, not looking at him at all, which he didn’t believe for a second. Evangeline at the far end of the table by the fire, silent, in grey, with a silver ring on her left hand, watching him and not blinking much.

And Elara beside him, talking for both of them.

She talked through the soup. She talked about the ward and the ferry and Mr. Yin, who’d sent a card in September to say his stoma had been reversed and he was back on his bus pass. She told the whole table that Xing Yue had once made a registrar cry with three sentences and that the registrar had sent him a thank-you card at Christmas. She told them about the cake, and the lamp, and the sugar, and the handkerchief. She talked so that nobody else would have to, and he understood that she was doing it for him, the way she’d done it for her sister in the room over the shop, and that she was frightened.

Lin Jian let her. He ate his soup and listened to his daughter with his eyes on Xing Yue.

When she stopped to breathe, he put his spoon down.

“Does she eat when she’s on nights?” he said.

The table went quiet. Even Raiden’s chair came down onto four legs.

It wasn’t the question Xing Yue had expected. He’d expected his family, his salary, his prospects, his intentions, the north. He’d been ready for all of them. He looked at Lin Jian and saw a man who had brought a three-year-old home from a children’s home and spent twenty years listening to her talk, and who had sat at this table watching her fall asleep over a dumpling in April, and who wanted to know one thing.

“Not unless someone puts it in her hand,” said Xing Yue.

Lin Jian looked at him. He asked whether Xing Yue did, then, and Xing Yue said yes, every time, and Lin Jian went on looking at him for a few seconds more and then picked up his spoon.

“Good,” he said, and went back to his soup.

Elara, beside him, let out a breath she’d been holding since the alley.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was Raiden who asked. Of course it was.

He asked over the fish, cheerfully, with his chopsticks in the air, as if he were asking about the weather in the north. “So,” he said. “Dr. Wang. What are your intentions towards my little sister? I have to ask. I’m the only son. It’s in the rules. Baba, it’s in the rules, isn’t it?”

“Raiden,” said Elowen.

“I’m only asking. Somebody has to. You’re all too frightened. Look at her, she’s gone purple.”

Xing Yue put his chopsticks down.

“To marry her,” he said. “Not today.”

The table went silent.

Elara, who had just taken a mouthful of soup, choked on it. She choked so badly that she had to put her bowl down and put her head between her knees, and he put his hand flat on her back without looking at her, and kept his eyes on Raiden.

Raiden stared at him. Then he started to laugh. He laughed out loud, the whole of him, tipped back in his chair with his hands on his stomach, the laugh going up the stairwell and round the house, until Ah Sim came out of the scullery to see what was wrong with him.

“Not today,” said Raiden, wiping his eyes. “He said not today. Baba. Baba, did you hear him?”

Lin Jian had heard him. He said nothing. But at the head of the table his eyes had gone wet at the corners, and Elara would talk about that in the car on the way home for twenty minutes.

At the far end of the table Evangeline looked at Elara, still bent double with her napkin over her face, and the corner of her mouth moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch Zhao stood up and looked at him and went out of the kitchen, and Xing Yue understood that he was meant to follow.

He followed him out of the red door into the alley. It was a grey afternoon and the noodle stall at the bottom had its shutters up and its steam going. Zhao stood by the wall with his hands in his pockets and looked at him.

He was a big man, broad and still, with a face that didn’t move. Xing Yue had stood beside the cake with him three weeks ago and asked how his side was. He’d seen the scar since, in his mind, every day, without ever seeing it: two wounds left open to drain, packed morning and evening for two weeks by a final-year student with stolen gauze.

“You saw her bags,” said Zhao.

Xing Yue said he had.

“You didn’t ask.”

“No.”

Zhao went on looking at him in the grey light. He didn’t say anything else. After a minute he nodded, once, the smallest movement of his head, and went back in through the red door, and left Xing Yue standing in the alley on his own.

He stood there for a few seconds. Then he went back in too.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara caught him at the bottom of the stairs.

“Come and see my room,” she said. “Come on. Quick. Before Raiden finds us and comes too. He’ll want to show you the drawings of the house. He’s got drawings of the house. He’s got drawings of every house. Come on.”

She took him by the hand up four flights of stairs, each narrower than the one before, past doors that were shut and a landing with a window onto the roofs of the Walled City and a cat asleep on the sill, to a small room at the very top of the house, under the roof, with a sloping ceiling and a window and a bed with a faded quilt.

There were posters on the walls. She hadn’t been joking. A band he’d never heard of, five boys with a great deal of hair. A film he’d never seen. A diagram of the human heart, cut out of a magazine, with arrows she’d added in pen. A map of the moons of Jupiter.

She stood in the middle of the room and told him about every one of them. Too fast. Much too fast. The band, and which one she’d liked, and why. The film, and how she’d seen it four times in one weekend when she was fourteen. The heart, and the arrows, and the mistake in one of them that she’d never fixed. She was breathless, and her face was bright, and she was talking the way she’d talked through lunch, to fill the room before anything could happen in it, and she was nervous of him in her old bedroom in a way she’d never been in his.

He shut the door.

“Elara,” he said.

She stopped.

She turned round and looked at him, standing against her bedroom door with his hand still on the handle, and she didn’t say anything, and he crossed the little room in two steps and turned her round and kissed her against the door.

She went up on her toes into it, at once, as though she’d been waiting for it since the alley. Her back hit the door. Her hands went into his hair. He kissed her hard, in her father’s house, under the poster of the five boys with their hair, with the sounds of the kitchen coming up the stairwell, Ah Sim’s voice and the clatter of dishes and Raiden laughing at something, every sound in the house coming up the stairs the way it always did. He kissed her until they were both breathing as though they’d run up the four flights, until she was pulling at the back of his shirt and he had her pressed to the door with his whole body and her hands had found the bare skin of his back.

He stopped first.

He stood with his forehead against hers and his eyes shut and his hands flat on the door on either side of her head, and breathed.

“Not in your father’s house,” he said.

She opened her eyes. She was flushed to the collar and her hair was everywhere.

“That’s a rule?”

“It is now.”

She stared at him. She looked so outraged, and so pink, and so pleased, all at once, that he had to stop himself kissing her again to make her stop looking like that, which would have broken the rule he had just made, inside a minute.

He stepped back. He straightened his glasses.

“Ask me again at home,” said Xing Yue.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left at five.

The whole family came to the door. Ah Sim gave him a bag of leftover dumplings and a look. Raiden shook his hand and said, “Not today,” again, and started laughing again, and Elowen took him by the arm and steered him away. Lin Jian stood in the hall at the bottom of the stairs and nodded to him, once, as Zhao had in the alley, and said, “Next Sunday,” and went back into the kitchen.

Evangeline was at the red door.

She was standing beside it, holding it open for them, in grey, with her silver ring. She looked at him as he went past her. She looked at him for a second or two, steadily, with her face doing nothing at all, and then she said one word, in a low flat voice that he would remember Elara telling him she’d heard perhaps twenty times in her life.

“Good,” said Evangeline.

Elara, beside him on the step, burst into tears.

✦ ✦ ✦

She cried in the car for ten minutes, and talked for twenty, about her father’s eyes and Raiden’s laugh and Zhao in the alley, which she’d seen from the landing window, and Ev, and Ev, and Ev. He drove and listened.

When they got home she took her shoes off and put them by the door, facing out. Then she stood in the hall, in her coat, and looked at him.

“I’m asking you again,” she said. “We’re home.”

He’d been waiting since the top of her father’s house.

She didn’t wait for him to answer. She took hold of the lapels of his coat and walked backwards up the stairs, pulling him with her, one step at a time, with her eyes on his, and he went. She kissed him on every third step. Halfway up she stopped and took his glasses off herself and put them in her own coat pocket, and he heard himself laugh. At the top of the stairs she let go of his coat and took her own off and dropped it on the landing, and then his, and then she took his hand and turned it over and kissed the inside of his wrist, the way he always did hers, deliberately, watching him, to show him she’d been paying attention.

He forgot about rules.

It was slow and it was not careful. She had been nervous all day, in her father’s house, with him beside her, and now the nervousness came out of her in a different shape, eager and laughing and greedy, and she pushed him down onto the bed and took her time with him, and talked the whole way through, telling him what she’d wanted to do in the bedroom at the top of the house, all of it, in detail, until he pulled her down and stopped her mouth with his.

Afterwards she lay with her head on his shoulder and said, into the dark, “To marry her. Not today.”

“I meant it.”

“I know you meant it.” She lifted her head. “That’s why I choked.”

chapters.title: An Yu Comes for Tea
chapters.desc: His brother flies down from the north for one afternoon and notices everything in a single cup of tea. Elara finds out how rich the Wangs really are, and then finds a card in her wallet.
chapters.epigraph: “He rang me to ask whether love at first sight was in the literature.” — Wang An Yu
chapters.content:
Elowen rang on the Tuesday, at eleven at night, which Elowen never did.

Elara was at the kitchen counter in her scrubs eating peach yoghurt out of the pot after a late shift. She answered with the spoon in her mouth.

“Ev’s engaged,” said Elowen.

Elara took the spoon out.

“On Saturday,” Elowen said. “The man. The one from February. The one you—” She stopped, because she didn’t know how much Elara knew, and Elara didn’t know how much she knew, and neither of them was going to say it on a phone. “He went to see Baba. In his office. There was a knife. Nobody’s hurt. Baba’s fine. Baba’s more than fine, Baba cried. And then they went to the market, the two of them, and he asked her at the orchid stall, the one she’s been going to since she was fourteen, and she said yes. In front of the orchid woman. Out loud.”

Elara put the yoghurt down on the counter.

“She said yes out loud,” she said.

“The orchid woman gave them a plant.”

Elara started to cry.

She stood at his kitchen counter with the phone against her ear and cried, hard, with her hand over her eyes, while Elowen told her the rest: his name, which was Lee Jun Hyuk, and that he was enormous and talked all the time and couldn’t cook, and that he’d told Baba in the office that Ev was his wife, with Ev standing in the doorway. Elara cried through all of it. She cried so much that Elowen said, “Elara. Elara, it’s good news,” and she said, “I know, I know it’s good news, that’s why,” and Elowen laughed down the phone, which Elowen almost never did.

When she put the phone down Xing Yue was standing in the kitchen doorway in his reading glasses with a journal in his hand.

“Evangeline,” he said.

“She’s getting married. To the man. The one with the knife wound. He’s called Lee Jun Hyuk and he’s enormous and he can’t cook.” She wiped her face on her sleeve. “I’m fine. I’m happy. I’m crying because I’m happy.”

“I know,” said Xing Yue. He came and took the yoghurt pot out of her hand, because she’d been holding it upside down. “You cry at everything good.”

“Not everything.”

“Dogs on the news. The banana prize. My handkerchief. Mr. Yin’s card.”

She thought about it. She couldn’t argue with any of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

His brother came on Sunday, between two flights.

Xing Yue told her on Friday, the way he told her about a change to the rota: An Yu was flying south on Sunday for a meeting, and back north the same evening, and would come for tea at three. He said it while he was cleaning his glasses, which meant he’d been thinking about how to say it for two days.

“Your brother,” said Elara. “An Yu. The one who rings on Sundays. The one who earns more before breakfast than you do in your life.”

“Yes.”

“He’s coming here. To the flat. Where I live. And you’ve told me on Friday.”

“He told me on Thursday.”

She spent Saturday cleaning, which she never did, and moving her things into piles, which he then moved into rows, which she then moved back. She bought a cake from the good bakery and then worried that it was the wrong sort of cake and bought another one. She asked him four times what An Yu was like. He said four times that An Yu was like An Yu, and she threw a cushion at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

An Yu came at three exactly.

He was shorter than his brother and broader, with the same serious face, but closed in a different way, like a door with a better lock. He wore a dark coat that, Elara thought, standing in the hall looking at it, probably cost as much as a small car, and when he took it off the suit underneath it cost as much as a larger one. He shook her hand. His hand was dry and brief. He said, “Elara,” and nothing else, and followed his brother into the big room.

He drank only tea. He brought it with him: a cake of old Pu’er in a paper wrapper that he gave to Xing Yue at the door, as though it were a bottle of wine. Xing Yue made it in the small brown pot. An Yu sat on the grey sofa with his cup in his hand and his back straight and let Elara talk.

She talked. She couldn’t help it. She talked about the cake from the bakery and why there were two of them, and the ferry, and Harbourside, and her ward, and the man on her ward who’d swallowed a key, and Mr. Yin’s card, and the camellias for Elowen’s wedding, and she heard herself doing it and couldn’t stop. An Yu listened. He drank his tea. He said nothing at all, except once, “Yes,” and once, “I see.”

But his eyes moved.

She watched them move round the room while she talked, the way Eliana’s moved over a screen. He looked at her shoes by the door, facing out, toes to it. He looked through the open door of the study at the low oak desk and the suturing board and the long-armed lamp. He looked at the kitchen counter, where there was a little pile of taxi receipts from the week, because she always got a receipt and never knew what to do with it. He looked at her lanyard on the stairs. He looked at the second toothbrush mug on the shelf by the bathroom door, which you could just see from the sofa.

And he looked at his brother.

Halfway through the man who’d swallowed the key, Xing Yue laughed. It wasn’t much. A short sound, under his breath, at the part where the man had asked for the key back. An Yu turned his head and looked at his brother laughing, and his face didn’t change at all, and he looked down into his tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

“He rang me,” said An Yu.

It was the first thing he’d said that wasn’t yes or I see. He said it to Elara, not to Xing Yue. He put his cup down.

“Two summers ago. In June. On a Saturday night. He doesn’t ring me. I ring him, on Sundays, to tell him he works too hard. He rang me, on a Saturday, at eleven at night, and asked me whether love at first sight was in the literature.”

Elara stared at him.

“I said what literature,” said An Yu. “He said medical. Psychiatric. Neurological. Anything with a reference. He said he’d seen someone on a ward and he hadn’t slept, and he wanted to know if there was a documented mechanism, or if it was just tiredness.” He looked at his brother. “I sent him three papers. One of them was about voles.”

“Voles,” said Elara.

“Pair-bonding in prairie voles. It’s a well-known paper.” An Yu picked his cup up again. “He read all three. He rang me back and said the voles were the only useful one.”

Elara turned round on the sofa and looked at Xing Yue.

He had taken his glasses off. He was cleaning them on his handkerchief, slowly, getting every corner of each lens, and his ears had gone dark red.

She started to laugh. She laughed so hard that she had to put her own tea down. She laughed until she was crying, which apparently she did at everything, and An Yu watched her with his serious closed face and the corner of his mouth moved, once, exactly the way his brother’s did.

✦ ✦ ✦

It came out sideways, after that, the way the most important things often did.

She asked An Yu, politely, what his meeting had been about. He told her, briefly. She didn’t understand most of it, but she understood the numbers, because there were a great many noughts in them and he said them as though they were small. She asked whether he enjoyed it. He said he did. Then she said, to be friendly, that Xing Yue had told her their father had some hospitals.

An Yu looked at his brother.

“Some,” he said.

“In the north. Your grandfather built them.”

“Fourteen,” said An Yu. “And the medical school that trains the doctors for them, and the land the hospitals are on, and the port the equipment comes into, and the house in the hills with the courtyard where my grandmother lives and sends Xing Yue a letter every month telling him to come home and get married.” He looked at Elara. “Some.”

The room was quiet.

Elara was a Lin. She’d grown up in a house where money came in through the back door at night in envelopes and went out the front in her father’s coat, where men stood up when her father came down the street, where there had been a car and a driver all her life and nobody had ever asked what anything cost. She’d thought she knew what rich was. She’d thought he was comfortable, and private about it, and had a flat.

This was another size of it. This was a size she didn’t have a word for.

She looked at Xing Yue. He’d put his glasses back on. He was looking at her, steadily, and he didn’t look sorry, and he didn’t look worried. He looked as though he were waiting to see which way she’d go.

✦ ✦ ✦

An Yu left at a quarter to four.

He put his coat on in the hall. He shook her hand again, brief and dry, and said, “Thank you for the cake. Both of them,” and she went red, because she’d thought he hadn’t noticed there were two.

She went into the kitchen with the cups. She heard them at the front door behind her, the two brothers, low.

“He’ll ask,” said An Yu. “At New Year. When you’re coming home.”

There was a short silence.

“I am home,” said Xing Yue.

She stood at the sink with a cup in each hand and didn’t move. The door shut. She heard his footsteps come back across the big room, and she turned the tap on so he wouldn’t know she’d been standing there listening, and he came into the kitchen and looked at the tap running into an empty sink and knew anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

She waited until she’d dried the cups.

Then she started.

“Fourteen,” she said. “Fourteen hospitals. And a medical school. And a port. A port, Xing Yue. You told me in May that your father had some hospitals and I thought you meant clinics. I thought you meant three clinics and a pharmacy. I told Elowen your family was in healthcare. I said it like it was a dentist’s. You let me think you were a normal person with a flat.”

“You never asked.”

“Don’t do that. Don’t say I never asked. You said it about your cousin. You can’t keep not telling me things and then saying I never asked, as though it’s my fault for not guessing that you’ve got a medical school—”

“You’re right,” he said.

She stopped. He never did that. He never said you’re right in a fight; he said it on ward rounds, about scans.

“You’re right,” he said again. “I didn’t tell you because I didn’t want it to be the thing about me. It’s been the thing about me my whole life. I came here so it wouldn’t be. That’s why. It’s not a good enough reason.”

He told her then. Plainly, standing in the kitchen, the way he’d have given a history. His grandfather had left him money in a trust that came to him at twenty-five. He’d bought the top of this building with some of it in 2019 and put the rest somewhere and hadn’t looked at it since, except when the letters came. He had a consultant’s salary now and spent almost none of it. He would never, as long as he lived, run anything in the north. His father knew that and didn’t believe it. His grandmother knew it and was the only one who did.

“None of it changes where I live,” said Xing Yue. “Or who with.”

She looked at him. She’d stopped being angry somewhere in the middle of it, and hadn’t noticed, and was annoyed with herself, so she started again.

She told him he should have told her. She told him that if they were going to get married, which she wasn’t saying they were, he’d said not today, she’d heard him, the whole table heard him, then she had a right to know if she was marrying a port. She told him about the time she’d told Raiden that Xing Yue drove an old car because he didn’t care about cars, when actually it was probably because he didn’t care about money because he had so much of it he didn’t have to—

He looked at his watch.

She stopped.

“Are you timing me?” she said.

“I’m giving you five more minutes,” said Xing Yue. “Then I’m kissing you.”

She stared at him. Then she went on, louder, because she wasn’t going to be told when she’d finished. She told him about his coat, which she now realised was probably worth more than her loupes. She told him about the second cake. She told him she’d spent all Saturday cleaning for a man who had looked at her taxi receipts. She was halfway through something about the receipts when she saw his eyes go to the second hand on his watch, and she broke off.

“You’re early,” she said. “That’s four. That’s not five, that’s four, I saw you look—”

He didn’t wait for the fifth.

He took her wrist, as if he were going to count her pulse against the second hand, and kissed her in the middle of the word, against the kitchen counter, with her back to the clean cups, and she made a furious noise into his mouth and grabbed his shirt in both fists and kissed him back, still furious, and then less, and then not at all.

“That was four,” she said, when she could.

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the card on Wednesday.

She was paying for a coffee at the hospital kiosk and opened her wallet and there it was, in the slot behind her ID, where it hadn’t been on Tuesday. A plain dark grey card from the taxi company that served the whole city, the one with the green cars, with her name on it, LIN ELARA, and an account number.

She rang him from the kiosk.

He told her what it was before she’d finished asking. An account. In her name. Every taxi she took, anywhere, at any hour, went on it. She’d never have to find cash at two in the morning outside a ferry terminal again, or stand by a road waving at cars that wouldn’t stop.

“Who gets the bill?” she said.

“I do.”

“So you’ll see every taxi I take. Where from. Where to. What time.” She was standing by the kiosk with the coffee going cold in her hand. “You’ll get a list of everywhere I go.”

“I already know where you go,” said Xing Yue.

She opened her mouth. She shut it. He did. He’d had her on his phone since February, a little blue dot, and she’d watched him look at it and never once told him to stop, and she didn’t tell him to stop now. She hung up on him instead, and was furious about it for an hour, in the way you’re furious at something you know perfectly well you’re going to keep.

At two in the morning she came out of Harbourside after a shift that had gone on six hours longer than it should have, into the rain, with no cash and no bus and her feet aching, and there was a green taxi at the rank.

She got in. She gave the driver the card. He swiped it and said, “Banyan Terrace, Dr. Lin?” because it was already on the account, and she sat in the back of the warm car with the rain on the windows and the harbour going past, and got her phone out.

Elara: Fine.

He was asleep. He answered anyway, inside a minute.

Xing Yue: Good.

chapters.title: He Is Bad at Holidays
chapters.desc: He works every holiday so other people can go home. On Lunar New Year’s Eve she brings dumplings to Ward 9B, and he breaks his own rule.
chapters.epigraph: “I said not in the hospital. I’m allowed to be wrong.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
In January Raiden’s girlfriend came to dinner at the red door for the first time, and Xing Yue was in theatre.

He’d been on the rota for weeks. He was always on the rota for the Saturdays nobody wanted. Elara had stopped asking him to swap, because the answer was always the same and she’d started to understand it, though he hadn’t explained yet. She went on her own, late, from Harbourside, in her scrubs under her coat, and at half past ten that night his phone rang in the pocket of his scrubs while he was standing at the end of a theatre table watching a registrar close.

He let it ring twice. Then he nodded to the scrub nurse, who took it out of his pocket, answered it and held it to his ear, because she’d done it for him for four years and knew who rang at half past ten.

“She came,” said Elara, without saying hello. “Jinx. She came inside. She’s never been inside, she’s been with Raiden for nearly three years and she’s never once come through the door, and she came tonight, and Baba opened it himself.”

“I’m glad,” he said.

“And Ev’s man was there, the big one, Jun Hyuk, and he stood up when she came in and nearly hit his head on the lamp and talked to her about engines for twenty minutes without stopping, about intakes, whatever they are, she builds motorbikes, and Ev just sat there and watched him with her face doing nothing at all, and I could tell she was proud. And then Ah Sim came out of the kitchen and looked Jinx up and down and said, He’s fat. About Raiden. To Jinx’s face. And Jinx said, He cooks. Just like that. And Ah Sim told her to sit down and eat because she was too thin too.”

On the table the registrar had put a stitch in the wrong place. It was the third. He’d watched the first two and said nothing because the first two had been his to get wrong.

“And then after dinner they were in the kitchen on their own, Baba and Jinx, drying up, and we were all upstairs arguing about Raiden’s drawings, and Baba laughed,” said Elara. “Out loud. The big laugh. It came all the way up the stairs and we all stopped. Nobody knows what she said to him. Raiden doesn’t know. She won’t tell him. Nobody’s made Baba laugh like that since—”

“Wait,” said Xing Yue.

He said it to her, and she stopped, because he never said wait to her. He turned his head an inch from the phone the scrub nurse was holding.

“Dr. Zou,” he said.

The registrar’s hands stopped.

“Take that out.” His voice didn’t go up at all. It went down. “And the one before it. You’re closing skin, not wrapping a parcel. If you close a wound like that on anyone of mine again, you can go and work in a shoe shop, where it won’t matter what the stitches look like. Again. Slowly.”

Dr. Zou took them out. Nobody in the theatre said anything. The anaesthetist found something urgent to look at on her machine.

Xing Yue turned his head back to the phone.

“Sorry,” he said. “Go on. He laughed.”

There was a pause on the line.

“You just told someone to go and work in a shoe shop,” said Elara. “In that voice.”

He said Zou would do it properly now.

Another pause. He thought she might be angry. He waited to find out. Then he heard her laugh, low, at the other end, in the back of a taxi somewhere on the harbour road.

“Poor man,” she said. “I’ll bring him a sweet on Monday. Which one’s Zou? Is he the one with the eyebrows?” And then, before he could answer, “I’ve heard Baba laugh like that about four times in my life. I want to know what she said.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She asked him on the phone, later that week, why he always took the holidays.

She didn’t ask it as a complaint. She asked it lying on the floor of the study with her feet up on the armchair and the phone on her chest, while he was on call again and walking down an empty corridor on the ninth floor at one in the morning, and he heard in her voice that she’d already guessed half of it and wanted him to say the rest.

He stopped by the window at the end of the corridor. The harbour was down there, black, with the lights of a ship going across it.

“The ones with children should go home,” he said. “Fei has two. Rao has a little girl. If I’m here, they’re not. That’s most of it.”

He could have stopped there. He’d always stopped there before, with everyone.

“The rest is that I don’t like them,” he said. “Holidays. I never have. At home they were dinners. Thirty people at a long table in my grandfather’s house, and my father at the end of it, talking about the hospitals. How many beds. How many new ones. Which of his sons would take over which. An Yu used to hide under the table with a book. I used to sit and wait for the courses to end.” He looked at the ship. “I’d rather be here. Here something happens that matters.”

She didn’t say anything for a few seconds.

“You told me that without me asking,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You’ve never done that before. Told me something about your family without me having to dare you or drag it out of you with a broom.”

He thought about it. She was right.

“Don’t get used to it,” he said, and she laughed so loud on the floor of his study that he had to hold the phone away from his ear.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Lunar New Year’s Eve he was on call, as he’d been every year since he came south.

She went to the Walled City at six, in a red dress she’d bought for it, with a box of mandarins and a bag of the green tea biscuits for Eliana, and from half past six his phone kept buzzing in his pocket on the ward.

Elara: Ev’s man brought a kumquat tree. A TREE. on his shoulder. up the alley.

Elara: raiden says he’s a wardrobe. 4 times so far

Elara: Aurelia Chen is here with her husband. she’s in red. she looks like she could buy the house and everyone in it. she keeps looking at Jun Hyuk

Elara: he’s been talking to me about wound packing for 25 mins. he knows a LOT about wound packing. I told him he had better technique than half my registrars and he went bright red. the whole of him. he’s enormous so it took a while

Elara: Baba and Jun Hyuk have been talking about tides by the window for an hour. both standing up. hands in pockets. Ah Sim says if they don’t sit down she’s giving their soup to the dog. we don’t have a dog

Elara: eliana just threw a bag of dumplings over the wall to the boy next door. your cousin. I saw. she doesn’t know I saw

He read them at the nurses’ station between patients, with his face perfectly straight, while Sister Shao, the night sister on 9B, watched him read them and pretended not to.

At ten he sent one back.

Xing Yue: Eat something.

Elara: I’ve eaten FOUR bowls. ah sim’s counting

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past eleven he was at the nurses’ station on 9B writing up the notes on a man with a bowel obstruction when the lift doors opened at the end of the corridor and she came out of them.

She was in the red dress with her coat over it and her hair coming out of its pins. She had a cardboard box in her arms, tied with string, the kind Ah Sim used, and a string bag of oranges hanging off her wrist, and her cheeks were pink from the cold.

She came down the corridor towards him past the dark bays, where the patients were asleep, and every nurse on the ward looked up, and Sister Shao put down her pen.

“Happy New Year,” Elara said, at the station, in a whisper, because of the patients. “I brought you dumplings. Ah Sim made them. Pork and cabbage, and there’s a coin in one of them, she says, but she won’t say which, and if you get it you have to tell her. And oranges. For luck. You have to have oranges.” She put the box down on the counter in front of him. “I got a taxi. A paid one. On the card. I thought you’d want to know.”

He looked at her. He looked at the box, and the oranges, and the red dress under her coat.

He put his pen down.

“Sister Shao,” he said, “I’ll be in the on-call room. Bleep me.”

Sister Shao looked at Elara, and at him, and at the box of dumplings.

“Of course, Dr. Wang,” she said. “Happy New Year, Dr. Lin.” She picked her pen back up. “Leave me two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The surgical on-call room on the ninth floor was a narrow room with a bed, a chair, a desk, a sink and a window that looked west over the hospital garden and the roofs, all the way to the old Walled City.

They ate the dumplings sitting on the bed with the box between them, out of the box, with the chopsticks Ah Sim had tucked in under the string. She told him about the dinner with her mouth full. The kumquat tree. The tides. Raiden and the wardrobe. Aurelia Chen leaning across to Evangeline and saying something, and Ev not answering, and Aurelia sitting back looking like she’d won something anyway. Her father at the head of the table in his funeral suit, laughing at something Jun Hyuk said, with his whole face.

“It was so loud,” she said. “It was the loudest New Year we’ve ever had. Everybody was there. Everybody except you.”

“I’m here.”

“I know. That’s why I came.” She put a dumpling in his mouth with her chopsticks before he could answer. “It’s not everybody if you’re not.”

He bit into the dumpling and his teeth hit something hard.

He took it out. A coin, an old one, wiped clean, warm from the dumpling.

She stared at it. Then she put both hands over her mouth and laughed into them until her eyes ran.

“You have to tell Ah Sim,” she said. “You have to ring her. Tomorrow. She’ll be furious. She’ll say you cheated. She’ll say I gave it to you on purpose. I didn’t. I swear I didn’t.”

He put the coin in the pocket of his scrubs.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight the fireworks went up over the Walled City.

They stood at the window of the on-call room with the light off and watched. They went up from the old piers and the roofs and the streets, red and gold and green, a long way off, in bursts, and the sound came a second after each one, faint, through the glass. Below them the hospital garden was dark, the big camphor tree black against the paths, and the old block with its verandahs, and the windows on the first floor of it dark.

She stood in front of him with her back against his chest, and he stood with his arms round her and his chin on the top of her head.

“Happy New Year,” she said.

“Happy New Year.”

The last of them went up. The sky went dark, and smoky, and quiet.

She turned round in his arms and looked up at him, and he saw her decide to be wicked.

“Your rule,” she said.

He’d made it in the autumn, on the first day she’d come up to 9B to bring him lunch, when one of the nurses had found them in his office with the door half open and had gone away again with her eyebrows in her hair. Not in the hospital, he’d said. Nothing inside the building. Not where his team were, not where his patients were. Outside the doors was outside. Inside was work.

“Not in the hospital,” said Elara. She stepped back from him, slowly, until her back was against the on-call room door, and leaned on it, and folded her arms, and looked up at him with her eyebrows up and her hair half down and the red dress showing under her coat. “That’s what you said. I’m in the hospital. You’re in the hospital. It’s very strict. I’m only saying, I wouldn’t want you to break it, you’d never forgive yourself, you’d have to go and work in a shoe shop—”

He came across the room and put his hand flat on the door beside her head, and shut it the last inch, and turned the lock.

“I said not in the hospital,” he said.

“You did.”

“I’m allowed to be wrong.”

He kissed her in the middle of whatever she’d been going to say next, with her back against the door and the lock under his hand, without any warning at all, and she made a sound of pure triumph into his mouth and uncrossed her arms and took hold of him. She tasted of oranges. Her coat came off somewhere. Her hands were cold from the window and she put them under his scrubs, on his back, on purpose, and he made a sound against her mouth he’d never made in this building, and she laughed, and he lifted her off her feet and carried her the two steps to the bed and sat down on it with her in his lap.

She kissed him like it was a holiday. Slow and then not slow, her hands in his hair, her knees either side of him on the narrow bed, his hands on her back through the thin red dress. She was kissing his throat. He had his eyes shut. He’d stopped thinking about the building at all.

His pager went off.

It went off on his waistband, loud, between them, and she jumped. He opened his eyes. She was looking at him from a few centimetres away, flushed and pink-mouthed and furious.

He unclipped it and read it, with her still in his lap.

Then he picked up the phone on the wall beside the bed and dialled.

“Wang,” he said. “Yes.” He listened. Her forehead had come down on his shoulder and she was shaking with silent laughter into his neck. “Yes. Coming.”

He put the phone down.

“Sister Shao,” he said. “Bed eight’s pressure is dropping.”

“Go,” said Elara into his neck, still laughing. “Go, go, go and save bed eight. I’ll wait. I’ll eat your dumplings.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Bed eight took two hours.

When he came back to the on-call room at a quarter past two she was asleep on the narrow bed in her coat and her red dress, curled on her side with her shoes still on, with the empty dumpling box on the floor beside her and an orange in her hand.

He sat on the chair and watched her sleep. Then he took her shoes off and put them side by side under the bed, facing the door.

At three he walked her down to the taxi rank at the main doors. It was cold and clear and the air smelled of the fireworks. A green taxi was waiting, and she stood beside it on the kerb with her coat pulled round her and turned and put something in his hand.

A red packet. A small one, a red paper envelope with a gold character on the front, folded flat.

“You’re not married,” she said. “Unmarried people get red packets at New Year. That’s the rule. Ah Sim says so. And anyone who works on New Year’s Eve gets one, she says, that’s an old rule, she might have made it up.” She put her hand over his, over the envelope. “Don’t open it till I’ve gone.”

She got in the taxi. He watched it go down the hill.

Then he opened it. There was no money in it. There was a slip of paper, folded in four, in her round quick handwriting, which anyone could read.

Come home for breakfast.

He stood on the kerb outside the main doors at three in the morning in his scrubs, in the cold, and read it, and put it in his pocket with Ah Sim’s coin, and went back up to his ward.

chapters.title: Staples on a Kitchen Table
chapters.desc: Her sister shoots a man in a noodle shop, and Elara staples the scalp of the giant who talks on the kitchen table. She comes home at one in the morning and shakes on the floor of the hall.
chapters.epigraph: “Next time ring me first. I’ll drive. I’ll wait in the car.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
At two in the afternoon she was on the surgical floor at Harbourside, eleven months into her intern year, explaining to an old man with a new hip why he couldn’t have a third pudding.

She was good at it. She was good at the whole floor. She’d been there since July and she knew every nurse’s children’s names and which porter would come fast if you asked nicely and which one would come fast if you didn’t. The old man was laughing. He’d stopped asking for the pudding and started asking whether she was married, which they all did in the end.

“Nearly,” said Elara. “Not today.”

Her phone rang in her pocket. A number she didn’t know. She stepped out into the corridor.

“Miss Elara. It’s Bao. I drive your sister. Evangeline.” A man’s voice, low and quick, with traffic behind it. “Nam’s Noodles, River Bridge Road. Somebody came for her. There’s been shooting. She’s not hurt. She’s not hurt. She shot one of them. There’s a boy hit, and the old lady, and Mr. Lee’s head’s open. She said call you. Nobody else.”

She was already walking.

✦ ✦ ✦

The emergency department at Harbourside was on the ground floor, and she went through it at a fast walk in her scrubs, smiling at everyone, the way you walked when you didn’t want anyone to look at you twice. By the door to the ambulance bay there was a shelf of green bags, the grab bags the paramedics took out to the big calls. She took one. Nobody saw. If anybody had, she’d have smiled at them and said she’d been sent.

There was a green taxi at the rank. She gave the driver the card and asked him to be quick, and he looked at her scrubs and was.

Her phone buzzed in her lap halfway over the bridge.

Xing Yue: ?

He’d seen the dot. He’d seen it leave Harbourside at ten past two in the middle of a shift, and cross the river, and go east into the old market district, where she had no reason in the world to be. She looked at the one question mark for a few seconds. She didn’t answer it. She didn’t know what she’d say.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came through the broken door of Nam’s Noodles at a quarter to three, with her hair falling out of its clip and the green bag over her shoulder, and stopped.

She looked at the room. The broken glass. The duck cabinet, with a hole in it. A calendar on the floor. A boy sitting against the wall with a tea towel pressed into his shoulder, crying steadily, like rain. A man in a pale shirt face down by the window with one of Zhao’s men sitting on his back. An old woman in a purple jacket in a kitchen chair with her wrist in a cushion, swearing.

And her sister, kneeling on the wet floor in a pale blue dress, with a man’s head in her lap.

“Oh, Ev,” said Elara.

Then she was a doctor.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did the boy first, because he was bleeding most.

She knelt beside him and looked at his shoulder. In and out. Through the muscle at the top of the arm, nowhere near the big vessels, nowhere near the bone. She felt her voice go clear and level and pleasant.

“You’re going to be fine. It went through. It missed the bone. You’re very lucky the person who shot you is a terrible shot.”

The boy stared at her. She packed the wound and taped it and told Bao, who was standing by the door with a face like a closed fist, that the boy needed an ambulance in the next hour and not before. Bao looked at the man on the floor by the window and said he’d see to it. She didn’t ask what that meant. She’d grown up in a house where you didn’t.

She did the old woman second. The old woman told her she was fine. Elara told her she had a broken wrist and probably a concussion and was going to the hospital whether she liked it or not, and the old woman gave her a long measuring look, from her trainers to her hair, and said, “You’re the doctor one,” and let her splint it.

Then she knelt down beside her sister.

The man with his head in Ev’s lap was the man from the phone. She knew it at once. She’d never seen him, and she’d have known him anywhere: the size of him, and the way her sister’s hand was on his hair. He was awake. He was lying on his side with his eyes open, watching the room slide about, and the floor beside him had been cleaned with a tea towel.

She parted his hair with her gloved fingers and looked.

“Six centimetres,” she said. “Down to the bone. It needs closing. He’s been sick?”

“Once,” said Evangeline.

“Did he lose consciousness?”

“For about a minute. Maybe two.”

Elara looked down at him. “Do you know where you are?”

“Nam’s,” said the man. “On the floor. In the soup. Your sister shot a boy.”

“He’s oriented,” said Elara. “Rude, but oriented.”

She told them about the scan. A head injury with loss of consciousness and vomiting got a scan, that was the rule, not her being careful. A bleed under the skull could look like nothing for six hours and then kill him.

“No hospitals,” said the man.

“Then he dies on the floor of a noodle shop,” said Elara pleasantly, “and I’ll tell everyone it was his own fault.”

Ev looked at her. Ev said there was a place on the hill above the old racecourse. Private.

“The Crestview,” said Elara. “It’s the most expensive hospital in the city. It costs more for one night than I earn in a month. Rich men go there to have their knees done and not be in the newspaper.”

“They don’t ask questions,” said Evangeline, “of people who pay.”

Elara looked at her sister. Then at the big man on the floor with his head in her lap.

“Can he pay?”

“Yes,” said Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

He refused to go anywhere with a hole in his head. He said so. Then he was sick again, without any fuss, into a bowl Ev was already holding.

So she closed it on Nam’s kitchen table.

There was a staple gun in the green bag, because there always was. She had him sit on the edge of the table in the back kitchen, among the flour sacks and the pots, with his head bent forward and Ev holding his hands, and she cleaned the wound and numbed it and closed it, staple after staple, along the line of the cut through his hair, fast and neat.

At twenty past three a tall policeman in a long coat came in through the broken door.

She heard him stop in the shop, the way everyone stopped. She heard him say “Evangeline,” and her sister not answer, and then a long conversation in the front of the shop about a passport. She didn’t stop. She didn’t look round. She had her hands in a man’s hair and a staple gun in her fist, and if the policeman wanted to watch her close a wound on a kitchen table, he could watch. She’d smiled at policemen all her life.

She’d finished when he came through to the back. He looked at the big man on the edge of the table. He looked at her, in her Harbourside scrubs, peeling off her gloves. He knew exactly who she was. She saw it. Everybody in the police knew her father’s face, and most of them knew his daughters’.

“Dr. Lin,” said Inspector Song Wei Long.

“Inspector,” said Elara, and smiled at him, and dropped her gloves in the bin.

He looked at her a second longer. Then he turned to the man on the table, and said his name, and a great many other things, and she went and washed her hands at Nam’s sink and didn’t listen to any of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Crestview was on the hill above the old racecourse, and it looked like a hotel.

They scanned his head at six. There was no bleed. There was a concussion, a bad one, and a fine crack in the skull that would heal by itself if he did nothing stupid for six weeks. The doctor on duty was a calm grey woman, who looked at the stapled wound under the light, and then turned and looked at Elara, standing at the end of the bed in her scrubs with the green bag still over her shoulder.

“Nice work,” she said.

Elara went pink to the ears. She didn’t say anything. She’d never been told it about a kitchen table.

She stayed until he was let go. She sat in the corridor outside his room on a chair that was nicer than her sofa, and at eleven she heard him through the door start on Ev about a sandwich, and then stop in the middle of a word, and not start again. She smiled into her coffee.

At a quarter past midnight they let him go, with a list.

She got a green taxi home on the card.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got as far as inside the front door.

She shut it behind her. She put her keys on the hook. She stood in the dark hall at Banyan Terrace in her scrubs, with the green bag still on her shoulder, and started to shake.

It came from nowhere. It came up from her knees. She’d been fine at Nam’s and fine at the Crestview and fine in the taxi, laughing at the driver’s jokes, and now she was in her own hall and she couldn’t stop. Her teeth went. Her hands went. She dropped the green bag. She put her back against the wall and slid down it, onto the floor, by the shoe rack, with her own shoes in front of her still pointing out, and sat there shaking with her arms round her knees.

The light came on upstairs. She heard him on the stairs.

He didn’t say anything. He sat down on the floor of the hall beside her, in his T-shirt and soft trousers, and put his arm round her and pulled her against him, sideways, so her head was on his chest, and held on.

She talked. She couldn’t not.

She told him all of it, in no order, through her teeth. The broken door. The ducks. The boy against the wall. The old woman with the purple jacket and her wrist. The policeman and the passport. The man who talked, with his head in her sister’s lap, and the staples, and the scan, and the sandwich.

“My sister shot someone,” she said. “Ev. Ev shot someone. She had a gun. She knew how to use it. Somebody came into a noodle shop to take her and she shot him and she sat on the floor afterwards holding a man’s head in her lap as calm as anything, and I’ve known her my whole life, and I didn’t know she could.” She was crying now, as well as shaking. “And I went. I didn’t think. I took a bag from the department and went. I’d do it again. I’d do it every time.”

He held her, and she felt him go still against her, in a way she’d never felt before. It was colder than his thinking stillness. It went all the way through him, like ice going through water, and she lifted her head and looked at his face in the light from the stairs and didn’t know it.

“Who?” he said.

“Who what?”

“Who came into the noodle shop.” His voice was perfectly level. “Who’s on the floor with one of Zhao’s men sitting on him. Who sent them. I’d like the names.”

“No,” said Elara.

He looked at her.

“No,” she said again. “I’m not giving you names. You’ll do something. I can see you’ll do something. You’ve got the face you had with Nie. And it’s not yours to do anything about. It’s Ev’s. It’s Zhao’s. It’s Wei Long’s, he was there, he’s dealing with it.” She held his T-shirt in her fist. “That world raised me. That’s my family. That’s where I’m from. Things come in through the back door at night and you help and you don’t ask. I’m not going to stop going when they ring. Don’t ask me to.”

He didn’t ask her to. He took it in, the whole of it, and she saw him put the names away somewhere, and the ice with them, and come back.

“I won’t,” he said. “Next time ring me first.”

She stared at him.

“I’ll drive,” he said. “I’ll wait in the car. I won’t come in. I won’t ask who. But I’m not finding out from a dot on a map that you’re in the old market district at half past two on a Saturday afternoon with no reason to be there, and then not hearing from you for ten hours.” His voice cracked on hours, a little, and steadied. “I watched it all afternoon. Nam’s. Then the Crestview. I didn’t know what you were doing. I didn’t know if it was you that was hurt.”

She hadn’t thought of that. She’d thought of everything else.

“Yes,” said Elara. “Yes. I’ll ring you first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When she’d stopped shaking he stood up.

He pulled her up with him, by both hands, off the floor, onto her feet. She thought he was going to take her upstairs.

He put her against the wall of the hall, with his hands either side of her face, and kissed her.

He didn’t say anything first. He didn’t take his glasses off. He kissed her hard, with his whole body holding her to the wall, the way you hold pressure on a bleed, steady and hard and not letting up for anything, as if he could stop something coming out of her by pressing hard enough. She held on. She held onto the back of his T-shirt with both fists and kissed him back with her mouth still wet from crying, and felt his heart going under her hands through his back, fast, much faster than his face had let her see.

When he stopped he kept his forehead on hers.

“You’re having a bath,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He ran it. She sat on the edge of it in her scrubs and talked about staples.

She’d calmed down enough to be interested in her own day. She told him about the staple gun in the green bag, and how they came in different widths, and how on a scalp you wanted the wider ones because of the hair, and how she’d once seen a registrar try skin glue on a scalp and glue the patient’s hair to his own glove. She got in. She sank down in the hot water up to her chin and kept talking. He knelt on the bathroom floor beside the bath in his T-shirt, with his elbows on the edge, and listened, and didn’t once look away from her.

“—and so there’s a gauge on the side, a little dial, and you’re meant to check it, and nobody checks it—”

She stopped.

She looked at him kneeling there on the tiles. Dry, in his T-shirt, with his glasses on, with his serious face, being sensible.

She took hold of the front of his T-shirt with one wet hand and pulled.

He came over the side of the bath before he knew it was happening. He came in with all his clothes on, glasses and all, in a wave of water that went over the edge and across the floor, and landed on her, half in and half out, with one knee on the bottom of the bath and his elbow in the soap dish, and came up gasping with his glasses crooked and his T-shirt plastered to him and water pouring off his hair.

She laughed so hard she slid under.

He pulled her back up by her arms. He was laughing too, out loud, the real one, the one she’d only heard a handful of times, in a bath with his trousers on, and she couldn’t stop, and he couldn’t stop, and the water went everywhere. He took his glasses off and threw them out onto the bathmat. He tried to get his T-shirt off and got stuck in it, and she helped, badly, and they laughed until the water started to go cold around them.

Then it wasn’t funny any more.

She didn’t know when it changed. She was holding his face. He was holding her in the water with both arms round her, as if she might go somewhere. She kissed him, slowly, for the first time that day without any hurry or fear in it, and he kissed her back the same way, and the bath went cold, and neither of them cared. She felt him shaking a little, under her hands, and understood it wasn’t the cold. She held him tighter.

He got them out in the end. He wrapped her in a towel and himself in another and took her up to bed, and they didn’t sleep until late, and then they did, tangled together with the wet towels still on the floor and his thumb on the inside of her wrist.

chapters.title: The Proposal at Dawn
chapters.desc: On the morning she finishes her intern year he meets her in the old garden at City Hospital and asks her to marry him. She’s talking, and says yes in the middle of a sentence.
chapters.epigraph: “Sorry, what? Say it again. I was talking.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The ring was made on Harbour Road, in a shop with a broken necklace in the window.

It had been mended in gold, the necklace, every break in it filled with a thin bright line, and it sat on black velvet behind the glass with no price and no label, and he had walked past it for five years on his way to the ferry without going in. In the second week of June he went in.

Aurelia Chen came out from the back herself. She was in grey, with her hair up, and she looked at him from his shoes to his glasses exactly the way she’d looked at him across Elowen’s shop in September, as if he were a stone she hadn’t decided whether to set.

“Dr. Wang,” she said. “Elara’s doctor.”

“I’d like a ring made.”

“Of course you would.” She sat down on the other side of the glass counter and folded her hands. “What did you have in mind?”

He’d had it in mind for a year. He told her. A star sapphire, not large, the grey-blue kind with the star that moves across it under a light. A plain gold band, narrow, nothing on it that could catch in a glove. Small enough for a surgeon’s hand.

“A star,” said Aurelia.

“Yes.”

She waited for him to explain. He didn’t. She looked at him a little longer and he saw her work it out, as Elara had at Old Bian’s, and the corner of her mouth moved.

“Star and moon,” she said. “Elara told Elowen what your name meant. Elowen told me. We both thought it was the most nauseating thing we’d ever heard.” She opened a drawer under the counter and took out a tray. “Enzo will set it. He’s the best goldsmith in the city and he’ll make you wait three weeks.”

“I need it in one.”

Aurelia looked up from the tray.

“Then it’ll cost you double,” she said, “for rushing a genius,” and named a figure.

He didn’t blink. He’d known she would, and he’d known she’d enjoy it. He took out his card.

She looked at the card, and at him. Then she put the tray of stones in front of him.

“I won’t tell Elowen,” said Aurelia. “Not because you asked. Because it’s the only time in ten years I’ll have known something about her family before she did, and I’m going to enjoy it for as long as it lasts.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He carried it for nine days.

In the inside pocket of his jacket, in a small box covered in grey silk. On the ward. In theatre, in the pocket of the jacket in his locker. In the car at night picking her up from the ferry. He carried it and didn’t give it to her because the day wasn’t right yet, and he knew which day was right, and he was waiting for it.

On the first of July she’d start as a surgical resident at City Hospital.

Professor Liao’s team. Colorectal and general, on the seventh floor, where she’d been a student with Dr. Fei two years ago. Not his team. Not his unit. She’d applied for it knowing that, and he’d sat on none of the panels and signed none of the papers and said nothing to anyone, and Professor Liao had read her reports from Harbourside and her prize and her logbook and taken her in a week, and said to Xing Yue in the lift afterwards, sucking a boiled sweet, “I don’t want to hear one word from you about her, Wang. Not one. Good or bad.” Nobody would ever stand in the line between them at work. She’d never have to wonder.

On the thirtieth of June she’d come off her last night shift at Harbourside, and her intern year would be over.

That was the day.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d said, a week before, that when she finished at Harbourside she wanted to go and look at her new hospital. Not the wards. Not the tower. The old part, the granite block with the verandahs, and the garden behind it, where she’d never once been in two years of coming and going, because she’d always been running.

“I want to see it when nobody’s there,” she said. “Before it’s mine.”

He’d said he’d meet her.

At five to seven on Sunday morning he stood at the garden gate behind the old block and watched the little blue dot of her on his phone cross the bridge, and come up the harbour road, and turn up the hill. He put his phone away when the taxi turned into the lane.

It had rained in the night. It was still grey and soft and the air was full of water, warm, as it always was in late June, and the paths through the garden were dark and shining and covered in fallen leaves. There was a big camphor tree in the middle, older than the hospital, with a trunk you couldn’t have got your arms halfway round, and its leaves dripped. There was a fish pond under it, round, with a low stone edge, and koi in it, orange and white and gold, moving slowly in the grey water. There were benches. There were the back windows of the old block, two floors of them, tall and arched, with the paint coming off the frames, and on the first floor a row of them that looked straight down onto the pond.

The taxi stopped. She got out.

She was in her scrubs with a cardigan over them, with her canvas bag over her shoulder and her hair falling out of its clip and the grey shadows of a night shift under her eyes. She saw him at the gate and her face lit up.

“You came,” she said. “You’re here at seven in the morning on a Sunday. You’re never off on a Sunday.”

“I swapped.”

“You never swap.” She came through the gate and stopped and looked round her, at the tree and the pond and the windows, and her mouth fell open. “Oh. Oh, it’s beautiful. Nobody told me. Two years and nobody told me there was this. Look at the tree. Look at the fish.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She walked round the pond, and talked.

She talked about her last patient, an old woman who’d had her gallbladder out on Thursday and who’d given Elara a knitted bookmark at four in the morning as a goodbye present, with a crooked cat on it. She talked about Harbourside, all of it, the whole year, the ferry and the floor and the porters and the third pudding, and she said she’d miss it, and her voice went wobbly. She talked about tomorrow.

“I’m scared,” she said. “I’m not scared of the work. I’m scared of Professor Liao. Everyone says he’s lovely and eats sweets on the round and he can tell from the way you hold a pen whether you’ll be any good. What if I hold a pen wrong? What if I’ve been holding pens wrong my whole life and nobody’s told me?”

She knelt on the stone edge of the pond and looked at the koi.

“Do koi sleep?” she said. “I don’t think I’ve ever known. Do they shut their eyes? They can’t shut their eyes, can they? They haven’t got eyelids. So how do you know if they’re asleep? Maybe they’re asleep now. Maybe they’re all asleep and they’re just moving out of habit. There’s one there, the big gold one, I think that one’s asleep, it’s—”

“Marry me,” said Xing Yue.

“—it’s just sort of drifting, look, by the stone, and they live for ages, don’t they, koi, I read somewhere they live longer than people sometimes, there was one in a pond somewhere that was two hundred—”

She stopped.

She turned her head and looked at him over her shoulder.

He was on one knee on the wet path behind her. He’d gone down without thinking about it. The leaves were soaking through the knee of his trousers. The air was so warm and wet that his glasses had fogged at the edges, and he could only see her through the middle of them, kneeling on the stone edge of the pond in her scrubs with her mouth open, and he held the little grey silk box out in his hand, open, with the ring in it.

“Sorry, what?” said Elara. “Say it again. I was talking.”

“Marry me,” he said again.

She stared at the ring. She stared at him.

“Yes,” she said, “but I was saying about the koi, there was one in a pond in—oh my God. Oh my God. Yes. I said yes in the middle of the fish. Wait. Wait, that doesn’t count, I want to say it properly, I want—”

He stood up and stopped the rest of it with his mouth.

He put his wet hand to the side of her throat, where her pulse was going like a bird’s, and kissed her standing on the path by the pond, with the box still open in one hand and the camphor tree dripping on them both, and she made a sound into his mouth that was half a laugh and half a sob and took hold of his shirt, and stood up on the stone edge of the pond to reach him better, and nearly went in. He held her. She kissed him back with her hands in his collar and the leaves dripping on them and the fish moving under the grey water below.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she let him go she said yes again. Properly, standing on the stone edge so her eyes were level with his, with both hands flat on his chest.

“Yes,” said Elara. “Yes. I’m saying it properly now. Yes.”

Then she cried.

She cried the way she cried at everything good, all at once, with her whole face, and he put the ring on her finger while she was doing it. It fitted. He’d known it would. He’d measured her finger in April, while she was asleep, with a piece of thread.

She held her hand up to the grey light. The star in the stone moved when she turned it, six thin lines of light across the blue-grey, sliding as the light changed.

“It’s a star,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You put a star on me.” She laughed through her tears. “Star and moon. That’s so embarrassing. That’s the most embarrassing thing anyone’s ever done. Everyone’s going to know. Aurelia’s going to know. Did Aurelia make this? This is Aurelia’s, isn’t it, this is Enzo, I can tell, look at the setting—”

“She charged me double.”

“Of course she charged you double. Has she told Elowen?”

“She says she’s going to enjoy not telling her.”

Elara laughed so hard she had to sit down on the bench under the camphor tree, and he sat down beside her, wet through at the knee, and she held her hand out in front of them both and turned it so the star moved, over and over.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It comes off for theatre,” she said, after a while. “Rings come off for theatre. I’ll have to take it off every day. Where do I put it? I’ll lose it. I lose everything. I’ll put it in a pocket and the pocket’ll go in the wash and some poor woman in the hospital laundry will find a star sapphire in a pair of scrubs—”

“There’s a hook,” he said.

She looked at him.

“In your locker. In the residents’ changing room on the seventh floor. Your locker’s the third from the end on the left. There’s a small gold hook inside it, on the door, at the top, where you can see it. For the ring.” He looked at the koi. “I asked the porters on Friday.”

She was quiet for a second.

“On Friday,” she said. “Before I’d said anything. Before you’d asked me. You had a hook put in my locker.”

“Yes.”

“What if I’d said no?”

He turned his head and looked at her.

“You didn’t,” said Xing Yue.

She hit him with her bag.

She hit him on the arm with her canvas bag, quite hard, with the knitted bookmark and the stethoscope and three phone chargers in it, and he let her, and she hit him again, and then she put the bag down on the bench and put her face in his shoulder and laughed until she was crying again.

She kept the hook.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went home and slept till three.

She fell asleep in the car before they were out of the lane, with her left hand held up in front of her face, looking at it, and her hand slowly coming down into her lap as she went. He carried her up the stairs at Banyan Terrace. She woke on the landing and said, “Did I say yes?” and he said she had, twice, and once in the middle of a fish, and she said, “Good,” and went back to sleep on his shoulder.

He woke at three to the afternoon sun coming through the blinds in stripes, the way it had the first morning, and found her awake beside him, propped on one elbow, looking at the ring on her hand in the light.

She saw him wake. She put her hand flat on his chest, with the ring on it, and looked at it there.

“I want to tell you something,” she said. “Before anything. Before we tell anyone.”

He waited.

“I love you,” said Elara. “That’s all. I just wanted to say it first, today, before anybody else says anything about it, before Raiden makes a joke.” She looked at him. “That’s all it was.”

He took her hand off his chest and turned it over and kissed the inside of her wrist, and then her palm, and then the ring.

It was slow. The whole afternoon was slow. There was nowhere to be, and nobody to ring, and nothing she had to start tomorrow that mattered as much as this, and they took all of it. She lay back in the striped light and let him take his time with her, and for once she didn’t talk, and then she did, and it was all his name and the word yes, over and over, as if now she’d started she couldn’t stop saying it. He kissed every bit of her he could reach. He kissed her as though he were learning her again, now that she was going to be his wife. When she pulled him down to her, the ring on her hand was cool against the back of his neck. He felt it there the whole time.

Afterwards she lay on her front with her chin on his chest and her hand beside her face, still looking at it.

“I’m going to be so annoying about this,” she said.

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she told the family chat.

She sat on the sofa with her feet in his lap and took a photograph of her hand on his knee, with the ring on it, and sent it with no words at all, and then put the phone face down on the cushion and put her hands over her face.

It buzzed, and buzzed again, and didn’t stop.

She turned it over and read them to him one at a time.

Elowen: ELARA

Elowen: Why didn’t Aurelia tell me

Eliana: Spreadsheet updated.

Raiden: First try? Show-off.

Raiden: I needed thirty-one. Some of us had to work for it.

Evangeline: Good.

Baba: Bring him on Sunday.

Elara read the last one twice. Then she put the phone down and looked at him.

“He’s coming every Sunday anyway,” she said. “Baba knows you’re coming every Sunday. Why’s he saying bring him?”

“Because he wanted to say something,” said Xing Yue.

She looked at him. She looked at the phone. She put her face in his shoulder, and cried again, at another good thing.

chapters.title: The Seventh Guest
chapters.desc: Elara kneels by a river at one in the morning with her green bag, and runs late up a lane to her sister’s wedding in scrubs. That night she says she doesn’t know who her own mother was.
chapters.epigraph: “Ev knows who her mother was now.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
In the autumn she was a surgical resident on Professor Liao’s team and learned that he could, in fact, tell from the way you held a pen. He told her on her second day that she held hers like a scalpel, and that this was correct, and gave her a boiled sweet.

The rest of the autumn went past her in pieces. One Sunday in October the whole family drove up to Ev’s new house on Fig Tree Lane in three cars, the first time all of them had gone up the lane at once, and Ev’s neighbours watched from over the wall. In November Jinx opened her own shop, three doors down from the garage near the Docks, and Elara came from a night shift in her scrubs and stood at the back eating a pastry and crying, because it was a good thing.

He wasn’t at either. He was on call for one and in theatre for the other. She told him both on the phone, all of it, and he listened.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Saturday in December, at half past ten at night, her phone buzzed on the arm of the sofa.

Evangeline: The bridge at the border. Boat. About thirty people. Some hurt. Old. Cold. Police coming. Bring your bag.

Elara read it twice. Then she looked up.

He was at the other end of the sofa with a journal, in his reading glasses, with her feet in his lap. He’d looked up when the phone went. He’d seen her face change.

She held up her phone so he could see it, and then took it back and rang him. He was sitting a metre away. His phone went off in his pocket.

He looked at it. He looked at her.

“You said ring you first,” said Elara. “I’m ringing you first.”

He answered it.

“I’ll drive,” he said, into his phone, looking at her down the length of the sofa. “Get your bag.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The green bag lived in the hall cupboard now. She’d never given it back to Harbourside. She’d restocked it herself, a little at a time, from places she didn’t think about too carefully, and he’d seen it in the cupboard every time he got his coat and had never said a word.

She knew he’d been through it. One night in October she’d packed it in a hurry and left the scissors on top, and in the morning they were in the side pocket where they belonged, and the out-of-date saline she’d been meaning to throw away was gone. He never mentioned it. Neither did she.

He drove north.

It was nearly two hours. Out of the city on the expressway, then the old road through the flat country with the fish ponds black on both sides and the lights of the border towns orange on the low cloud. She talked for the first hour about nothing, because she was frightened and didn’t know of what. She told him about Ev’s house, the fig tree and the stream and the green door and the menu taped inside it. She told him about the cat. She went quiet for the second hour and held her bag on her knees.

There was a checkpoint before the bridge, with police cars across the road and their lights going, and an ambulance, and people in blankets being brought up a track from the river, slowly, one at a time.

He stopped the car on the verge outside the checkpoint and turned the engine off.

“I’ll be here,” he said.

“You can’t sit in the car all night.”

“I said I’d wait in the car.”

She looked at him. He’d said it in June, on the floor of the hall, and he was going to do exactly that, and nothing she said would make him get out and come down that track, because she’d told him it wasn’t his, and he’d listened.

She leaned over and kissed him, hard, once, on the mouth.

Then she got out with her bag and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

A tall policeman in a long coat was standing by his car at the checkpoint, in the light from the bridge, watching people in blankets come up from the jetty. She knew him. Inspector Song. Twenty past three on Nam’s kitchen table, a passport, a long look.

He looked at her as she came past with her bag, and nodded, as if he’d expected her.

Then she saw him look past her, at the dark blue car on the verge, at the man sitting in it with his hands on the wheel. Wei Long’s long face did nothing at all. He lifted one hand off the roof of his car, a small movement, and in the car on the verge Xing Yue lifted his off the wheel.

She stopped.

“You know him?” she said.

“He’s Yu Chen’s cousin,” said Wei Long. “The other side of the family. Yu Chen talks about him.” He looked at her. “The old ones are at the bottom of the track. One of them’s bad.”

She went down.

✦ ✦ ✦

The old one who was bad was a woman called Auntie Lian, who’d been at the front of the deck, and who was sitting on the track in a foil blanket with her lips blue and her breath coming short and her hand on her chest.

Elara knelt down beside her on the wet stones and opened her green bag.

She didn’t think. She never did, once she’d started. She was warm and cheerful and clear, and she told Auntie Lian her name and asked hers, and she listened to her chest and counted her breathing and wrapped her in a second blanket under the first and held her cold hands in her own until they started to warm. Behind her an old woman in a purple jacket with her wrist in the splint Elara had put on it in June was standing at the top of the track directing police officers to her back room, as if they were her staff. Somebody was crying further down. The river went past under the bridge, black and slow.

She went from one to the next. A man with a cut on his leg from the deck. A girl of about fifteen who wouldn’t let go of her own hands. A boy with his ankle swollen. An old man who was only cold, and frightened, and wanted to tell her where he’d come from, and she let him, and listened, and nodded, and wrapped him up.

At some point she looked up and saw Ev’s man by Wei Long’s car, enormous in the light from the checkpoint, handing something over. A long case. She saw Wei Long look at it, and at him, and take it.

She didn’t know what it meant. She knew it meant something. She went back to Auntie Lian.

✦ ✦ ✦

They drove home at four.

She talked at first. She told him about the thirty: where they’d come from, the boat, the cold, the old man who’d wanted to tell her about his village, the girl with her hands, Auntie Lian, whose breathing had come back to normal by three and who’d held Elara’s face in both her hands and said something in a dialect Elara didn’t know. She told it all in pieces, too fast, with her bag on her knees.

Then she stopped.

She sat beside him in the dark with the fish ponds going past and didn’t say anything at all. He looked across at her. She knew he was looking. She’d never been quiet in his car. She’d never been quiet anywhere, with him, for more than a minute, in two years.

“Ev’s man gave away his rifle,” she said, a long way further on. “To Wei Long. At the bridge. I saw him. I don’t know what that means.”

He didn’t say anything.

She reached across in the dark and took his left hand off the gearstick. She held it in both of hers in her lap, and then lifted it, and pressed her mouth to the middle of his palm, and held it there against her face with her eyes shut, for a long way down the old road.
