He drove one-handed all the way to the expressway, and didn’t ask for it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Ev got married two weeks later, on the longest night of the year, in the garden at Fig Tree Lane, with six guests.

Elara was supposed to be the seventh. She was on a twelve-hour night shift at City Hospital, and couldn’t swap it, and had begged, and nobody would. She sent a message to the family at four in the morning from the doctors’ room: On a twelve-hour. Two crash calls already. Will come when I can. Start without me. And then, a minute later, because she couldn’t bear it: DON’T START WITHOUT ME.

She came off at eight. She had a patient to hand over who wouldn’t stop bleeding and she stayed with him until he did, which was eleven. She got a taxi on the card at noon from the main doors, in her scrubs, with her lanyard still round her neck, because she forgot, and fell asleep in the back of it, and woke on the reservoir road with the hills going past and the driver saying, “Fig Tree Lane, Dr. Lin?”

She ran up the lane from the bottom. She’d made the driver stop at the bottom because she thought it would be quicker to run. It wasn’t. Her hair came out of its clip halfway up. She was shouting before she got to the gate.

“I said don’t start without me!”

She came in through the green door at a quarter to two and found them all at the long dark table in the front room with the windows open, eating long noodles. The viola case was on the window seat. There was white silk tied round the neck of a jar on the table. Everybody looked up at her in the doorway.

Her sister was at the head of the table, in white.

Ev was in white, with a bent silver pin in her hair, and she was laughing. Not the small movement at the corner of her mouth that was all Elara had ever seen. Laughing out loud, at something Jinx had said, with her whole face, with her head back, in front of everyone.

Elara burst into tears.

“Seventh guest,” said Raiden, and pulled out a chair for her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got home at seven that evening, in a taxi, with a jar of salted lemons that Ev had pushed into her hands at the green door, and a container of noodles from Ah Sim, and her eyes swollen.

He was home. He was off for once, a whole weekend, the first in months. He was in the kitchen when she came in and he took the jar and the container from her and put them on the counter, and she sat on the stool and told him.

The garden in the frost. The herbs Ev had carried instead of flowers, from her own glasshouse, tied with white silk. The six guests and the neighbours on two chairs over the wall with a ginger cat between them. The noodles you weren’t allowed to cut. The viola.

“It was her mother’s,” said Elara. “Ev’s mother. Her real one. She played the viola. Ev found out this year. There was a man who knew her, and he told Ev she spoke just like her, and she had the viola sent, and she’s learning. And the hairpin in her hair, the silver one, that was her mother’s too.” She was turning the jar of lemons round on the counter, round and round. “Ev knows who her mother was now.”

He waited.

“I don’t know who mine was,” she said.

She heard herself say it. She’d never said it before, not to her father or her sisters, not even out loud to herself.

“I don’t know her name,” she said. “I don’t know what she looked like. I don’t know if she was alive when they took me to the children’s home, or if she’d died, or if she gave me away, or if somebody took me. I don’t know if she talked. I don’t know if I talk because she did.” She stopped turning the jar. “I’ve never said I wanted to know. I never thought I did. I always thought, I’ve got a family, I’ve got the Lins, I’ve got Baba, and that’s enough, and it’s greedy to want another one.” Her eyes filled again. “And then I watched Ev laugh at her own wedding with her mother’s pin in her hair, and I wanted it so much I couldn’t breathe.”

He came round the counter. He didn’t hold her yet.

“What do you know?” he said.

“Nothing. That’s what I’m saying. Baba brought me home from a children’s home when I was three. That’s all. That’s all there’s ever been.”

He didn’t say anything to that. He put his arms round her on the stool and she put her face in his shirt and cried, for Ev, and for herself, and for a woman she couldn’t picture, until she was hiccupping.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine she said she wanted to sleep.

She’d been up for thirty-six hours. She’d done a night shift and a bleeding man and a taxi and a lane and a wedding and cried for most of the day. She lay down on the sofa with her head in his lap and her eyes shut and said she was going to sleep for a week.

He was stroking her hair. He’d been stroking it since she lay down. His hand stopped.

“Please,” said Xing Yue.

She opened her eyes.

He never said please. He’d said it maybe once in two years, at the hospital, to a porter, under extreme circumstances. She looked up at him from his lap, and he was looking down at her, serious, in the lamplight, with his glasses on, and he didn’t say anything else. He didn’t explain. He’d been sitting beside her all evening while she cried for something he couldn’t give her.

She gave in at once. She hadn’t been going to hold out, really.

She sat up and took his glasses off and put them on the arm of the sofa, and kissed him.

It was slow and sleepy and warm. They didn’t get as far as the stairs. They didn’t try. She was so tired she was clumsy, and she laughed at herself, and he didn’t laugh, he just held her, as if she were the thing he’d asked for and he wasn’t going to waste any of it. His hands were slow on her back, under her scrubs top, which she’d never changed out of. His mouth was slow on her throat. She pulled him down with her onto the cushions and wound herself round him, and everything was soft and heavy and close, the lamp low, the frangipani branches tapping at the study window, his breath on her neck and his name in her mouth. She felt like she was being held together. She let him do it.

Afterwards she lay on top of him on the long grey sofa under the blanket from the back of it, with her ear on his chest, and found she wasn’t sleepy at all.

“I want ours outdoors,” she said.

His hand moved on her back.

“Our wedding,” said Elara. “Ev’s was in a garden. In the frost. And it was the best one I’ve ever been to, and Elowen’s was in the shop, and that was beautiful too, but I want ours outside. Early. In the morning. When the light’s coming. Somewhere with trees.” She thought about it. “Somewhere nobody’s ever bled.”

“All right,” he said.

She told him he wasn’t allowed to organise it, and he said all right to that too.

“You are, a bit,” she said, and fell asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning she came downstairs at seven and he was at the kitchen counter already, dressed, with a cup of tea and his prescription pad.

He was writing something on it. When she came in he tore the sheet off and folded it and put it in his shirt pocket.

“Patient?” she said, yawning.

“Something I need to look up,” said Xing Yue, and made her tea.

She didn’t think about it again. She had no reason to. She sat on the stool in his T-shirt and drank her tea and ate the salted lemon Ev had given her, sliced thin, with honey, and told him what she wanted for breakfast, and he made it, and it was a year later, in an envelope, that she saw what he’d written on it that morning.

Her birthday. The words children’s home, with a question mark. And under it, underlined twice, in handwriting that only she could read: Find her.

chapters.title: A Name in a Ledger
chapters.desc: He finds the old matron of the children’s home and the birth name Elara has never heard. He decides to keep it for their wedding day.
chapters.epigraph: “They called her the bell girl. She never stopped.” — Matron Sima
chapters.content:
He started with what he had, which was almost nothing.

A birthday. The words children’s home. The age of three. A tall house in the Walled City behind a red door, and a man who had his postman checked every Lunar New Year. He kept the sheet from the prescription pad in his wallet behind his driving licence, and on the nights when he wasn’t on call and she was, he sat at the kitchen counter at Banyan Terrace with his laptop and looked.

He rang the children’s homes that were still open, from his office between clinics, and the women who answered were kind and told him nothing, because the records of a child placed with a family were closed to anyone but the child. The homes that had shut had sent their files to the welfare archive behind the courts. He went there on a Saturday in January. There was a card in the index for Plum Steps Children’s Home, closed 2011, and boxes of files, and nothing he was allowed to open.

What he found, in the end, was a newspaper.

A short piece from the week the home closed, with a photograph: a small woman in a cardigan standing at an iron gate with a bag of keys, looking at the camera as though she didn’t think much of it. Matron Sima Huijun, it said, who has run Plum Steps for thirty-one years. He found her through the church on the steps below the old home, where she still did the flowers. It took three weeks for her to agree to see him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lived on the fourth floor of an old building with no lift, in two rooms that smelled of camphor and cooking oil. There was a photograph of her husband on the wall in a black frame, with a dish of oranges in front of it. She was eighty-one and tiny, and she made him take his shoes off and sit on a stool that was too low for him, and she poured his tea and didn’t pour her own.

“You’re a doctor,” she said.

“A surgeon. At City Hospital.”

“And you want a child.”

“I want to know about one. She doesn’t know I’m here.” He put his cup down. “She was brought to you in October 2002. She was nearly three. She went to a family in November. Her birthday’s the second of November. She talks.”

Matron Sima looked at him with her small hard eyes.

“Why should I tell you anything?” she said.

He had a story ready. He didn’t use it.

“She told me she doesn’t know who her mother was,” he said. “She’s never said it to anyone else. She said she wanted it so much she couldn’t breathe. I’m going to marry her. I’d like to be able to give it to her.”

The old woman didn’t answer that.

She got up. She went into the other room, and he heard a cupboard open, and a lot of things being moved, and something heavy put down. She came back with a ledger bound in red cloth with the corners worn through, and put it on the table between them, and sat down, and didn’t open it.

“The bell girl,” she said.

He waited.

“That’s what we called her. The girls in the kitchen named her. She talked from the minute she woke up to the minute she went to sleep, and in her sleep too, and she followed you round all day like a bell on a cat. You always knew where she was.” For the first time something like a smile went over the old face. “She asked the boy who fixed the roof if his ladder had a name. She never cried, all those weeks. The other ones who came from a fire cried in the night, or wouldn’t eat. That one talked. She sat on the end of my bed and told me about the boats.”

“Boats,” said Xing Yue.

“Her father’s boats. The little ones that go out to the ships.” She opened the ledger.

✦ ✦ ✦

He read it upside down at first. Then she turned it round for him.

Every child who had come through the iron gate in thirty-one years was in it, in the same small upright hand, in blue ink. The official files, she said, had gone to the archive when the home closed, and the government could keep them. This one was hers. She’d written in it every night.

October 2002. A line near the bottom of the page.

Qu Xiaoyue. Then two characters he knew: little moon. Born 2 Nov 1999. Brought by police, 12 Oct, from the fire at Qu Lighterage, Walled City piers. Found in a laundry basket under wet towels. Father Qu Mingde, lighterage, deceased. Mother Shi Yuning, nurse, deceased. No relatives found.

And under it, in the same hand, in different ink:

16 Nov. Gone to a family. Papers came back with another name.

He read it three times.

“The papers came back with another name,” said Matron Sima. “So I wrote the first one down. I always did. If somebody’s going to take a child’s name away, somebody should keep it.” She tapped the line with one finger. “A man came in a black car. He paid for the roof. The roof had leaked for six years and the government never paid for it, and he paid for all of it in cash, and the next week he came back for her. I don’t know his name. I never asked. You didn’t, then.” She shut her mouth tight on whatever else she knew. “She went down the steps holding his hand and talking. He didn’t say a word. He looked like he’d been hit.”

Xing Yue didn’t say anything.

He asked if he could photograph the page. She said no. He asked if he could copy it out by hand. She looked at him, and then she got up and fetched him a pencil and a sheet of paper from a drawer, and he copied it out at her table on the low stool, every word, in square block capitals, so that anybody could read it.

When he stood up to go she held onto his sleeve at the door.

“Does she still talk?” said Matron Sima.

“All the time.”

The old woman nodded and let him go.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found the clipping that afternoon, in the newspaper room at the central library, on a machine that showed old pages on a screen that flickered.

Saturday, 12 October 2002. Page nine.

Fire at Walled City lighter office kills two.

Four short paragraphs. The office of a small lighterage company by the old piers, and the flat above it. The owner and his wife, found dead by firemen. The boats undamaged. Police suspected the fire had been set. No one charged.

There was no child in it. Nobody had told the paper about a basket. There were no other names, and nothing that pointed at anyone at all. He had it printed and paid the man at the desk.

He sat in his car outside the library with the printout and the pencilled page on the passenger seat and didn’t start the engine.

Her mother had been a nurse. Her father had run boats out to the ships. Someone had put a child in a laundry basket under wet towels when the building was burning, and it had worked. And six weeks later somebody had looked at a girl called little moon and called her Elara, because Elara was a moon too, so she’d keep a piece of it without knowing she had.

He thought of her in Old Bian’s, delighted, telling him there were about eighty moons. My mother chose it. My father says she liked the sound.

He put the papers in a brown envelope from the glovebox, next to her hair clip, and sat there until the car park lights came on.

He’d give it to her on their wedding day. In the morning, before anyone else was up. He’d put it in her hands, and she’d have her mother’s name on the day she got married, and nobody else’s voice would be in the room when she read it.

He didn’t ask himself whether he had the right to choose the day. He thought about that later.

✦ ✦ ✦

That week, at dinner, they set the date.

On the Wednesday she came home from a long day on Professor Liao’s list, sat down at the counter with a bowl of his noodles, and said she’d decided it was the hospital garden.

“Where you asked me,” she said. “Under the tree. By the fish. It’s the only place I can think of that’s outdoors and has trees and where nobody’s ever bled. I checked. I asked Sister Shao. Sister Shao’s been there thirty years and she says nobody’s ever bled in the garden, except a porter who fell off a bench, and that was his nose, and it doesn’t count.”

“It’s a hospital garden,” he said. “You’ll have the windows full of patients.”

“Good. They can wave.”

She wanted May, after her first surgical exams next spring, because she’d cry at both and couldn’t be expected to cry that much in one month. She held her phone up across the counter and scrolled, and he watched her finger go through the whole of 2025 and into 2026 and stop.

“The ninth of May,” said Elara. “It’s a Saturday. Next year. That’s fourteen months. Is fourteen months too long?”

He looked at her. He thought of the envelope in the glovebox.

“No,” he said. “It’s good.”

She put it in her calendar and then in his, on his phone, by taking it out of his pocket while he was eating, and she typed WEDDING in capitals and then, under it, DON’T BOOK ANY LISTS.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the second week of March he came out of theatre between cases and heard her before he saw her.

She was in the corridor outside the women’s changing room, in scrubs and a paper hat, with her phone against her ear, laughing.

“Raiden, you’re being an idiot,” she was saying. “You’re being an idiot with great conviction, and I’m proud of you. But a king signed it. You can’t win against a king. I’ve got a gallbladder, I’m going back in—”

She saw him and waved the coffee.

He kept walking. It was about Evangeline’s birthday, he knew that much, and he didn’t ask what a king had to do with it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The driver came in on a Thursday night at the end of March.

Xing Yue was the consultant on call. He’d been down to resus for an old man with a twisted bowel, and he was standing at the nurses’ station writing up the old man’s notes when he saw her across the department, in cubicle eleven, with the curtain half open.

She was the surgical resident on call. She’d been sent down to see a man with a hand injury, and he knew the man.

He didn’t know his name. He knew the face, the way you know a face you’ve seen at the bottom of a hill road at four in the morning. One of Zhao’s drivers. A thick quiet man who’d brought the car down from the house to the bus shelter some mornings and looked at nothing. He was sitting on the trolley now with his left hand on a pillow, wrapped in a towel that had been white, and his face was the colour of the towel.

A police constable was standing at the curtain. Young, with a notebook.

Elara was talking to him.

She was talking to him the way she talked to everybody, warm and cheerful, with a boiled sweet in her cheek. She unwrapped the towel. She looked at the hand. He saw her face from across the department while she looked at it, and for one second there was nothing on it at all, nothing warm or cheerful, just a cold clear flat attention that went over the wound and the man’s face and the constable’s notebook and came back. Then it was gone, and she was smiling at the constable and saying something that made him laugh.

She closed it at the trolley, fast, and talked the constable through the whole of it, about tendons and luck and a man she’d once seen shoot a nail through his own boot. The constable had stopped writing.

Xing Yue finished his notes on the old man. He signed them. He went up to theatre.

He read her notes in the morning, at seven, before the round. Nail-gun injury, building site. Through and through, left hand, between second and third metacarpals. Tendons intact. Washed out and closed. PC present at assessment; patient declined to give a statement.

He wrote under it, as the consultant on call, Seen and agreed, and signed it.

At the round Dr. Zou looked over his shoulder at the screen.

“Funny kind of nail gun,” said Dr. Zou. “That’s a big hole for a nail.”

Xing Yue didn’t look up.

“Did you see him?” he said.

“No, I was—”

“Then you don’t know what size the hole was. Bed four’s drain chart has nothing on it since midnight. Go and find out why, and when you’ve found out, find out why you didn’t know at six.”

Dr. Zou went. The nurse with the drug trolley looked at the floor.

Elara never mentioned the driver. Neither did he. That night she was asleep on the sofa when he came in, with one foot hanging over the edge, and he thought about her face in cubicle eleven and found he didn’t want her to be any different at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

She caught him on the first Sunday in April.

He wasn’t good at hiding things. He’d taken a Friday off in March, which he never did, and told her he’d been to the dentist, and she’d looked at his teeth. He cleaned his glasses whenever she asked what he’d been doing on a Saturday, and she’d started asking just to watch him do it.

That evening she came and sat on the sofa beside him while he was reading, and then on the arm of it, and then she took the journal out of his hands and put it on the floor and climbed on him.

“You’re hiding something,” she said.

She sat across his lap with her hands on his shoulders and looked down at him the way she looked at a chart she didn’t trust.

“Since Christmas. Saturdays. A Friday off. An envelope in the car, next to my hair clip, which I’ve known about for two years, by the way. And every time I ask you a question you clean your glasses.” She took his glasses off his face, so he couldn’t, and held them up out of reach. “So. One. Is it bad? Two. Is it about the hospital? Three—”

“It’s not bad.”

“Three is the important one. Three is, is it about me? Because if it’s about me—”

He put his hand flat on her back, between her shoulder blades, under her jumper, and pulled her down, and stopped her mouth with his.

She made a noise of pure outrage against his lips. She didn’t let go of his glasses. She didn’t stop kissing him either. She held on to his shoulder with one hand and his glasses with the other and kissed him back, hard, as if she were still arguing with him and had just found a better way to do it, and his hand stayed spread on her back and held her there.

When she pulled back she was pink to the ears.

“That’s cheating,” she said. “That’s what you do. You do that to stop me talking.”

“It works.”

“It works because I let it.” She sat back on his knees and looked at him. “Is it about me?”

“It’s a wedding present,” said Xing Yue.

She went still on his lap.

“You can have it on the day,” he said. “In the morning. Before anybody else is up.”

He watched her want it. She opened her birthday presents on the bus on the way home; she’d once read the end of a crime novel in a bookshop and put it back. Then he watched her get annoyed, properly, and that was harder.

“You’ve decided,” she said. “You’ve decided when I get to know something. It’s mine, isn’t it. Whatever it is, it’s mine, and you’ve got it, and you’ve picked a day for me to have it.”

He didn’t answer. He didn’t have a good answer and he didn’t want to give her a bad one.

“I hate that,” said Elara.

“I know.”

She sat on him, frowning, with his glasses in her hand. Then she folded them and put them on the table, the way he did, and took his face in her hands.

“Fine,” she said. “Keep it. But it had better be a good one. It had better be better than the loupes, and the loupes were the best present anyone’s ever given me, so you’ve made it hard for yourself.” She kissed him on the forehead. “And I’m writing down that I hate it. I’m writing it down, so that on the day, when I cry, you’ll remember I was cross first.”

She got up and wrote it on the list on the fridge, under peach yoghurt and above sesame paste: XY’S SECRET — CROSS ABOUT IT. Then she came back and sat in his lap again and kissed him until he’d forgotten the envelope was anywhere at all.

It stayed on the fridge for months. He saw it every morning when he made the tea.

chapters.title: Again?
chapters.desc: At five in the morning her brother and his wife come in from a fire with burned hands. For six weeks she spends her days off fixing switches in the rebuilt shop, humming.
chapters.epigraph: “You’ve got good hands. Steady. I’d hire you.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
At ten to five in the morning a nurse from the emergency department rang the ward and asked for Dr. Lin.

Elara was on nights, covering the surgical floors, and she’d just sat down for the first time since midnight with a cup of tea and a biscuit she’d been saving. She took the phone at the nurses’ station with her mouth full.

“Your brother’s down here,” said the nurse, who’d known her since she was a student and knew whose sister she was. “And his wife. Smoke, and burns. They’re both all right. I thought you’d want to know before somebody else told you.”

Elara put the biscuit down.

She didn’t remember the stairs. She remembered the doors at the bottom, and the corridor, and the two trolleys side by side in the bay at the end, with the curtain pulled back. Raiden on one with an oxygen mask on his face and both his hands wrapped in white, held up on his chest like two clouds. Jinx on the other with a mask too, and a dressing on her left forearm, and black still in her hair and in the lines round her eyes, looking at the ceiling. Raiden’s head was turned towards her. Jinx’s hand was on his wrist, above the bandage.

Four years ago he’d been on the sixth floor of this hospital after a van.

“Again?” said Elara.

It went right up the corridor. A porter looked round. Raiden turned his head on the trolley and looked at her over his mask, and his eyes creased, which meant he was trying to grin.

✦ ✦ ✦

She checked everything, because she couldn’t not.

She read their notes. She lifted the edge of Raiden’s dressings and looked at his palms and put them back, and she didn’t say anything about the blisters, because he was watching her face and she kept it nice. She listened to both their chests. She asked the nurse what their oxygen levels had been when they came in and what they were now, and she asked twice, because the first time she didn’t hear the answer.

The shutter, Raiden said through his mask. He’d put his hands on it. He hadn’t known where Jinx was.

Then she did Jinx.

Jinx let her. She lay on the trolley and let Elara turn her arm over and look at the burn on the inside of it, across the edge of a tattoo of a fish, and didn’t say anything at all, which Elara had learned was how Jinx said thank you.

“You’ll want silicone gel on that,” said Elara. “When it’s healed over. Not before. It’ll stop it going thick and red. I told you that at Elowen’s wedding about your exhaust burns, and you didn’t do it, I could see you didn’t do it, they’re still there—”

“You told me,” said Jinx, through her mask.

“Well, I’m telling you again. And this time you’ll do it, because it’s on the same arm as the fish, and you’ll want the fish to stay a nice shape.”

Jinx looked at her. One corner of her mouth went up, nearly.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six Xing Yue came in for his day.

He walked to work at that time every morning and came in through the main doors, not the ambulance bay, and he had no reason to come through the emergency department at all. He came through it. She was standing outside the bay with her back against the wall, and he came down the corridor in his coat with his bag on his shoulder and two cups of tea from the bakery, and stopped beside her, and gave her one.

She held it in both hands. She didn’t drink it.

He didn’t say anything. He didn’t ask if they were all right; he’d have read the board on the way past. He stood next to her against the wall with his own tea and looked at the trolleys, and his shoulder was against hers, and that was all.

After a while she leaned her head on his arm.

“His hands,” she said. “He draws with his hands. That’s all he does.”

“Second degree,” he said. “Partial thickness. I looked. They’ll heal.”

“I know they’ll heal. I know that. I’m a doctor.” Her voice went up. “I’m just—it’s the second time. It’s the second time I’ve come down a corridor in this building and found him on a trolley.”

He put his hand on the back of her neck, under her hair, and left it there.

“Drink the tea,” he said. “Then eat something. Then go back up, because you’ve got two hours left and somebody on nine is going to need you, and you won’t be any use to them on one biscuit.”

She wanted to argue. She drank the tea instead. He’d put sugar in it, which he never did, and she knew why.

✦ ✦ ✦

They rebuilt the shop in six weeks.

Elara came on her days off. She’d told Elowen she would and then lay awake wondering what use she’d be, among men with scaffolding and Aurelia’s glazier and Eliana on the floor with a laptop and wires, and Jun Hyuk carrying steel. On the first day she found out. Nobody wanted the small jobs. The switch plates, the light fittings, the little brackets for the shelving and the hooks for the tools, the hundred fiddly things that had to go back on walls once the walls were painted. She did them all.

She liked it. She hadn’t expected to. She stood on a stepladder with a screwdriver in her teeth and a bag of fixings in her pocket and did one bracket after another, and her hands knew what to do, the way they did with a suture, small and quick and exact. She hummed. She didn’t know she was doing it.

Jinx came and stood at the bottom of the ladder on the second Saturday.

She’d been on the floor all morning with a broken machine and black on her hands, and she stood there in her overalls with her bandaged arm and watched Elara do a bracket. Then another one. She didn’t say anything. Elara had stopped expecting her to. They’d been sisters-in-law for a year and spoken maybe forty sentences, most of them about burns.

“You’ve got good hands,” said Jinx. “Steady. I’d hire you.”

Elara stopped with the screwdriver in the air.

“I’m a surgeon,” she said.

“I know. I’d still hire you.” Jinx looked up at the bracket. “That’s level. Nobody does them level. Eliana’s are all a degree off and she says it’s the wall.”

“It’s not the wall,” said Elara.

“No,” said Jinx.

That was the first real conversation. It went on, off and on, through the afternoon. Jinx told her what the brackets were for. Elara told her about bananas. Jinx said she’d tried to stitch her own hand once, at nineteen, under a flyover, with fishing line, and Elara came down the ladder to look at the scar and was so appalled that Jinx laughed out loud, the short rough laugh Elara had only ever heard her give Raiden. They ate noodles sitting on a crate. Jinx didn’t say anything else nice all day, which was plenty.

✦ ✦ ✦

One Thursday in July Lin Jian came.

He came in the black car, with Uncle Mok, in his good coat, and stood in the middle of the shop floor and looked at the walls going white and the new window going in. Jinx’s father was there, as he was every week, an old man with a broom in a shirt with the sleeves rolled up, sweeping round the benches. Lin Jian watched him for a while.

Then he took off his coat and folded it over the back of a chair, and took the other broom from against the wall, and started sweeping on the far side.

Elara was on the stairs to the mezzanine with a box of switch plates. She stopped.

The two old men swept the floor for two hours. They didn’t talk. They didn’t look at each other. They went up and down the shop in long slow lines, one on each side, and when they got to the middle they passed each other and kept going, and the dust went into two neat piles by the door. Somewhere up on the mezzanine she knew Jinx was watching too.

Elara put the box down on the step and went out to the street.

She stood on the cobbles outside with her back to the shop and her hands over her face for a few minutes, because she didn’t know what had happened between those two men, years ago, under a flyover, and she knew it had been something, and her father had taken off his coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the tenth of July, Yu Chen and Eliana graduated on the same afternoon in the Great Hall, in two different gowns.

Xing Yue sat with her near the front. He was Yu Chen’s mentor and had been for four years, and he’d been asked to come, and he’d come in his dark grey suit and sat beside her with his back straight. When Yu Chen went up for his degree, Xing Yue didn’t clap any harder than anybody else, and Elara looked at him sideways and saw that his jaw was tight.

Afterwards on the steps Eliana kissed Yu Chen in front of everyone. Everyone saw it. Elara burst into tears and then went and hugged her little sister so hard her cap fell off and rolled down two steps, and Eliana let her, stiffly, with her arms out, saying, “Okay. Okay. You can stop now.”

Yu Chen came over with his ears red and shook his cousin’s hand.

“Emergency,” said Xing Yue. “You’ll be good at it. You don’t panic and you don’t like being thanked.”

Yu Chen looked at him as if he’d been given something heavy and didn’t know where to put it down. He said thank you. Xing Yue nodded and let go of his hand, and on the way down the steps Elara put her arm through his and didn’t say anything about his jaw.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ladder happened on a Tuesday afternoon in the last week of the rebuild.

She was off. He’d had a clinic in the morning and nothing after, which happened about twice a year, and he came down to the shop because she’d told him she’d be there and he wanted, he said, to see what she’d been doing with her days off for a month.

She was at the top of the tall ladder by the back wall, putting up the last of the tool hooks, with her hair tied up in a scarf of Jinx’s and a screwdriver in her hand.

She felt the ladder go still under her.

She looked down. He was at the bottom, in his work shirt with the sleeves rolled up, with one hand on the ladder and the other round her ankle.

“Let go,” said Elara. “I’m fine. I’ve done about two hundred of these.”

“You’re humming.”

“I always hum.”

“You’re humming and leaning out to the left,” he said. “And the left foot of the ladder’s on a drain cover.”

She looked. It was. She went red and finished the hook anyway, and he didn’t let go of her ankle the whole time, his hand warm round it above her trainer, his thumb on the bone, and she felt it all the way up.

When she started to come down he didn’t move out of the way. She came down rung by rung until she was nearly level with him, and then, on the rung above the bottom, she caught the back of her thumb on the edge of the last bracket and said a word Ah Sim would have washed out of her mouth.

He took her hand.

He turned it over and held it up to the light from the new window, the way he’d have looked at a cut in clinic. A small one. A line of red across the back of her thumb. He looked at it closely, frowning, as if there might be something in it.

“It’s nothing,” she said. “It’s a scratch. Don’t you dare put a plaster on it, I’ll never hear the end of it from Jinx.”

He didn’t put a plaster on it. He kissed it, the back of her thumb. Then, before she’d finished telling him it was nothing, he kissed her mouth.

She came off the last rung into his arms. She dropped the screwdriver. She put her arms round his neck and kissed him back in the middle of the half-built shop, with sawdust in the air and the smell of new paint, and he held her up off the floor against him with her feet not touching anything, and she laughed into his mouth and didn’t stop kissing him to do it.

Somewhere behind them a man coughed.

Raiden was in the arched doorway with a tray of coffees and his healing hands and an expression of enormous innocence.

“I’ll come back,” said Raiden. “I’ll come back in about ten minutes. Or tomorrow. Jinx says the hooks are level.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She had plaster dust in her hair that night, and in her eyebrows, and down the back of her neck.

She sat on the bathroom counter at Banyan Terrace in her vest while the shower ran hot, and picked dust out of her own fringe, and talked. She told him about the switch plates. She told him about Jinx and the fishing line, and the two old men with their brooms, and how she’d had to go out to the street. She told him the hooks were level and Eliana’s brackets weren’t.

He was standing in the bathroom doorway with his arms folded, listening.

She stopped picking at her hair. She looked at him there, being sensible, in his clean shirt, at the end of a day when he’d held her ankle on a ladder and she’d felt it all afternoon.

She hooked two fingers into his belt and pulled him in between her knees.

“You’ve got dust on you,” she said. “From me. On your shirt. And in your eyebrows. Both of them.”

“I haven’t.”

“You have. Look.” She turned him by the belt to face the mirror, and he looked, and he did, a grey streak through one eyebrow from where she’d had her hands in his hair at the shop. She laughed so hard she nearly fell off the counter, and he caught her, and she was still laughing when she started on his buttons.

It was mostly laughing, after that. The dust wouldn’t come out of her hair and she made him wash it for her under the shower, standing behind her, and he got shampoo in her eyes and she swore at him and he laughed against her shoulder. She soaped the dust off his face with great care, as though she were cleaning a wound, and told him to keep still, and he didn’t. They knocked the shampoo off the shelf. The water ran grey and then clear. He kissed her with the water running down both their faces and she stopped laughing for a while.

Later, in bed, she lay across him with her wet hair spread over his chest and listened to his heart.

“You held my ankle all afternoon,” she said.

“Ten minutes.”

“It felt like all afternoon.” She lifted her head. “Don’t do that on a ladder again. I couldn’t think. I nearly put a hook in upside down.”

He put his hand round her ankle under the sheet, the same one, his thumb on the bone, and she put her face back on his chest and gave up arguing.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Friday before they reopened, she put up the last bracket.

It was by the new stair door at the back, a small brass one for a fire blanket, and Jinx had saved it for her. The others had gone. Eliana’s cameras blinked in the corners of the ceiling. Raiden was upstairs at his desk behind the new glass with his hands unwrapped at last, drawing. Elara stood on the low step and put in the screws, one, two, three, four, and tested it with her hand, and it didn’t move.

She turned round. Her father was standing at the bottom of the step.

She hadn’t heard him come in. He was in his good coat. He was looking at her hands.

“You have your mother’s hands,” said Lin Jian.

Elara laughed. She came down off the step and put her screwdriver in her pocket.

“Mama’s?” she said. “Ah Sim always says Mama couldn’t sew a button. She says Mama burned rice. She says she was the worst cook in the Walled City and you married her anyway.”

Her father didn’t say anything. He was still looking at her hands, and his face had gone the grey it went sometimes when somebody brought up the old days at the table.

“She did burn rice,” he said, after a while.

He didn’t say anything else. He put his hand on her shoulder, which he almost never did, heavy and brief, and went out to the black car where Uncle Mok was waiting, and she watched him go and thought how tired he looked, and that she’d tell Elowen he looked tired, and then she forgot, because Jinx was calling down from the mezzanine that the coffee had come.

chapters.title: The Knife at the Red Door
chapters.desc: After Sunday lunch a man in a seaman’s jacket comes for her father with a knife. Elara gets in the way, and Xing Yue keeps her alive on the stones of the alley.
chapters.epigraph: “Stop diagnosing yourself. I know what’s cut.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
Sunday lunch was soup.

Ah Sim had made the pork bone one with the lotus root that took two days, because it was November and the first cold week, and because Elara had turned twenty-six a fortnight before and Ah Sim still thought she was too thin. There were seven of them at the long table. Elowen and Zhao had come for the soup and gone again by two. Raiden and Jinx were at one end arguing about a carburettor. Evangeline sat beside Jun Hyuk, who was explaining lotus root to Lin Jian, who had been eating it all his life.

Elara talked about the wedding.

It was six months away. She had a dress now, which none of them were allowed to see. She’d asked Sister Shao whether the koi would mind, and Sister Shao had said the koi had seen worse. She told the table his grandmother was coming from the north with a stick she pointed at people, and Raiden said he’d like to see her try it on Baba, and Lin Jian laughed, the big rusty one, into his soup.

At three, when everyone was getting their coats, Lin Jian said he’d see them out.

They’d come by taxi. Lin Jian wouldn’t hear of a taxi. Uncle Mok had the car at the mouth of the alley, he said, and he’d walk them down to it himself, and he got his good coat from the hook by the stairs, and Ah Sim put a box of leftover soup and three dumplings into Xing Yue’s hands and told him to make her eat them.

Lin Jian opened the red door.

✦ ✦ ✦

The alley was grey and cold, with the light already going. The noodle stall at the mouth of it had its shutters half down. The black car was there beyond it, at the kerb, with Mok in the driver’s seat.

A man was standing by the stall.

Xing Yue noticed him because there was nobody else in the alley. Sixty, about. Thin and weathered, in an old navy jacket with a high collar, the kind seamen wore on deck. His hands were in his pockets. He was looking at the red door, and when it opened he took his hands out.

“Lin Jian,” the man said. “Do you remember the Qu boats?”

Lin Jian stopped on the step.

Xing Yue saw his face go grey, all at once, the way a patient’s does when the blood pressure goes. He heard the name and something in him caught on it, the way your foot catches on a step in the dark. Qu.

Then the man had a knife in his hand and was coming up the alley.

He didn’t run. He walked fast, straight at the old man on the step, with the knife held low, and his face was perfectly calm, and Lin Jian didn’t move. Lin Jian stood in his good coat in his own doorway and watched him come and didn’t lift a hand, as though he’d been waiting twenty years for exactly this and had decided long ago that he wouldn’t.

Elara was closest. She was on the step below her father, buttoning her coat.

She didn’t think. Xing Yue saw that she didn’t. She put up her right arm and grabbed at the man’s wrist, the way you’d put your hand out to catch something falling.

The blade went across the inside of her wrist.

✦ ✦ ✦

He dropped the box.

He heard it hit the stones, and the soup go everywhere, and he was already there. His hands were round her wrist before she’d started to fall. He had her by the forearm, both hands, hard, and the blood came through his fingers anyway, bright, too bright, in spurts that went with her heartbeat, and he knew exactly what that meant and put it away.

“Lie down,” he said. “Elara, lie back for me. Keep it up.”

He got her down on the stones with her back against the step and her arm up, straight up, over her head, his hands locked round it above the wrist. She was looking at it. She was looking at her own hand with an expression of great interest, as though it belonged to a patient.

Behind him somebody shouted. He didn’t look.

He heard a body hit the ground. He heard Uncle Mok, who never said anything, saying something low and terrible. He heard the red door bang open behind him and a sound like a wardrobe falling over, and when he glanced up for half a second the man in the seaman’s jacket was face down on the stones with Mok’s knee in his back and Jun Hyuk sitting on top of both of them, enormous, holding the man’s arms, with the knife skittering away into the gutter.

There was blood on Lin Jian’s coat. None of it was his.

“Belt,” said Xing Yue. “I need a belt. I need someone to hold her arm.”

Footsteps. Somebody came from next door at a run, out of the gate of the Song house, a tall thin young man in a grey jumper, and knelt on the stones beside him. Yu Chen. He didn’t ask anything. He put his big careful hands round Elara’s forearm where Xing Yue showed him and held it up and held it hard.

Xing Yue pulled his own belt out of his trousers in one movement.

He put it round her upper arm, high, near the shoulder, and pulled it as tight as it would go, and held it, and the spurting slowed, and then it stopped. He looked at his watch and said the time out loud, so that Yu Chen would remember it if he didn’t.

“Car,” he said, to nobody. “Get the car into the alley.”

“I’ll clear it,” said a girl’s voice, and he looked up and saw Eliana in a hoodie at the gate of the house next door, already walking up towards the mouth of the alley, where people had started to come out of their doors and stand. She said something to them. They went back in.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elara was talking.

Of course she was. She was white to the lips and her coat was soaked down one side and she was sitting on the cold stones of her father’s alley with her arm up in the air, held by two men, and she was talking.

“It’s the ulnar,” she said. “The artery. That’s why it’s spurting like that. You’ve stopped it. Good. That’s good. And the tendons, it went deep, I felt it go deep, I felt it go through the tendons, it’s the flexors, it’s at least three of them, I can’t bend my fingers—” She tried, and stopped, and he saw her see it. “And I can’t feel my little finger. I can’t feel my little finger or half the next one. That’s the ulnar nerve. It’s cut. And the thumb’s wrong as well, the thumb’s numb, so it’s the median too, it’s both of them, Xing Yue, it’s both nerves—”

“Stop diagnosing yourself,” he said. “I know what’s cut.”

She stopped.

His voice was calm. He heard it. It was calmer than he’d ever heard it in his life, and level, and slow, and it came from somewhere a long way below his chest, where nothing was happening at all.

“I’ve got you,” he said. “I know what’s cut. Keep your arm up. Look at me.”

She looked at him. Her pupils were huge. She had blood on her chin. She looked at him and her mouth shook once, and then she pressed it shut and nodded.

Raiden came out of the red door.

He didn’t say anything. He didn’t make a single joke. He looked at his sister on the stones, and he went white, and then he bent down and lifted her, all of her, in her soaked coat, as if she weighed nothing, while Xing Yue held her arm up and Yu Chen let go. Raiden carried her down the alley at a fast walk with her head on his shoulder, past the noodle stall, past the people Eliana had sent back indoors, to the black car, which Mok had left with the engine running and the back door open.

Xing Yue got in first and Raiden put her in across his lap, and he held her arm up against the roof of the car with one hand and the belt with the other.

Uncle Mok got in behind the wheel. Xing Yue didn’t see where he’d come from. His trousers were torn at the knee and he had somebody else’s blood on his hands, and he didn’t say anything at all. He drove.

He went through every light between the Walled City and the hill, red or not, and never once used the horn, and the old car went up to the ambulance bay faster than any ambulance.

She talked the whole way, about the soup, and how Ah Sim would be furious about the box. Her voice was getting slower, and he held her arm up against the roof and talked back to her, which he never did, about nothing, about the box, about the soup, so that she would go on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Resus at City Hospital on a Sunday afternoon was Dr. Toh’s.

They ran her in on a trolley with his hands on her arm, and the registrar on duty met them at the door of bay two. A young man, competent. Xing Yue had seen him run a cardiac arrest and been satisfied.

The registrar looked down at the trolley and saw who it was, and stopped. He stood there with his gloved hands up and looked at Dr. Lin from the surgical floor, who brought sweets to the department at Lunar New Year and knew his girlfriend’s name, lying white with her coat soaked through. He looked two seconds too long.

“Get out of my resus,” said Xing Yue.

The registrar looked at him.

“It’s not your—”

“Get out. Get me two large lines, get blood sent for cross-match, six units, and get Dr. Meng from plastics on the phone. If she’s at home, get her out of it. Then go and stand somewhere I can’t see you.”

The registrar went. A nurse had a line in Elara’s left arm before he’d finished. Xing Yue had his hands on the right one and didn’t take them off.

Dr. Toh came in from the next bay, small and brisk, and looked at the trolley and at him.

“Wang,” she said. “This is my department.”

“Then you can tell me if I’ve missed anything,” said Xing Yue.

She looked at him. Then she went round to the other side of the trolley and started checking everything he’d done, from the top, and didn’t send him out.

Professor Liao came at twenty to four. Somebody had rung him at home. He came into the bay in a cardigan with his car keys still in his hand, and looked at Elara, and his face went still.

“Step back, Wang,” he said.

Xing Yue didn’t move.

“You can’t treat her. You know you can’t. Step back and let the department do it.”

“When Meng’s here,” said Xing Yue.

Liao looked at him across the trolley. He didn’t say it again.

Dr. Meng Shuhua came at five past four in a tracksuit, with her hair still wet, and pushed through the curtain and looked at the wrist, all of it, quickly, turning it in her hands, and looked up.

“Theatre,” she said. “Now. I’ll take it.”

Xing Yue took his hands away.

He took his hands off her arm and stood back from the trolley and held them up in front of him, and they shook. They hadn’t shaken in the alley or the car or the bay, and now they shook so hard that he had to put them in his armpits, and stand there, while the trolley went out past him and down the corridor towards the lifts.

✦ ✦ ✦

The repair took five hours.

He shouldn’t have been in the room. Everybody in it knew that. He was her partner, and he was a surgeon, and there were rules about both. Dr. Meng looked at him when he came in scrubbed and gowned and gloved, and he said, “I won’t touch anything,” and she looked at him a moment longer and nodded at the corner by the anaesthetic machine, and went back to her microscope.

He stood in the corner with his empty gloved hands held up in front of his chest and watched.

Meng did the tendons first, one by one, and then the artery, and the hand went pink. Then she brought the microscope down for the nerves and spent most of three hours on them, with stitches finer than a hair, so slowly that the scrub nurse shifted her feet. Nobody spoke. The theatre was cold, and he could see Elara’s left hand on the board on the other side, small and pale and still, with the ring on it.

Nobody hummed.

At twenty past nine Meng sat back and took off her loupes and rubbed her eyes, and then she came over to the corner, stripping off her gloves.

“The repair’s good,” she said. “As good as I can make it. It was a clean cut and she’s young and you got her here fast.” She looked at him. “She’ll keep the hand. Whether she keeps the surgeon’s hand, nobody can tell you for a year.”

He nodded.

He knew all of it already. He’d known it on the stones. He nodded again, because he didn’t trust his voice, and Meng put her hand on his arm, briefly, the way you do with a relative, and went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke in recovery at ten.

He was beside the trolley on a stool. Her right arm was in a thick splint up to the elbow, raised on pillows, and he’d been watching her face for forty minutes.

Her eyes opened. They wandered over the ceiling and the monitor and found him.

“Oh,” said Elara. “It’s you.”

Her voice was thick and slow. She frowned at him.

“You look terrible,” she said. “Has somebody died? You’ve got your—your bad face. The one for registrars.” Her eyes went half shut and opened again. “Is it me? Did I die? I don’t think I died. I think if I’d died I’d be cross about the soup.”

“You didn’t die.”

“Good.” She tried to lift her right hand and the splint didn’t let her, and she looked at it, and he saw her remember. Her face went still. Then she looked back at him and made her mouth smile, crookedly, the drugs in it. “Well,” she said. “At least it wasn’t my talking hand.”

He couldn’t answer that.

She saw that he couldn’t. She looked at him from the pillow with her eyes swimming.

“Xing Yue,” she said. Just his name.

He stood up and bent over the trolley and kissed her forehead. He held his mouth there, on her cold skin, under the edge of the paper cap, for as long as he could. Then he lifted her left hand, the good one, with the ring on it, and turned it over and kissed the inside of her wrist where the pulse was, and felt it under his mouth, slow and steady and there.

“I’m here,” he said.

She was already asleep again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wei Long came up to the ward at midnight.

Xing Yue was in the chair beside her bed in a side room on the plastics floor. Lin Jian was in the corridor outside on a plastic chair, where he’d been since six, in his coat with the blood dried on it, and wouldn’t go home, and wouldn’t come in. Raiden had taken Jinx home. Ev and Jun Hyuk were in the relatives’ room.

Wei Long stood in the doorway in his long coat and looked at the splint, and then at Xing Yue, and beckoned him out to the window at the end of the corridor, away from her father.

“He’s not saying much,” said Wei Long. “He’s not denying anything either. He came for Lin Jian. He says he didn’t mean to touch anyone else. He keeps asking if she’s all right.”

“Who is he?”

“Qu Wenjun. Fifty-seven. A seaman. Merchant ships, thirty years, a prison term in between for a fight.” Wei Long was watching his face. “He says Lin Jian burned his brother’s boats in 2002 and killed his brother and his brother’s wife. He says Lin Jian killed the child too. He says the whole family died.”

Xing Yue stood at the window and looked out at the dark car park.

Qu.

Qu Lighterage, Walled City piers. Qu Mingde. Shi Yuning, nurse. A child in a laundry basket under wet towels. A man in a black car who paid for a roof in cash, and came back the next week, and went down the steps without a word, looking as though he’d been hit.

No relatives found.

He went cold. It started in his hands, where her blood had been, and went up his arms and into his chest, and he stood at the window and let it.

“Xing Yue,” said Wei Long.

“I’m all right.”

“You don’t look it.”

“I need to go back in,” said Xing Yue. “She wakes up and talks. I don’t want her to wake up and find nobody there.”

He went back down the corridor past Lin Jian on his plastic chair. The old man lifted his head and looked at him, and Xing Yue looked back, and neither of them said anything. Then he went in and sat down by her bed and took her left hand and put his thumb on her pulse, and kept it there until the window went grey.

chapters.title: The House Is Too Quiet
chapters.desc: Lin Jian tells her where she came from and what he did. She learns Xing Yue has known her name for eight months, and stops talking to everyone.
chapters.epigraph: “The house is too quiet, Elara.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
The pain came in the night, and it came like electricity.

The cut itself was a dull hot ache under the splint that the drugs mostly held. The nerve pain was a shock that went from her wrist to the tips of her fingers and made her whole arm jump on the pillow, and then nothing, and then again. Nerve pain. She’d explained it to patients and written it in notes, and never once known it felt like someone switching you on and off.

Two and a half of her fingers weren’t hers any more. The little one and half the next were nothing at all. The thumb side came and went, numb, then buzzing, then numb. When she looked at her hand lying in the splint she had to tell it to move, and it didn’t, and she lay and looked at it and did the sums.

Nerves grew back about a millimetre a day, if they grew back at all. She knew the distance from her wrist to her fingertips. She’d done the sums on the first night, with the drip in her other arm, and she did them again every night after that, and they came out the same. Months. And the small muscles of the hand, the ones that did the fine work, the ones that tied a knot one-handed in the dark, came back last, if they came back.

Dr. Meng came on the Monday and said all of it, honestly, and Elara nodded at every sentence, because she’d already said it to herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday afternoon her father asked for an hour.

He’d been in the corridor since Sunday, in the same coat with the blood on it. He hadn’t come in. Every time the door opened she saw him out there on the plastic chair, enormous and grey, with his hands between his knees.

On Tuesday he came to the door and asked Xing Yue if he could have an hour with his daughter, alone, and Xing Yue looked at her, and she nodded, and he went.

Her father sat down on the chair by the bed. He didn’t take his coat off.

“I have to tell you something,” said Lin Jian. “I should have told you when you were seven. When you asked me. I told you that you came from a children’s home and that I wanted you.” He looked at his hands. “Both of those things are true. They’re not all of it.”

She waited.

He told her.

He told it badly, in pieces, slowly, a man who’d never in his life said this many words in a row. There had been a man called Qu Mingde, who had four lighter boats at the old piers in the Walled City, small ones, that went out to the big ships and brought the cargo in. He was a good boatman. He laughed a lot. His wife was a nurse at City Hospital. Her name was Shi Yuning. They lived in the flat above the office with their little girl, who was nearly three.

In 2002 a man called Zuo Hanlin wanted the piers. All of them. Lin Jian had boats too, then, and men, and Zuo had more, and Zuo wanted Qu Mingde gone. He came to Lin Jian and asked for the night schedule of the Qu boats and the name of the watchman, and Lin Jian sold them to him.

“I thought he’d burn the boats,” said her father. “That’s what they did, then. You burned a man’s boats and he went away. I thought he’d burn the boats and Qu would take his family somewhere else, and I’d have the piers that Zuo didn’t want, and that would be all.” His voice didn’t change at all. “Zuo’s men didn’t touch the boats. They set the office alight at two in the morning. And the flat above it.”

Elara lay still.

“You were in a laundry basket,” said Lin Jian. “In the back, by the washing machine. Under wet towels. Somebody put you there. Your mother, I think. The firemen found you in the morning. You weren’t burned at all. You were asleep.”

He’d gone to the children’s home on Plum Steps a week later and looked at her through a window. He’d paid for the roof. He’d gone back and taken her home, and done the papers so that the name Qu went away, so that nobody would ever look at the fourth Lin child and wonder. His wife had known all of it. She’d held the child on the first night and asked what her name was, and been told, and said that Xiaoyue meant little moon, and that there was a moon called Elara, a small one, and that they’d call her that, so she’d keep a piece of her name.

“She was ill already,” said her father. “With Eliana. She had three months with you. She said you never stopped talking.” He stopped. “She said I’d done the worst thing I’d ever do, and that the only thing left was to love you more than the others, and not let you see it. I tried.”

Then he told her the last part. The man in the alley was called Qu Wenjun. He’d been at sea in 2002. Somebody had told him the whole family died in the fire, the child too. He’d been told this year who sold the schedule.

“He’s your uncle,” said Lin Jian. “Your father’s brother. He came for me. He didn’t know it was you.”

Elara looked at the ceiling.

She couldn’t look at her father. She could hear him breathing, and a nurse laughing at the station, and none of it was real except his voice, and she couldn’t bear it.

“Please go,” she said.

He stood up. He didn’t argue. He didn’t say anything else. He stood by the bed in his coat for a second, and she thought he was going to touch her and she’d scream, and he didn’t. He went out and shut the door behind him without a sound.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xing Yue came in.

He’d been in the corridor. She saw it on his face: he’d seen her father come out. He sat down in the chair her father had been in, and looked at her, and waited, the way he always waited, and she turned her head on the pillow and looked at him.

Something in her had gone cold and clear. It was the voice she used on the wards at three in the morning. She heard it come out of her mouth.

“Did you know?”

He didn’t clean his glasses. He didn’t look away.

“I knew your name,” he said. “Qu Xiaoyue. Since March. I found the matron of the children’s home. She’d kept a book. Your father’s name, your mother’s. The fire. I found a newspaper.” He stopped. “I didn’t know about him. On Sunday night, when Wei Long told me the man’s name, I guessed. I didn’t know before that.”

“Since March.”

“Yes.”

“The envelope,” she said. “In the car. Next to my hair clip. That was it. That was my wedding present.” Her voice was perfectly steady. “You had my name for eight months. My mother’s name. You had it in your glovebox. And you were going to give it to me in the morning on my wedding day, and you’d decided that, and you didn’t ask me, and I wrote on the fridge that I was cross about it and I didn’t even know what I was cross about.”

“I was going to give it to you on the day,” he said. “I thought—”

“I know what you thought.”

He stopped.

She turned her head back and looked at the ceiling, and after that she didn’t say anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t speak for three weeks.

Not to him. Not to Elowen, who came every day and held her good hand. Not to Raiden, who tried every joke he had. Not to Eliana, who sent a message every night that said only here, or to Professor Liao, who left a bag of boiled sweets on the table and went.

Ev came on the Friday and sat in the chair and didn’t say anything either. It was the only visit Elara could bear.

On Saturday they let her go home. Xing Yue drove her to Banyan Terrace and carried her bag up the stairs, and opened the door, and stood back to let her in.

The flat was silent.

For two years it had been full of her voice, in every room, in the shower, in her sleep. Now she sat on the long grey sofa with her splint in her lap and said nothing, and the flat went back to what it had been before her, and worse.

She knew he was frightened of it. She could see it. He was more frightened of the silence than he’d been in the alley.

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked after her.

He opened every door before she got to it. He cut her food into small exact squares, all of it, the rice cakes and the fish and the pork, so she could eat it with a spoon in her left hand, and put the plate in front of her, and sat across the counter and watched her eat every square. He buttoned her shirts in the mornings, kneeling on the bedroom floor, one button at a time, from the bottom. He washed her hair in the bath, with her right arm held up on a folded towel on the edge, the way he’d done it the night she moved in, and he didn’t say anything while he did it, because she didn’t.

He did the finger exercises with her. The therapist had shown him on the ward, and he’d written it all down in his unreadable hand, and twice a day he sat beside her on the sofa and took her splinted hand in his and moved her fingers for her, gently, bending and straightening, the way he’d been shown, counting under his breath.

She let him. She said nothing.

She heard him on the phone in the study one evening with the door half shut, to a registrar who’d discharged somebody too early. “You read the result and sent him home anyway. Tell me why. No, tell me the real reason.” His voice was flat and cold and exact, and she could hear the registrar on the other end start to come apart. “Ring him tonight. Get him back in. Then write down what you did, all of it, and put it on my desk.”

Then the door opened and he came out and saw her on the sofa, and his face changed completely, and he came and sat down by her feet and put his hand round her ankle and didn’t say a word.

She lay awake at night beside him and listened to him not sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Saturday in December, three weeks in, he couldn’t stand it any more.

She was on the sofa, as she always was now, looking at the window. He came and sat down beside her. Then he put his hands under her arms and pulled her across onto his lap, splint and all, careful of the arm, and settled her there sideways with her back against the arm of the sofa.

She looked at him. She didn’t say anything.

He took her right hand in both of his.

He went over it like a ward round. He pressed each nail where it came out of the splint and watched the pink come back. He looked at the swelling. He ran his thumb down the side of her little finger, where she couldn’t feel anything, and watched her face while he did it, and she kept her face still.

“I’m inspecting your hand,” he said. “I’m going to do it every day. Twice. You can’t stop me.”

She didn’t say anything.

He put two fingers on the inside of her good wrist, on the pulse.

“The house is too quiet, Elara,” he said. “If you don’t say something soon, I’m going to start checking your pulse every hour. Day and night. I’ll set an alarm. I’ll wake you up for it.”

She laughed.

She didn’t mean to. It came out of her, a small cracked noise, and she put her good hand over her mouth, and then she was crying. She cried with her face in his shoulder and her splint held up between them, and he held her and didn’t say anything at all, and then she started to talk.

She talked for two hours.

She talked about the mother she couldn’t remember. A nurse. Shi Yuning. She said the name out loud for the first time and it sounded like nothing, like a stranger’s, and she said it again until it didn’t. She talked about the basket, and the wet towels, and somebody putting her in it with the building on fire, and how she’d always hated the smell of a wet towel and never known why. She talked about the moon. She talked about Mama, the Lin one, who’d known, who’d held her the first night and named her and had three months and told Baba to love her more and not let her see it, and how she’d never once in her life thought she was loved less, not once, and now she didn’t know what that meant. She talked about Baba in the alley, not lifting a hand.

“He wanted it,” she said. “He was waiting for it. He stood there and let that man come at him with a knife, because he thought he deserved it, and I got in the way.”

She talked about her uncle. A man who’d been told she was dead. Who’d come for the man who killed his brother and cut his brother’s daughter instead.

Then she talked about her hand.

She’d been saving it for last. She told him the sums. She told him the millimetre a day, and the distance, and the small muscles, and how she’d read every paper there was on the first night with the drip in, on her phone, with her left thumb, and how she knew the numbers better than Dr. Meng did, and how she’d done the sums every night since and they never came out any different. She told him that she’d held a needle holder since she was eighteen and that she didn’t know who she was if she couldn’t. She told him she was frightened all the time.

Then she ran out.

She sat on his lap with her face wet and her mouth open and nothing left in it.

He kissed her.

Slowly, without a word, holding her face in one hand and her splinted arm in the other, as if she might break. She kissed him back. She hadn’t kissed him in three weeks. She put her good hand in his hair and held on and felt him shaking.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards he went to the study and came back with an envelope.

It was brown, a bit creased, from the glovebox. He put it in her lap.

“It was always yours,” he said. “I shouldn’t have kept it.”

She opened it with one hand. A sheet of paper with a matron’s book copied out on it in square block capitals, every word, so that anyone could read it. A printout of a newspaper page, four paragraphs. And a sheet from a prescription pad, folded small, with her birthday on it, and children’s home with a question mark, and under that, underlined twice, Find her.

She looked at the last one.

“When did you write this?”

“The morning after Ev’s wedding.”

She held it in her good hand and then looked at him.

“You should have told me,” she said. “The day you found it. You should have rung me from the car.”

“Yes.”

“I’m still cross about it.”

“I know.”

“I’m not cross about this.” She held up the prescription-pad sheet. “This is the nicest thing anyone’s ever done for me. You went and found my mother because I said one sentence on a stool. I’m cross about the day. I’m not cross about the rest.”

He didn’t say anything. She saw his throat move.

She didn’t forgive her father. She didn’t try. She didn’t speak to him, and when the family chat had his name in it she didn’t read it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the middle of December she told him she wanted to postpone the wedding.

She wasn’t going to walk down a garden in May with a hand that didn’t work and a name she’d only just found out, and smile at forty people and pretend.

“Postpone,” he said. “Not cancel.”

“Postpone.”

“Then all right,” said Xing Yue. He rang the people who needed ringing that afternoon.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Christmas Eve he cooked.

He’d learned four things from Ah Sim over two years of Sundays, and he made all four. She sat at the counter in his jumper with her splint on a cushion and talked a little, the way she talked now, in short runs with long gaps. He put her plate in front of her. The pork was cut into small squares. So was the fish. So were the green beans.

She looked at the plate.

“I’m going to learn to cut my own food,” she said. “With my left hand. And then with my right. And you’re going to hate it.”

He looked at her across the counter.

“Yes,” he said.

She reached across with her good hand and took hold of his collar and pulled him down over the counter until his face was level with hers, and kissed him, with the squares of pork between them going cold. Then she let him go and picked up her spoon.

chapters.title: She Gives the Ring Back
chapters.desc: Out of the splint, Elara puts the ring in his hand and goes to stay with the sister who knows what it is to learn why you were kept. He sits on the verandah step every night for five weeks.
chapters.epigraph: “You asked a surgeon to marry you.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The splint came off on the first Monday in January.

Dr. Meng took it off in her clinic at the Crestview, in a room with a view of the old racecourse, and turned the hand over in her own and looked at it without saying anything. It was thin and pale and stiff, and the scar ran across the inside of the wrist and up the forearm in a red zigzag where Meng had opened it further to find the ends. The fingers curled in a little, as if they were cold.

“Good,” said Meng. “It’s healed well. Now the work starts.”

The work was a hand therapist called Ms. Cui, on the floor below, a tall strict woman with short grey hair who didn’t smile and who’d made a professional footballer cry in her first session. Xing Yue had asked for her by name. He paid for it. He’d have paid for anything; he’d have bought the floor. Elara knew, and didn’t argue, which frightened him more than if she had.

She went three times a week. He drove her and waited in the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday she gave him the ring back.

He woke at seven and she wasn’t beside him. She was sitting on the edge of the bed in his jumper with her back to him, and when he sat up she turned round.

She’d got the ring off her left hand by herself. He could see the red mark on her finger where she’d worked it off against her knee, slowly, with her left thumb, because her right hand couldn’t help. She held it out to him on her open left palm.

“Take it,” she said.

He didn’t move.

“Please. Take it. I’m not breaking anything. I’m not leaving you. I just can’t wear it.” Her voice was steady and he could see what it cost her. “You asked a surgeon to marry you. You asked me on the edge of a fish pond and I said yes in the middle of a fish, and I was a surgeon. I’m not one any more. I don’t know what I am. I don’t know my own name. I don’t know if I’m going to be able to hold a pen properly by the summer.”

“No,” he said.

“I’m not asking.”

She took his hand off the duvet and turned it over and put the ring in his palm, and closed his fingers over it with hers.

“I’m going to Ev’s for a while,” she said. “She knows what it’s like. To find out why you were kept.” She looked at his closed hand. “Don’t come in with me. Drive me. Then go home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her to Fig Tree Lane that afternoon with her bag on the back seat.

The reservoir road went up through the hills with the water grey on the left, and she didn’t talk. She looked out of the window. He kept the ring in his shirt pocket, and he could feel it there, a small hard weight, on every bend.

The green door was open before they’d reached the gate.

Jun Hyuk came out onto the verandah. He was the biggest man Xing Yue had ever seen in person, bigger than his photographs, in an apron, with a wooden spoon. He looked at Elara with her bag and her thin bare hand, and then at Xing Yue, and something on his broad cheerful face went careful.

Evangeline came out behind him. She went straight past her husband and down the steps to her sister and looked at her.

“Stay,” said Evangeline.

Elara went in. She didn’t look back. Xing Yue stood at the bottom of the verandah steps with his hands at his sides and watched the green door close.

Jun Hyuk sat down on the top step.

“You’ll want to sit down,” he said. “No, you will. Here. Sit.” He moved over. “Do you know about rosemary? Nobody knows about rosemary. Everyone thinks you just put it in the ground. You don’t. You have to be cruel to it. You have to give it bad soil and no water and the worst corner of the garden, and then it’s happy, and if you’re kind to it, it dies. I had four die before I understood that.”

Xing Yue sat on the step.

Jun Hyuk talked about rosemary for an hour. Then he talked about thyme. He didn’t once mention the woman inside, or her hand, or the ring in Xing Yue’s shirt pocket, and at the end of the hour he went in and came back with a cup of tea and put it in Xing Yue’s hand and went in again.

When he’d drunk it, Xing Yue drove home.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came back the next night. And the one after.

He came every night for five weeks. He finished his list, or his clinic, or his ward round, and drove out along the reservoir road in the dark, and parked by the gate, and went and sat on the verandah step of No. 9 Fig Tree Lane.

She didn’t come out.

He hadn’t expected her to. He sat on the step anyway. Some nights it rained and he sat under the edge of the verandah roof with his coat collar up. Some nights it was so cold that his breath went white in the light from the window. He could see her window from the step, on the left of the green door, with the lamp on behind the curtain. He sat and watched it.

Jun Hyuk brought him tea, every night, and talked. Rosemary. Lemons. The man on the harbour who’d tried to bring a crate of frozen eels in as furniture. The cat. A sermon he’d heard as a boy on an island in the south. He talked until the tea was finished and then went in. Evangeline came out once a night with a blanket, and put it round Xing Yue’s shoulders without a word, and went back inside. She never said anything. He was grateful for both.

He checked the dot on his phone every night before he came, and every night after he left, in the car, at the bottom of the lane. It never moved much. The house. The garden. Once, in the afternoon, a slow wander down to the stream at the bottom of the lane and back.

She knew he looked. He knew she knew. She could have turned it off with two touches of her left thumb, and she didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the third week his phone went on the step, at nine at night.

A registrar. A woman had come back from theatre with a falling blood pressure, and the registrar had waited two hours to ring him because he’d thought it would settle.

“Two hours,” said Xing Yue. “You watched a woman’s pressure fall for two hours and thought it would settle. Take her back to theatre. I’ll be there in forty minutes. If she’s not on the table when I get there, don’t bother coming in tomorrow.”

He hung up.

Jun Hyuk was standing in the green doorway with the tea. He looked at Xing Yue for a second, with his eyebrows up, the way a big friendly dog looks at a much smaller dog that has just growled.

“I’ll put it in a flask,” he said.

Xing Yue looked up at her window. The lamp was on. The curtain had moved.

He went to theatre. The woman lived.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the fourth week she came out.

It was a Thursday. It was cold and clear, with stars over the hills and frost on the lemon tree in its pot by the door. He heard the green door open behind him and didn’t turn round, in case it was Jun Hyuk, and then she sat down on the step beside him.

She was in one of Ev’s coats, too long in the sleeves, with her hands pulled up inside them. He could see the right one through the cuff, curled.

She didn’t say anything at first. Neither did he.

“Go home,” said Elara.

“When you do.”

She looked at him. Her face in the light from the window was thinner than it had been in November, and tired, and something in it had come back that hadn’t been there in the flat at Banyan Terrace. She looked at him as though she were seeing him properly for the first time since the alley.

“You’ve been sitting here for four weeks,” she said. “Jun Hyuk tells me. Every night. He tells me what you said and what you drank. He told me you shouted at a registrar.”

“I didn’t shout.”

“He said you didn’t shout. He said it was worse.”

He didn’t say anything to that.

She looked down at her hands in the sleeves of Ev’s coat. Her breath was white. He wanted to kiss her more than he’d wanted anything in his life. He’d wanted it for four weeks, and three before that, and every night on the step. He’d never once asked her. He’d kissed her mid-word on a step in September, and in a car at midnight, and against a wall.

She’d left him now. She’d put the ring in his hand and closed his fingers over it. He wasn’t going to take anything she hadn’t offered.

“Can I kiss you?” said Xing Yue.

She went still.

She turned her head and looked at him on the step, and he saw her understand, and her eyes filled.

“Yes,” she said. “Then go home.”

He put his hand up to her face, slowly, giving her time to move. She didn’t. He kissed her on the cold step with the frost on the lemon tree, carefully, the way you touch something you’ve been told you might not get back. Her mouth was cold. After a second she made a small sound and took her right hand out of her sleeve, the bad one, curled and stiff, and put it against his cheek, and held it there.

He felt it shaking on his face. He didn’t move.

When she drew back she kept her hand where it was.

“Go home,” she said again. “Please. You’ve got a list in the morning.”

He went home.

She didn’t come home. But after that she came out every night, and sat on the step beside him in Ev’s coat, and talked. Not much, at first. Ms. Cui, who had made her cry on Tuesday and then given her a tissue as if she were handing her a scalpel. The cat, who sat on her feet at night. Ev’s garden. A book. Then more. By the second week she was telling him stories in three parts and losing the third, and he sat on the step and listened to every word, and drove home at midnight with the window down, and couldn’t stop smiling at the road.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Lunar New Year’s Eve, Ev and Jun Hyuk went to the Walled City.

Elara wouldn’t go. She hadn’t spoken to her father since November. She told Ev so in the kitchen, and Ev looked at her and said nothing, and then came out onto the verandah, where Xing Yue was sitting on the step at six in the evening because for the first time in nine years he wasn’t working New Year.
