Fei had taken it. Fei had told him he’d better not come in, or she’d tell everyone everything at Christmas, and he’d said it was February, and she’d said she knew.

Ev stood over him on the step.

“Stay with her,” said Evangeline.

He looked up at her.

“Tonight.” She turned and went down the steps to where Jun Hyuk was holding the car door open, talking about tides, and got in.

So he stayed.

Jun Hyuk had made dumplings. A great many of them, in neat rows on trays in the fridge, with a note in a cheerful round hand that said BOIL 6 MIN DON’T LET HER COOK. They were terrible. The pastry was too thick and the filling had too much ginger in it and they fell apart in the water. He and Elara sat at the long dark table in the front room with the windows shut against the cold and a bowl each, and ate them, and she laughed at the first one until she choked.

“They’re awful,” she said. “They’re the worst dumplings I’ve ever had. Don’t tell him. He’s so proud of them. He made two hundred.”

She ate eleven.

He watched her eat them. She was holding the chopsticks in her left hand, badly, and chasing the broken dumplings round the bowl, and she wouldn’t let him help. When she dropped one on the table she looked at it and then at him, daring him to cut anything into squares, and he kept his hands on his side of the table.

Fireworks started over the hills to the south at midnight, far off, small, like someone else’s. She went out onto the verandah to watch them in Ev’s coat, and he went with her, and she leaned against him on the top step, and he put his arm round her.

“Happy New Year,” she said.

He kissed her hair. She didn’t ask him to go home.

He slept on Ev’s sofa under the blanket from the verandah, and in the morning she brought him tea.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second day of the New Year, Eliana’s birthday, he drove her to the grave.

The family went at dawn every year. Her father took them. Elara wouldn’t go with her father, so she asked Xing Yue to drive her at ten, when they’d have gone. He waited at the gate of the cemetery in the car, the way he always waited, and watched her walk up the hill between the stones in Ev’s coat with a bunch of white flowers in her left hand.

She was there an hour. When she came back down she sat in the passenger seat and held her phone to her mouth and recorded a voice message for Eliana. It went on for six minutes. He didn’t listen to the words. He listened to her voice, going on and on, cracking in places and laughing in others, and he looked out of the windscreen at the hill and the stones and let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

That afternoon a motorbike came up Fig Tree Lane.

He was on the step. He’d driven her back and stayed, because it was a holiday and she’d said he could. Jinx pulled up at the gate, took her helmet off, and came up the path in her leather jacket with a roll of graph paper under her arm and a sketchbook in her other hand. She nodded to him. She didn’t say anything. She went in through the green door without knocking.

He heard them through the window. He didn’t mean to; the window was open, and the kitchen was on the other side of it.

“I don’t know hands,” said Jinx. “I know linkages. Let me try.”

Nothing. Paper being unrolled on a table. He sat on the step with his back to the window and his elbows on his knees and didn’t move.

“Yes,” said Elara.

He didn’t go in. He didn’t ask afterwards. When Jinx came out an hour later she stopped on the step beside him, and looked down at him, and for a second he thought she was going to say something.

“Calipers,” said Jinx. “I’ll need to measure. Every day for a week.”

“Do you need anything?”

She thought about it. “No,” she said, and went down the path to her bike.

Inside, Elara was at the kitchen table with the graph paper flattened under a teapot and a jar of salted lemons. On it, in hard pencil, was the outline of her own right hand, traced round, with numbers all down every finger in a small fierce engineer’s writing. She was looking at it. She looked up when he came to the doorway, and her face was frightened and alive at the same time.

“Don’t ask,” she said.

He didn’t.

chapters.title: Jinx Builds a Machine
chapters.desc: At five every morning, before the garage opens, Elara works her ruined hand on a steel rig Jinx built for her. Her uncle pleads guilty, and she watches from the gallery.
chapters.epigraph: “Five in the morning, before I open. Nobody needs to know.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
She went home on the first Sunday in March.

He came to Fig Tree Lane to fetch her with the car, and Jun Hyuk carried her bag down to it and talked the whole way about the lemons she was taking, and Ev stood on the verandah and didn’t say goodbye, because Ev never did. Elara hugged her anyway. Ev let her, stiffly, and then at the last moment put one hand on the back of her sister’s head and held it there.

At Banyan Terrace her shoes went back by the door, facing out. He’d kept the place exactly as she’d left it. Her cardigan was still over the back of the study chair. Her mug was still on the draining board, upside down.

The ring was in the top drawer of his bedside table, in its grey silk box, beside the coin from Ah Sim’s dumpling and a red packet with her handwriting on it. She knew because she looked, the first night, while he was in the shower. She didn’t take it out. She shut the drawer and got into bed and lay on her side with her hand on the pillow, looking at it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rig stood in the garage near the Docks, under the old sign that said TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS.

Jinx had built it in two and a half weeks, on her own, at night, from the measurements she’d taken at Ev’s kitchen table with calipers every afternoon for a week. It was bolted to the end of the long bench under the window, and it looked, the first time Elara saw it, like something you’d find in a museum of torture.

Then she looked closer.

There was a steel frame with a padded rest for her forearm, so the hand hung out over the bench. There were slings for each finger on thin springs, and the springs could be swapped, a row of them on a rail, from soft to stiff. There was a pinch gauge with a dial, for her thumb and each finger in turn. There was a pegboard of pins, the first row as thick as her little finger, the last row as thin as a needle. There was a wire bent into a long wobbling track with a ring on a handle, that buzzed if you touched the ring to the wire. And there was a small camera on an arm, pointing down at a practice pad of fake skin, with a screen beside it, so she could see what her hand was doing even where she couldn’t feel it.

Every part of it adjusted by a quarter turn of a knurled knob.

“Five in the morning,” said Jinx. “Before I open. Nobody needs to know.”

Elara looked at her.

“I don’t want anyone to know,” she said. “Not Baba. Not Elowen. Not him. If it doesn’t work, I don’t want to see anybody’s face.”

Jinx nodded, as if that were obvious, and went back to the bike she’d been working on.

✦ ✦ ✦

She started on the first Saturday in March.

A taxi came for her at a quarter to five every morning. She paid for it on the card, because she was too tired to think of anything else, and because he’d see it anyway, and because she’d told him, on the first night home, that Jinx had built her something for her hand and that she was going to use it at five in the morning, in the garage, and that she didn’t want him to come.

He’d said he wanted to.

“No,” said Elara.

He looked at her across the kitchen counter. She saw him want to argue, and decide not to.

“Then tell me one thing,” he said. “Every night. Anything you like. One thing that happened in your day.”

“Not the garage.”

“Not the garage.”

So she told him one thing a night. The first night it was a pigeon on the window ledge at the medical school. The second it was a student who’d fainted at the sight of a skeleton. She never told him the garage, and he never asked, and every morning at a quarter to five the taxi came and the card paid for it and the statement went to him, and they both knew where she went, and neither of them said a word about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first morning, she couldn’t do any of it.

She put her forearm on the rest and her fingers in the slings with the softest springs on, and tried to bend them, and they bent about as far as a door you’ve just started pushing. She did the pinch gauge, and the needle on the dial hardly moved. She tried the thickest pins on the pegboard and dropped two on the floor and couldn’t pick up the third. She tried the wire.

It buzzed, and buzzed again, so often that the noise of it went into the walls.

Jinx was under a bike on a creeper at the other end of the garage, with her back to the bench, and she didn’t turn round. She didn’t say anything. She worked on the bike with the radio on low, as if Elara weren’t there at all, and Elara understood after a while that it was the kindest thing anyone had done for her since November.

At half past five Raiden came down the stairs from the flat in his dressing gown, put a cup of coffee on the end of the bench by her elbow, and went back up without a word.

She did ninety minutes. At the end of it her hand was shaking and her face was wet and she hadn’t got the ring to the end of the wire once.

“Same time tomorrow,” said Jinx, from under the bike.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second of March, the day after she came home, she became a tutor in anatomy.

Professor Liao had found it for her. He’d come to Banyan Terrace in February with a bag of sweets and sat on the sofa and told her that the medical school needed someone to teach the first-years in the dissection rooms, three days a week, someone who knew the body and could talk about it, and that he couldn’t think of anyone in the city who talked about it more. She’d cried. He’d looked at the ceiling until she stopped.

The anatomy rooms were in the basement of the old medical building on the hill, under the skills lab where she’d won the bananas. They were long and cold and smelled of preservative, and the first-years came in clutching their notebooks against their chests, the way she had.

They loved her by the end of the first week.

She couldn’t help it. She talked. She stood at the end of the table with a long wooden pointer in her left hand and told them the names of everything, and why it was called that, and what it did, and a story about it, usually a patient, usually funny. She told them about the man who’d swallowed a key. She told them the moon she was named after. She showed them the nerves in a forearm, the median and the ulnar, laid out on the table under the light, and she talked about them so well that a girl at the front asked her how she knew so much about the forearm in particular, and she smiled and said she’d had a lot of time to read.

She came home and complained about the other lecturers.

“There’s one who’s been teaching the hand for thirty years,” she told him, at the counter, eating noodles with her left hand. “And he still calls the little finger the fifth digit. Every time. Fifth digit. Nobody’s ever called it that in their life. The students think he’s talking about a phone number.”

He listened. He didn’t point out that she was telling him two things, not one.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the third week, she could feel the springs.

Not much. Not in the fingers she couldn’t feel at all, the little one and half the next. But the others had started to answer her. She’d moved up two springs on the index and the middle. She’d got the needle on the pinch gauge past the first mark. She’d got a fat pin into the pegboard, and then a slightly thinner one, and dropped the third and picked it up again with her teeth gritted and her eyes stinging, and got it in.

The wire still buzzed. It buzzed and buzzed. Some mornings she wanted to rip it off the bench.

One morning she did try. She took hold of the wire track with her left hand and pulled, and it didn’t move, because Jinx had bolted it into the bench from underneath, and she stood there with her left hand on it and her right hand hanging and swore at nobody, every word she knew, loud enough that Raiden’s feet stopped on the stairs.

Jinx rolled out from under the bike on her creeper and looked at her.

“It’s bolted,” said Jinx.

“I know it’s bolted.”

“I’ll bolt it harder,” said Jinx, and rolled back under.

Elara laughed. She didn’t mean to. She stood at the bench with her face wet and laughed until she had to sit down on the stool, and Jinx’s boots stuck out from under the bike and didn’t move, and after a while Elara put her hand back on the rest and picked up the ring and started again at the beginning of the wire.

✦ ✦ ✦

He asked her at breakfast, at the end of the second week, whether she was eating before she went.

She was. Mostly. A biscuit in the taxi.

“A biscuit isn’t breakfast,” he said. “You’re doing an hour and a half of physical work at five in the morning on a biscuit and then going and standing in a cold room for six hours. You’re losing weight. I can see it in your face. Your hand needs protein to heal, it’s not optional, there’s a whole literature on nerve regeneration and nutrition, and you know it better than I do, and you’re eating a biscuit in a taxi—”

She leaned across the counter and kissed him.

She didn’t take his glasses off. She didn’t warn him. She put her left hand on the back of his neck and pulled him down and kissed him in the middle of the literature on nerve regeneration, hard, until he stopped talking about it, and then past that, until he’d forgotten the biscuit and had both hands on the counter on either side of her bowl.

“That’s what you do,” she said, when she let him go. “To me. That’s your trick. I’m allowed it too.”

He looked at her. His ears had gone pink.

The next morning there was a pork bun in a paper bag on the hall table, by her shoes, and a carton of soy milk with the straw already in. She ate both in the taxi.

✦ ✦ ✦

At night he’d started kissing her fingers.

He’d done it first in the second week back, in bed, in the dark. She was lying on her side facing him, with her right hand between them on the pillow, and he picked it up and kissed the tip of her thumb. Then the index finger. Then the middle one.

“What are you doing?” she said.

“Checking sensation.”

She knew what he was doing. He was doing what she did on the rig every morning, what Ms. Cui did with a little plastic tool in her clinic, testing which bits of her came back. He kissed the tip of the ring finger, on the thumb side, and she felt it, faintly, like something through a glove. Then the other side of it.

She didn’t feel it.

He kissed the little finger. She didn’t feel that either. She knew he’d kissed it only because she was looking at him.

She started to cry.

She hadn’t meant to. She’d been doing so well. She’d done ninety minutes that morning and got a pin in she hadn’t been able to touch a week before, and taught fifty students the brachial plexus and made them laugh, and now she was lying in bed crying because a man had kissed her little finger and it might as well have been somebody else’s.

He put her hand down on the pillow, carefully. He didn’t say anything. He moved closer and kissed her mouth.

He kissed her slowly, without any hurry at all, and kept on. He kissed her until she’d stopped crying and was kissing him back, and then he kept going. His hand went into her hair. His mouth went to her jaw and down her throat, and stayed there, on the place he’d put his fingers on the steps outside Old Bian’s, the first time, and she felt her pulse go against his mouth and knew that he could feel it too. She put her left hand on his back, under his T-shirt, and held on. She forgot her hand. She didn’t know when. She only knew, much later, lying with her face in his shoulder, that she hadn’t thought about it once.

She stopped him there. She was the one who stopped. She put her hand flat on his chest and he stopped at once, and lay with his forehead against hers, breathing.

“Not yet,” she said. “I want to. I just—not yet.”

“All right.”

He kissed her fingers again the next night. And the next. He did it every night, all five, in the same order, and she lay and felt the ones she could feel and watched him kiss the ones she couldn’t, and she stopped crying about it in the second week.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Friday in March her uncle was sentenced.

He’d pleaded guilty in February, to wounding, through his lawyer, without a trial. Wei Long had told her the date. She’d told Xing Yue she wanted to go. He’d taken the day off without saying a word about it and driven her there, to the court building behind the archive, and they sat together in the public gallery at the back, high up, on a wooden bench.

Qu Wenjun came up the stairs into the dock between two officers.

He was thinner than in the alley. His hair was cut short. He was in a grey shirt instead of the seaman’s jacket, and he stood in the dock with his hands in front of him and looked at the floor while the judge talked about the seriousness of the offence and the injury to an innocent bystander, a young doctor, whose career might be over, and about his plea and his previous record and his age.

Six years.

He didn’t react. He nodded once, at the floor.

Elara sat on the bench in the gallery with her hands in her lap. Xing Yue’s hand was on her knee. He’d put it there when the judge started talking and he hadn’t moved it since, and she’d put her left hand over it and was holding on so hard her nails were in his skin.

As they took him down, her uncle looked up.

He looked up at the gallery. She didn’t know why. Maybe people always did, at the end. He looked straight at the back bench, at the two of them, at her, small, in her good coat, with her right hand in her lap, and his face didn’t change at all. He looked at her the way you’d look at anyone. Then the officers turned him and he went down the stairs.

He didn’t know who she was.

She sat on the bench until the court was empty.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside on the steps Wei Long was waiting in his long coat.

She took the envelope out of her pocket. She’d written it at the kitchen counter over three nights, with her left hand, in big careful letters that sloped downhill. She held it out to him.

“For him,” she said. “Will you give it to him? And tell him who I am.”

Wei Long looked at the envelope. He looked at her, and then at Xing Yue standing a step behind her with his hands in his coat pockets, and back at her.

“Are you sure?” he said.

“No,” said Elara. “Give it to him anyway.”

He took it and put it inside his coat, and nodded to both of them, and went down the steps.

She stood on the court steps in the March wind with her hands in her pockets.

“One thing,” said Xing Yue, beside her.

She looked up at him. It took her a second to understand. Then she laughed, a cracked short laugh, and leaned on his arm.

“I got a pin in yesterday,” she said. “The third row. I’ve been trying for nine days. I got it in and I didn’t drop it.” She looked at the street. “That’s the garage. That’s all you’re getting.”

He didn’t say anything. He put his arm round her, and they went down the steps together.

chapters.title: Her Mother’s Window
chapters.desc: In a prison visiting room her uncle gives her the only photographs of her parents. She finds her mother’s ward window over the hospital garden, and Xing Yue asks her again.
chapters.epigraph: “My mother was a nurse. She worked here.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The prison at Cold Water Bay was an hour down the coast, on a headland, behind two fences and a car park full of puddles.

Xing Yue drove her. He’d have come in if she’d let him. She didn’t. She left him in the car with the engine off and walked across the car park on her own in her good coat, with her bag over her left shoulder and her right hand in her pocket, and went through the gate, and through a room where a woman in a uniform took her bag and her phone and her coat and looked in her mouth, and into a long room with small tables bolted to the floor.

He was already sitting at one of them.

He stood up when he saw her. An officer at the wall said something and he sat down again, fast, with his hands flat on the table in front of him.

She sat down opposite.

Wei Long had told him. She could see it. He looked at her the way you’d look at someone who’d come back from the sea after you’d buried them. His face was the colour of the table. His mouth moved, and nothing came out of it, and he shut it and opened it again and still nothing came.

She waited. She’d decided in the car that she’d wait.

“Xiaoyue,” he said, in the end.

Nobody had ever called her that. She felt it go through her like the nerve pain.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then he couldn’t stop.

He talked the way she talked. She heard it after a minute and it frightened her more than anything else in that room. He talked in long runs, fast, with his hands moving on the table, going back to the beginning and losing the end and starting again. He told her he’d been on a ship off the coast of somewhere when they got word. A cargo ship. Three weeks out. He told her they’d said all of them, the whole family, Mingde and Yuning and the baby. He’d come home and there was a black square of building at the piers with a fence round it, and nobody would tell him anything, and he’d gone back to sea because he couldn’t stand the city.

“I’d have come for you,” he said. “If I’d known. I’d have come back. I’d have taken you. I’d have—” He stopped. “I don’t know what I’d have done. I was thirty-four. I’d have done something.”

He told her about the bookkeeper. An old man who’d worked for Zuo, dying in a hospice by the harbour last spring, who’d sent for him and told him who sold the schedule. He told her he’d waited by the noodle stall three Sundays.

“I came for him,” said her uncle. “Not you. I didn’t know there was a you. When you put your arm up I didn’t know who you were. I didn’t even see your face.” He looked at her right hand, on the table, the scar running out of her sleeve. “I’m sorry. I’m sorry. I’m sorry about your hand.”

He put his face down on his arms on the table.

The officer at the wall looked over. Elara didn’t move. She sat across from her father’s brother with her ruined hand on the table and watched his shoulders shake, and she didn’t touch him, and she didn’t look away.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he sat up he’d stopped crying, and he talked about her parents.

Her father laughed all the time. He was bad with money and good with boats. He’d once taken a lighter out in a typhoon to bring in a man who’d fallen off a ship, and been fined for it. Her mother was a nurse on the children’s ward at City Hospital, in the old building, and she was quiet, and clever, and stubborn, and she’d married Mingde because he’d made her laugh at a bus stop.

“Hers,” he said. “You’ve got her face. Not his. You’ve got his mouth. You never stop talking. Neither did he. My mother used to say he was born talking.” He looked at her. “Do you know you do it?”

“Yes,” said Elara.

He laughed. It was a cracked, surprised sound, and it was hers. She had to look at the table.

At the end he spoke to the officer at the wall, and the officer went out and came back with a small brown envelope from his property and gave it to her, not to him.

“I kept them,” said her uncle. “All those years on ships. And inside. They’re the only ones. The rest were in the flat.”

She opened it. Two photographs, small and square, the colour gone soft and orange the way old photographs went.

A woman in a white nurse’s uniform at a tall window, with a baby on her hip. Laughing at whoever held the camera, with her head turned. The baby had a lot of black hair and its fist in its mouth.

A man on the deck of a small boat with a rope over his shoulder, coiled, wet, in a vest, laughing so hard his eyes had shut.

Elara looked at them.

She didn’t know she was humming until he stopped talking. She looked up. He was staring at her, and his face had gone strange.

“That,” he said. “What’s that? What you’re doing.”

“I hum. I always do. I don’t know what it is.”

“She sang it,” said Qu Wenjun. “Yuning. On the ward. To the babies, to make them go to sleep. And at home, washing up. Mingde used to say she only knew one song.” His voice went. “You were two. You can’t remember that.”

“No,” said Elara.

She’d hummed it all her life. In theatre. Over bananas. At the top of a ladder, putting up brackets. She didn’t know where it had come from. She’d never once wondered.

She put the photographs back in the envelope.

“I don’t forgive you,” she said.

He nodded. He seemed to have expected nothing else.

“I’ll come back,” said Elara, and stood up, and the officer took her out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xing Yue was standing by the car.

He’d got out. He was leaning on the driver’s door in his coat with his hands in his pockets, in the drizzle, and he’d been watching the gate. She saw him straighten up when she came through it.

She got in. He got in. He started the car and didn’t ask anything.

She talked all the way up the coast road.

She didn’t mean to. It came out of her the way it had on his lap in December, all at once, in no order. The room with the tables. Her uncle’s hands. The ship three weeks out. The hospice and the bookkeeper. Her father in a typhoon, fined for saving a man. Her mother at a bus stop. The photographs, which she took out of the envelope and held up for him to see at the traffic lights, and he looked at them for exactly as long as the lights were red. She told him about the humming, and that her uncle had said she had her mother’s face and her father’s mouth, and that he’d laughed, and that it was her laugh, and how she hadn’t known what to do with that.

“My mother was a nurse,” she said.

He pulled over.

There was a lay-by beside the sea wall, a strip of wet tarmac with a bin and a view of nothing but grey water. He pulled into it and stopped the car and turned the engine off.

She looked at him. She’d been crying for some of the last twenty minutes and she’d only just noticed.

He leaned across and took her chin in his hand and turned her face towards the window, towards the grey light off the sea, the way you’d turn a patient’s face to look at their eyes. He looked at her. He ran his thumb under one eye, and then the other, slowly, wiping them, frowning a little, as though he were checking for something and wanted to be sure.

“Your mother was a nurse,” he said.

Then he kissed her.

It was hard and slow at once, his hand still on her jaw, her face still wet, and she grabbed the front of his coat with her good hand and pulled him over the gearstick towards her and kissed him back with everything she’d carried out of that room. The rain went on the windscreen. A lorry went past on the coast road and shook the car. Neither of them noticed. She held onto his coat and felt his heart going under her fist, and when he stopped he didn’t let go of her face.

“She worked on the children’s ward,” said Elara, against his mouth. “At City Hospital. In the old building. Your hospital. My hospital.”

He went still.

She took the photograph out again, the one with the window. Her hand was shaking. She held it up between them in the grey light, and she saw it, and so did he: on the white wooden frame of the tall window behind her mother’s shoulder, in black paint, a ward number.

She knew those windows. She’d walked under them on her way in for nearly two years. Two floors of tall arched windows at the back of the old granite block, the first-floor row looking straight down on the garden and the koi pond.

He’d asked her to marry him under them.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the middle of April, in the shower, she felt the water.

It was a Thursday night. She was standing under it with her eyes shut, too tired to think, with her right hand held up against the tiles the way she always held it now, out of the way. The water was running down over it. She wasn’t thinking about it at all.

The tip of her index finger tingled.

She opened her eyes.

She held her hand under the water and looked at it. She moved it out of the stream and back in. A tingle, faint, like the pins and needles when a foot wakes up, on the pad at the end of the finger, where she held a needle holder. It was the water. She could feel the water.

She stood in the shower with her hand in front of her face and her mouth open.

“Xing Yue—” she said.

He was in the bedroom. She heard him stop moving.

“Elara?”

She looked at her finger. She thought of his face if she told him, the way it would change, the hope in it. She thought of his face in three weeks, or three months, if the tingle went away and never came back, if it was nothing, if it was the nerve doing something stupid and meaningless, the way nerves did. She thought of telling him and then having to watch him be careful about it for the rest of her life.

“Nothing,” she said. “Can you bring me a towel? I forgot.”

He brought it. He hung it on the rail and went out.

She stood under the water until it ran cold, with her finger in it.

✦ ✦ ✦

A week later, on a Thursday at six in the evening, she went to the garden.

She had the photograph in her pocket. She’d been carrying it every day. She walked round the back of the old block and through the gate into the garden, under the camphor tree, past the benches, to the edge of the round pond where the koi were going slow in the cooling water, and she stood there and looked up.

The first-floor windows. She counted them from the end. She took the photograph out and held it up and looked at the frame in the picture and the frames on the wall. It was the fourth one. The paint on the number had gone, years ago, and the window had been painted cream since, and there was a stack of folders on the sill inside where once there had been a woman with a baby on her hip.

It was the records office now. Somebody had left a mug on the sill.

She stood with the photograph in her left hand and looked up at it.

She heard the door of the old block open behind her and footsteps on the path, and she knew whose they were before she turned round. He’d have seen the dot. He’d have seen it come round the back of the old block at six and stop by the pond, and he’d have finished whatever he was doing and come down.

He stood beside her. She gave him the photograph.

“My mother was a nurse,” she said. “She worked here.”

He looked at the photograph, and then up at the window, the fourth one, with the mug on the sill.

He didn’t say anything. He stood with the photograph and looked at the window her mother had laughed out of with her on her hip, and then he looked at the pond, and the camphor tree, and the path where he’d knelt in the wet in his good trousers two summers ago.

He gave the photograph back. Then he took something out of his coat pocket.

The grey silk box.

“I’ve had it with me since January,” he said. “Every day.”

She looked at it.

“I’m asking again,” said Xing Yue. “Same question.”

He didn’t kneel this time. He stood in front of her on the path under her mother’s window with the box open in his hand, and his face was plain and tired and completely certain, and she looked at the small star sapphire and thought of the water on her finger, and that he didn’t know, and that she wasn’t going to tell him.

“Yes,” said Elara.

He put it on her. Her left hand, the good one. It went over the knuckle easily. She held it up and looked at it, with the window behind it and the camphor tree, and she cried, because she always did.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night he was too careful.

She’d known he would be. It was the first time since the alley. She’d stopped him in March, in the dark, and he’d stopped, and he’d never pushed, not once, not by a breath. Now she pulled him upstairs by his tie, the way she’d once pulled him down a banister, and pushed him down on the bed, and he went, and then he held her as though she might come apart.

He kissed her wrist, the scar, all the way up the zigzag, slowly. He held her right hand away from everything, out on the pillow, as though it were something that might be knocked. He kept stopping to look at her face, as if he were reading a monitor.

“Stop being a doctor,” said Elara.

He looked up at her.

“You can stop being a patient, then,” he said.

She laughed. She sat up on him in the lamplight, with her hair coming down and the ring on her hand, and she stopped being a patient.

She took his glasses off and put them on the table. She took her own shirt off with her left hand, badly, and laughed at herself, and wouldn’t let him help. She kissed him the way she’d wanted to for five months, slow and then not slow, with her good hand in his hair and her bad one flat on his chest, where she could feel his heart under it through the skin even if she couldn’t feel his skin. She set the pace, and told him where and when, and he let her. He lay under her and let her have all of it, every bit of it, his hands on her waist holding her and not steering, his eyes on her face, and his breath going ragged, and her name. She leaned down and kissed him through it and didn’t stop talking, and then did, and then said his name instead, over and over, into his mouth, until there wasn’t any room left in her for anything else.

Afterwards she lay on top of him with her ear on his chest.

He’d taken her right hand. He was holding it against his collarbone, his thumb moving over her fingertips, one by one, the way he did every night.

When he got to the index finger, she felt it. Faint, through the glove that wasn’t there.

She didn’t say anything. She kept her face on his chest so he couldn’t see it, and listened to his heart, and let him go on.

chapters.title: A Surgeon Who Doesn’t Exist
chapters.desc: At one in the morning her father rings for the first time in eight months: his driver’s grandson is bleeding on the kitchen table. Elara picks up the instruments herself, and her hands don’t shake.
chapters.epigraph: “Ask me things, Baba. That was the deal.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
In May the springs went up.

She moved the index finger to the fourth spring on the rail, and the middle to the fourth, and the ring finger to the second, which made Jinx put down her spanner and look across the garage for a whole second before going back to the bike. The pins went thinner. She got to the second-to-last row on the pegboard, the ones like knitting needles, and then in June to the last, the ones like real needles, and dropped every one of them for a week and then didn’t.

The wire went quiet.

Not all at once. One morning she got the ring from one end of the wire to the other and it buzzed only twice. Then once. Then, on a Tuesday in the middle of June, with Raiden’s coffee going cold by her elbow and the radio on low, she took the ring the whole length of the wire, round every bend, and back again, and it didn’t make a sound.

She put it down. She looked at Jinx’s boots sticking out from under the bike.

“Did you hear that?” she said.

“I didn’t hear anything,” said Jinx.

“That’s what I mean.”

The boots didn’t move. Then Jinx rolled out on her creeper and looked up at her from the floor, and she didn’t smile, and then she reached up and put her black oily hand flat on the bench beside Elara’s, for one second, and rolled back under.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ninth of May went past.

She’d known it would. It was a Saturday. She woke at six and lay in bed and thought, this is the morning, and listened to him make tea in the kitchen below, and didn’t go down for an hour. Nobody in the family mentioned it. Elowen sent a photograph of a single white peony at nine and nothing else. That night he took her to Old Bian’s and didn’t say anything about the date, and she ate too many dumplings and didn’t either.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the Crestview, Dr. Meng tested her hand every month.

She did it the way she did everything, flat and thorough. Two little plastic points on the fingertips, close together and then further apart, to see whether Elara could tell one from two. A dial gauge for the grip and the pinch. A pegboard of her own, timed. Pictures of the small muscles between the bones of the hand, filling out again under the skin.

In June she sat back and looked at the numbers on her screen and then at Elara.

“This is good,” said Meng. “This is better than I’d hoped. I want to know what you’re doing.”

“Therapy,” said Elara. “And something else. A thing a friend built. Every morning.”

Meng waited.

“I’d like it to stay between us,” said Elara. “The numbers. All of it. Please. I don’t want it in a letter to anyone. I don’t want Ms. Cui writing it up. I don’t want my fiancé to see it.”

Meng looked at her over her screen. She’d been a hand surgeon for twenty years and she had probably heard stranger things in that room.

“It’s your hand,” she said.

Then, as Elara was putting her coat on: “He came to see me, by the way. Your fiancé.”

Elara stopped with one arm in the sleeve.

“Last week. He caught me in the corridor outside theatres. Colleague to colleague, he said. He wanted to know how your recovery was going. He wanted to see the notes.” Meng’s face didn’t change. “I told him to ask you. He told me what he thought of a hand surgeon who wouldn’t share a result with a consultant in her own hospital. He was quite specific about it. I told Professor Liao.”

“Oh God,” said Elara.

“He didn’t ask you, I take it.”

“No.”

Meng nodded, as if that told her something, and went back to her screen.

Elara stood in the corridor outside the clinic with her coat half on.

He’d gone to Meng. He’d stood in a corridor and tried to get her notes, the man who’d never once written a lie in a record until he met her, and been rude enough about it that Meng had gone to Liao. And then he’d come home and said nothing, and kissed her fingers in the dark, all five, in the same order, and not asked.

She wanted to shout at him. She wanted to go home and climb into his lap and hold on. She couldn’t do either without talking about the hand, so she went home and did neither.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home, she pretended.

She held her cups in both hands. She’d done it for months without thinking, when she had to, and now she did it on purpose. She fumbled her buttons in the mornings, standing in front of the bedroom mirror, and let him come up behind her and do them, one by one, from the bottom, with his chin on her shoulder. She let him open jars. She let him cut the pork at dinner, sometimes, and pretended she hadn’t noticed, and watched him do it so carefully, every square the same size, and ate them.

It made her feel sick. Every time.

She did it anyway. She couldn’t stop. If she stopped, he’d see. And if he saw, he’d hope, and then every time she picked up a pen she’d feel him watching to see if it shook, and if it all went backwards, if the nerves did something stupid, he’d have to watch that too.

She told herself that was the reason. Some nights she believed it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past one on the second Saturday in July her phone rang on the bedside table.

She was awake. She’d been awake since midnight, lying on her side in the dark with her right hand on the pillow, moving her fingers one by one against the cotton. He was asleep behind her, with his arm over her waist.

The screen said BABA.

She looked at it. He hadn’t rung her in eight months. He’d sent messages through Elowen. He’d let her stop coming on Sundays and never once asked her to come back.

She slid out from under Xing Yue’s arm and went out onto the landing and answered it.

“Elara,” said her father.

His voice was low and fast. She’d never heard him sound like that.

“It’s Mok’s grandson. Jiale. His daughter’s boy. He’s nineteen.” He breathed. “He’s been knifed. In the leg, in an alley, over some money he owes. He’s on bail. If he goes to a hospital they’ll ring the police, and they’ll take his bail, and he’ll go to prison. Mok brought him here.” He stopped. “I’ve got Hou. Old Hou. He’s drunk, and his hands are shaking. I need you to talk him through it. On the phone. That’s all. I’m not asking for anything else. Just tell Hou what to do.”

She stood on the dark landing with the phone against her ear.

“Is it bleeding?”

“Yes.”

She’d already turned towards the bathroom, where her clothes were.

“Bright? Coming in spurts?”

“Mok’s pressing on it. I don’t know. It’s a lot.”

“I’m coming,” said Elara.

“No. I’m not asking that. I only—”

“I know you’re not,” she said. “I’m coming anyway.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She dressed in the bathroom with the light off.

She wrote a note on the kitchen counter, on the pad he used for shopping lists, with her left hand, because her right would have been too neat and he’d have seen. Ah Sim’s not well. Gone to the Walled City. Back by morning. Don’t worry. She put it under the teapot, where he’d find it.

It was the first lie she’d ever told him.

She stood in the dark kitchen for a few seconds looking at it. Then she got her bag and her shoes, which were by the door facing out, and went down the stairs without turning on a light.

✦ ✦ ✦

The kitchen in the Walled City had every light on.

Ding Jiale was on the long table, on a sheet over the plastic cloth, a skinny boy in a torn shirt with his jeans cut off at the top of one leg and Uncle Mok’s big hands pressed into a towel on his thigh. The towel was red right through. Mok’s face was grey. He didn’t look up when she came in. Ah Sim stood at the stove in her dressing gown with a kettle and a pan of boiling water and her mouth in a line.

Old Hou was in a chair by the fire.

She’d known him all her life. The Walled City’s back-room doctor, seventy-four, who’d stitched up half her father’s men in the old days and taken out Raiden’s splinters and given Elara her first injection. He had his black bag open on his knees and the instruments laid out on a tea towel on the chair beside him, and he was holding a needle holder, and his hand was shaking so hard the needle holder rattled against the chair arm.

He looked up at her. His eyes were wet and red.

“Little sparrow,” he said. “I can’t.”

Her father was standing at the end of the table. He looked at her, and then at her right hand.

She didn’t say anything to him. She went to the sink and washed her hands. Both of them. All of it, the fingers and the backs and the wrists, the way you were taught and nobody did after the first year. She dried them on a clean tea towel from the drawer. She took the gloves out of Hou’s bag and put them on, the left and then the right, and she felt the right glove go on over her fingers and felt it, most of it, the stretch of the rubber, the cool.

She picked up the needle holder from the chair in her right hand.

It didn’t shake.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Mok,” she said. “Keep pressing. Don’t move till I tell you. Baba. The lamp.”

Her father picked up the lamp from the dresser, the old one with the long neck, and held it over the table without a word.

She worked.

She didn’t think about her hand. She didn’t have room. She numbed the skin round the wound, and had Mok lift the towel a little, and saw what it was: a deep cut through the muscle of the thigh, and a vessel in the bottom of it, a small artery, not the big one, pumping. She got it. She got a clamp on it and then a tie round it, and the knot went down under her fingers, and she felt it go down, and she tied the second throw and the third, and it held. The bleeding stopped.

She washed it out. Ah Sim brought the boiled water, cooled, in a clean bowl, and held it, and Elara washed the wound until it ran clear. Then she closed it in layers, the deep part first and then the skin, small stitches, close, one after another, and her hands went down the line the way they’d gone down a banana once in a skills lab, small and quick and exact.

She didn’t talk. She hummed, and under the humming, the way she always did, she said, “Okay, okay, there, okay.”

Her father held the lamp and didn’t move it a centimetre.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four the boy was asleep on the table with a dressing on his leg and Mok sitting beside him holding his hand.

She stripped off the gloves. She stood at the sink with her hands on the edge of it and her head down, and breathed. Behind her she heard Hou say something to Mok, and Mok not answer, and Ah Sim go out, and the kettle start.

When she turned round her father was sitting at the table.

He’d put the lamp down. He was sitting in his own carved chair at the head of the table, grey all through, with his big hands flat on the wood in front of him, looking at her hands.

“Your hand,” said Lin Jian.

“Yes.”

“How long?”

She dried her hands on the towel before she answered. “A few months. It’s getting better. It’s nearly there.”

He looked at her face. “Does he know?”

“No.”

He didn’t say anything to that. He sat there in his chair. She waited for him to say that she had to tell him, or that she mustn’t, or anything at all about it.

Then he asked her.

He asked her slowly, choosing every word, the way Elowen had taught him to years ago, when he’d had to learn. He asked whether he could ever ask her to do this again. He didn’t say it was for the family. He didn’t say she owed him. He said that if she said no, he’d never ring her about it again, and that Hou would do what he could, and that would be the end of it.

She stood at the sink with her wet hands.

“Ask me things, Baba,” said Elara. “That was the deal. Ask me, and I’ll say yes or no.” She dried her hands. “Yes. On my rules. I’ll tell you what they are.”

He nodded.

Ah Sim came back with the tea. Her father got up and took the pot from her, which he never did, and poured a cup and put it in front of Elara, at her place at the table, and stood back.

She sat down. He stood beside her chair.

She reached up with her right hand and put it on his shoulder.

She felt his coat under her fingers. She felt the weight of him, and how still he went. It was the first time she’d touched him since November. She left it there for as long as it took to drink half the tea, and he didn’t move once.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got home at half past five.

The flat was dark. She came in with her shoes in her hand so they wouldn’t make a sound, and went into the kitchen, and he was there.

He was sitting at the counter in the dark in his T-shirt, with her note in front of him and a cup of tea that had gone cold. He looked up.

“Ah Sim,” he said.

“Her chest,” said Elara. “She was coughing. She couldn’t get her breath, and she frightened Baba, and he rang. It’s all right. It’s a cold. She’s fine. I made her sit up and drink something hot and she shouted at me for coming.” She heard herself say it. It came out easily. It came out smiling. “She’s fine.”

“Good,” he said.

He stood up and came round the counter. He took her right hand, carefully, the bad one, the one that had tied a vessel and closed a wound in layers on her father’s kitchen table two hours ago. He held it in both of his, gently, as though it might break, and rubbed it with his thumbs, because her fingers were cold.

She couldn’t stand it.

She pulled her hand out of his and took his face in both hands and kissed him, hard, so she wouldn’t say anything.

He made a surprised sound against her mouth. She didn’t stop. She kissed him the way she’d needed to all the way home in the taxi, with her whole body, pushing him back against the counter, her hands in his hair and his T-shirt and on his face. He caught her round the waist. He lifted her up onto the counter, onto the cold marble, and stood between her knees and kissed her back, and his hands were warm on her back under her shirt, and she held onto his shoulders and didn’t let go.

She was shaking. She couldn’t stop. She was shaking with what she’d done, and half of her was so proud of her hand that she wanted to shout, and the other half was so ashamed of her mouth that she wanted to cry, and she couldn’t tell him either, and she kissed him instead.

He felt it. He pulled back an inch and looked at her face in the grey light from the window.

“You’re shaking,” he said.

“It was a long night.”

He thought it was fear. She saw him decide it was fear: Ah Sim, a cough, an old woman who’d raised her, her father ringing in the night. She saw him decide to be gentle about it.

He picked her up off the counter. He carried her up the stairs with her arms round his neck and her face in his shoulder, and laid her down, and she pulled him down after her before he could say anything kind, and he didn’t say anything at all.

chapters.title: The Cellar Under the Rope Store
chapters.desc: Raiden builds her a room under the building next to the garage, and Evangeline comes to hand her the instruments. The ghost never says a word.
chapters.epigraph: “I’ll hand you things.” — Evangeline Lee
chapters.content:
Raiden showed her the cellar on the Saturday after.

He didn’t say why. He came down the stairs from the flat at a quarter to six with two coffees instead of one, put hers on the bench by the rig, and stood there in his dressing gown until she’d finished the wire, and then said, “Come and look at something,” and went out of the side door into the street.

The building next to the garage was the old rope store. He and Jinx had owned it since the winter they bought the garage, and it had stood empty all that time, with its shutters down and TAI HING painted over the door in letters even older than the sign next door. He unlocked a small door at the side, off the street of chandlers, behind a stack of pallets, and went down a flight of stone steps with a torch.

It was a cellar. Long and low, with a brick floor and a vaulted ceiling and a smell of damp and old hemp. There was nothing in it at all except a drain in the middle of the floor and a tap on the wall.

He shone the torch round it.

“Baba rang me,” said Raiden. “On Sunday. About Mok’s boy.” He didn’t look at her. “He didn’t tell me anything else. He said you might need a room one day, and he didn’t want it to be his kitchen table. That’s all he said.”

Elara stood at the bottom of the steps.

“I can make it a room,” said Raiden. “If you want. I won’t ask what for.” He turned the torch on the drain, and the tap, and the bare brick walls. “There’s water. There’s a drain. There’s power next door. Nobody comes down this street at night except cats. Two weeks.”

She looked at her brother in his dressing gown with his torch, being careful not to look at her.

“Yes,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took him twelve days.

He did it the way he did everything that mattered, without telling anyone, with drawings nobody saw. A steel door at the top of the steps, painted to look like the old wooden one. Lights. A floor that could be washed. A big steel sink against the wall with taps you worked with your elbows. A long table with a padded top, and, over it, a proper operating light, a big round one on an arm, which he’d bought from a clinic on the other side of the harbour that had closed in the spring. Oxygen in tall cylinders chained to the wall. A fridge. A cupboard with a lock. A chair for whoever was waiting.

When it was done Jinx came down the steps behind her and stood looking at it with her hands in her overalls.

“Your room,” said Jinx.

Eliana came on the thirteenth day.

She came on her own, in a hoodie, in the afternoon, with a bag of cables, and Elara didn’t know who’d told her and didn’t ask. She put a phone on the wall by the door, an old-fashioned one with a cord, that would ring only there. She put a small camera over the steel door outside, pointing at the street, with a screen by the phone so you could see who was on the step before you opened it. It took her two hours. She didn’t say anything about what the room was for. She looked round it once, at the light and the table and the sink, and then at her sister.

“It’ll ring from Baba’s number,” said Eliana. “Or from one of Mok’s. Nobody else can get through.”

“Thank you.”

“I didn’t do anything,” said Eliana, and left.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first night it rang, Elara called Evangeline.

She knew why her. She stood in the cellar at one in the morning with the phone still warm in her hand and her father’s voice still in her ear, a dock worker, a crane, a hand caught under a crate, and the first person she thought of was her sister who didn’t talk, who’d sat on the floor of a noodle shop with a man’s head in her lap and a gun on the counter, and hadn’t flinched at any of it.

Ev answered on the first ring, the way she always did.

“I need someone to hand me things,” said Elara.

There was a pause on the line. Elara could hear Jun Hyuk somewhere in the background, asking who it was.

“I’ll hand you things,” said Evangeline.

She came in forty minutes, in a dark grey jumper with her hair tied back, and came down the steps and looked at the room without a word and went to the sink and started washing her hands, the way Elara showed her, every finger, both sides, to the elbow.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d decided before the first one came that the ghost wouldn’t speak.

Not a word, not to the patients and not to whoever brought them. A voice was something you remembered. A voice could be heard again, in a corridor, in a hospital, on a ward. A face could be covered with a mask and a cap, and eyes could be anybody’s, but a voice was yours.

So she didn’t speak. She wore scrubs she’d bought herself and a paper cap and a mask and her own red loupes, and she pointed, and Ev handed her what she pointed at. Two sisters in masks, in a cellar, in silence. If Ev had something to say she said it in one word, and usually she didn’t.

The dock worker was first.

They brought him in at half past one, two men from the docks with their arms round him, and laid him on the table, and his hand was in a towel. She unwrapped it.

She couldn’t look at it at first. She stood there with her own right hand in its glove and looked at his, crushed across the back, and she felt her wrist go cold. Then Ev’s hand touched her elbow, once. Elara looked up. Ev was looking at her over the mask with her calm grey eyes.

Elara started.

He was working without papers, and a hospital meant the police and a boat home, and without somebody he’d have lost the hand. She kept all his fingers. It took three hours. The men who’d brought him sat on the chair and the floor by the door and watched the masked woman work under the big light and didn’t say anything either, and when it was over and the hand was splinted and the dock worker was awake, one of them came over and bowed to her, low, the old way, the way people bowed to her father in the street.

“Thank you, Doctor,” he said. He looked at her mask, and her cap, and her eyes. “Doctor Ghost.”

She didn’t answer. She couldn’t.

That was the name, after that. She didn’t choose it. It went round the docks and the Walled City in a week, the way names did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came to the cellar on the first Sunday in August, in the afternoon, when it was empty.

He came down the steps slowly, in his good coat, and stood in the middle of the room and looked at the light and the table and the sink and the phone on the wall, and went grey, the way he did when the old days came up at dinner.

She’d written the rules out on a sheet of paper. She gave it to him.

He read them standing up. Only people who couldn’t go to a hospital and would die or lose a limb without her. No questions about what they’d done, from her or from him. No money to her, ever, from anyone. Anyone who could go to a hospital afterwards went, whatever it cost them, and the family made sure they did.

“And I can say no,” said Elara. “To any of them. Any time. You ask, and I say yes or no.”

He nodded. He folded the sheet and put it inside his coat, and then he took it out again and asked her for a pen, and signed the bottom of it, and gave it back to her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The girl came in the first week of August.

She was about seventeen. Someone had broken a bottle and used it on her face, in a bar, across the cheek, and her mother had brought her because her mother had worked for Lin Jian’s men twenty years ago and knew who to ring, and because the girl’s father was the one who’d done it. Elara closed it under the light for two hours with stitches so small that Ev had to pass them to her on the tip of her finger.

The girl didn’t cry. She lay on the table and looked at the ceiling and her mother held her hand, and when it was over the mother looked at the line on her daughter’s face, fine and close, which would go white and thin in a year and then be almost nothing, and put her hands over her own mouth.

The runner came the week after.

Her father had rung about him differently. He’d said a name she knew from the house on the hill, from Elowen’s dinners, a man who sat at the end of the table with a quiet face and a camel coat, and said this one was his and that he, her father, vouched for him. The runner was a boy of twenty with a bullet in the muscle of his calf, and it was shallow, and she took it out and washed it and packed it and left it open, and he swore at her the whole time, and she didn’t say a word back. When he limped out at dawn between two men in dark jackets, one of them stopped at the steel door and looked back at her and nodded, once.

She hummed through every one.

She didn’t know she was doing it. She never did. Ev knew. Ev stood across the table from her, handing her things, and listened to her sister hum the same tune she’d hummed at the top of the ladder in the shop, and on the morning in the kitchen on the hill, and in every theatre she’d ever stood in, and never said anything about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told Xing Yue she couldn’t sleep.

It was true. She hadn’t slept properly since November. She told him that some nights, when she couldn’t, she went to Jinx’s and used the rig, because it was the only thing that made her hand stop buzzing, and because Jinx and Raiden didn’t mind, and because it was better than lying awake beside him and keeping him awake too.

He looked at her across the counter.

“At night,” he said.

“Sometimes. Not often. When it’s bad.”

He didn’t say anything for a few seconds. She watched him put it away somewhere, the way he put things away.

“Take a taxi. On the card. Both ways.”

“I will.”

She did. About three nights a month she got up in the dark and took the black bag from the study cupboard, the one with her loupes and her cap and her mask in it, and went down the stairs with her shoes in her hand, and the taxi took her to the street of chandlers, and the card paid for it. He’d see it. She wanted him to see it. It was true, the taxi and the street and the garage door; it was only the cellar next door that wasn’t.

The first time, her phone buzzed in her pocket at two in the morning, while she was scrubbing.

Xing Yue: ?

She dried her hands and texted back with her left thumb.

Elara: rig. can’t sleep. go back to sleep

Xing Yue: Ring me when you’re leaving.

She did. She rang him from the street at four, with the black bag on her shoulder and the dock worker’s blood washed off her arms, and he answered on the first ring and said, “All right,” and she knew he’d been lying awake the whole time, looking at a small blue dot on the street of chandlers.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the day she was the anatomy tutor.

She was louder than she’d ever been. She knew it. The first-years thought she was the funniest person in the building. She stood at the end of the long cold tables with her pointer in her left hand and taught them the heart and the lungs and the long nerve that went from the brain to the belly and wandered, and she told them a story about every one. She made a boy who’d fainted in the first week laugh so hard he had to sit down. She brought sweets. She complained at the coffee machine about the man who called the little finger the fifth digit.

She went home at five and fell asleep on the sofa with her shoes on.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Sunday in August he looked at her across the breakfast counter and put his tea down.

“You’re exhausted,” he said.

“I’m fine.”

“You’ve got shadows under your eyes. You fell asleep on the sofa three times this week before seven. You fell asleep in the bath on Wednesday and I had to come and get you out.” He picked up his tea again. “Doctor’s orders. Bed. Four o’clock. Two hours. I’ll wake you.”

“You can’t prescribe me a nap.”

“I just did.”

She looked at him. He looked back, completely serious, a consultant on a ward round.

“Yes, Doctor,” said Elara. “Of course, Doctor. Four o’clock, Doctor. Shall I take it with food?”

She went on like that all day. She went on about it at lunch. She saluted him at three. At five to four she marched up the stairs announcing every step, and got into bed in her T-shirt, and lay on her back with her arms straight at her sides, and said, “Ready, Doctor.”

He came up after her. He didn’t laugh. He pulled the sheet and the blanket up over her, to her chin, and tucked them in down both sides, firmly, the way the nurses did, the way he’d done on the first morning, so she was wrapped up tight.

He bent over her and kissed her forehead.

“Two hours,” he said.

She got one arm out of the blanket, which took some doing, and caught the front of his shirt, and pulled.

He came down onto the bed half on top of her, with the blanket between them, and she held onto his shirt and looked up at him.

“Doctor,” she said. “I can’t sleep. There’s somebody standing over me.”

He looked down at her. Then he got under the blanket.

It was the slowest afternoon of the summer. The blinds were half down and the light came in in stripes, the way it had once, and the fan turned overhead, and neither of them hurried. He kissed her as though he had nowhere else to be all year.

She took his shirt off a button at a time with her right hand, slowly, and he watched her do it, and she didn’t see his face because she was looking at her own fingers on the buttons, and when she’d finished he took her hand and kissed the palm.

She pulled him down to her. She felt the weight of him, and his breath at her ear, and his hands, careful and then not, and the long slow climb of it, with the fan going round and the light moving on the ceiling, until she forgot the cellar and the black bag and the phone on the wall and there was nothing in her but him. She said his name. She said it into his shoulder, and into his mouth, and once out loud, and he laughed against her neck.

She did sleep, afterwards. Two hours exactly. He woke her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lay on her side in the evening light with his arm over her, and looked at his face.

He was half asleep. His glasses were on the floor. He had his thumb on the inside of her wrist, the way he always did, on the pulse, over the scar.

She thought about telling him.

She could. She could say it now, in this bed, in this light. Xing Yue. My hand works. I’ve got a room under the rope store. I took a bullet out of a boy’s leg on Friday and he swore at me the whole time. She could feel the words in her mouth. She could feel how easy it would be, and how he’d open his eyes.

She didn’t.

He was the only part of her life that nobody had bled on. She’d told him that once, in his car, on her birthday, when the worst thing she was keeping from him was a red door. It was truer now. Everything else had blood on it. Her father’s kitchen table. Her own hand. The cellar. This bed didn’t. He didn’t.

She shut her eyes and kept it that way, and felt his thumb on her pulse, and pretended to go back to sleep.

chapters.title: The Pillowcase
chapters.desc: He wakes at two in the morning to find her sewing up a torn pillowcase by the light of her phone. He knows a surgeon’s hands when he sees them, and a week later he follows her to a steel door.
chapters.epigraph: “Go back to sleep. It’s only a pillowcase.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
He woke at two because the light was wrong.

It was a small cold light, low down, on her side of the bed. He lay on his back with his eyes almost shut and turned his head a little on the pillow, and saw it was her phone, propped against the lamp on the bedside table, with the torch on and the beam pointed at her lap.

She was sitting up against the headboard with her knees drawn up, in his old grey T-shirt, and his pillowcase was across her knees.

His pillowcase. He was lying on the bare pillow. He hadn’t noticed her take it. He looked at it in the small light and saw the long tear down the side seam, where her watch strap must have caught it when she turned over, and the thread hanging out of it, and the needle going in and out.

She was sewing it.

She had the little travel kit from his washbag open beside her on the duvet, the one he’d been given on a plane years ago and never used, with the three colours of thread and the two needles. She’d chosen the white. She had the edges of the tear pinched together in her left hand and the needle in her right.

Her right.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t move.

He lay with his eyes nearly shut and watched her through his lashes, and his whole body went still, the way it went in theatre when something started bleeding that shouldn’t.

She was doing a running stitch down the seam. Small stitches, close together, evenly spaced. The needle went in and came out and went in again, and her fingers turned it each time without looking, the way you’d turn a needle in a holder. She didn’t hesitate. She didn’t fumble. When she got to the end of a stretch she changed to a locked stitch, looping the thread back through itself so it wouldn’t pull, and the tension on every one was exactly the same as the one before. He could see it from where he lay. Every stitch sat flat.

At the end of the seam she tied it off.

She did it with her fingers, without the needle, in the half-dark, one-handed. Her right hand. She made the loop and threw the knot and pulled it down, and did it again, and again, the way he’d been taught to tie a knot deep inside a body where there was no room for two hands, the way he’d watched her tie them in a skills lab on a banana four years ago, faster than him. She snipped the thread with the little scissors from the kit.

She was humming.

He knew the tune. He’d heard it in theatre the first day, over Mr. Yin, under her breath. He’d heard it in his kitchen over a cake with sugar camellias. He’d told her once that it went up at the end, and she hadn’t known she did it.

She hadn’t hummed it since November. He hadn’t heard her hum anything since November at all.

She was humming it now, under her breath, in the light from her phone, with a needle in her right hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

He must have breathed. She looked round.

She saw his face on the bare pillow, and her hands went still on the pillowcase.

“Go back to sleep,” said Elara. “It’s only a pillowcase. My watch tore it. I couldn’t sleep, so I thought I’d—” She stopped. “Go back to sleep.”

He made a sound, something sleepy, and turned over away from her, onto his side, and shut his eyes.

Behind him he heard her let out her breath. He heard the travel kit close. He heard the phone light click off and the bed move as she lay down, and he lay on his side in the dark with his eyes open and his heart going so hard he thought she’d feel it through the mattress.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went through it like a case.

He couldn’t help it. It was what he did with anything that frightened him. He lay still in the dark and laid it all out, every finding, in order, the way he’d present a patient at the morning meeting.

The cups. She held every cup in both hands. She’d done it since January, and in the spring she’d started doing it more, not less, and he’d seen her once in the study through the half-open door pick up a mug of tea in her right hand without thinking, and then see him, and put her left hand under it.

The buttons. She’d fumbled her buttons in June worse than she had in March. He’d done them for her every morning, from the bottom, and once, on a day she was late, she’d done the top three herself in the mirror without looking, fast, before she remembered he was there.

Dr. Meng, in the corridor outside theatres, telling him to ask Elara. He hadn’t asked.

The note under the teapot, in July. Ah Sim’s not well. Written left-handed, which she only did now when she didn’t want the writing to look like anything. Ah Sim’s chest. Elara coming home at half past five, shaking, and kissing him on the counter as if she were drowning. He’d thought it was fear. He’d been wrong.

The black bag in the study cupboard. Three nights a month. The taxi statements, every one, to the street of chandlers by the Docks, between one and four in the morning. The rig. She couldn’t sleep. She went to the rig.

Evangeline, who never left Fig Tree Lane at night, whose car he’d passed once in August at four in the morning on the harbour road, driving home from a call. He’d thought nothing of it.

And the tune, tonight. In the dark. Over a needle.

He lay and looked at all of it, and it was as plain as a scan.

Her hand was back, and not as a tingle in a fingertip: a surgeon’s hand, fast and exact and sure, tying one-handed knots in the dark. And she was using it, three nights a month, on people who couldn’t go to hospitals, somewhere near the Docks, with her sister handing her things.

And she hadn’t told him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He got up at half past two and went to the bathroom and shut the door.

He sat down on the edge of the bath in the dark without turning on the light.

The relief came first. He hadn’t expected it to be the first thing. It came up through him so hard it hurt, like a cramp, and he put his face in his hands and sat there on the cold edge of the bath with it going through him. Her hands. Her hands were back. Nine months of the sums, a millimetre a day, the small muscles that came back last if at all. Nine months of cutting her food into squares and doing her buttons and kissing her fingers in the dark and feeling her not feel it. And she’d sat up in bed and sewn his pillowcase faster than he could have done it himself.

He stayed with that. He let himself.

Then the fear came. Because he knew what a cellar near the Docks at two in the morning meant in this city. He’d closed the notes of a man with a nail-gun injury from a building site. He’d sat at the bottom of a hill road in his car for two weeks. He knew what came in through the back doors of the Lins’ lives at night, and what it took to fix it, and that she’d go towards it every time it rang, because she’d told him so, sitting on the floor of the hall with her shoes pointing at the door. Don’t ask me to.

Then, under both of those, smaller and worse, the hurt.

She hadn’t told him. She’d felt her hand come back, finger by finger, and she hadn’t told him. She’d lain in bed and let him kiss her fingertips every night and pretended she couldn’t feel them. She’d let him do her buttons. She’d let him cut her food.

He sat with that one longest.

And then, because he was who he was, he went back to the supply room. Three and a half years ago, at twenty-five past three in the morning, a girl in scrubs with a bag of fluid in each hand, shaking, saying don’t ask me, please, if you ask I’ll tell you and then it’s yours too.

I won’t ask.

He’d said it. He’d meant it. He’d kept it through the drips and the hill road and the stock book and the bridge and the noodle shop, and he was going to keep it now.

He sat on the edge of the bath until the window went from black to dark grey, and decided.

He wouldn’t ask her. He wouldn’t make her stop. He’d never once wanted her to stop; he’d watched her face in cubicle eleven with the constable and loved it. And he wouldn’t let her be alone with it either. He didn’t know yet how. He’d find out.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he went back she was asleep, or pretending.

She was lying on her side facing the window. The pillowcase was back on his pillow, smoothed flat, the seam turned to the underside where he wouldn’t see it.

He got in behind her. He put his mouth against her shoulder through the T-shirt and kissed it, once. Then he found her right hand on the sheet in front of her and took it in his, and turned it over, and put his thumb on the inside of her wrist, on the pulse, on the scar.

It was quick and light. She was awake.

He didn’t say anything. He held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning he looked at the pillowcase in daylight while she was in the shower.

The seam was perfect. Small even stitches the whole length of the tear, locked at the end, with a knot so neat he had to look for it. Better than his. He’d have been pleased with it on a face.

He put the pillowcase back on his own pillow, on his own side of the bed, seam side up, and didn’t change it for a month.

✦ ✦ ✦

At dawn on Sunday, he woke her.

He hadn’t planned it. He woke before her, the way he always did, and lay in the grey light and looked at her asleep with her hair across the pillow and her right hand curled on the sheet between them, and he took it.

He turned it over, slowly, palm up. He looked at the scar. It had gone from red to pink over the summer, a line across the inside of the wrist and the zigzag up the forearm where Meng had opened it. He’d looked at it so many times. He’d looked at it as a surgeon, checking it, and as the man who’d held it shut on the stones of an alley.

He bent his head and kissed it. The wrist first, across the line. Then up the zigzag, a kiss at every angle of it, slowly, all the way to her elbow.

She was awake before he’d got halfway.

She didn’t open her eyes at first. He felt her wake, the change in her breathing, and her fingers move in his. Then she made a sleepy sound and pulled her hand out of his and put it in his hair, her right hand, and held on, and pulled him up to her mouth before she could have been sure it was even morning.

He let her pull.

It was slow. It was the slowest he’d ever been with her, slower than the first morning, slower than her birthday. He kissed her as though he had all the time in the world and was going to use it. He took her T-shirt off in the grey light and kissed every bit of her he could reach. He held her right hand down on the pillow beside her head with his fingers through hers, and felt her fingers grip back, hard, with a strength that hadn’t been there in March, and didn’t say anything about it. She said his name. She said it into his shoulder in that low voice with no stories in it, and arched up against him, and held on.

She thought he was gentle because of her hand. He could see her think it. She looked up at him once, with her eyes half shut and her face flushed, and he saw her decide that he was being careful of her.

He was being grateful, and nothing else. He was thanking her body for coming back to her, every part of it, slowly, and he didn’t stop until the room was full of light and she’d forgotten to think anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the next Friday night she got up at twenty to two.

He was awake. He’d been awake every night that week, lying on his back with his eyes shut, waiting. He heard her slide out from under his arm. He heard her dress in the bathroom in the dark, and the study cupboard open, and the soft sound of the black bag being lifted out, and her bare feet on the stairs, and the front door.

He gave her two minutes. Then he got up and dressed and went down to the car.

He knew where she was going. He’d known for weeks where her taxis went at night. He didn’t need to see her dot on his phone. He looked anyway, at the lights at the bottom of the hill, and it was going east along the harbour road towards the Docks, the way it always went.

He followed it.

He didn’t think about whether he should. He’d decided on the edge of the bath that he wouldn’t ask. He hadn’t decided that he wouldn’t look.

✦ ✦ ✦

The street of chandlers was narrow and dark and smelled of the harbour.

He parked at the top of it, by the marine paint shop, with the lights off. It had started to rain. He could see the garage halfway down, under its old painted sign, with the shutter down and no light behind it. Next to it was the old rope store, empty for years, with its shutters down too.

Her taxi was pulling away from the kerb outside it.

She was on the pavement with the black bag on her shoulder. She looked up the street and down it, and he sat still in the dark car and didn’t breathe, and she didn’t see him. Then she went to a door at the side of the rope store, behind a stack of pallets, a door that looked old and wooden in the streetlight, and knocked, twice, and it opened from inside, and she went in.

He waited ten minutes. Then he got out of the car and walked down the street in the rain.

The door was steel. Close to, under the paint, he could see it. Steel painted to look like old wood, with no handle on the outside, and a small black camera above it under the eave, pointing at the step where he was standing. He looked up at it. He thought of Eliana, and didn’t move away.

He put his hand flat on the door.

It was cold and wet. He stood there with the rain coming down the back of his collar and his palm on the steel and listened.

At first there was nothing. The rain. A cat somewhere. The water in the gutter.

Then, faint, from a long way down, through the steel and the stone, he heard her humming.

The same tune. Going up at the end.

He stood in the rain and listened to it. He didn’t know how long. Long enough for the rain to soak through the shoulders of his coat. Then there was another voice, a woman’s, low and flat, saying one word.

“Clamp.”

Evangeline.

He took his hand off the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in bed when she came back at four.

He heard the front door, and her feet on the stairs, and the bathroom, the tap running a long time. Then she came in and got into bed behind him, carefully, so as not to wake him, and lay there.

He kept his eyes shut and his breathing slow.

She was cold. She’d come through the rain. After a while she moved closer and put her forehead against the back of his neck, and her arm round his waist, and her hand flat on his chest, her right one. He felt it shaking a little, the way it had on the counter in July, and he knew now what that was: what was left in your hands at the end of a long case.

He didn’t turn over. He didn’t say anything. He put his hand over hers on his chest, and found her wrist, and put his thumb on her pulse, and held it there until she went to sleep against his back.

chapters.title: Notes in the Margins
chapters.desc: He starts leaving surgical journals open on the kitchen table at the hardest cases. She can’t resist writing in the margins, and he answers.
chapters.epigraph: “Come to bed.” — Wang Xing Yue, in pencil
chapters.content:
The first one was open on the kitchen table when she came down at one in the morning for water.

A trauma journal. He had them delivered, four or five a month, and read them at the counter with his tea and left them in a pile on the shelf by the Pu’er. This one was on the table, open, flat, with the lamp on over it, as if he’d been reading it and gone up to bed in the middle.

It was a case report. A young man, a motorbike, a torn artery behind the knee, and what the surgeons in some city hospital had done about it, in what order, with photographs.

She read it standing up with her glass of water.

She read it again sitting down. She got to the part where they’d gone straight to repairing the artery, which had taken them three hours, while the leg below the knee went without blood the whole time, and she sat back and looked at the ceiling. There was a pencil in the gutter of the journal. She picked it up, in her right hand, and wrote in the margin beside the paragraph, small:

I’d have shunted first. Get blood to the leg, then take your time.

She looked at it. Then she put the pencil back in the gutter where she’d found it and went up to bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, under her note, in handwriting that looked like a heart monitor having a bad day, he’d written:
