Agree. But they’d no shunts on the shelf. What would you have used?

She read it at the counter with her tea. He’d already gone to work. She read it three times, and her face went hot, and she didn’t know why it should, and she picked up the pencil and wrote under it:

Anything. A bit of tubing. A drip line. I read once about a man in a war who used a

She stopped. She rubbed out the last four words with the end of the pencil, hard, until the paper went thin. Then she wrote Anything clean, and left the journal open and went to the medical school.

✦ ✦ ✦

It went on for three weeks.

He never said anything about it. Not at dinner, not in bed, not over the tea in the morning. There’d just be a journal on the table at night, open at a page, with the lamp on, and the pencil in the gutter. A gunshot to the liver. A woman whose spleen had torn days after a fall. A boy with a knife wound in the neck, and the photograph of it, which she looked at with her hand flat on the table. She’d read it, and write in the margin, and in the morning there’d be an answer under hers.

He asked her questions. Real ones, the kind you’d ask a registrar you trusted at three in the morning. What would she do if the pressure didn’t come up. When would she stop and pack and come back tomorrow. Whether she’d have waited for the scan.

She answered every one.

She couldn’t help it. She’d sit at the kitchen table at one in the morning in his T-shirt with her hair coming down and her right hand moving across the margin, small and quick, and she’d forget where she was. She’d write things she’d done, without ever saying she’d done them: how you’d manage under a big round light, with your sister handing you things. Once she wrote it’s easier than it looks if you’ve got someone holding the light still, and looked at it, and rubbed it out.

She was a little hurt, too. She knew she was being stupid about it.

He didn’t say anything. He wrote back, every time, careful, interested, and never once said you could do this or you’ll do this again. He talked to her in the margins as if she were a surgeon thinking about surgery. As if that were all it could ever be: thinking. He thought she sat at a table at night and imagined it.

She wanted to shake him. She wanted to say: I took a bullet out of a boy’s leg in August. I closed a girl’s face so fine it’ll be gone in a year.

She wrote in the margins instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Thursday in September the journal was open at a diagram.

A repair to a big vessel in the thigh, drawn in thin black lines, with arrows, the way they drew them in the textbooks. She’d come down at half past twelve because she couldn’t sleep, which was true for once, and she’d seen the lamp on and come over.

She studied the diagram. She picked up the pencil and wrote beside it: I’d put the stitches closer at the back wall, where you can’t see, because that’s where it leaks, and you won’t know till

There was already something written under the diagram, at the bottom of the page. She hadn’t seen it.

Come to bed.

She looked at it. She looked up at the ceiling, where he was. She bent over the journal again and wrote under it, firmly: Five minutes.

She went back to the back wall.

She’d got as far as and if you’ve got a second pair of hands, they should when she heard him on the stairs. She didn’t look up. She heard him come into the kitchen behind her in his bare feet, and stop, and she went on writing, faster, because she was nearly at the end of the sentence.

“That’s six,” he said.

“I’m nearly—”

He took the pencil out of her hand.

He took it in the middle of the word should, between her fingers, and she looked up to protest, and he bent down over her where she sat bent over the journal, and kissed her.

He kissed her upside down, from behind and above, with one hand flat on the open journal and the other on her jaw, tilting her face up to his. She made a sound against his mouth. Her elbow knocked the lamp. She got her hand up behind her into his hair and held on, and he didn’t stop, and the journal slid sideways on the table under his hand, and he didn’t stop then either.

When he did, he stayed bent over her, with his forehead on hers, upside down.

“Five minutes,” he said.

“I said five. You came at six. I can’t help it if you can’t tell the time.” She was laughing. “I hadn’t finished the back wall.”

“Finish it in the morning.”

He pulled her up out of the chair by her hands, both of them, and she went, and halfway up the stairs she remembered that she’d been holding the pencil in her right hand and writing small and fast for twenty minutes and that he’d taken it out of her fingers, and she looked at him on the step above her, and he didn’t say anything about it at all.

In the morning, under should, in his writing, it said: be holding the light still. You told me that two weeks ago. And under that: Then rubbed it out.

She sat at the counter with her tea and went cold, and then hot, and then decided she’d imagined it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Yu Chen came to dinner on the last Saturday in September.

He came most months. He’d started his emergency training at City Hospital in August, and Xing Yue was still his mentor, though nobody had made him be for over a year, and he still came. He brought a bag of oranges and sat at the counter in a grey jumper with his ears going red every time Elara asked him about Eliana, and she asked him about Eliana every few minutes on purpose.

After dinner she went to get the tea from the cupboard by the stairs, and she heard them in the kitchen through the half-open door.

“How did you know?” said Yu Chen. His voice had gone low. “When to ask her. How did you know she’d say yes?”

There was a pause. She could see a slice of Xing Yue through the gap, leaning on the counter with his arms folded.

“I didn’t know the first time,” he said. “I had a hook put in her locker anyway.”

“That’s not—”

“The second time I knew. She’d given it back. I asked anyway.” He looked at his cousin. “You don’t ask because you know. You ask because you can’t not.”

Yu Chen didn’t say anything. She saw him look at his hands on the counter.

Elara stood in the hall with the tea tin against her chest. She went back in a minute later, loudly, and put the tin on the counter and looked from one to the other with her eyebrows right up.

“What are you two whispering about?” she said. “You’ve both gone pink. You’ve both got exactly the same pink ears. It must be in the family. Yu Chen, are you asking him about girls? He’s no use. He proposed to me next to a fish.”

Yu Chen went scarlet. Xing Yue cleaned his glasses.

She didn’t tell Eliana. She kept it to herself, and it nearly killed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hillclimb was on the first Sunday in October, on the old pass in the north.

They drove up the night before, the whole family, in four cars. The road closed for one weekend every year, and the finish was at the top of the pass, on a wide gravel shoulder beside the timing hut, with the mountain falling away on one side into a valley full of cloud.

They stood at the finish line in a row in the cold. Her father in his good coat. Elowen in green, and Zhao in black behind her like a wall. Ev in pale blue with Jun Hyuk, who’d brought a flask and a folding chair for Baba and a bag of pastries for everyone and was explaining to the marshal next to him how the sidecar’s steering worked. Eliana with a laptop and a camera on a stick, and Yu Chen beside her, holding the laptop. Jinx’s father, with a pigeon in a basket that he’d been told not to bring. Serafina on the wall by the timing hut, in a red jumper, with her husband, shouting.

Elara stood next to her father, with Xing Yue on her other side.

She’d started going back to Sunday lunch in August. Not every week. She and Baba didn’t talk about November. They talked about Ah Sim’s knees and the price of fish. Today, when she’d come to stand by him, he’d moved over on the gravel to make room for her without looking, and she’d taken it.

The two old outfits from the north went first. Four minutes nine, and four minutes seven.

Then the black one.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t watch Raiden. Everyone else watched Raiden, hanging off the side of the chair with his whole body out over the road on the right-handers, so far that Elowen put her hand over her mouth.

Elara watched Jinx’s hands.

On the bars. Through the last corners, the long right before the finish, flat out. She could see them through the visor of her helmet, as the outfit came up the last straight towards them. Small and sure and still. Not fighting the bike. Holding it, exactly as hard as it needed, not one bit harder, at a hundred and something kilometres an hour with the chair going light.

She knew those hands. She’d watched them every morning for seven months, black with oil, at the other end of a garage, building something for her.

Four minutes five point six. One point four seconds.

The outfit stopped on the gravel in front of them. Raiden was off the chair before Jinx had her helmet off. He took it off for her, and put it on the tank, and kissed her, there, in front of everyone, with both hands in her hair, and she grabbed the front of his leathers in both fists and kissed him back so hard they both went over against the bike. Somebody whistled. Somebody else said hm. Her father laughed, the big rusty one, right across the top of the mountain, and Elara laughed too, and found she was crying.

Over Raiden’s shoulder, Jinx opened her eyes and looked straight at her.

Jinx didn’t smile. She looked at Elara across the gravel for a second, with her brother’s hands in her hair, and Elara looked back, and they both knew what they were both thinking about: a steel frame bolted to a bench, and a wire that had stopped buzzing.

Elara looked away. She found Xing Yue watching her.

He’d seen it. She could tell. He’d seen her look at Jinx and Jinx look at her, and he was standing there beside her in his dark coat, and he didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

It got cold on top of the mountain as the afternoon went.

She was in a jacket that wasn’t warm enough, because she never had the right coat, and she was standing behind the timing hut out of the wind with her hands under her arms when he came round the corner. He looked at her. He unbuttoned his coat, the long dark wool one, and opened it, and put her inside it, and buttoned it again round both of them as far as it would go, which was nearly to her chin.

She stood inside his coat with her face against his shirt and her hands round his back, getting warm.

“You were crying,” he said.

“I cry at everything good.”

“I know.”

She tipped her head back and looked up at him from inside the coat.

She didn’t say anything. She pulled her hands out from round his back and took his face in them and kissed him, standing on her toes on the gravel behind the timing hut, with the cloud coming up out of the valley and the noise of the family on the other side of the hut, and Serafina still shouting. He bent his head to her. She kissed him slowly, with her cold hands warming on his face, until she’d stopped shaking from the wind, and then for longer.

“I want that,” she said, against his mouth. “One day. What they did. I want to win something with someone. Not on my own. Not with nobody knowing. With someone holding the other side.”

He looked down at her.

“You will,” he said.

He said it as though he knew. As though it were a result he’d already read. She looked up at him from inside his coat and nearly asked him what he meant.

She didn’t. She put her face back against his shirt instead, and he held her, and on the other side of the timing hut she heard her father laugh again.

chapters.title: Doctor Ghost
chapters.desc: A young man on a trolley hears Elara humming and calls her Doctor Ghost. Xing Yue lies in the notes, goes through her black bag in the night, and nearly breaks his promise.
chapters.epigraph: “Doctor Ghost? It’s you, isn’t it?” — Ding Jiale
chapters.content:
On Tuesdays she brought him lunch.

She’d started in September, on the days she taught only in the morning. She came down the hill from the medical school at half past twelve with two boxes from the noodle place opposite the ambulance bay and came in through the main doors and down the corridor past the emergency department to the lifts, and they ate on the stairs in the east stairwell, where nobody went, on the landing between the eighth floor and the ninth.

On the third Tuesday in October he was in the emergency department already, at the nurses’ station, writing up a referral, when he heard her coming.

She was humming. She was walking down the corridor with the noodle boxes in a bag in her left hand, in her cardigan, with her lanyard from the medical school round her neck, and she was humming under her breath without knowing she was doing it. The tune that went up at the end.

On a trolley against the corridor wall, waiting for a bay, a young man lifted his head.

He was skinny, about nineteen, with a drip in his arm and a sheet over his legs, and he’d been lying with his eyes shut. He opened them. He pushed himself up on his elbows and stared after her as she went past.

“Doctor Ghost?” he said. “It’s you, isn’t it?”

She didn’t stop. She didn’t turn her head. She kept walking at exactly the same speed, humming, and turned the corner to the lifts and was gone.

The young man lay back down on the trolley. He was staring at the ceiling.

Xing Yue put his pen down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty minutes later the emergency registrar asked him to see the young man in bay six.

“Thigh wound,” she said. “Infected. He says it’s old. He says he came off a scooter last week and split it open and left it. But it’s been stitched, and it’s—” She stopped. “Can you just look at it?”

His name was Ding Jiale. He was on bail. It was in the notes in red, in the box for police involvement, and there was a constable’s number beside it.

Xing Yue drew the curtain and looked at the leg.

The skin had opened along one end of an old scar on the front of the thigh, red and hot, with pus in it, where somebody had been careless with a scooter and then with the wound. Under that, where it hadn’t opened, the scar was a fine straight line. He pressed along it with two gloved fingers and felt what was underneath: the deep layer closed, and the layer above that, and then the skin, every stitch where it should be, small and close and even.

He’d seen that closure before. On a banana. On a pillowcase.

He looked up. The boy was watching him.

“Who closed this?” said Xing Yue.

“Nobody. A clinic.”

“Which clinic?”

“I don’t know. A private one. I was out of it.” The boy’s eyes went to the curtain and back. “My grandad took me. I had my eyes shut. I didn’t see anything.” He swallowed. “I only heard her. She hummed. The whole time. And everyone says—”

Xing Yue leaned down.

He put one hand flat on the trolley beside the boy’s head and bent until his face was close to the boy’s, and spoke low, so that nobody on the other side of the curtain could have heard a word of it.

“If you say that word again in this building,” he said, “to anyone, to a nurse, to a porter, to the man in the next bay, I’ll have you discharged straight into the back of a police car. I’ll ring the number in your notes myself. You’ll be in a cell tonight with your leg like this.” He watched the boy’s face. “Do you understand me?”

The boy had gone white. He nodded.

“Say it.”

“I understand.”

Xing Yue straightened up. He opened the curtain. He told the nurse what the boy needed: the wound opened up and cleaned properly, the antibiotics, a surgical review in the morning. Then he sat down at the computer outside bay six and wrote in the notes, under the registrar’s history, in his own name:

Old laceration, left anterior thigh, primary closure at a private clinic in July. Superficial wound breakdown and infection after trauma. Deep layers intact.

He read it once. He signed it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was on the landing in the east stairwell with the noodles open on her knees.

She looked up when the door banged. She’d been waiting twenty minutes, and she was going to say so; he could see it in her face. She had her mouth open to say it.

He crossed the landing in two steps and pulled her up off the stair by her arms, and the noodle box went over, and he put her against the wall and kissed her.

He didn’t say anything first. He kissed her hard, with his whole body holding her to the cold painted wall of the stairwell and his hand on the back of her head, the way he’d kissed her once in a hall at one in the morning when she’d come home from a noodle shop. She made a startled sound against his mouth. Then she grabbed his shirt, both fists, and kissed him back, and her lanyard caught between them, and somewhere above them a door opened on the ninth floor and shut again.

When he let her go she stayed against the wall, breathing hard, looking up at him.

“That was the hospital,” she said. “You said not in the hospital.”

“I know what I said.”

She didn’t let go of his shirt. She was looking at his face, and whatever she saw there made her own go still.

“What happened? Who did you shout at?”

“Nobody.”

“You’ve got your bad face. The one for registrars.” She put her hand on his cheek. “Bad morning?”

“Bad morning,” said Xing Yue.

She looked at him for a second. Then she bent down and picked up the noodle box, which had landed the right way up, by some miracle, and sat back down on the stair and held his out to him.

“Eat that,” said Elara. “Then you can tell me or not tell me.”

He sat down beside her and ate it. He didn’t tell her. She didn’t ask. Halfway through, she leaned against his shoulder, and he felt her start to hum, and then stop herself, and he didn’t say anything about that either.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Friday Yu Chen was hurt in the emergency department, and Xing Yue spent the night in the hospital with his cousin. He got home at seven in the morning and Elara was awake on the sofa, and she didn’t ask about any of it, only held out her arms.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went through the black bag on the last Saturday in October.

He’d known since the pillowcase that he would. He’d gone through the green bag in the hall cupboard two years ago, more than once, and moved the scissors to the side pocket and thrown out the old saline, and never said a word. This was the same. He told himself it was the same.

She was asleep. It was three in the morning, a night she hadn’t gone out. He went down the stairs in the dark and opened the study cupboard and took the bag out, a black sports bag with a broken zip-pull she’d replaced with a paperclip, and carried it into the kitchen and put it on the table under the lamp, and opened it.

Her red loupes, in their black case, with E.L. inside the arm.

A paper theatre cap, folded. Two masks. A pair of dark scrubs he’d never seen, washed and rolled. Gloves, her size, in a box with the hospital’s name on it. A head torch. A roll of tape. A packet of sterile drapes from the skills lab at the medical school, the kind they used for teaching. A handful of sutures, some of them the good ones, most of them the cheap teaching kind that frayed. A small set of instruments in a cloth roll, old, worn, that he didn’t recognise and that had probably belonged to Old Hou. One needle holder with a stiff hinge.

He laid it all out on the table in rows and looked at it.

She was working with this. In a cellar, at two in the morning, on people who’d die without her. With teaching sutures and a stiff needle holder and drapes meant for a banana.

He wrote a list on the prescription pad.

He put everything back exactly as he’d found it, every item in its place, the loupes on top, the zip closed to the paperclip, and put the bag back in the cupboard. He went back to bed. She hadn’t moved.

On Monday he rang a surgical supplier he’d used for years, the one the private hospitals in the north used, and ordered on his own account. Good sutures, the ones he’d want himself. A set of fine instruments, the best they made, in a case. Sterile packs. A proper needle holder. He had it delivered to his office.

It went into the bag a little at a time, over the next two weeks, at night, while she slept. A box of sutures under the scrubs. The new needle holder in the cloth roll, where the stiff one had been. The instrument case at the bottom, under everything.

She noticed on the third night. He saw her in the study in the morning with the bag open on the desk, holding up the needle holder, turning it in the light from the window, with her mouth open.

That afternoon he heard her on the phone in the study to Jinx, asking carefully, without saying what, whether Jinx had put anything in her bag. Then to Evangeline. Then she stood at the study window with the needle holder in her hand.

She decided it was Ev. He could see her decide it. At dinner she was cheerful and said nothing at all about it, and he cut his own food and didn’t look up.

✦ ✦ ✦

He knew the nights now.

About three a month. Always the same black bag. Always the same street on his phone, the street of chandlers by the Docks, between one and four in the morning, and always the same taxi on the statement afterwards, out and back. He knew which nights she’d come home and stand in the shower for twenty minutes. He knew which nights she came home and didn’t, and got straight into bed cold, and put her hand on his chest.

He didn’t hate himself for looking. He’d thought he might. He didn’t. He’d look again, every time, for as long as she went. If anything ever went wrong down those stone steps, he wanted to be the one who knew where she was.

✦ ✦ ✦

An Yu rang on Sunday, the way he did every Sunday, to tell him he worked too hard.

Xing Yue took it on the roof terrace. She was downstairs in the kitchen, singing along to the radio, badly.

“You sound wrong,” said An Yu.

“I’m fine.”

“You’re not. You sound like you did the year before you came south.” A pause. His brother never wasted words; he waited until he’d chosen them. “Is it her?”

Xing Yue looked out over the hospital tower and the harbour.

He told him. Not all of it. Not the cellar or the street or the steel door. He told him that she was doing something she hadn’t told him about, something that could hurt her, and that he knew, and that she didn’t know he knew.

“Ask her,” said An Yu.

“I promised I wouldn’t.”

There was a silence on the line. An Yu didn’t ask what he’d promised or when. He never did.

“Then don’t ask her,” he said. “Tell her.”

Xing Yue didn’t answer.

“Tell her you know,” said An Yu. “That isn’t asking. You keep your promise and she stops being on her own with it. Isn’t that what you want?”

“Not yet.”

“Why not?”

He didn’t have an answer. He stood on the roof with the phone at his ear and the wind coming up off the harbour and thought about her face in the study window with the needle holder, deciding it was Ev, because it was easier than deciding it was him.

“Because she hasn’t told me,” he said. “If I tell her first, I’ve taken it.”

An Yu didn’t say anything.

“You’ve always been like this,” he said. “You’d rather wait at the bottom of a hill for two weeks than walk up it.” Then, before Xing Yue could answer: “Eat something. Ring me next Sunday.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the second Friday in November she went out at twenty to two.

He heard her go. He lay on his back in the dark and listened to the study cupboard and the stairs and the door, and didn’t get up. He didn’t follow her. He’d done that once. He lay there and looked at his phone on the pillow, at the small blue dot going east along the harbour road, and then stopping, on the street of chandlers, and staying there.

It stayed there two hours. He watched it the whole time.

At four it moved. He put the phone face down on the bedside table and turned on his side, away from her side, and shut his eyes.

She came in at twenty past. The shower ran. Then she came and got into bed behind him, and lay on her back, and he could hear that she wasn’t asleep and wasn’t going to be.

The room was dark. Neither of them moved.

“Xing Yue—” she said.

He waited. He didn’t move. He kept his breathing slow and even, and every muscle he had was waiting.

She didn’t say anything else. He felt her turn her head on the pillow towards his back. He heard her breathe in, as if she were going to start, the way she started a story, with three things to say and the third one the important one.

“Nothing,” said Elara. “Go back to sleep.”

He lay with his eyes open in the dark until it got light.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six he turned over and kissed her.

She was asleep at last, on her side, facing him, with her hair over her face. He took her face in his hands and kissed her awake, hard, the way he’d kissed her in the stairwell, as though nothing had happened and as though something had.

She woke into it. She made a sound against his mouth and grabbed him, both arms round his neck, and held on too tight. She pulled him down onto her and held on as if he were going somewhere. He kissed her until she was gasping, and then she pulled back an inch and looked up at him in the grey light with her eyes wet.

“I love you,” she said. And then again, at once, before he could answer, “I love you.”

She said it the way you say sorry.

“I love you,” said Xing Yue.

He said it once. He said it the way you make a promise, looking at her, and then he bent his head and kissed her again before she could say anything else, and she let him, and held on.

chapters.title: Two Surgeons, One Table
chapters.desc: Zhao’s guard is shot at the armory gate and is bleeding faster than one surgeon can stop. Elara makes the call she swore she’d never make.
chapters.epigraph: “Call him. Tell him to bring blood.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
At five past one her phone buzzed on the bedside table, and the screen said BABA.

She took it out onto the landing. She’d learned to wake and move in the same second, without a sound, the way he did when his pager went.

“It’s Zhao,” said her father. “His man’s been shot. At the armory gate, ten minutes ago. In the leg. It’s bad. Zhao’s own surgeon is at the Crestview and the Crestview’s half an hour, and he says the boy won’t last half an hour.” He breathed. “I’ve given him the door. He’s taking him there now. He doesn’t know who’s behind it. I didn’t tell him.”

“Who is it?”

“Peng,” said her father. “From the gatehouse.”

She stood on the dark landing with the phone against her ear.

Peng. The young guard who’d rung her at twenty past three on a March night three and a half years ago, his voice high and breaking, she said steal it if you have to. Who’d driven her up the hill road every morning for two weeks and down again, and never once asked her anything, and always had the heater on.

“I’m going,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t look back at the bed. He was asleep. She told herself he was asleep.

She dressed in the bathroom in the dark, took the black bag from the study, and went down the stairs with her shoes in her hand. There was a taxi on the rank at the bottom of the hill, the way there always was. She gave the driver the card and said the street of chandlers, and fast, please, and he looked at her face in the mirror and was.

She rang Ev from the taxi.

“Forty minutes,” said Evangeline. “Bao’s getting the car.”

“Come as fast as you can.”

The line went dead. Elara sat in the back of the taxi with the black bag on her knees and looked at the harbour lights going past and made herself breathe, slowly, the way he’d told her to on the phone the day Zhao’s fever went up. Breathe first. Then tell me.

✦ ✦ ✦

The steel door was open when she got there. Raiden was standing in it in a T-shirt and tracksuit bottoms with his hair everywhere, and he’d turned every light in the cellar on.

She went past him and down the steps and stopped.

Peng was on the table.

He was grey. He was lying on his back on the padded table under the big round light, in the dark uniform of the gatehouse, with one leg of his trousers cut away, and there was blood on the table, and on the floor, and running down off the edge into the drain. Zhao was standing over him with both hands pressed into a bundle of cloth high on the inside of Peng’s thigh, right up by the groin, and the cloth was black with blood and so were his hands, to the wrists, and his sleeves.

Two of Zhao’s men were by the wall. They were as grey as Peng.

Zhao looked up.

He looked at her in the doorway. She had her mask on already, and her cap, and her red loupes pushed up on her forehead, and her scrubs. She’d put them on in the taxi. He looked at her over the top of Peng’s body, at her eyes, and nothing in his face moved.

“Elara,” said Zhao.

She didn’t answer. She went to the sink.

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at the wound while she scrubbed. She made herself.

It was high. Too high. Right up in the crease at the top of the thigh, where the big vessels came down out of the belly and into the leg, and the blood was dark and bright at once, coming up round Zhao’s fingers in a way that told her this was no small artery in the muscle. It was the big one, or the vein beside it, or both. Torn.

She’d have needed a theatre for this. A theatre and a vascular surgeon and an anaesthetist and six units of blood and a team. She had a cellar and a table and her brother.

“Jinx,” she said.

Her voice came out of her mouth in that room for the first time. It sounded strange to her, flat and fast and level, a voice from the wards at three in the morning. Zhao’s men looked round. Raiden, at the top of the steps, went still.

Jinx was already coming down. She’d come from the flat over the garage in a T-shirt and bare feet, with her hair tied up, and she looked at the table once and her face went white and stayed calm.

“Wash your hands,” said Elara. “Here. Like this. Every finger, both sides, to the elbows. Then gloves. They’re in the box. Then you stand there, and you hand me what I point at, and if I say a word you give me the thing that’s called that, and if you don’t know what it’s called, I’ll point.”

“Yes,” said Jinx.

“Raiden. The light. Bring it down. Lower. Hold the arm. Don’t move it.”

He came down the steps and took hold of the arm of the big light and held it, and didn’t move it a centimetre.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took over from Zhao.

She put her own hands where his were, and pressed, and he took his away, and the blood came up anyway, through her fingers. She pressed harder. It slowed. She held it. She held it with all her weight, both hands, leaning on it, and looked at Peng’s face under the light.

He was awake, a little. His eyes were open. His lips were going grey.

“Peng,” she said. “It’s Elara. Little sister. You drove me up the hill. Do you remember? You always had the heater on.” She didn’t know if he heard. “I’ve got you. Hold on.”

His eyes moved to her face, over the mask. She thought they knew her.

Then she tried to do it.

She tried. She’d never tried harder at anything. She needed to keep the pressure on with one hand and open the wound with the other and find the torn vessel and get control of it above the tear and below the tear, and she couldn’t. She couldn’t do all of it. There were only two of her hands, and the moment she lifted one to work, the blood came up and filled everything and she couldn’t see, and she had to put the hand back and press again. Jinx handed her things. Jinx did everything she was told, fast and exact, and it wasn’t enough. Jinx didn’t know where to put a retractor. Jinx didn’t know what she was looking at. Nobody in the room did except Elara.

She tried three times. On the third time she got a glimpse of it, deep in the crease, the tear in the wall of the big vessel, the length of her fingernail, and then the blood came up and hid it and she had to press again.

She looked at the fridge.

There was no blood in it. There’d never been blood in it. They’d never planned for this. She’d made the rule herself, on a sheet of paper her father had signed: anyone who needs more than the room goes to a hospital, whatever it costs. Peng needed more than the room. Peng needed a hospital. And the nearest hospital that could do this was twenty minutes away, and Peng had about ten.

She looked at his lips.

She knew exactly what she was looking at. She’d watched it on wards. She’d watched it on a kitchen table on the hill, once, and in an alley, from the other side, with her own arm in the air. He was going to die on this table with her hands in him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had always known who she’d call. That was the worst of it.

She’d known since the night she sewed the pillowcase. Since before that. Since the supply room, maybe, three and a half years ago, when he’d read the label on the instrument case and put the right one in her bag. She’d built all of this, the cellar and the rules and the mask and the silence, so she’d never have to call him. So the one part of her life that nobody had bled on would stay that way.

She looked at Peng’s grey face. She thought of him at the bottom of the hill road with the heater on.

“Call him,” said Elara. “Tell him to bring blood.”

Raiden looked at her over the light.

“Who?”

“Xing Yue.” She heard her voice. It was steady. It didn’t feel like hers. “My phone’s in the bag. Two units of O negative and a vascular tray. Tell him where. Tell him now.”

Raiden didn’t ask anything. He let go of the light with one hand, which he’d been told not to do, and got her phone out of the bag with his other, and rang, and put it to his ear.

It rang once.

She heard her brother say, “It’s Raiden. She needs you. She says two units of O negative and a vascular tray. The garage near the Docks, the building next door, there’s a steel door at the side behind some pallets—” He stopped. He listened. He looked at Elara with a strange face. “He says he knows where,” said Raiden, and put the phone down.

She didn’t have room to think about that. She pressed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in thirteen minutes.

She heard the car stop in the street and the door slam, and feet on the stone steps, fast, and then he was in the doorway with a blue cool box in one hand and a sterile pack in the other, in his coat over a T-shirt, with his glasses on.

He looked at her once. At her eyes, over the mask, and her hands on the wound, and her red loupes.

He didn’t say anything. He put the cool box down on the side and opened it and took out two bags of blood and gave them to Zhao, and said, “Hold those up,” and Zhao held them up. He put the pack on the side table by Jinx. He took his coat off and went to the sink and scrubbed, every finger, both sides, to the elbows, fast, the way he’d done it ten thousand times, and put on gloves from her box, and came to the other side of the table, opposite her.

He put the line into Peng’s arm and the blood in. He did it in less time than it took her to breathe twice.

Then he picked up the retractor from the tray.

“Show me,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They worked.

They didn’t talk. Not about anything that wasn’t the leg on the table. He put his hands where she told him, and then where she didn’t have to tell him, above the tear, and pressed, and held it, and for the first time since she’d walked into the cellar she could see. She could see all of it. The torn vessel, the length of her fingernail, deep in the crease, with the blood slowed to almost nothing because his hands were on it, steady as a clamp.

She repaired it.

She didn’t do it the way you’d do it in a theatre. There wasn’t a theatre. She did enough to stop it, enough to get blood going down into the leg again, a temporary thing that a vascular surgeon at the Crestview would take apart in the morning and do properly. It took most of an hour. It took everything her right hand had. Her fingers were small and quick and exact inside the wound and she felt every one of them, and the needle holder that had turned up in her bag in November was in her hand, and it was the best one she’d ever held.

She hummed. She didn’t know she was doing it. He didn’t say anything about it.

When the first stitch held he said, “Good.”

When the second held he said it again. That was all he said, all night. Good. Each time she got something right. And each time he said it she felt it go through her, steady, like a hand on her back.

At some point Ev was there. Elara didn’t see her come. She was just there at Jinx’s elbow, in her grey jumper with her hands washed and gloved, and Jinx stepped back from the tray, white, shaking, and Ev took her place without a word and handed Elara the next thing before she’d pointed at it.

At some point the second bag of blood went in.

At some point Peng’s lips weren’t grey any more.

Xing Yue looked at the monitor Raiden had brought down from somewhere, a little one on a stand, and then at Peng’s face, and then at her.

“His pressure’s coming up,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six the street outside went grey.

Zhao’s men came down the steps with a stretcher and two more men behind them. A van was in the street with its back doors open. Peng was awake. He was white and sweating and his leg was bandaged from the groin to the knee, and he looked up from the stretcher at the masked woman standing by the table with her gloved hands held up in front of her, red to the wrist, and his mouth moved.

“Miss Lin,” he said.

She nodded. Her throat had shut.

They carried him up the steps. Zhao went after them, and stopped at the top, by the steel door, and turned round, and looked down at Xing Yue, who was standing at the sink with his gloves off and his hands under the tap.

“Thank you,” said Zhao.

“He needs a vascular surgeon by eight,” said Xing Yue. “Not nine. Eight. That repair won’t hold past the morning. Tell them that.”

“He’ll have one,” said Zhao.

He looked at Elara. He didn’t say anything to her. He nodded, once, and then he said, to nobody in particular, “I’ll tell Elowen. I don’t lie to her,” and went out into the grey morning, and the van doors shut, and it drove away.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her home.

Ev took Jinx upstairs. Raiden stood in the steel doorway with his hands at his sides and watched them go and didn’t make a single joke.

She sat in the passenger seat in her scrubs with her gloves still on and her hands in her lap. She’d forgotten to take them off. She looked down at them. They were red to the wrist and they weren’t shaking. They lay in her lap, still, the right one and the left one, as steady as they’d ever been.

Neither of them said anything.

He drove along the harbour road in the early light with one hand on the wheel. Halfway home he took the other off the gearstick and put it over both of hers, gloves and blood and all, and left it there, and she didn’t move.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the lift at Banyan Terrace he leaned down and rested his forehead on hers.

He didn’t kiss her. He just stood there in the small lit box with his forehead on hers and his eyes shut, while the lift went up, and she stood with her red hands at her sides and her eyes shut, and she felt him breathing, and it was the closest she’d ever felt to anyone in her life.

In the kitchen he took her gloves off.

He did it one at a time, the way you’d take them off a patient, peeling each one down from the wrist and off the fingers, and dropped them in the bin. Then he took her to the sink and ran the tap warm and washed her hands. All of them. Every finger, both sides, the backs, the wrists, slowly, with the soap, until the water ran clear. He dried them on a clean tea towel. Then he turned her right hand over and bent his head and kissed the scar.

He took her upstairs. He took off her scrubs and put her in his T-shirt and put her into bed, and pulled the sheet and the blanket up to her chin, and tucked them in down both sides, firmly, the way he always did.

“Go to sleep,” he said.

She looked up at him from the pillow. She opened her mouth.

He shook his head, once. She shut it.

He lay down beside her on top of the blanket, in his clothes, and took her right hand and held it against his chest. She lay and listened to the city starting outside the window, and neither of them said anything about any of it, and somewhere in the middle of not saying anything she fell asleep.

chapters.title: I Know
chapters.desc: The blood bank finds two missing units with his name on them and he’s suspended, and he tells her nothing. She finds the letter, and he tells her he’s known since the pillowcase.
chapters.epigraph: “You told me not to ask. I didn’t.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
For a week neither of them said anything about it.

They were kind to each other. That was how he knew they were both pretending. She cooked every night, things that took hours, and folded the dumplings with her left hand, slowly, in front of him. He held doors open for her that she didn’t need held. She didn’t hold her cups in both hands, and neither of them mentioned that either.

On the Tuesday she put her hand on his arm at the counter and opened her mouth. He waited. She took her hand away and asked if he wanted more tea.

Peng was in the Crestview. A vascular surgeon had taken him to theatre at half past seven on the Sunday morning and done it properly, and he was going to keep the leg. Zhao sent a message on the Thursday, to Xing Yue’s phone, which Zhao had never had the number of. It said: He’s walking to the bathroom. Nothing else.

He showed it to her. She read it and went into the study and shut the door, and he heard her crying through it, and didn’t go in.

✦ ✦ ✦

The blood bank’s monthly check ran on the first Monday in December.

Every unit of blood that left the bank in the basement of City Hospital was matched, at the end of each month, to a patient and a record. Two O-negative units had been signed out on the night of the twenty-eighth of November at twelve minutes to two in the morning, on the emergency request form, in the name of Dr. Wang Xing Yue, consultant, general and trauma surgery. There was no patient. There was no record. There was no theatre booking and no ward and nobody in the emergency department who’d received them. The units had gone out of the bank in a cool box and had never come back.

The medical director’s office asked an auditor to look at Dr. Wang’s other records. She was a thorough woman. She went back three years.

On the Saturday night page of the theatre stock book for the twenty-fifth of March 2023, against an emergency appendix, she found an entry in his writing for an instrument set opened and contaminated, and fluids, and dressings, and a great deal of gauze. It was more than an appendix used. It was initialled. It was too old to mean much, she wrote in her report, and too small, but she was putting it in.

He heard about it on the Wednesday. Dr. Xia’s secretary rang him and asked him to come to a meeting on Thursday at four.

He didn’t tell Elara.

✦ ✦ ✦

The meeting was in a room on the top floor of the old block with a long table and windows over the garden.

Dr. Xia Wanqing, the medical director, sat at the head of it with the papers in front of her. Professor Liao sat on her left with a bag of boiled sweets he didn’t open. There was a woman from human resources with a laptop, and the blood bank manager, who wouldn’t look at him.

Xing Yue sat at the other end of the table.

Dr. Xia read him the facts. He agreed with all of them.

“You signed out two units of O-negative blood at one forty-eight in the morning on the twenty-ninth,” she said, “and took them out of the hospital. Is that right?”

“Yes.”

“For a patient.”

“Yes.”

She turned a page, though he could see she didn’t need to.

“Which patient?”

“A patient who would have died without them,” said Xing Yue.

Dr. Xia looked at him over her glasses.

“Where?”

“Not in this hospital.”

“Where, Dr. Wang?”

He didn’t answer. She waited. He let her wait. Outside the windows the camphor tree moved in the wind over the pond.

“Was anyone else involved?” said Dr. Xia.

“No.”

“You took blood products out of this hospital without a record, for a patient you won’t name, at a place you won’t name, on your own.”

“Yes.”

She made a note. She looked up again.

“Do you understand how serious this is? Blood is the one thing in this building we cannot lose track of. If that blood had gone into the wrong person, at the wrong place, with nobody checking—”

“It went into the right person,” said Xing Yue. “I checked.”

“Do you understand the seriousness of it?”

“Yes,” he said. “I’d do it again.”

The woman from human resources stopped typing.

“I’d do it again tonight,” said Xing Yue. “The patient is alive. He’s walking. He has both his legs. That’s more than this meeting could have managed for him, and more than the blood bank’s form could, and if you’d like me to apologise for it, I can’t, because I’d be lying, and I’ve been told that’s the one thing I mustn’t do in this room.”

Professor Liao looked at the table.

Dr. Xia looked at him without saying anything. Then she wrote it down. He watched her write it, every word, in her neat hand, and underline something.

✦ ✦ ✦

The letter came on Friday morning, by hand, in an envelope with the hospital’s crest on it.

Suspended from all clinical duties for three months, pending a review of his professional conduct. Not to attend the hospital site for any purpose without permission. His patients handed to colleagues. His pager to be returned to the switchboard.

He read it standing in his office and put his pager on the desk.

Professor Liao came in without knocking and shut the door behind him.

He stood in his cardigan with a boiled sweet in his cheek, looking at the pager on the desk. He’d been Xing Yue’s professor for nine years. He’d taught him half of what he knew.

“I’m not asking as your head of department,” said Liao. “There’s nobody here. I’m asking as an old man who’s known you since you came down from the north with one bag.” He took the sweet out of his mouth. “Is it Elara?”

“No,” said Xing Yue.

Liao looked at him. Xing Yue looked back.

It was the first lie he’d ever told this man. He’d told lies for her in notes and stock books and a meeting yesterday. He’d never told one to someone’s face who’d trusted him for nine years, and he found it was easy, and he found he didn’t mind.

Liao put the sweet back.

“All right,” he said. “Go home. Sleep. Eat something. Don’t come in here again till March, because if you do, I’ll have security walk you out, and I’ll enjoy it.”

He went out. He left the door open.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t tell her.

He went home that evening and said nothing. He put the letter in the journal on the kitchen table, the trauma one, the one they’d been writing in since September, at the page with the diagram of the vessel repair, where it said Come to bed at the bottom in his writing and Five minutes under it in hers. He couldn’t throw it away, and he couldn’t put it anywhere she’d never look, and he didn’t decide which of those he wanted.

On Monday he got up at half past six, the way he always did, and showered, and dressed for work, and kissed her on the forehead while she was still asleep, and went down to the car.

He drove to Fig Tree Lane.

Jun Hyuk opened the green door at a quarter past seven in his apron, and looked at him, and didn’t ask a single question.

“Lemons,” said Jun Hyuk. “You’re just in time. I’ve got a mountain of them from a man in the south, and Ev won’t help, she says she’s got a viola lesson, she hasn’t. Come in. Have you ever salted a lemon? Everyone thinks you just put salt on it.”

So he salted lemons.

He went every day that week. He spent six hours a day in the kitchen at Fig Tree Lane with his sleeves rolled up, cutting lemons and packing them with salt into jars while Jun Hyuk talked about everything in the world except the reason Xing Yue was in his kitchen. Evangeline came and went. She brought him tea. Once she reached past him and pressed the lemons in a jar down harder with her thumb, and went away again.

Neither of them said a word about a cellar. He was grateful for both.

He drove home at six every evening smelling of lemons and told Elara the ward had been busy.

✦ ✦ ✦

That Friday she took him lunch.

He didn’t know until he came home. He came in at six with his hands smelling of salt and lemon peel and went into the kitchen, and she was sitting at the table.

The journal was open in front of her at the page with the diagram. The letter was beside it, flat, unfolded, with the hospital’s crest at the top.

She looked up at him. Her face was white.

“I took you lunch,” said Elara. “To 9B. Noodles. I thought I’d surprise you. I went up to the ward and asked for you, and Sister Shao looked at me, and said, He’s not here, love. Not since the eleventh.” Her voice was rising. “Not since the eleventh. A week. A week, and you’ve been getting up every morning and putting your work clothes on and kissing me on the head and going out, and coming home and telling me the ward was busy, and you haven’t been on the ward, you haven’t been in the building, you’ve been suspended—”

“Elara.”

“You let them suspend you.” She stood up. “You let them take your job away for three months, for me, for blood you took for me, and you didn’t tell me. You sat in a meeting and told them it was nobody, didn’t you? I know you did. You told them it was you, on your own, and you came home, and you didn’t say a word, and you went out every morning and—where did you go? Where have you been all week?”

“Fig Tree Lane. Salting lemons.”

She stared at him.

“Jun Hyuk knew?” she said. “Ev knew? Everyone knew except me?”

“You didn’t tell me either,” said Xing Yue.

She stopped.

“That’s different,” she said.

“How?”

She opened her mouth. She shut it. She stood at the kitchen table with her hands flat on either side of the open journal, breathing hard.

“You don’t even know what I’ve been doing,” she said. “You don’t know anything. You came to a cellar in the middle of the night because my brother rang you, and you didn’t ask me a single thing, and you think it was one night, you think it was just Peng, you don’t know what I’ve been doing for five months—”

“I know,” said Xing Yue.

✦ ✦ ✦

The kitchen went silent.

She looked at him. He watched her hear it. He watched it go into her and stop her, the way her voice had stopped on the steps outside Old Bian’s when he’d put two fingers on her throat.

“You know,” she said.

“Yes.”

She put one hand on the back of the chair, as though the floor had moved.

“Since when?”

“Since the pillowcase.”

She didn’t move.

“You sewed it at two in the morning,” he said. “In August. With your right hand. You did a running stitch and then a locked one, and you tied it off one-handed, in the dark, and you hummed. I was awake. You told me to go back to sleep.” He came round the table. “I lay there and went through it like a case. The cups. The buttons. Ah Sim’s chest. The black bag. The rig at night. Ev’s car on the harbour road at four in the morning. I’d seen all of it. I hadn’t looked at it.”

“The journals,” she said.

“The journals were for you.”

Her face changed. He watched her see it, all of it, the margins, the questions, what would you have used, you told me that two weeks ago, then rubbed it out.

“You never asked,” she said. “Four months. You never asked me once.”

“You told me not to ask,” said Xing Yue. “In the supply room. I didn’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There wasn’t any fight left in either of them after that.

She sat down on the kitchen chair as if her legs had stopped. She put her hands over her face and cried, not the way she cried at good things, but all the way down, the way she’d cried on his lap a year ago when she’d run out of words. He knelt on the kitchen floor beside the chair and put his arms round her and held on.

“Why didn’t you tell me to stop?” she said, through her hands. “You knew. You knew what I was doing. Why didn’t you ever say stop?”

He sat back on his heels and looked at her.

She took her hands off her face and looked at him, and saw how he was looking at her, as though she’d asked him why he hadn’t told the sun to stop coming up.

“Why would I?” said Xing Yue.

She laughed. It came out wet and cracked and astonished.

He took her right hand. He held it in both of his on her knee, palm up, the scar across the inside of the wrist and the zigzag up the forearm, and looked at it, and then up at her.

“Show me,” he said.

She looked at him. Then she moved her fingers.

All of them. Fast. One after the other, thumb to little finger and back, the way she’d done it on the rig every morning for nine months, and then all together, a fist and open, and then each finger touching her thumb, quick as a pianist, and then she took his hand and laced her fingers through his and squeezed, hard, harder than she’d been able to in March, harder than she’d ever squeezed it in her life.

He laughed out loud.

He knelt on the kitchen floor and laughed, the real one, the one she’d heard a handful of times, with his head down on her knee and her hand crushed in his, until she was laughing too, through the crying, with her other hand in his hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her about the bag.

He told her he’d been through it in October while she was asleep and written a list, and about the supplier, and the case at the bottom, and the needle holder.

She sat up straight on the chair.

“That was you,” she said. “That was you. I rang Jinx. I rang Ev. I thought it was Ev. I’ve been thanking Ev for a month with my eyes and she’s been looking at me like I’ve gone mad—you went through my bag.”

“Yes.”

“In the night. While I was asleep.”

He told her it was twice a week. He didn’t say sorry, and she didn’t seem to want him to.

“That’s not normal,” said Elara. “That’s not a normal thing to do.”

She looked at him. Her face was furious. Then it wasn’t, and she put both hands on his face and pulled him up off the floor and kissed him.

“How did you know where?” she said against his mouth. “That night. Raiden said you said you knew. You came in thirteen minutes.”

“I followed you once,” he said. “In August. A week after the pillowcase. I stood outside the steel door in the rain with my hand on it and listened to you hum. Ev said clamp.”

She stared at him. Then she started to laugh again, helplessly, with her forehead on his, and couldn’t stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was the one who started it.

She stood up and took him by his shirt, the shirt that smelled of lemons, and walked backwards out of the kitchen and up the stairs pulling him after her, and she talked the whole way. She talked about the cellar. She told him everything now that she could, all at once: the dock worker, the girl with the bottle, the boy who swore, the first time she’d spoken in the cellar, to Jinx, the night of Peng, and how her voice had sounded.

She told him while she took his shirt off. She told him while he took hers off. She told him about the rig and the wire that had stopped buzzing on a Tuesday in June, and how she’d wanted to run across the city and tell him, and hadn’t, and had sat on the stool in the garage and cried instead.

And for once he talked too.

He’d never talked in bed. He did now. He told her what it had been like to lie on the bare pillow at two in the morning and watch her sew through his lashes. How his heart had gone. How he’d had to turn over so she wouldn’t see his face. How he’d sat on the edge of the bath until it got light. He said it into her neck, into her hair, against the inside of her right wrist, and she listened to every word, with her hands on him, and her right hand felt every bit of his skin, and she told him so.

It was the most open they’d ever been. Nothing left in either of them that the other didn’t know. She held his face and looked at him the whole time, and he let her see everything that was in his, and when she said his name at the end it was in her ordinary voice, the talking one, as though she were just telling him something she’d always meant to say.

chapters.title: Rules for a Ghost Surgeon
chapters.desc: They write the ghost’s rules together on the back of his suspension letter. Then he takes her north for New Year, where his grandmother points her stick at everyone.
chapters.epigraph: “Rule one. Nobody does this alone.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
They wrote the rules on the back of the letter.

It was his idea. She’d wanted to burn it. She’d held it over the gas ring on Saturday morning, the hospital’s crest curling at one corner, and he’d taken it out of her hand and blown it out and turned it over and put it on the kitchen table, blank side up, and got a pen.

“It’s the only paper in this flat that’s got both of us on it,” he said.

She looked at it, at the scorch mark on the corner, and sat down.

“Rule one,” he said. “Nobody does this alone.”

He wrote it at the top, in square block capitals, so that anyone could read it.

1. NOBODY DOES THIS ALONE.

She read it upside down. She took the pen out of his hand and wrote the second one under it, in her round fast writing.

2. Anyone who needs more than the room goes to a hospital. Whatever it costs. Whoever they are.

They went on like that, passing the pen across the table. No money, ever, to either of them. He was on call for her, and she was on call for him. Her father asked, and she could say no. He wrote that one, and underlined asked.

Then he took the pen and wrote, before she could say anything:

Nobody makes the other one stop.

She looked at it. She looked at him across the table.

“You wrote that one first,” she said. “You wrote it before you wrote no money.”

“It’s the one that matters.”

She didn’t say anything for a second. Then she took the pen and wrote, at the bottom, No more lies. Not even kind ones, and pushed it back to him, and he read it and nodded.

She took the pen back. She was smiling now. She wrote, in small letters, in the margin: XY stops checking my dot.

He leaned over and read it, and took the pen off her, and drew a single straight line through it.

“No,” he said.

“I knew you’d say that.”

“Then why did you write it?”

“To see your face.” She took the pen back again and wrote, under the crossed-out line: E gets his dot too. She held her hand out across the table. “Phone.”

He gave it to her. She did it there and then, with her right thumb, fast, and held it up so he could see his own name come up on her screen, a small blue dot in a kitchen on Banyan Terrace, the way she’d once held hers up for him at breakfast.

“There,” said Elara. “Now I’ll know every time you go and salt lemons.”

He signed the bottom of the sheet. She signed under him.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday they took it to the Walled City.

She went back through the red door for lunch with the letter folded in her coat pocket, and after the soup, when Ah Sim had gone back to the stove and Raiden had taken Jinx out to look at a motorbike in the alley, she put it on the table in front of her father.

He read it. He read the back first, the rules, all of them, with his heavy grey face perfectly still. Then he turned it over and read the front, the hospital’s crest, suspended from all clinical duties, and his mouth went tight and shook, once, which she’d never seen it do, and he turned it back.

He looked across the table at Xing Yue.

“Do you want this?” said Lin Jian. “Any of it. This is mine. It’s my house and my family and the things I did. You’ve got a name nobody in this city has ever had to whisper. You can walk away from all of it and she’ll still marry you.”

Xing Yue didn’t look away from him.

“I want her to stop doing it alone,” he said.

Her father looked at him a moment longer. Then he took a pen out of his inside pocket, the old fountain pen he signed everything with, and signed the bottom of the sheet, under both of them, and pushed it back across the table to her without a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday Elowen came to Banyan Terrace.

She came at eleven in the morning in her good coat with a bunch of white chrysanthemums from the shop, and Elara opened the door and knew from her sister’s face that Zhao had told her. Zhao had told her three weeks ago. Elara had known he would; he’d said it on the stone steps with Peng’s blood on his sleeves. I don’t lie to her.

Elowen put the flowers on the counter. She didn’t take her coat off.

“I made you this,” she said.

Elara looked at her.

“In March 2023. In my kitchen. I rang you at three in the morning and told you to steal everything you could carry and come, and you came, and you saved his life on my table, and I never once asked you afterwards what it cost you.” Elowen’s voice was perfectly cool and her eyes weren’t. “And Baba rang you in July, and you went. And I didn’t know. I didn’t know you’d got your hand back. I didn’t know about a cellar. I didn’t know you’d been doing it in the dark for five months with Ev, and I’m your sister, and I’m the one who started it.”

“You didn’t start it.”

“I rang you.”

“You rang me because I’m good at it,” said Elara. “You didn’t make me anything. I was already this. I’ve been this since I was nine and Ah Kuen cut his hand on a rope and I held the towel on it in the kitchen till Old Hou came.” She put her hand on her sister’s arm. Her right one. “You just knew who to ring.”

Elowen looked down at the hand on her arm.

She looked at it the way she looked at a stem before she cut it, carefully, all the way down. Then she put her own hand over it, and her mouth crumpled the way it hadn’t since their mother’s grave, and she cried, standing in Elara’s kitchen in her good coat, without making a sound.

✦ ✦ ✦

Peng came on New Year’s Eve.

He came up the stairs at Banyan Terrace on crutches, slowly, one step at a time, with one of Zhao’s men behind him carrying a basket, and refused to let the man help him with the last flight. He stood in the doorway breathing hard. He was thin, and pale, and the leg was in a brace from the hip to the knee, and he was grinning.

The basket was full of mandarins. Small loose-skinned ones, the kind she liked, with the leaves still on.

“From the gatehouse,” said Peng. “The tree by the gate. Mrs. Zhao said you like them.” He held the basket out. “Dr. Lin.”

She took it. She’d been braced for the other name, the one from the docks. He didn’t use it. He stood in her doorway on his crutches and called her what she’d been called on the wards, as though it were the only name he’d ever known her by.

She cried. Of course she did. She put the basket down and hugged him round the crutches, and he went red to the ears, and behind her Xing Yue took the basket and put it on the counter and asked Peng whether the brace was rubbing at the top, and Peng said a bit, and Xing Yue made him sit down on the sofa and showed him how to pad it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The plane went north at four that afternoon.

It was the Wangs’ plane. She hadn’t known they had one. She hadn’t known anyone had one. It was small and white and waited for them on the far side of the airport, away from the terminal, with a man in a cap holding the door, and inside it there were eight leather seats and a woman who brought her tea in a real cup.

“You said a flight,” said Elara. “You said, we’ll fly up for New Year. You didn’t say it was your flight.”

“It’s my father’s.”

“That’s worse.”

He was looking out of the window. He couldn’t work for three months, and he’d said that if he couldn’t be a doctor, she couldn’t be one either, not for a week, and she’d said he was a terrible patient, and he’d agreed.

She looked at him in the leather seat in his good coat. Then she unbuckled her belt and got up and sat in his lap, which you were absolutely not supposed to do on a plane, and the woman with the tea looked at the ceiling, and he put his arms round her and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house in the north was in the hills, behind a wall, round a courtyard, and it was snowing.

She’d never seen snow. She stood in the courtyard in the dark with her face turned up and her mouth open and let it fall on her, and forgot about the family coming out of every door to look at her, until Xing Yue said her name.

His grandmother was in the doorway of the main house with a stick.

She was small, smaller than Elara, wrapped in a fur-lined coat, with white hair pulled back hard and a face like a walnut. She came down the steps without help, one at a time, and across the courtyard through the snow, and stopped in front of Elara, and pointed the stick at her.

“Why are you so small?” said Nainai.

Elara opened her mouth.

“Do you eat? You don’t look like you eat. He doesn’t eat either. He never did. I sent him south with a bag of dried meat and he gave it to a porter.” She turned the stick on her grandson. “You. Why didn’t you bring her before? I’ve been writing to you for nine years. Nine years. Come home, get married. And you write back, Nainai, I’m busy. Busy.” She poked him in the chest with the stick. “Is this busy?”

“Yes,” said Xing Yue.

His grandmother looked at him. Then she looked at Elara again, all the way down and back up, and her walnut face cracked into something that was nearly a grin.

“Good,” she said. “Come inside. You’ll freeze. You’ve got no fat on you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother read her scar at dinner.

Dr. Lou Huiyi was a retired cardiologist, tall and grey and quiet, and she’d said almost nothing all evening. Then, over the soup, she reached across the table and took Elara’s right hand without asking, and turned it over, and pushed her sleeve back, and looked at the scar the way you’d look at an ECG, from one end to the other.

“Who repaired this?”

“Dr. Meng. At City Hospital.”

Dr. Lou ran one finger along the zigzag. “She extended it there. To find the ends. That was right. Most people wouldn’t have.” She looked at the fingertips. “And you’ve got it all back.”

“Nearly all.”

“Then she did it well,” said Dr. Lou, and gave her hand back, and went on with her soup.

His father asked at the end of the meal.

Wang Jingtang sat at the head of the long table, a big quiet man with his son’s face gone heavier, and he’d been polite to Elara all evening, and asked her about her work and listened to the answer. Now he put down his cup and looked down the table at his elder son.

“When are you coming home?” he said. “There’s a hospital in the east city with no head of surgery. There’s been no head of surgery since August. I’ve kept it for you.”

The table went quiet. An Yu, at the far end, who’d said four words all evening, looked at his tea.

Xing Yue didn’t raise his voice. He never did.

“I’m not,” he said. “Give it to someone who wants it. I’ve got a hospital.” He looked at his father down the length of the table, as flat and cold as she’d ever heard him with a registrar. “Come south and visit. You’ve never seen where I work. Come and see it.”

His father looked at him.

Then Xing Yue turned to Elara beside him and put another piece of fish in her bowl, as gently as if nobody else were at the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight there were fireworks over the hills, and the whole family went out into the courtyard to watch, and the snow had stopped and lay thick and white and untouched across the middle of it.

She looked at it. She looked at him in his good coat, the long dark wool one, with his hands in his pockets, watching the sky.

“I dare you,” said Elara.

He looked down at her.

“Lie down in it. In the snow. In your coat. Make an angel. You move your arms and legs, like this, and it leaves a shape. I’ve seen it in films. I dare you.”

She thought he’d say no. He was a consultant in a good coat in his grandmother’s courtyard with his whole family watching. He looked at the snow, and at her, and then he walked into the middle of the courtyard and lay down on his back in it.

Somebody gasped. Nainai laughed out loud, a cackle that went round the courtyard walls.

He moved his arms and legs. Slowly, seriously, as if it were a procedure. Then, before she could stop laughing, he reached up and caught her wrist and pulled, and she came down on top of him in the snow with a shriek.

He kissed her.

He kissed her lying on his back in the snow with his glasses crooked and snow in his hair and the fireworks going over them, and his hands were cold on her face, and his mouth wasn’t. She kissed him back. She forgot the family. She forgot everything except the cold coming through her coat and the warm under her, and his laugh against her mouth.

When she sat up there was a perfect angel in the snow under him, with a second, smaller one, lopsided, on top of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

His boyhood room was on the far side of the courtyard, with a big old bed under a mountain of quilts, and shelves of school books, and a model of a human heart he’d made at twelve, with the chambers painted in red and blue.

She talked. She couldn’t help it. She talked while they got under the quilts, about the heart, which was good for twelve, and about his grandmother’s stick, and about the plane, and about the snow. She talked while he kissed her neck. She told him the quilts weighed more than she did, and that she’d suffocate, and that it would be his fault, and that Nainai would point the stick at him at the funeral.

He laughed into her shoulder.

He laughed so much that he had to stop kissing her. He lay under the quilts in the room he’d slept in as a boy and laughed with his face in her neck, and she lay there delighted with herself, and then she stopped talking, because his hands had started again, slow and warm under the weight of the quilts, and there was no air left over for anything except his name.

✦ ✦ ✦

On New Year’s Day she woke before him.

She lay under the quilts and looked at the ceiling of his boyhood room, at a crack in the plaster in the shape of a river, and thought about it.

She’d been thinking about it since the cellar. Since Peng’s lips came back pink. Since his voice saying good, every time a stitch held.

She’d done it in the dark for six months. She could do it in the dark for the rest of her life, and she would. But she could do it in the light as well, with her name on a theatre list and someone holding the other side.

The window for applications to surgical training opened in February. She’d need a hand assessment. A skills test. A reference from somebody who’d seen her hands since November, and she didn’t know who that could be, unless it was a hand surgeon who’d kept her notes in a drawer for a year.

She turned over. He was awake, watching her, with his head on the pillow.

“I’m going to apply,” she said. “To go back. To training. In February.”

He reached out under the quilts and found her right hand and held it, hard.

“February,” he said, as if he were writing it on a list.

She put her forehead against his and lay there in the cold bright morning and let him hold on.

chapters.title: No More Pretending
chapters.desc: At Lunar New Year, in the middle of Raiden’s toast, Elara picks up her teacup with one hand. Then she tells the whole table.
chapters.epigraph: “Pass the tea. No, leave it. I’ve got it.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The long table in the Walled City had every chair filled for the first time he could remember.

Lin Jian at the head, in his carved chair. Elowen on his right in green, with Zhao behind her shoulder like a wall even sitting down. Raiden and Jinx, with Raiden in a red waistcoat with embroidered dragons that Jinx had refused to sit next to and then sat next to. Evangeline in pale blue, and Jun Hyuk beside her, already talking. Eliana at the far end with Yu Chen, who’d come over the wall at seven with a bag of oranges and been put in a chair by Ah Sim before he could say no, and who was holding Eliana’s hand under the table where everybody could see it. The old high chair nobody moved, empty, in the corner. Ah Sim in the kitchen doorway with her arms folded, watching all of them eat.

Elara was beside him. She was in red, a dress he’d never seen, with her hair up in pins that were already coming down.

She’d been quiet in the car. Not silent. She’d told him three stories on the way across the city and lost the third one at the fish market. But under the stories she’d been quiet, the way she was before a list, and when they’d stood in the alley outside the red door she’d stopped and looked at the stones for a second before he knocked.

He’d knocked. He’d opened the door for her when Ah Sim unlatched it. He always did.

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone went during the fish.

He’d stopped carrying his pager in December. He hadn’t stopped carrying his phone. It was Dr. Zou, on call on 9B, and he took it in the hall by the stairs.

“Sorry. I know you’re not—I know you’re suspended. But there’s a man in bed eleven and his scan—”

“I’m suspended,” said Xing Yue. “You’re not. You’ve got a consultant on call. Ring him. If you’ve rung me because you’re frightened of him, look at the scan yourself first, so you’ve got something to say when he answers.”

“I just thought—”

“If you ring me again tonight,” said Xing Yue, “I’ll tell Professor Liao on Monday that you can’t read a scan without someone holding your hand. Look at it. Then ring him.”

He hung up. When he came back to the table Elara looked up at him with her eyebrows raised, and put a piece of fish in his bowl, and he sat down and ate it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden stood up to make a toast after the dumplings.

He’d made one every year since he was fourteen, Elowen said, and none of them had ever been under six minutes. This one was about a crane. It was nearly always about a crane. He stood at his end of the table with his cup raised and talked about a crane he’d drawn in 2019 that the builders had put up backwards, and the family groaned, and Jun Hyuk asked a serious question about the counterweight, and Raiden answered it at length.

Xing Yue was watching Elara.

She’d put her teacup down in front of her when Raiden stood up. She always held it in both hands at the table, in front of the family. She’d done it at every Sunday lunch since August, the right hand under the cup and the left round it, so that nobody would see.

Now she reached out with her right hand alone.

She picked the cup up by the side, the way anybody would, her fingers round it, her thumb on the rim, and lifted it off the table, full, to the level of her chin, and held it there. It didn’t shake. Not a drop went over.

Raiden was halfway through the counterweight. He stopped.

The table saw it. He watched it go round, face by face. Jinx saw it first, because Jinx had been watching for it; her mouth went tight at one corner. Then Elowen. Then Ev, who didn’t move. Then Eliana, with her phone half up, and Yu Chen beside her looking at Eliana’s face to see what she was seeing. Jun Hyuk stopped mid-sentence. Zhao didn’t change at all, but his eyes went to the cup and stayed there. Ah Sim in the doorway unfolded her arms.

Lin Jian, at the head of the table, put his chopsticks down.

Elara drank. She put the cup down on the table with her right hand, carefully, and left her hand beside it, flat.

“Pass the tea,” she said, to nobody, and then, as Jun Hyuk reached for the pot, “No, leave it. I’ve got it.”

She picked up the pot with her right hand and poured herself another cup.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then she told them.

She told them sitting down. She didn’t stand up; she said afterwards that she’d have fallen over. She sat at the long table with her hand flat beside her cup and told them all of it, in order, which for her was a miracle.

Her hand had come back. Most of it. All of the important parts. She told them about the rig in the garage, under the old sign, at five in the morning, every morning for nine months, and the springs and the pins and the wire that buzzed. She told them about the tingle in the shower in April. She told them that in July Baba had rung about Mok’s grandson and she’d gone, and that in August Raiden had built her a room, and that since then she’d been working at night under the rope store, three nights a month, on people who couldn’t go to hospitals, with Ev handing her things.

“In a mask,” she said. “I don’t talk. Not a word. They call me Doctor Ghost. Somebody at the docks started it.” She looked at her hand on the table. “There are rules. We wrote them. Baba’s signed them.”

She told them about Peng. She looked at Zhao when she did, and Zhao looked back.

“And I’m applying,” said Elara. “To go back into surgical training. In the light, this time. With my name on the door. I’ll still be the other thing at night. I’m not stopping that. But I’m going back.”

She stopped.

Most of them had known a piece. He could see it on their faces, each one, the piece they’d been holding. Jinx had known the rig. Raiden had known the room. Ev and Jun Hyuk had known the cellar. Zhao and Elowen had known since November. Lin Jian had known since July. Eliana had probably known everything since before it happened. None of them had said a word of it at this table. Not to each other, and not out loud.

Now it was out on the table between the dumplings and the fish, and nobody had to hold any of it on their own any more.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden cheered.

He cheered so loudly that a dog started barking in the alley. He came round the table and picked Elara up out of her chair, red dress and all, and swung her round and put her down again, and then he stood back and turned and looked at his wife.

“You built her a machine,” he said. “A whole machine, in our garage, at night, in February, and you didn’t tell me. I thought you were doing a gearbox.”

“You built her a room,” said Jinx.

Raiden opened his mouth and shut it. He sat down and sulked magnificently for almost a minute, about rooms and machines and which of them was worse to keep from your wife, and Jinx reached across and took his hand and let him.

“I knew,” said Eliana, from the far end, not looking up from her phone.

Ev looked at her sister across the table.

“Good,” said Evangeline.

Then Jun Hyuk started. He put both hands flat on the table and told everyone, at length, how proud he was. He’d been proud since the first night Ev came home from the cellar at five in the morning and washed her hands for twenty minutes and didn’t say why. He’d been proud every time. He went on for several minutes. Nobody stopped him.

Under the table, Xing Yue saw Elowen reach across and take Elara’s hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then Elowen let it go.

She sat back. She looked round the table at all of them, and her face went cool and exact, the face he’d heard about and seen once across a flower shop, the one she used on men who’d crossed her family.

“We were all kept out,” said Elowen.

The table went quiet.

“Every one of us,” she said. “Each of us had a bit of it, and each of us kept our bit to ourselves, and nobody said a word at this table for nine months. I found out from my husband at seven in the morning with someone else’s blood on his sleeves.” She looked at Elara. “You let us all sit here every Sunday and watch you hold your cup in two hands. You let Baba watch it.”

Elara didn’t look away from her.

“I’m sorry I lied,” she said. “To all of you. I’m sorry about the cups. I’m sorry you had to find out from Zhao.” She put her right hand flat on the table between them. “I’m not sorry about the cellar. I’d do it again. I’ll do it next week.”

Elowen looked at her.

“All right,” she said. “Then next time you tell me first.”

“I’ll tell you first.”

Elowen took her hand back under the table and held it, and didn’t let go again.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Jian got up.

He didn’t say anything. He pushed his carved chair back and stood, and went through the kitchen past Ah Sim, and out of the back door into the yard. They heard the door shut behind him.

Nobody went after him. Ah Sim looked at the back door, and then at all of them, and then went into the kitchen.

He came back after a few minutes. His face was wet. He sat down in his chair and picked up his chopsticks and ate a piece of fish, and nobody said anything about it at all.

✦ ✦ ✦
