Ah Sim brought the last plate of dumplings.

She put it on the table and then took one off it with her own fingers and put it in Elara’s bowl, and stood there with her arms folded and watched her eat it.

Elara bit into it and stopped. She took something out of her mouth. A coin, an old one, the kind Ah Sim put in one dumpling every year for luck.

“Ah Sim,” said Elara.

“Luck,” said Ah Sim. “It’s luck. Eat.”

She went back to the kitchen doorway and folded her arms again. Xing Yue looked at the plate she’d taken the dumpling from. It was the only one on it she’d touched. He’d had the coin himself once, out of a box of Ah Sim’s dumplings on a ward at midnight. He’d known then it wasn’t luck either.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left at eleven.

Everyone was in the hall at once, getting coats, the way they always were. He got Elara’s coat off the hook and held it for her and she put her arms in it. Then he went to the red door, the way he always did, and put his hand out for the latch.

He stopped.

He’d opened every door for her for over a year. Every door, every jar, every button. He’d done it because she couldn’t, and then he’d gone on doing it after she could, because she let him, and because it was a way of holding on to her that he hadn’t known how to stop.

He took his hand back. He stood aside.

She looked at him. She looked at the door. Then she reached past him with her right hand and opened it herself, the old brass latch, the heavy red door, and held it, and the cold and the noise of the New Year came in from the alley.

She went out first.

✦ ✦ ✦

The alley was hung with red lanterns from end to end, and the fireworks had started over the Walled City, going up in loud bursts above the roofs and coming down in gold. People were in their doorways. Somebody’s children were letting off crackers by the noodle stall.

She stopped halfway down the alley, on the stones.

He knew where. He’d known before she stopped. It was the place.

“Here,” she said. “It was here. I was on the step, and then I was here, and you had my arm up, there, and Yu Chen was here, and Baba was on the step, and the man was over there by the stall—”

She was pointing at the stones, one after another, with her right hand. Her voice was going fast and high. She’d started crying without noticing.

“—and you put your belt on me here, right here, you knelt there, I remember your knee was in the soup, you’d dropped the soup—”

He took her right wrist.

He turned it over, under the red lanterns, palm up. He put his thumb on the inside of it, on the scar, where the pulse was. It was going fast, hard, the way it had on the steps outside Old Bian’s the first time. He felt it under his thumb, strong and sure.

He kissed her there, in the place where he’d knelt in November with her blood coming through his fingers. He kissed her mouth in the middle of her sentence, before she’d finished pointing at the stones, with his thumb still on her pulse.

She made a furious sound against his mouth.

She was crying. She hit his chest once with her left hand. She hadn’t finished. She’d wanted to tell him all of it, every stone, and he’d stopped her, and she was angry, and she didn’t let go of him. She grabbed the front of his coat with her left hand and held on, and kissed him back, hard, with her face wet and the fireworks going up gold over the roofs behind her.

When she pulled back she didn’t let go of his coat.

“I hadn’t finished,” she said. “You always do that. You always stop me in the middle.”

He didn’t say sorry. He’d never once been sorry for it, and she knew that, and she was still holding on to his coat.

She looked up at him with the lanterns red on her wet face. Behind them the red door was still open, with the light from the hall coming out of it, and her whole family standing in it, watching, and none of them pretending they weren’t.

She put her right hand flat on his chest, over his heart, and left it there.

chapters.title: He Goes Back to Work
chapters.desc: The review gives him a warning and his job back. She walks him to the hospital gate like it’s his first day at school, and he shows her the house he’s bought.
chapters.epigraph: “Wear the bananas. Everyone will love you.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The review was on a Thursday afternoon in the same room on the top floor of the old block, and she waited for him in the garden.

He’d told her not to. She’d told him she wasn’t asking. She sat on the bench by the koi pond in her coat with a bag of mandarins from the gatehouse tree, which Peng had sent again on his crutches, and peeled them one after another and ate them and looked up at the top-floor windows, and didn’t know which one he was behind.

It took over an hour. She ate most of the bag.

He came out of the side door of the old block at ten past four with an envelope in his hand and walked across the garden to her, and sat down on the bench, and handed it to her.

A written warning. For removing blood products from the hospital without a patient record. It would stay on his file for two years. The theatre stock entry from March 2023 had been looked at and set aside, as too old and too small to act on. He could go back to clinical duties on Monday. There was a paragraph in the middle she read twice. The panel had received a letter from Inspector Song Wei Long, confirming that a firearm injury to a security guard had been reported to the police by the employer’s lawyer on the morning of the twenty-ninth of November, and that the injured man had been treated and transferred to a private hospital that morning, and that there was no police interest in any doctor.

“Wei Long wrote to them,” she said.

“Zhao’s lawyer rang him that morning. Before seven. He’d already written it down.” Xing Yue looked at the pond. “Dr. Xia read it out. Then she asked me if I had anything to add. I said no. She said, next question.”

Elara put the letter in her lap. She put her hand over her mouth.

He took the last mandarin out of the bag and peeled it, and gave her half.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday morning at half past six she walked him to the hospital gate.

It was ten minutes down the hill from Banyan Terrace. He’d walked it every working morning for eight years, except the mornings since December, when he’d driven to Fig Tree Lane instead and salted lemons. She walked beside him in her coat over her pyjamas, with her hair in a knot, holding his hand.

At the gate, under the old stone arch with CITY HOSPITAL cut into it, she stopped him.

“Wait,” she said. “Bend down.”

He bent down. She took a scrub cap out of her coat pocket. It was the tie-on kind, the cloth ones some surgeons wore instead of paper, and it was yellow, and it was covered in small cartoon bananas with faces.

He looked at it.

“I had them made,” said Elara. “Six. One for every day and one spare. There’s a woman at the market who sews them. I told her bananas and she asked if I wanted faces and I said obviously.”

“Elara.”

“Wear the bananas,” she said. “Everyone will love you.”

She put it on his head. She tied it at the back herself, under his neat short hair, with her right hand, a quick firm knot, and patted it, and stood back and looked at him in the grey morning light under the stone arch in his dark coat and his glasses and a yellow hat covered in smiling fruit.

He didn’t take it off.

She put her hands on his face and stood up on her toes and kissed him, there, at the gate, with a porter going past with a trolley and two nurses coming off nights, and one of the nurses said, “Morning, Dr. Wang,” and kept walking with her eyebrows up somewhere in her hair.

“It’s your first day back,” said Elara. “You’re supposed to be nervous. I’m doing the thing parents do at school.”

“I’m not nervous.”

“I know you’re not. I’m nervous for you. Go on.” She turned him round by the shoulders and pushed him through the gate. “Eat your lunch.”

He walked up the drive to the main doors. He didn’t look back. She stood at the gate in her pyjamas and coat and watched the yellow cap go all the way up and in through the doors.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came back at lunchtime with noodles.

The round had gone on late. Of course it had; he’d been gone three months and he’d read every chart on the floor. She came out of the lift on the ninth floor at five past twelve with the bag in her hand and heard it before she saw it, the way you’d hear weather coming in: his voice at the far end of the ward, never raised, flat and cold and exact.

He was at bed fourteen, in his yellow banana cap, with his whole team round him.

A resident she didn’t know, a tall young man with a new white coat, was standing at the end of the bed holding a set of notes. He’d gone the colour of the notes.

“The blood result came back at eight last night,” said Xing Yue. “It’s in the system. It’s flagged in red. It’s on the front page. You looked at this patient’s chart at ten, at two and at six, and you wrote bloods pending three times.” He didn’t move. “They weren’t pending. They were back. They were telling you his kidneys were failing. You didn’t see them because you didn’t look. You copied what you’d written the time before.” He held his hand out for the notes. “If I hadn’t come back this morning, he’d have been on dialysis by Wednesday. Go and ring the renal team. Then go and find out why you couldn’t read a red number on a screen, and when you’ve found out, tell me, and don’t tell me you were busy.”

The resident went. He went fast. He went straight past the nurses’ station and into the staff toilet at the end of the corridor, and she heard, through the door, that he was being sick.

The patient in bed fourteen was watching all of it with enormous interest.

Elara put the noodles down on the nurses’ station. She went down the corridor and waited outside the toilet door, and when the resident came out, white, wiping his mouth, she took a boiled sweet out of her cardigan pocket and put it in his hand.

He looked at it. He looked at her.

“Lemon,” she said. “It helps. He did it to me on my first day as well. I’m marrying him anyway.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Professor Liao found her at the lifts.

He was in his white coat with a bag of his own sweets, and he looked at her for a second, at the noodle bag and her lanyard from the medical school, and pressed the button for her and stood beside her while they waited.

“I’ll say this once,” he said. “To you, not him. If you tell him I said it, I’ll deny it, and I’ll take you off the anatomy rota.” He sucked his sweet. “He’s the best he’s ever been. Since he came back. Since you.” He looked at the lift doors. “He was always good. He was always right. Now he’s right and he looks at the patient while he’s being right. He didn’t used to do that.”

The lift came. He didn’t get in it.

“Go and give him his lunch,” said Liao, and walked off down the corridor.

She stood there with the doors open in front of her until they closed again.

Later the nurses on 9B told her the other thing. They told her the way nurses told you things, at the station, over tea, all at once. He smiled on rounds now. Not much, and not at the patients, and certainly not at the residents. He smiled at the door, every time it opened, in case it was her.

✦ ✦ ✦

They set the wedding for the end of May.

Saturday the twenty-ninth, at dawn, in the hospital garden, under the camphor tree, by the pond, under the fourth window along on the first floor. She’d rung Sister Shao to ask if nobody had bled in the garden in the last year, and Sister Shao had said one porter, his nose again, same bench, and it still didn’t count.

His parents rang from the north on the Wednesday. His mother said they’d be coming south for it, all of them, and that Nainai was bringing her stick, and that the family would like to give a banquet afterwards, at the Harbour Hotel, for both families, three hundred people, and they’d like to pay for all of it.

“Three hundred,” said Elara, when he’d put the phone down.

“That’s small, for them.”

She thought about it. She thought about the Wangs in their courtyard in the snow, and his father asking when he was coming home, and his grandmother with her stick, and his mother reading her scar over the soup. She thought about the Lins at the long table with their eleven chairs that didn’t match.

“Let them,” she said. “The garden’s ours. They can have the hotel.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Thursday evening he put an envelope on the kitchen counter in front of her.

She looked at it. The last envelope he’d put in front of her had had her mother’s name in it.

She opened it. It was the deed to a house.

2 Camphor Hill. A 1920s house above the hospital, on the road behind it, that everyone at City Hospital called the old doctor’s house, because a physician from the hospital had built it a hundred years ago and lived in it until he died. She’d walked past it a hundred times. It had a long low front with green shutters and a garden behind a wall, and a camphor tree you could see over the top of the wall.

The deed was in two names. WANG XING YUE. LIN ELARA.

It was dated a fortnight ago.

“You bought a house,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You bought a house two weeks ago. You bought a house and you put my name on it and you didn’t tell me. You didn’t ask me. I’ve never been inside it. I don’t know how many rooms it’s got. I don’t know if it’s got a bath. You decided where I’m going to live.”

“It’s got a bath,” he said.

“That’s not—”

“It’s got a long kitchen. It’s got a back room with a north window for the rig. It’s got a garden with a camphor tree in it. It’s ten minutes to City Hospital and twenty-five to Harbourside.” He looked at her. “I wanted you to have it.”

She was so angry she couldn’t speak, which for her was a medical event.

She put the deed down on the counter and went upstairs and shut the bedroom door, and stayed there. She stayed angry all evening. She was angry all night, on her side of the bed, with her back to him. She was angry all Friday morning, through her anatomy class, which got the brachial plexus at a speed that frightened them. She was angry that he’d done it again: the room before she’d moved in, the hook in her locker before he’d asked, and now a house, a whole house, decided, bought, with her name on it, without one word.

And under the anger she was something else, and she knew it, and she was angry about that too.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday afternoon her application went in.

She did it at the desk in his study, at the desk he’d built at her elbow height three and a half years ago, on the training board’s website, with her right hand on the mouse. Re-entry to basic surgical training. Her intern year, her surgical residency, her career break with a reason she’d written and rewritten twenty times and kept short. Injury to dominant hand, November 2025. Full recovery. Independent assessment requested. They’d want a hand assessment from a surgeon who wasn’t hers. They’d want a skills test. They’d want her in a room in front of a panel.

She pressed the button. She sat back and looked at the screen.

Then she went downstairs and found him in the kitchen and said, “Show me the house.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He had the keys in his coat pocket. Of course he did.

It was empty. Every room was empty and swept and smelled of old wood and dust, and the evening light came in through tall windows with green shutters folded back. She walked in through the front door and down a short hall and stopped.

The kitchen ran the whole width of the back of the house. Long and low, with a stone floor and a big old range at one end and a wall of windows over the garden at the other, and through the windows the camphor tree, enormous, with its leaves going gold in the last of the sun. There was room for a table. A long one. Room for eleven chairs.

“Yes,” said Elara.

He was behind her in the hall.

“You haven’t seen the rest of it.”

“I don’t care. Yes.” She didn’t turn round. “I’m still angry. I’m going to be angry about it for a year. I’m going to tell everyone at the banquet that you bought me a house without asking and I’m going to tell your grandmother so she can hit you with her stick.” She turned round. “Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They had a picnic on the kitchen floor.

He went back to the car and came back with a bag of food from Old Bian’s, because he’d bought that too, before they’d left the flat, in case. They sat on the bare boards by the open window with the garden going blue outside and the camphor tree black against the sky, and ate dumplings out of the boxes with their fingers.

She planned it out loud.

All of it, room by room. The table would go there, along the windows, a long one, so they could have everyone. The rig would go in the back room, with the north window, and she’d ask Jinx to come and bolt it down, because Jinx and Raiden were moving across the lake this month anyway and the garage would need the bench. The study would be upstairs, at the front, for him, and she’d have a desk in it too, at her height. Books on every wall. Her shoes by the door, facing out. A bed by the window where you could see the tree. She was talking faster and faster, waving a dumpling, getting up to show him where things would go and sitting down again—

He kissed her.

He leaned across the boxes and took her face in both hands and stopped her mouth with his in the middle of the bookshelves in the second bedroom. She made a muffled sound of protest. Then she dropped the dumpling.

She pulled him down onto the bare boards. He went. The window was open and the evening air came in cool off the garden, and the light was going, and the house was so empty that every sound they made went round it. She laughed at that, against his mouth, and he did too. She took his glasses off and put them on the windowsill. She undid his shirt with her right hand, button by button, fast, and he caught her wrist and held it and kissed the scar, and then let her go on.

It was slow after that. Slower than she’d meant. The boards were hard under her back and she didn’t care. He was warm over her and the air from the window was cool on her skin, and the camphor tree moved outside in the dusk, and she held onto him and watched the ceiling of their kitchen go from gold to grey to dark over his shoulder, and said his name into the empty house and heard it come back.

Afterwards they lay on the floor under his coat with the window open and the stars coming out over the tree.

“I’m still angry,” she said, into his chest.

“I know,” said Xing Yue.

“The table goes there,” she said, and pointed at the dark windows with her right hand, and he turned his head and looked where she was pointing.

chapters.title: The Skills Test
chapters.desc: A hand surgeon she’s never met tests her strength and feeling, and examiners time her on a model bowel. He isn’t allowed in, so he waits in the car park for three hours.
chapters.epigraph: “Stop coaching me. Let me do it my way.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The hand surgeon was called Mr. Situ, and he worked at Harbourside, and he had never met her. That was the point of him.

The training board had sent three names. Elara picked the one she’d never heard of. Xing Yue had heard of all three, and he’d have picked Situ too, because Situ was the hardest of them and nobody would ever say he’d been kind to her. He didn’t say so. She hadn’t asked.

He drove her across the harbour on the first Thursday in April and parked in the multi-storey at Harbourside, on the level with the bridge into the outpatient block.

“You can’t come in,” she said.

“I know.”

She’d put on a grey jacket over a white shirt, and her hair was in a clip that was already losing, and her right hand was in her jacket pocket, which was where she kept it when she was frightened. She leaned across the gearstick and kissed his cheek and got out. He watched her walk across the bridge. She didn’t look back. She never did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dr. Zou rang twenty minutes later.

He was on call on 9B with a man in bed four whose drain had changed colour in the night. The registrar had told him to ring Dr. Wang, because Dr. Wang was the consultant this week and had said on Monday, in front of everyone, that he wanted to hear about drains.

“When did it change?” said Xing Yue.

“Some time in the night. The nurses noticed at six.”

“It’s ten past nine. What have you done in three hours?”

“I sent bloods.”

Xing Yue asked if they’d come back, and there was a silence on the line.

He sat in the car with the engine off, looking at the bridge she’d walked across, and told Zou what he thought of a registrar who sent bloods and didn’t look at them, and what the drain meant, and what the man in bed four would need before lunch, and who was going to book it. He didn’t raise his voice. Zou said “Yes” at the end of each sentence, faster each time.

“If you send something and don’t look at it,” said Xing Yue, “don’t send it. You’ll save the lab the trouble.”

He put the phone face down on the passenger seat. Then he turned it over and looked at her dot, a small blue circle on the third floor of the outpatient block, perfectly still, and turned it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came out at half past eleven with her right hand tucked under her left arm.

He got out of the car. She came straight to him and didn’t say anything, which was how he knew how hard the morning had been, and took her hand out and held it up.

It was white. The fingers bloodless to the second knuckle, waxy and stiff, the nails a faint grey-blue. He’d seen it go like that in theatres and in the lecture rooms at the medical school and once in the frozen aisle of the supermarket. It always came back. It always frightened him.

“He keeps the room freezing on purpose,” said Elara. “I asked. He said half his patients have cold hands after an injury and he wants to see what they do in a real theatre, not a nice warm clinic. I said that was sensible and quite evil, and he wrote something down.”

He took her hand.

He opened his coat and the top of his shirt, there in the car park, and put her hand flat against his chest, against his skin, and held it there under his own. She was so cold he caught his breath. She stopped talking.

He felt the stiffness go out of her fingers one at a time. After a minute he lifted her hand out and turned it to the light. Pink was coming up from the base of each finger. He pressed the nail of her index finger with his thumb and let go, and watched the white spot fill in under a second.

“It’s back,” he said.

“It always comes back.”

He kissed her. With her hand still in his, still against his open shirt, on the third level of the Harbourside multi-storey, with a woman unloading a pram from the next car. She made a small surprised sound and then her other hand was in his coat, holding on, and she kissed him back as if she’d been waiting all morning to do it. Her fingers moved against his chest. He felt each one.

The woman with the pram took her husband’s arm and went away.

“I passed,” said Elara against his mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him in the car in three parts. The grip machine first, her right hand against her left, and the right had been stronger, which Situ looked at twice and wrote down, and she’d said that was a year of springs, and he’d said he’d like to meet the springs. Then the nylon threads on her fingertips with her eyes shut, and the blunt points of the calipers, and she’d got every one but the edge of her little finger, which she’d told him before he found it. Then the third part, which was important, something he’d said at the end—

She’d lost it. It came back twenty minutes later on the hill road below Banyan Terrace, in the middle of a story about the ticket machine.

“He said he’d let me operate on him,” she said, and burst into tears, and he pulled over by the bakery and gave her his handkerchief and went in and bought her an egg tart while she cried into it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Saturday Jinx moved the rig.

She came up Camphor Hill at seven in Raiden’s van, with the frame wrapped in blankets in the back and a box of tools on her knees. She’d unbolted it from the end of the long bench on Friday night, where it had stood for thirteen months under the old painted sign. They’d moved across the lake in March, and the garage was nearly empty, and Jinx had said the bench could go when the rig went and not before.

She didn’t let anyone carry it but Raiden, and only his end. They took it through the empty house to the back room with the north window, and Jinx stood on the bare boards and looked at the light and the wall and where the afternoon sun would come, and then got down on her knees with a drill.

Xing Yue stood in the doorway.

He’d never seen it. He’d watched her dot go to the garage at a quarter to five every morning for a year. He’d heard it described in pieces, at the table, in bed. He’d never once gone to look, because she hadn’t asked him to.

It was smaller than he’d thought. A frame, a forearm rest, a rail of springs, a dial, a board of pins from fat to fine, a thin wire track with a buzzer at one end, a camera over a practice pad. Every part had a knurled steel knob.

“Quarter turn,” said Jinx from the floor. “All of them. So she can make it harder without asking anybody.” She drove the last bolt and sat back on her heels and looked up at him. “Don’t touch them.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You think the third spring’s too low.”

He did think that. Raiden laughed out loud in the hall. Jinx put her drill away, and when Elara tried to thank her she said she had a gearbox in the van and left.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then he started coaching her.

He didn’t decide to. He found himself doing it, the way he found himself checking her dot. The skills test was on the sixteenth, and the interview a week after that if she passed, and every night at Banyan Terrace he sat across the table and asked her the questions they’d ask. Why surgery. Why now. Tell me about a mistake. Tell me about your injury. How do you know you’re ready. He asked them the way he’d been asked them in the north, by five men in grey suits, and told her how to make her answers better.

In the mornings he went up the hill with her and sat on a crate in the back room at Camphor Hill and timed her knots with the second hand of his watch. He told her she was holding the needle holder too far down. He told her to stop talking while she sutured, because examiners didn’t like it.

She did what he said for four days.

On the fifth night, in the middle of his sixth question, she put her chopsticks down.

“Stop coaching me,” said Elara. “Let me do it my way.”

“I’m trying to help.”

“I know. You’re the best teacher I ever had.” She pushed her bowl away. “But you’re doing it to me the way you’d do it to a resident, and I’ve been doing this on my own in the dark for a year. I hold the needle holder there because that’s where it works for my hand now. It’s a different hand. Jinx built a whole machine round it. And I talk when I sew. I’ve always talked. If the examiners don’t like it they can tell me.”

He didn’t say anything.

“And you keep rewriting what I say about the knife. You weren’t the one who had it.”

That one went in. She saw it go in and reached across the table, but she didn’t take it back.

“I know you were holding it shut,” she said. “But it’s my hand. I want to say it my way, even if my way’s worse.”

He took his glasses off and cleaned them on his handkerchief. She waited, and didn’t fill the silence, which for her was a kind of mercy.

“I’ve never been nervous for a test,” he said. “Not mine. I’m nervous for yours.”

Her face went soft all at once.

“I know,” said Elara. “That’s why you have to stop.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He managed two nights.

On the Thursday, the night before, they were on the long grey sofa with her feet in his lap, and she was telling him about the first-years and the brachial plexus, and he heard himself say, “If they ask why you left Harbourside after your intern year—”

She sat up and put her hand over his mouth.

Her right hand, flat and firm, the heel of it on his chin. She looked at him over it, close, with her eyebrows up.

“You promised,” she said. “On this sofa. I’m going to take my hand away. If you ask me another question, I’ll put it back.”

She took it away, and before he could decide whether he was going to say anything, she kissed him, hard, where her hand had been.

He laughed. It came up out of him into her mouth. She pulled back an inch, delighted, and kissed him again before it had finished. He pulled her down onto him and she came, knees on either side of him and her hands in his hair, and kissed him until he’d forgotten every question anyone had ever asked him in the north.

“You need an early night,” he said, when he could.

She told him that was a question. He told her it was an order, and she said she’d allow it, and pulled him off the sofa and up the stairs.

She was gentle with him, which surprised him. Slow and warm and laughing, with the window open and the city going on outside, as if he were the one with something to do in the morning. She took her time over every button. She kissed the place on his chest where her cold hand had been, and told him so, and he pulled her down to stop her telling him anything else. When she fell asleep she went all at once, on his chest, with her right hand open over his heart, and he lay awake for an hour and didn’t move it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The surgical college was a grey stone building near the courts, with a porter at the door checking names on a list. Candidates only, the sign said.

“I’ll be three hours,” she said. “Go home.”

“No.”

She nodded, as though she’d expected that, and kissed him once through the car window and went in.

He sat in the car park for three hours with a journal open on the steering wheel at a paper on bile duct injuries, and read the first paragraph eleven times. He checked her dot. It sat a little left of the middle of the building and didn’t move. He knew it wouldn’t. He checked it every ten minutes anyway, the way you check a pressure after a big case, not because it would tell you anything.

He knew roughly what they’d give her. A pad of fake skin and a row of stitches against the clock. Knots tied down onto a post that told the examiner if they’d slip. Then the one that mattered: a length of model bowel cut across, two ends to join by hand, and two surgeons marking every stitch for spacing and depth and how she handled the tissue. He’d done it himself at twenty-five. He remembered being bored.

At the end of the second hour Professor Liao rang.

“Are you in the car park?” he said.

Xing Yue didn’t answer. Liao made a sound that might have been a laugh, and rang off.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came out at twenty past one and stopped on the top step and found the car. Then she ran.

She ran across the car park between the parked cars with her bag banging on her hip and her hair coming out of its clip, and he was out of the car before he knew he’d opened the door. She didn’t slow down. She jumped, and he caught her, and she hit him hard enough to knock him back against the car. Her arms went round his neck and her legs round his waist and she kissed his mouth and his cheek and his glasses, which went crooked, and his mouth again, laughing, while the porter watched from the steps with his list under his arm.

“I talked,” she said. “All through the skin pad and the knots and the start of the bowel. And the examiner, Zhai, a colorectal man, he’s ancient, he looked up and said, Dr. Lin, would you mind not talking. I said sorry, I talk when I sew. He said, then try sewing without it.” She was still in his arms. “So I stopped. And I got faster. I don’t know why. I hummed instead. I finished with four minutes on his watch, and he and the other one turned the bowel over and looked at the back of it, and she ran her finger along the line. And Zhai said, where have you been for a year?”

He went still.

“He meant the career break. It’s on his sheet. He meant, you’re good, where’ve you been.” She put her forehead on his. “But I nearly told him. I nearly said, under a rope store.”

He put her down then, onto her feet by the car. She took his coat off him and put it on, because her hand had gone cold again in the college, and didn’t give it back.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home she stood in the kitchen with the sleeves down over her fingers.

“That’s what frightens me,” she said. “Not the hand. They’ll ask about the hand and I can tell them. It’s that. Where have you been?” She looked at him over his collar. “What if they ask if I’ve operated since the knife?”

He knew what he’d say. He’d said it to Liao with a sweet in the old man’s cheek, and to an inquiry, and in a dozen notes. One word. The easiest one there was.

“You could say no,” he said.

She looked at him for a second.

“You did say no,” said Elara. “You’ve been saying no for me for four years. I’m not going to make you the only one in this house who lies about it. And I’m not lying to them. We wrote that down.”

“That rule was for us.”

“I know who it was for.” She pushed the sleeves up. “I won’t lie, and I won’t tell them anything they don’t ask. If they ask straight out, I’ll say I’m not answering. If that’s the end of it, it’s the end of it.”

He wanted to argue. He wanted to tell her that the end of it would be a letter and a shut door and her standing on the steps of a grey building with nowhere to go, and he’d watched her stand on enough steps.

He didn’t. She hadn’t asked what he thought. She’d told him what she was going to do.

“All right,” said Xing Yue.

She came across the kitchen in his coat and put her cold right hand flat inside his shirt, on purpose, to make him jump, and he did.

chapters.title: The Board Asks About the Accident
chapters.desc: At her interview they ask about the knife and the year after it. She tells the truth, and when they ask the one question she won’t answer, she says so.
chapters.epigraph: “I won’t lie to you, and I’m not going to answer that.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The suit was navy, and Elowen had chosen it, and Elara hated it.

It was a good suit, which was the trouble. It fitted like a decision someone else had made. The jacket was stiff across the shoulders. The trousers had a crease you could have cut bread with. She stood in front of the bedroom mirror at Banyan Terrace at half past six on the Thursday morning and looked like a lawyer who’d come to tell somebody bad news.

“I look like I’m about to sue someone,” she said.

Xing Yue was behind her, doing up his watch. He was on a list at eight, and she’d told him she didn’t want him to come.

“You look like a surgeon,” he said.

“Surgeons wear blue pyjamas and paper hats.” She pulled at the jacket. “I didn’t sleep.”

“I know.”

He came round in front of her. He took the small pen torch out of his shirt pocket, the one he carried on every round, and clicked it on, and before she could ask what he was doing he tipped her chin up with one finger and shone it in her left eye, and then her right.

“Really,” said Elara.

He clicked it off. He looked at her for a second longer, at her eyes, close, the way he’d look at a patient who said they were fine.

“Pupils equal,” he said. “You didn’t sleep.”

“I just told you I didn’t—”

He kissed her. He put the pen torch back in his pocket without looking and took her face in both hands and kissed her, there in front of the mirror, slow, as if he had nowhere to be at eight and no list at all. She held onto the front of his shirt. Her stiff navy shoulders went loose for the first time since she’d put the jacket on.

When he let her go she was pink to the ears and the clip had come out of her hair.

“Now you look like a surgeon,” said Xing Yue, and picked the clip up off the floor and gave it to her, and went to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

The interview was on the top floor of the training board’s offices, in a room with a long table and a jug of water nobody touched.

There were four of them. A woman in her fifties at the end, Ms. Dong, who ran the surgical training programme and had a face like a closed door. Mr. Zhuang, a consultant from Harbourside, broad and bald, with his reading glasses on his head. A man from the college who was introduced as Mr. Qi and who wrote things down and didn’t speak once. And at the other end, with a folder in front of her, Dr. Xia Wanqing, the medical director of City Hospital, sitting in for the hospitals.

Elara sat down opposite them in the navy suit with her hands in her lap. The ring was on her left hand. She’d thought about taking it off and hadn’t.

They began with the ordinary questions. She talked too much in every answer and watched Ms. Dong’s face not move, and kept talking anyway, because she’d told him she’d do it her way.

Then Ms. Dong turned a page.

“Your career break,” she said. “Tell us about the injury.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She told them plainly.

She’d decided in the taxi that morning that she would. Not the whole of it. Not her father or the boats or the man by the noodle stall. But the parts that were hers.

“It was a knife,” said Elara. “In November 2025. A man came to my father’s house and I got in the way. It went across the inside of my right wrist. It cut most of the flexor tendons and both the big nerves and the ulnar artery.” She turned her hand over on the table, palm up, and pushed her cuff back so they could see the scar and the zigzag. “Dr. Meng at City Hospital repaired it the same night. Splint for six weeks. Then therapy at the Crestview three times a week. Ms. Cui. She made a footballer cry once. She made me cry a lot.”

Mr. Zhuang’s mouth moved at one corner.

“Then my sister-in-law built me a machine,” said Elara.

She told them about the rig. She couldn’t help it. The springs and the pins and the wire that buzzed, and the knobs that turned a quarter at a time, and a year of a quarter to five every morning in a garage near the Docks while her sister-in-law fixed motorbikes with her back turned. The first tingle, in the shower. Her right hand stronger than her left now, which Mr. Situ had written down twice.

“It still goes white in the cold,” she said. “It’ll do that for the rest of my life. I warm it under my arm before I scrub. Nobody notices.” She put her hand flat on the table. “That’s it. That’s where I’ve been.”

Dr. Xia, at the end, hadn’t written anything. She was looking at Elara’s hand on the table.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Zhuang took his glasses off his head and put them on.

“Your hand’s been tested in a lab,” he said. “Mr. Situ’s report is good. Your skills test is the best this year, which Zhai tells me is annoying, because he wanted to fail you for talking.” He looked at her over the glasses. “But a lab isn’t a theatre. A pad isn’t a person. How do you know it holds up at three in the morning with someone bleeding in front of you?”

“Because it has,” said Elara.

The room went still.

She hadn’t meant to say it. It had come out the way the truth always did, before she could get in front of it, and she felt her face go hot and then cold.

Mr. Zhuang didn’t move.

“Where?” he said.

She thought of Peng on the table under the big light, and a girl with a bottle across her cheek, and Xing Yue’s hands above the tear, steady as a clamp. She thought of the inquiry room on the top floor of the old block, and Xing Yue saying nobody else was involved to the woman sitting at the end of this table.

She didn’t look at Dr. Xia.

“I won’t lie to you,” said Elara. “And I’m not going to answer that.”

Nobody said anything.

Mr. Qi stopped writing. Ms. Dong put her pen down. Mr. Zhuang sat back in his chair and looked at her with his glasses on, for what felt like a whole minute, and she looked back, and didn’t say one more word. It was the hardest thing she’d ever done in a room full of people. Every part of her wanted to fill it. She sat on her hands, almost, and kept her mouth shut.

At the end of the table, Dr. Xia closed her folder.

“Next question,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside, on the pavement, she shook.

She stood against the wall in the stupid suit and shook from her feet up, so hard her teeth went. She got her phone out with both hands and rang him.

It rang and rang. Then someone picked up, and there was the noise of a theatre behind it, the beeping and the suction and somebody asking for a swab, and a woman’s voice she knew.

“It’s Sister Shao, love,” said the voice. “He’s scrubbed. I’d come down with a patient and they’ve given me the phone because I’m the only one in here with nothing to do. I’m holding it to his ear. Go on.”

“Elara,” said Xing Yue.

She couldn’t speak. She stood against the wall and breathed.

“Was it bad?” he said.

“I don’t know. I told them. I told them the truth and then I told them I wouldn’t answer, and nobody said anything, and then Dr. Xia said next question.” Her voice cracked. “I don’t know if that’s bad. I think it might be the end of it.”

There was a pause. She heard the suction, and him say something short and cold to somebody at the table, and then his voice again, close.

“Come home,” he said.

“You’re not home.”

“I will be. Go home. I’ll be there at six.”

“Doctor,” said Sister Shao’s voice, from further off, “your registrar’s waiting,” and the line went.

✦ ✦ ✦

She waited three weeks.

She taught louder than she’d ever taught in her life. The first-years got the hand that week, every bone of it, with a story for each, and a girl laughed so hard at the hamate she had to leave the room. The man who called the little finger the fifth digit started having his lunch somewhere else.

The ghost phone didn’t ring. Her father had promised her it wouldn’t. He’d rung on the Thursday night, the night of the interview, and asked how it had gone, and listened to the whole thing, and then said, “Nobody rings you till you know. I’ll tell them.” She’d asked what if somebody was dying. He’d said then he’d take them to a hospital himself and carry them through the doors.

She didn’t sleep much. She went up the hill to Camphor Hill at three in the morning, some nights, and sat on the rig in the back room with the north window black and the springs on the hardest setting, and worked until her hand ached.

On the second Tuesday he came up after her.

She heard the front door, and his feet in the empty hall, and he came and stood in the doorway in his coat over his pyjamas, and looked at her on the rig.

He didn’t say anything about the springs. He didn’t tell her where she was losing time. He sat down on the upturned crate by the wall with his hands between his knees and watched her run the wire, the whole length of it, silent, and back.

“You can say something,” said Elara.

“I’m not coaching you.”

“You can say something that isn’t coaching.”

He thought about it.

“You’re beautiful at four in the morning,” said Xing Yue.

She laughed so hard she touched the wire, and it buzzed, for the first time in months, and she put her forehead down on the forearm rest and laughed into it until he came and lifted her off the stool.

✦ ✦ ✦

The letter came on a Friday, the fourteenth of May, at twenty to eight in the evening, in an email.

She was at the kitchen counter at Banyan Terrace eating peach yoghurt out of the pot. She read it standing up. Then she read it again sitting on the floor, because her legs had stopped.

A place in basic surgical training. Harbourside General. Starting on the first of July.

Harbourside had been her first choice on the form. She’d put it first on purpose, in March, at his desk, with him downstairs not asking. Not his hospital. Not his department, not his professor, not his name on the board outside the ward. Nobody would ever be able to stand at a nurses’ station and say that Wang got his wife a job.

He was on call. He’d been in theatre since five.

She didn’t ring him. She put her shoes on without socks and ran.

✦ ✦ ✦

She ran down the hill from Banyan Terrace with her phone in her hand and her hair coming down, ten minutes on a working morning, six tonight, through the stone arch with CITY HOSPITAL cut into it and up the drive and in through the main doors.

At the lifts on the ground floor she nearly ran into Dr. Xia.

The medical director was going home. She had her coat on and her bag over her shoulder and her folder under her arm, and she stopped, and looked at Elara, out of breath, in a cardigan with yoghurt on it and no socks.

Elara stopped too. She didn’t know what to say. She held the phone against her chest.

Dr. Xia looked at the phone. Then she looked at Elara’s face.

“Your fiancé,” she said, “is a stubborn man.”

Elara opened her mouth.

“Make sure he isn’t stubborn on his own again,” said Dr. Xia. “It’s expensive. For everyone.” She pressed the lift button for her, the way Liao had once, and walked away across the hall to the main doors, and didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at the nurses’ station on 9B.

He’d come straight up from theatre. He was still in his scrubs, and he was still wearing the cap, the yellow one with the bananas, and there was an intern in front of him, a girl with a fluid chart in her hand that he’d just taken out of it.

“You’ve written this man up for the same bag every eight hours since Tuesday,” he was saying. “He’s been nil by mouth since Tuesday. Look at his weight. Look at his sodium. Look at him. He’s in the bed behind you. Turn round—”

Elara walked up the corridor, past the side rooms and the drug trolley and Sister Shao at the end of the station with a mug of tea, and took the fluid chart out of his hand.

He stopped. He looked down at her.

She put her phone in his hand instead, with the email open on it.

He read it. She watched him read it. She watched his face as he got to the word Harbourside, and then the date, and she saw it go through him, all the way down, and she didn’t wait for him to finish.

She took the front of his scrub top in her fist and pulled him down and kissed him.

In front of the intern, and the fluid chart, and Sister Shao, and two porters with a trolley, and the man in bed six, who’d sat up. In the middle of the ninth floor at City Hospital, where he’d said not in the hospital three and a half years ago and meant it. She kissed him hard, standing up on her toes in her yoghurt cardigan, with his phone and hers both somewhere between them, and after a second his hand came up to the back of her head and held her there.

Behind her somebody started clapping. She knew who. It was slow and loud and pleased with itself, and then the porters joined in, and then the man in bed six.

She let him go.

He was looking down at her in his banana cap, and it was all over his face, and the whole ward could see it. The intern saw it and went pink.

“I got in,” said Elara. “Not your hospital. Not your anything.”

She took the banana cap off his head.

She held it up in her right hand, by its strings, and walked backwards down the corridor with it, away from the station, towards the door at the end where the on-call room was, and he stood there for one second in front of the whole of 9B. Then he handed the fluid chart back to the intern without looking at her, and said, “Do it again. Properly,” and followed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The on-call room on the ninth floor still had the narrow bed and the chair and the desk and the window over the hospital garden. She’d brought him dumplings in it once at midnight, on a Lunar New Year’s Eve, and he’d locked the door.

She locked it this time.

She turned the key with her back against the door and the banana cap still in her hand, and he was there, and she dropped the cap and put both her hands in his hair and pulled him down to her.

It wasn’t slow. It had been three weeks, and an interview, and a pavement, and a whole ward clapping, and she kissed him as if she’d been holding her breath since April. She pushed him back until his legs hit the desk and he sat on the edge of it, and she stood between his knees and kissed his mouth and his jaw and the place under his ear that made him stop breathing.

He got his hands under her cardigan, warm on her back. She pulled his scrub top up and he pulled it off for her. Somewhere a trolley went past outside in the corridor, and she laughed against his neck, and he held her tighter, and his mouth was at her throat and then lower, and she said his name the way she said it at home, not caring who was on the other side of the door.

His pager went off on the waistband of his scrubs.

He swore, which he never did. She got there first. She took it off his waistband and held it up to the light from the window and read it.

“It’s from the station,” said Elara. “It says bed eight fine, nothing needed. You have twenty minutes. S.”

He took his glasses off.

He put them in the pocket of her cardigan, the way he had on the steps outside Old Bian’s the night of the bananas, and took the pager out of her hand and put it face down on the desk, and pulled her into his lap.

“Twenty minutes,” he said.

“She’ll be counting.”

“Let her,” said Xing Yue, and stopped her mouth before she could say anything about Sister Shao, or the hospital, or the rules, and she didn’t try hard to finish.

chapters.title: The Wedding Under Her Mother’s Window
chapters.desc: They marry at six in the morning in the hospital garden, with the night staff in scrubs at the back. She talks too long, and he says one sentence.
chapters.epigraph: “Talk as long as you like. I’m staying.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
At five in the morning the garden was still grey, and the porters were putting out the chairs.

Two rows on each side of the path, folding wooden ones from the old lecture theatre, set out on the grass under the camphor tree. The pond was dark and still, with the koi asleep somewhere at the bottom. Above it the back of the old block went up in its two floors of tall arched windows, and the fourth one along on the first floor had a light on in it. Dr. Xia had given Elara the key to the records office for the morning. She was up there now, with her sisters, getting dressed in the room where her mother had worked.

Raiden’s arch stood at the end of the path.

He’d built it from hospital bed frames. Old iron ones, the head and foot ends from the 1930s wards, which had been sitting in the basement store under the old block for fifty years until Professor Liao signed them out to him for a token sum and a promise. Raiden had cleaned them and painted them white and bolted four of them together into a tall curved arch, with the little brass wheels still on the bottom, and Elowen had wound it in white camellias from her shop, hundreds of them, so that the iron only showed in places.

“It’s structurally perfect,” said Raiden, to anyone who passed. “You could hang a car off it.”

Xing Yue stood under it in his dark grey suit and waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

A woman from the photographer’s firm came up the path at twenty past five with a clipboard and a light meter.

She looked at the back of the garden, where people had started to gather behind the last row of chairs. Nurses in blue scrubs with coffee in paper cups. Two porters. A registrar he recognised from the emergency department, still in her lanyard, sitting on the low stone edge of the pond with her shoes off. Sister Shao in the middle of them in her navy uniform, with her arms folded, having come straight off the night on 9B.

“Could we move those people?” said the woman. “They’re in the back of every shot. Could they go behind the tree, or—”

“No,” said Xing Yue.

She looked at him.

“They’re coming off a night shift,” he said. “Some of them have been on since eight last night. They came out here instead of going home to bed. They stay where they are, and you’ll photograph them, and if any of them is cut out of a single picture, your firm won’t be paid.” He didn’t raise his voice. “Is that clear?”

The woman went pink and said it was, and went and stood somewhere else.

An Yu, beside him, said nothing at all. He’d flown down the night before with their parents and Nainai, and he was standing at his brother’s shoulder in a suit that cost more than the arch, holding a flask of Pu’er, and when the woman had gone he unscrewed the lid and poured some into the cup and handed it to Xing Yue without a word.

Xing Yue drank it.

“You’re shaking,” said An Yu.

“I’m not.”

“Your tea is,” said his brother, and took the cup back.

✦ ✦ ✦

The chairs filled.

The Lins on the left. Elowen’s chair was empty, because Elowen was upstairs, but Zhao sat beside it in black, enormous, perfectly still, with one white camellia in his lapel. Jinx in the second row in a dress she’d plainly been made to wear, and Raiden beside her, still looking at his arch. Jun Hyuk, with a packet of tissues already open on his knee. Eliana at the end with a camera on a stick, and Yu Chen beside her, his ears already red.

Ah Sim in a dark blue jacket she’d had for thirty years, with Uncle Mok next to her, who’d driven her and hadn’t let her walk the last bit from the gate. Peng on the aisle with a stick and his leg out straight, in his gatehouse uniform, pressed. And on the end of the front row, in a black straw hat with a white flower on it, an old woman with a bag on her knee who had kept a red cloth ledger for thirty-one years, and had come down the church steps and across the city on two buses because Elara had written and asked her.

The Wangs on the right. His mother, tall and grey and calm. His father, who’d come south, who’d been told come and see where I work and had come, and who’d stood for a while that morning at the gate under the old stone arch looking up at the tower with his hands behind his back. Nainai in the front row with her stick across her knees, looking at the bed-frame arch with deep suspicion.

At the back, behind the Wangs, Professor Liao with a bag of boiled sweets he was handing out to the night nurses. Dr. Meng, and beside her Ms. Cui, upright as a pole, not smiling. Dr. Fei with her two children, who’d been promised breakfast. Mr. Yin, in his bus driver’s jacket, who’d sent a card every September since his stoma was reversed and had answered this invitation by return.

Nainai turned round in her chair and pointed her stick at him under the arch.

“She told me about the house,” she said, loud enough for the back row. “You bought her a house without asking.”

“Yes.”

“Good,” said his grandmother. “But you should have asked.” And turned back round.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten to six the light came up over the old block and touched the top of the camphor tree, and the side door opened.

Elowen came out first, in green, and Evangeline in pale blue, and they walked down the path, and Elowen went to her chair beside Zhao and Ev to hers beside Jun Hyuk, who took one look at her and started crying already.

Then Elara came out on her father’s arm.

Lin Jian was in his funeral suit, which was still his only suit after every wedding. He’d had it pressed. He came down the step from the side door slowly, as if he were afraid of going too fast. Elara had asked him in April, at Sunday lunch, at the long table, in front of everyone. Will you walk me? He’d put his chopsticks down and said, Yes. If you want. And she’d said, I asked, Baba.

Her dress was white, and simple, and came to just above her ankles, and it had short sleeves.

That had been the only thing she’d known for certain when she went to the dressmaker. Short sleeves. So the scar showed. She’d said she’d spent a year hiding that hand inside her own pocket and she wasn’t hiding it at her own wedding. And there it was, in the first light, across the inside of her right wrist and up her forearm in its zigzag, pale now, silver at the edges, on the arm she’d linked through her father’s.

She was carrying white camellias. Tucked into the middle of them, so you’d only see it if you looked, was a small square photograph with white edges: a young man on a boat with a rope over his shoulder, and a young woman in a nurse’s uniform at a window. The window was up there, above them. The fourth one along.

Her hair was up, and already coming down.

She was looking at him all the way down the path.

✦ ✦ ✦

The celebrant was a small brisk woman from the registry who had married people in stranger places, she’d told them, but never under hospital beds.

Elara gave her bouquet to Elowen. Then, before anything else, she took an envelope out of the pocket of her dress, because of course the dress had a pocket, and unfolded a single sheet of lined paper, and turned to the chairs.

“My uncle wrote,” she said. “He can’t be here. He’s not allowed out till 2029. He wrote three pages and I’m only reading one line, because the rest is mostly about the food in prison.” A few people laughed. Her voice was shaking. “He says, Your mother would have talked through the whole thing, and your father would have let her.”

She folded it up again. She put it back in her pocket. Lin Jian, in the front row, looked down at his own hands.

Then she turned back to Xing Yue and started talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t keep it short.

She’d said she would. She’d said it three times that week, and he’d said she could talk as long as she liked, and she’d said no, she’d keep it short, she had three things to say and she’d written them on her hand. He could see the biro on the inside of her left wrist. 1. 2. 3. That was all she’d written. Numbers.

The first thing was the ward round. She told the whole garden about it: bed fourteen, the leak, Mr. Yin’s heart rate, a chief resident in glasses who’d looked at her as if she were a drug chart someone had got wrong, and how she’d been sure he would ruin her life. Mr. Yin, in the back row, said, “He nearly did,” and the night nurses laughed. She said he’d taken her logbook away before lunch and she’d marched into his office to apologise for being right.

The second thing was the supply room. She didn’t say what for. She looked at him, and told the garden that once, at three in the morning, when she was frightened out of her mind and had two bags of fluid in her hands and no right to them, he’d found her and swapped her instrument case for a better one and said three words, and kept them for three and a half years, through things that would have broken anyone else’s promise in half. Her voice went at the end of that. She stopped and breathed.

“The third thing,” said Elara.

She looked down at her wrist.

“The third thing’s the important one,” she said. “I know it is. I wrote it down so I wouldn’t—” She turned her wrist to the light. “I only wrote the number.”

The whole garden laughed. Even Ms. Cui’s mouth moved. Nainai cackled from the front row.

Elara stood under the bed-frame arch in her white dress with the scar showing and her wrist turned up, laughing too, and crying, and looking at him, and he saw her start to panic about the lost third thing, saw her open her mouth to start again from the beginning—

“Talk as long as you like,” said Xing Yue. “I’m staying.”

That was all he said.

She shut her mouth. She looked at him.

In the second row Jun Hyuk made a sound like a kettle and put his face in Evangeline’s shoulder, and Ev put her hand on the back of his head and held it there, and looked straight ahead, and didn’t move.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rings were plain gold. Aurelia had made them, because Aurelia had made the first one, and had said that if anyone else made the second she’d take it personally.

He took Elara’s left hand to put hers on.

He held it the way he’d held it a hundred times, palm down in his, and he looked at the fourth finger, where the star sapphire already was. Then he bent his head and kissed that finger, just above the knuckle, where the band would go. He put the band on. He looked up at her, and her eyes had gone wide, and before the celebrant could say the line she was waiting to say, he kissed her mouth.

She grabbed his lapels with both hands. She kissed him back under the arch, under the camellias, under her mother’s window, in the early light, with the night staff at the back of the garden putting their coffee down on the grass to clap.

The celebrant said it anyway, afterwards, for the record.

✦ ✦ ✦

He gave her the frames on the path, after the photographs, while everyone stood about on the grass and Nainai poked the bed-frame arch with her stick to see if it would fall down.

There were two, in plain dark wood, wrapped in brown paper. He’d found them in March in the welfare archive and in the old harbour licensing office, and had them copied and framed. Her mother’s nursing registration: a small photograph stapled to a card, a young woman in a cap with a round face and quick dark eyes, looking straight at the camera as if she were about to say something. Her father’s licence for a lighter boat, with his name typed across the top and a photograph of a laughing man who’d plainly been told not to laugh.

There was a card with them, folded once. One line on it, in his writing.

Elara looked at the frames and didn’t speak. Then she opened the card and read it, and put her hand over her mouth.

“What does it say?” said Raiden, over her shoulder. “I can’t read it. Nobody can read it. What does it say?”

“No,” said Elara.

She put the card inside her dress, against her heart, and wouldn’t say another word about it, and Raiden sulked about it until the banquet.

✦ ✦ ✦

The banquet was enormous. It was at the Harbour Hotel, in the big ballroom, and there were three hundred people at it, and his parents had paid for every one of them.

He hardly remembered it afterwards. He remembered pieces. His father standing up to speak and saying, to his own surprise, that he’d been to the hospital that morning and that it was a good hospital, and sitting down again. Sister Shao calling across the room, “Dr. Wang,” and both of them turning round. Nainai, at the top table, reaching across the tablecloth with her stick and hitting him on the arm with it, hard, and saying, “House,” and Elara laughing until she had to put her head down on the table.

He remembered Aurelia, across the ballroom in red, leaning over to Elowen and saying something, and Elowen going stiff.

“What did she say?” he asked Elara.

“She said this one counts as a point for nobody,” said Elara. “Because Elowen did the flowers and Aurelia did the rings, so they’ve cancelled out.” She watched her eldest sister’s face. “Elowen’s going to argue about it for a year.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She wanted to go home. Not a hotel. She’d said so in March, on the bare kitchen boards, and she’d said it every week since. Home.

They’d moved into Camphor Hill a fortnight before, on the Saturday after her letter, with Uncle Mok’s car and Raiden’s van and Jun Hyuk talking the whole way about where the lemons should go. The long table was along the kitchen windows. The bed was by the window upstairs, where you could see the tree.

They got there at half past eleven at night. She took her shoes off in the hall and put them by the door, facing out, and stood in her white dress in the dark kitchen with her hair half down.

Then she turned round, and reached up, and took his glasses off.

He let her. She folded them, carefully, with her right hand, and put them in the breast pocket of his suit, and patted the pocket flat, and looked up at him.

“There,” said Elara. “Now it’s my turn.”

She took him upstairs.

It was slow. Slower than anything. She undid his tie and his buttons one at a time, and he undid the long row of small buttons down the back of her dress, every one, which took a while, and she laughed at how long it took and said the dressmaker had done it on purpose, and then stopped laughing. The window was open. The camphor tree moved outside in the dark.

He laid her down on the bed under it and kissed her wrist, the scar, the inside of the elbow, her shoulder, her mouth, as if they had all night, which they did. She said his name. She said it into his neck with no story in it. He felt her hands on him, both of them, and she held on, and he went slowly, all the way, until she was arching up against him and holding his face and looking at him, and he let her look.

Afterwards she lay with her head on his chest and her new ring against his skin.

“I remembered,” she said into the dark. “The third thing.”

He waited.

“I was going to say I’d look after you too,” said Elara. “That’s all. You’ve looked after me for five years. I was going to say I’d do it back. I’m going to do it back.”

He put his hand over hers on his chest. He didn’t say anything. He didn’t trust his voice, and she knew it, and she didn’t make him.

chapters.title: Not Under Her Husband
chapters.desc: Her first day back in surgical training is across the harbour, under a registrar younger than she is. That night the ghost’s phone rings in their kitchen drawer, and they go together.
chapters.epigraph: “Drop me at the corner. Nobody needs to see your car.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
He drove her, because she’d let him, and because she’d been sick with nerves at half past four.

The car was the dark blue saloon he only used at night, clean inside except for the passenger side, which had her sweets and pens in every pocket.

“Drop me at the corner,” said Elara, as they came off the harbour road.

He looked at her.

“By the newspaper shop.” She was already undoing her seatbelt. “Nobody needs to see your car. Nobody needs to see a consultant from City Hospital dropping his wife off on her first day. I’m going to walk in like everyone else, with my own bag.”

“It’s three hundred metres.”

“I can walk three hundred metres.”

He pulled in by the newspaper shop. He leaned across her and opened the glovebox.

She thought he was getting her a sweet. He took out something yellow, folded small, and put it in her hand.

It was the sixth banana cap, the spare. He’d worn the other five in turn since March, and she’d thought this one was lost in the move.

Behind it, at the back of the glovebox, she saw a plain brown plastic hair clip with one tooth missing. She’d lost it on the steps outside Old Bian’s the night he first kissed her, and she’d known for two years that he still had it.

“Spare,” said Xing Yue.

She looked at the cap in her hand, and at him, and at the clip.

“You’re ridiculous,” said Elara, and kissed him, and got out of the car, and walked three hundred metres to Harbourside General with a cap covered in smiling bananas in her pocket and her face burning.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her registrar was called Dr. Jin, and he was younger than she was.

Not by much. He’d gone straight through, without a knife or a year in a garage, and he looked at her placements on the team sheet and then at her, and she watched him do the sum.

“You were a resident at City Hospital,” he said. “On Liao’s team. And then you stopped.”

“Yes,” said Elara.

He waited. She didn’t say anything else. She’d learned that, at least, in a room with four people and a jug of water.

“Right,” said Dr. Jin. “Bed two needs a cannula, bed seven’s bloods are back and nobody’s looked at them, and the list starts at half eight. You’re with Mr. Zhuang. He’ll want to see you do something.”

“Yes,” said Elara.

She did what she was told. She put in the cannula in bed two and told the old woman a story about the ward kettle, and the old woman said she hadn’t felt a thing. She rang the pharmacist about bed seven’s potassium before Dr. Jin asked her to. It was the job of the person at the bottom, and she’d thought it would feel like going backwards. It felt like coming home through a door she’d been told was bricked up.

✦ ✦ ✦

The theatres at Harbourside were colder than City Hospital’s. They always had been.

She felt it the second she went through the doors into the corridor. Her right hand went first. By the time she’d changed and put the yellow cap on and got to the scrub sink, the fingers were white to the second knuckle and stiff, and she stood by the sink with her back to the room and tucked her hand into her left armpit under the scrub top, and counted, and waited, and talked to the anaesthetist about his holiday.

Nobody noticed. She watched to see. The scrub nurse was laying out her trolley. Dr. Jin was on the phone. The anaesthetist told her about a beach.

When she took her hand out it was pink. She scrubbed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Zhuang came in at twenty to nine with his glasses on his head and looked at the list on the board, and then at her, at the cap.

“Bananas,” he said.

“My husband’s,” said Elara. “He’s got five more.”

He’d sat across a table from her in April and asked her where, and he’d never mentioned it since. He didn’t mention it now.

“Hernia,” he said. “On the left. He’s awake, it’s under local. You’re doing it. I’m watching. If you’re slow I’ll take over, and if you’re rough I’ll take over, and if you’re good I’ll go and have a coffee.”

The patient was a taxi driver called Mr. Che, awake behind the drapes with a nurse holding his hand, and frightened. Elara talked to him the whole time.

She told him what she was doing in plain words, and when she ran out of that she told him about getting lost in Harbourside’s basement as an intern and coming out in the mortuary. Mr. Che laughed under the drapes. The nurse holding his hand laughed. Her hands did the rest on their own, quick and small and sure, the way they’d done it on a rig at a quarter to five in the morning and under a light in a cellar, and she didn’t look up once to see if Mr. Zhuang was watching.

Halfway through, she heard the theatre door open and shut behind her.

When she’d finished, and the dressing was on, and Mr. Che had told her she was the best doctor he’d ever met and he’d drive her anywhere for free, the scrub nurse leaned over and said, “He went for his coffee at the twenty-minute mark, Dr. Wang.”

“Did he say anything?”

“He said you talk too much,” said the nurse. “And then he said, keep her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the changing room at the end of the day she opened her new locker.

It was third from the end on the left. She hadn’t asked for that.

Inside the door, at the top, there was a small gold hook.

She stood and looked at it.

She’d taken her rings off before theatre that morning and put them in the zip pocket of her bag, because there’d been nowhere else. Now somebody had screwed a small gold hook into locker fourteen, exactly where the other one was in her old locker at City Hospital.

She got her phone out.

Elara: did you put a HOOK in my LOCKER

Xing Yue: Wednesday. The estates manager owed me a favour. Nobody saw the car.

She was furious for nearly a minute. Then she took the rings out of the zip pocket and hung them on the hook, the sapphire and the band together, and they swung there, catching the light, and she shut the locker door on them and leaned her forehead against it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father came at six with a cardboard box.

He came up the path at Camphor Hill on his own, slowly, with the box held in both hands, and stood in the hall as if he weren’t sure he’d been asked in, though he’d been asked every Sunday since May.

“Old Hou’s stopped,” he said. “He went to his daughter’s last week. Across the water. He says his hands are finished and he’s going to sit in a chair and watch the sea.” He held the box out. “So it’s only you now. And it’ll ring more.”

She opened it on the long kitchen table. Inside was a small black phone, old, plain, with a charger wound round it. Eliana had taken the line out of the cellar wall on Sunday and put it in this, so it would ring wherever it was. Baba’s number. Mok’s numbers. Nobody else.

“It was ringing in an empty room,” said her father. “With Raiden and Jinx gone over the lake. Nobody to hear it.” He looked at the phone and not at her. “I thought it should be where you are. If that’s still all right.”

She looked at him, standing by her table in his good coat with his big grey hands at his sides.

“Is it still all right?” said Lin Jian. “You’ve got the hospital now. In the day. You can say no. It’s on the paper. You can say no to all of it.”

“It’s still all right, Baba,” said Elara.

She opened the drawer at the end of the kitchen counter, the one by the back door with the tea towels in it, and put the phone in on top of them, and plugged the charger into the socket beside it, and shut the drawer.

Her father nodded. He looked at the drawer for a second. Then he said he wouldn’t stay for dinner, because Mok was waiting, and went back down the path, and at the gate he turned round and lifted one hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xing Yue had cooked.

She could smell it from the hall when she came back in. He was at the range at the far end of the long kitchen with his sleeves rolled up and a tea towel over his shoulder, and he’d made the one dish Jun Hyuk had taught him in the three months of salting lemons: a whole steamed fish with salted lemon and ginger and spring onion, which Jun Hyuk had made him cook eleven times at Fig Tree Lane until he stopped overdoing it.

It was good. She told him so with her mouth full.

She took his plate out from under his chopsticks before he could start. She took the fish off it and put it on the board, and picked up a knife, and with great care and her right hand she cut his fish into exact squares. Small, even, neat, every one the same size, every bone out. It took her five minutes. She didn’t hurry. He sat at the long table and watched her do it, and she could see his mouth going at one corner from the second square onwards.

She put the plate back in front of him.

“There,” she said. “Eat that, and then you can argue with me.”

He laughed.

He put his head down on the table, on his arms, next to the plate of perfect squares, and laughed until his shoulders shook, and she stood over him with the knife and was enormously pleased with herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

She told him about Dr. Jin over dinner. She told him the whole day, nearly in order, and when she got to the registrar she got going.

“He’s younger than me,” she said. “And he looked at my placements and did a face, like he was adding up what was missing, and he said, and then you stopped, like I’d gone on holiday, and I wanted to say I didn’t stop, I was very busy actually, I was taking a bullet out of someone’s leg under a—”

He leaned across the table.

He put his hand round the back of her neck, under her hair, warm, and his thumb along the front of her throat, at the side, light, where it would feel everything. He felt her swallow. She felt him feel it. She stopped in the middle of the word.

He kissed her across the table, over the plates, with his hand at her throat and the fish going cold.

She made a small sound and put her own hand flat on his chest, over his shirt, and held on. He kissed her slowly, and then not slowly, and she half stood up out of her chair and knocked her chopsticks on the floor and didn’t care.

“You’re on at seven,” he said, against her mouth.

“I know.”

“You need to sleep.”

“I know,” said Elara, and took him upstairs at half past eight, which was the earliest she’d gone to bed since she was nine.

She didn’t sleep straight away. He made sure of that, and then made sure of it again, slowly, with the window open and the tree moving outside it, until she was boneless and laughing and saying his name into the pillow. Then he tucked her in, firmly, down both sides, and lay down beside her with his thumb on the inside of her wrist, and she fell asleep in the middle of telling him what Mr. Che had said about the free taxi.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past eleven the drawer rang.

She heard it through the floor. A small flat ring, muffled by tea towels, from the kitchen. She was out of bed before she was awake. So was he.

They stood on the landing in the dark and looked at each other.

Neither of them said anything. She saw him look at her, at her face, the way he’d looked at her face over a mask in a cellar once with blood coming up through her fingers, and then he turned and went into the bedroom and started getting dressed.

She went down and answered it. It was Mok.

A girl from the Walled City, about eighteen. She’d put her hand through a window that wasn’t hers, Mok said, and she was on probation, and if she walked into a hospital with that cut the police would know whose window. Her mother had rung Lin Jian. The hand was bad. Mok was taking her to the street of chandlers now.

“Twenty minutes,” said Elara.

She went back upstairs. He was dressed, and had her black bag from the hall cupboard on the bed, open, and was checking it.

He looked up.

“Ev?” he said.

“No,” said Elara. “You.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The street of chandlers was dark, and the garage under the old painted sign was empty now, its shutter down for good, and the rope store next door was the same as ever, with its pallets and its steel door painted to look like wood. She had her own key. She’d had it since June.

Mok was waiting in the old black Mercedes with the girl in the back and a young man beside her, holding a towel round her hand.

They went down the stone steps. She turned on the lights and the big round lamp over the table. She scrubbed. Xing Yue scrubbed at the sink beside her, every finger, both sides, to the elbows, and neither of them spoke.

The young man tried to come down the steps after the girl.

Xing Yue turned round from the sink with his hands up and dripping, in his mask and cap, and looked at him.

“Sit on the top step,” he said. “If you come down these stairs, I’ll put you back up them. You’ll be told when she’s done.”

The young man went back up. He sat on the top step. Mok sat beside him in the doorway, a big quiet shape against the street, and said nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

The cut was across the back of her hand, deep, from the knuckles nearly to the wrist. Glass. Elara washed it out under the light and looked, and found a tendon lying white in the bottom of it, whole, not cut, and breathed out. She looked for glass. She found two pieces and took them out. She checked the girl could move every finger, and feel every fingertip, and she could.

She pointed. He handed it to her.

That was all he did. All night. He stood across the table from her in his mask and gloves, with his long clean hands that had done ten thousand operations and knew exactly how he’d have closed this one, and he handed her what she pointed at, and held the light where she wanted it, and held the edges when she nodded, and didn’t say one word.

He didn’t correct her. Not once. She was doing it her way: the deep layer first, then the skin, small and close, with the girl staring at the vaulted ceiling and the tune going under Elara’s breath. She knew he’d have done it differently. She knew, because she could feel him not saying it. It came off him across the table like heat off a range.

She looked up at him once, over her loupes, halfway through.

His eyes over the mask were fixed on her hands. He was holding the light so still it might have been bolted there. He looked up and met her eyes, and she saw what it was costing him, and she saw that he was going to pay it anyway, every time, for as long as she wanted him in this room.

She hummed louder and went back to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were home by two.

He drove. She sat with the black bag on her knees and her hands in her lap, clean, the girl’s hand splinted and bandaged and gone back to the Walled City in Mok’s car with the young man holding her good one.

Halfway up Camphor Hill she told him she knew he’d have done the skin differently, with a different stitch, and that she’d felt him not say so the whole way through.

He didn’t answer. He changed down for the steep bit by the gate, and parked, and turned the engine off, and sat for a second with his hands on the wheel.

“It nearly killed me,” said Xing Yue.

She laughed. She leaned across the gearstick in the dark and put her forehead on his shoulder and laughed into his coat, and he put his hand on the back of her head and held it there, and they sat in the car outside their own gate until the laughing had gone and she was nearly asleep, and then he carried the bag in, and she carried herself.

chapters.title: A Mass Casualty Night
