chapters.desc: A footbridge comes down at the lantern fair, and every hospital in the city fills. Across the harbour from her husband, Elara closes her first patient on her own.
chapters.epigraph: “I wasn’t scared of my hands. Only of the bleeding.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
At twenty past nine on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, the footbridge over the harbour road came down.

Elara heard about it the way everyone at Harbourside heard about it: all at once, from every direction. She was on the surgical floor, eleven weeks into her training, eating a mooncake one of the nurses had brought in, and every pager on the floor went off together. Then the overhead speakers. Then her phone, three times, and the ward phone, and a porter running past the station without a trolley.

Major incident declared. All surgical staff to the emergency department.

She put the mooncake down and ran.

The lantern fair had been on the waterfront all evening, the whole city out in the warm dark with paper rabbits and fish and stars. The footbridge crossed the harbour road from the fair to the ferry piers, and thousands of people had been on it at once.

She didn’t know that yet. She knew only that she came down the back stairs into the emergency department and it was already full.

✦ ✦ ✦

It filled for six hours.

They came in by ambulance and in taxis and in the back of a fruit lorry, carried by their friends, with broken bones and cut heads, and a man who’d been under a piece of the deck. People who weren’t hurt at all and were only screaming. People who were hurt badly and were perfectly quiet, which was worse, and she’d been taught that, and knew it, and walked towards the quiet ones first.

The consultants weren’t there. They were coming. They were stuck. The harbour road was shut in both directions with the bridge lying across it, and the tunnel was jammed, and Mr. Zhuang rang the ED from his car at a quarter to ten to say he was on the bridge road and hadn’t moved in twenty minutes.

So it was the registrars, and the trainees, and the nurses, and the emergency doctors, and whoever had been in the building when the pagers went.

Elara did what she was told. She went where Dr. Jin pointed. She put in lines and held pressure and wrote numbers on people’s foreheads in marker pen because there wasn’t time for anything else, and talked to every one of them while she did it, about nothing, about the fair, about the moon, until their eyes stayed on her face. When a man’s wife screamed at her in a corridor that her husband had been waiting forty minutes, she turned round and took the woman by both arms and said, “I know. He’s next. Hold his hand. Talk to him. Don’t stop,” in a voice so level the woman stopped screaming and did it.

There was a new nurse on the ED that night. Elara saw her a dozen times without knowing her name. A small one with short hair, two weeks in, Elara heard someone say. Somewhere after eleven Elara passed a cubicle with the curtain half open and saw her sitting on the floor beside a girl who was being sick into a bowl, holding the girl’s hair back off her face with one hand, and with the other holding the bowl, and her face perfectly calm.

“Nuo,” someone shouted from the station. “Nuo, bay four.”

“Coming,” said the nurse, and didn’t get up until the girl had finished.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past midnight Dr. Jin took her into theatre.

The man was in his forties, a ferry clerk on his way home. He’d been under the edge of the deck when it went. His belly was full of blood. The scan, which there’d been barely time for, showed his liver torn and his spleen torn, and his pressure was falling every time they looked at it.

“You’re with me,” said Dr. Jin. He was white. He was twenty-six years old and every consultant in the hospital was stuck in a car on the bridge road. “You open. I’ll take it from there.”

The theatre was cold. The theatres at Harbourside were always cold. She stood at the scrub sink with her back to the room and her right hand tucked under her left arm, inside her scrub top, against her own skin, and counted, and thought about a hand flat on a man’s chest in a multi-storey car park, and when she took it out it was pink and steady, and she scrubbed.

She opened. Dr. Jin took it from there. It was as bad as the scan had said.

They’d been working for forty minutes, packing, finding the worst of the bleeding and getting it under control a corner at a time, when the theatre door banged open and a nurse put her head in.

“Dr. Jin. Theatre two. The chest. He’s going.”

Dr. Jin looked up. He looked at the man on the table, at the packs, at the blood still coming in the corner by the liver. He looked at Elara.

“Go,” said Elara.

“You can’t—”

“Ring Mr. Zhuang,” she said. “Put him on speaker. Go.”

He went.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Zhuang’s voice came out of a phone propped on the anaesthetic machine, from a car stuck on the bridge road with the engine running. He made her tell him everything. She told him in short words, which she’d never managed about anything in her life except this.

“You’re not fixing it,” said Zhuang. “You hear me? You’re not a hero tonight. Pack it. Pack the liver, pack where the spleen was, get the bleeding stopped with pressure and swabs, and close him temporarily and get him to intensive care. We go back tomorrow when he’s warm and there’s blood in the bank and somebody’s had some sleep. That’s all. Pack it and close.”

“Yes,” said Elara.

She packed it.

She did it the way he said, and the way she’d read about in a journal on a kitchen table with a pencil in the gutter and somebody else’s handwriting in the margin. She held the torn liver together between her hands, longer than she wanted, and felt the bleeding slow under them. She packed it. She packed the corner where the spleen had been. She watched the field, and it stayed dry, and stayed dry, and she watched the anaesthetist’s face over the drapes, and he nodded.

Her hands didn’t shake.

She noticed that at the end. During it there was no room for noticing anything but the blood. At the end, when she was closing him, the temporary closure, quick and safe and ugly, the kind you did when you were coming back tomorrow, she looked down at her own hands in the light and they were as steady as the table.

She hummed. The scrub nurse looked up and then away.

When it was done, and the man was going out of the doors to intensive care with his pressure holding, she stood at the table with her gloved hands held up in front of her, red to the wrist, and the scrub nurse said, “Well done, Dr. Wang,” and she nodded, and couldn’t say anything at all.

Dr. Jin came back at half past one, grey. The man in theatre two had lived. He looked at the empty table and the packs count on the board and at her.

“You closed?”

“Mr. Zhuang told me to pack and close.”

“You did it on your own,” said Dr. Jin. He looked at her for a second, as if he’d only just seen her. Then he said, “Right,” and went to find the next one.

✦ ✦ ✦

The family chat had been going all night.

She hadn’t looked. She looked at three in the morning, in the toilet, the only place in the building she could be alone for a minute, sitting on the closed lid in her scrubs with her phone.

Elowen: Are you safe? Elara. Tell me you’re safe.

Elowen: Xing Yue’s not answering either.

Raiden: [a photograph, from the old garage roof by the Docks, where he’d driven over to look: the harbour road at night, blue lights from end to end, and the footbridge lying across all six lanes like something dropped]

Raiden: Elara are you at work

Jinx: Sidecar’s outside your ED if you need moving. Anything or anyone. I’m on the corner by the newspaper shop.

Eliana: YC’s in resus at City. He’s fine. Busy.

Evangeline: Good.

And at the bottom, sent at eleven minutes past one, from a number that had never once in her life typed anything into a family chat, because he rang, he always rang, he said he didn’t trust words without a voice:

Baba: Eat.

She sat on the toilet lid in Harbourside General at three in the morning and laughed out loud, and then cried, and then texted all of them safe, working, ate a mooncake, it was disgusting, and went back out.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past three the food came.

Two delivery vans pulled into the ambulance bay, and men in caps carried boxes into the staff room, stacks of them, two hundred boxes, noodles and dumplings and rice and soup in sealed cups, still hot, and flasks of tea. There was no name on any of it. The delivery slip said only that it had been paid for.

Elara opened a flask and smelled it, and smiled.

Pu’er. Old, good, the kind that came in a pressed cake with a paper wrapper and cost more than a trainee earned in a week. The same flasks turned up in the staff rooms at City Hospital at the same time, she found out later, and nobody there knew who’d sent them either.

She didn’t tell anyone. She ate a box of noodles standing up and drank her brother-in-law’s tea and went back to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

By six it wasn’t over, but it was finished for now. The ED was full of people who’d been seen and were waiting for beds and scans and families, and the theatres were full of the ones who couldn’t wait, and the consultants were in the building at last, with their car keys still in their pockets, taking over.

Elara went outside.

She went out through the ambulance doors in her scrubs, which had blood on them, someone else’s, dried brown at the knees and the cuffs, and sat down on the kerb at the edge of the ambulance bay in the grey morning with a paper cup of coffee from the machine, which was terrible, and held it in both hands for the warmth.

Her phone buzzed. It was a number she knew: his scrub nurse at City Hospital, the one who’d held his phone for him in theatre on a January night nearly four years ago.

Suyin: He’s on his way to you. Thought you’d want to know he threw Mr. Lang out of his theatre at 4am. Mr. Lang was “helping.” Nobody’s speaking to him. He doesn’t care. x

She read it twice. She laughed into her coffee.

She wasn’t surprised. She didn’t mind at all. She drank the terrible coffee and thought about it, him in a theatre at four in the morning in a banana cap with his voice going flat and cold, and some poor consultant being walked out of the door in front of everybody, and she loved him so much she had to put the cup down.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at ten past six.

She saw the dark blue saloon turn in at the end of the ambulance bay and stop where it wasn’t allowed to stop. He got out. He was still in his scrubs too, under his coat. He’d come straight from his last case. He looked as if he hadn’t slept, which he hadn’t, and as if he’d driven round the closed road checking her dot at every red light, which he had.

He came across the bay and sat down on the kerb beside her.

He didn’t say anything at first. He looked at her scrubs. He looked at the blood at her knees, and her cuffs, and her hands round the cup. He took her right hand off the cup and turned it over and looked at it, the palm and the fingers and the scar, as if counting them.

“Not mine,” said Elara. “Any of it.”

He let out a breath.

“I closed one,” she said. “On my own. My registrar got called to another theatre halfway and Zhuang was in his car on the bridge road and he told me to pack and close, so I packed and closed. A liver. A man who works at the ferries.” She looked at her hand in his. “My hands didn’t shake. I kept waiting for them to. They didn’t.”

He held on to her hand.

“I wasn’t scared of my hands,” said Elara. “That’s what’s strange. I thought I would be. I thought I’d be standing there thinking, is this the night it goes, is this the night the nerve gives out. I wasn’t thinking about my hands at all. I was only scared of the bleeding.”

“Good,” said Xing Yue.

She looked at him.

He was looking at her. His face was grey with tiredness and there was a mark across the bridge of his nose from a mask, and he was looking at her in a way she’d only seen a few times, at the pond edge with a ring, on a kitchen floor with her hand crushed in his.

“I’m proud of you,” he said.

He didn’t say that kind of thing. She’d always known he thought it. He’d never once said it to her face. She sat on the kerb at the edge of Harbourside’s ambulance bay and felt her eyes go hot.

“Suyin says you threw a consultant out of your theatre,” she said.

“He was in the way.”

“She says nobody’s speaking to you.”

“Good,” said Xing Yue again, and she laughed so hard she had to lean on him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She fell asleep on his shoulder.

She didn’t mean to. She’d only leaned on him to laugh, and the sun had come up over the harbour behind the ambulances, and he was warm, and she’d been awake since five the morning before. She closed her eyes for a second, with her head on his shoulder and her coffee going cold on the kerb, and when she opened them the shadows had moved.

He’d let her sleep twenty minutes, she found out later, without moving, with an ambulance crew stepping round his feet.

What woke her was his handkerchief.

She felt it on her cheek, the ironed cotton, damp at one corner, wiping something off her cheekbone, carefully, the way you’d clean round a wound. She opened her eyes. He was close, frowning at her cheek, with the handkerchief in his hand.

“Blood,” he said. “I was checking it wasn’t yours.”

He folded the handkerchief and put it back in his pocket, and then he took her face in his hand, his palm along her jaw where he’d just cleaned it, and kissed her.

Slowly, on the kerb of the ambulance bay, with the morning shift coming in through the doors behind them and a paramedic saying “Morning, doctors” as she stepped over their feet. She kissed him back half asleep, with her hand curled in his coat, and tasted terrible coffee and the morning, and didn’t care who walked past.

Then he stood up, and picked up her bag, and held out his hand, and she took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home he ran her a bath.

She sat in it in the long bathroom at Camphor Hill with the window open to the garden and the camphor tree full of birds, and he knelt on the floor beside it with his sleeves rolled up and washed her hair, the way he had on the night she moved into Banyan Terrace, with his fingers slow on her scalp and the water warm, until she stopped thinking about the ferry clerk’s liver.

She pulled him in.

Not all the way. He was still half in his scrubs, and the water went over the edge and onto the floor, and he swore, and she laughed, and then she stopped laughing and kissed him with her wet hands on his face, slow, hungry, the way you kiss someone at eight in the morning after a night like that, when you’re too tired to be anything but honest.

He took her to bed. He took his time. He was slower than she’d ever known him, as if he had the whole day and meant to use it, and the light came in round the edges of the curtains and the tree moved outside, and she held onto him and felt him everywhere, warm and careful and then not careful, and when it was over she was already half asleep.

He tucked her in. Down both sides, firmly, to her chin.

“Go to sleep,” he said, and she told him he should too, and he said he would.

He lay down beside her on top of the covers, and found her right hand, and turned it over, and put his thumb on the pulse over the scar. She fell asleep with it there. She didn’t know if he did. She thought, the last thing before she went, that he’d probably lie awake an hour and watch her, and that she’d let him, and that it was the most looked-after she had ever been in her life.

chapters.title: Twin Scrub Caps
chapters.desc: A year married. Two pagers and a ghost’s phone on the kitchen counter, all quiet, and a pair of silly caps.
chapters.epigraph: “Everything’s quiet. Don’t say it out loud.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
At eight in the evening there were three things on the kitchen counter at Camphor Hill, in a row, by the bread bin.

His pager. Hers. And the small black phone from the drawer, which she’d taken out and put beside them when she came in, as if it were a third pager, as if it were on call too.

None of them had made a sound since six.

Xing Yue stood at the board by the windows with a knife, cutting a carrot. The long kitchen was full of the last of the light, gold along the stone floor, and the windows were open onto the garden, and the camphor tree filled all of them, enormous and dark and moving a little in the evening air. A grey cat sat on the garden wall under it, watching the kitchen with great patience. It wasn’t theirs. It came over the wall from the old house next door every evening at about this time, because Elara fed it, and Elara fed it because it had once sat on the windowsill and watched her eat a pork bun with an expression she said she recognised.

In the back room, through the open door at the end of the hall, he could see the rig against the north window in the dusk. The springs were on the hardest setting. They’d been there since February. She still did it every morning before work, a quarter of an hour, because she said that if she stopped her hand would notice.

She was cooking. Badly. She was frying something in the big pan on the range with too much oil and the flame too high, and talking.

“—and the registrar said, Dr. Wang, have you been on the hernia list before, and I said yes, about forty times, and he said, oh, and went pink, and Mr. Zhuang laughed at him in front of the whole theatre. He’s new. The registrar. He’s younger than Jin was. Everyone’s younger than me now. I’m going to be the oldest first-year trainee in the history of the city.” She shook the pan. “Is this burning? It’s not burning. It smells like it’s burning.”

“It’s burning.”

“It’s caramelising,” said Elara, and turned the flame down.

✦ ✦ ✦

He cut the carrot into squares.

He did it without thinking. Small, exact, even, every one the same, the way he’d once cut her food for a year when she couldn’t. Then the spring onions, into lengths, and the pepper into squares, and he laid them out on the board in neat rows and pushed the board along the counter towards her.

She looked at it. She looked at him.

Then she reached over, still talking, and with one finger moved three of the squares out of their row, and turned one of them on its corner, so that it sat like a diamond among the rest, and pushed the board back.

He looked at the diamond.

“Don’t,” said Elara. “Don’t put it back. I can see you wanting to.”

He didn’t put it back. He watched her scrape the whole board into the pan anyway, squares and diamond and all, and stir it with a wooden spoon, and burn it slightly, and tell him it was supposed to be like that.

✦ ✦ ✦

The day had been ordinary.

He’d done a list in the morning, a gallbladder and two hernias and a man whose bowel had twisted, and on the round afterwards he’d taken a new registrar apart at bed nine for writing patient settled about a man who was plainly about to stop breathing. The registrar had gone white and then gone and done everything right in under ten minutes. Elara had heard about it by lunchtime, across the harbour, from somebody who knew somebody on 9B. She’d texted him a picture of a boiled sweet.

She’d done a list too. She’d closed on her own twice. Nobody at Harbourside remarked on it any more. Mr. Zhuang had stopped watching her in March and now only came in at the end to look at the wound and say fine, which from Mr. Zhuang was a parade.

They’d both come home at half past six, from opposite sides of the water. She’d taken the ferry. He’d walked up the hill. They’d met at the gate, by accident, and stood there kissing in the road until the cat came along the wall and stared at them.

It was their anniversary. Neither of them had said so yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate at the long table by the windows, with the light going and the tree going dark.

The table was the one she’d planned on the bare boards fourteen months ago, with room for eleven. It had had eleven at it three times, and her father every other Sunday, and once Nainai, down from the north for a week in the winter, who’d sat at the end of it with her stick across her knees and told Elara her cooking was the worst she’d ever eaten and asked for more.

He glanced at the counter. At the three small black things in a row by the bread bin. Still quiet. He opened his mouth.

She pointed her chopsticks at him.

“Everything’s quiet,” said Elara. “Don’t say it out loud.”

He shut his mouth. She went back to her burnt vegetables, satisfied.

Neither of them said it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

She gave him the present after dinner. She couldn’t wait any longer; he could see her not waiting, all through the meal, the way her knee kept going under the table.

It was wrapped in brown paper and tied with a bit of suture, black silk, which she said was all she could find. Inside were two scrub caps, the tie-on cloth kind, both navy.

His had small white stars on it. Hundreds of them, tiny, scattered all over the navy like a sky.

Hers had small white moons.

“Star moon,” said Elara. “Your name. Half each. Same woman at the market, she remembered me, she asked how the bananas went. I said they’ve worn through, they’ve been washed three hundred times, the bananas have got no faces left.” She held the star one up. “These are for theatre. For both of us. Every day. You at yours and me at mine, and we’ll match, and nobody at either hospital will know why except us.”

He looked at the caps. He turned the star one over in his hands.

“They’re silly,” he said.

“I know they’re silly. You wore bananas for a year.”

“I’ll wear it tomorrow,” said Xing Yue.

She grinned at him across the table, the whole of her face, the grin he’d fallen for by a lift on the sixth floor at seven in the morning seven years ago, before she’d known he existed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then he gave her his.

It wasn’t wrapped. He took it out of his pocket and put it on the table in front of her. It was yellow, and faded, and it had small cartoon bananas on it that had lost most of their faces in the wash.

The sixth one. The spare. Hers, from the glovebox, from the newspaper shop corner on her first day. She’d worn it on her own lists at Harbourside all year, every day, until it was nearly white.

She picked it up. She looked at him.

“Turn it over,” he said.

She turned it inside out. On the band, on the inside, where it would sit against her forehead, someone had sewn her name.

ELARA.

In white thread. In small stitches, a running stitch and then a locked one at each end, the way she’d sewn his pillowcase at two in the morning nearly two years ago by the light of her phone. It wasn’t good. The E was too big and the second A leaned sideways, and the tension was all over the place, tight in the L and loose in the R, and at the end the knot had been tied three times, as if whoever had tied it hadn’t trusted the first two.

She stared at it.

“You taught me,” he said. “In January. You thought I was being polite.”

She had taught him. He watched her remember. A Sunday in January, after her father had gone home, on the sofa, with the little travel kit from his washbag that she’d mended the pillowcase with, and a square of old sheet. He’d asked her how she’d done it. She’d shown him, laughing at him, guiding his fingers, telling him he held a needle as if it might go off. He’d practised every night after that, in his study, at the desk he’d built at her height, with the door shut, until she’d started asking what he was doing in there.

“It’s terrible,” said Elara. Her voice had gone. “The tension’s terrible. The second A’s falling over.”

“I’m not as good as you,” said Xing Yue.

She burst into tears. She put the faded banana cap against her face and cried into it, at the long table, in the dusk, with the cat on the wall outside watching her through the open window, and he got up and came round the table and she stood up into his arms without letting go of the cap, and cried into his shirt instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was still sniffing when he kissed her.

He didn’t plan it. She was standing against the counter with the cap in one hand, telling him in a wet voice that she was going to wear it every day until it fell apart, and then she was going to frame it, and hang it in the hall, and tell everyone who came in that her husband had done it and that he couldn’t sew. Her stethoscope was on the counter beside her, where she’d dropped it with her bag when she came in. He picked it up.

She stopped.

He held the bell of it in his closed hand for a second, to warm it, the way you did for children and old people, and then he put the earpieces in and set the bell against her chest, over her shirt, on the left, and listened.

Her heart was going fast. Fast and strong and absolutely regular, under his hand.

She watched him listen. Her mouth was open, and her eyes were wet, and she’d gone quite still.

“Well?” she said.

He took the earpieces out. He put the stethoscope down on the counter beside the three quiet black things in a row, and took her face in his hands, and kissed her.

She made a sound against his mouth, half a laugh and half the end of the crying, and wound her arms round his neck with the banana cap still in her fist, and pulled him down to her, and kissed him back the way she’d kissed him on the steps outside Old Bian’s, as if she’d only just found out she could.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, upstairs, she checked his dot.

He saw her do it. She was sitting on the edge of the bed in his T-shirt with her phone, and she opened the map, out of habit, without thinking, and looked at the small blue circle that was him. It was in a bedroom on Camphor Hill. He was standing two metres away from her by the window, taking his watch off.

She looked at it a second longer than she needed to. Then she put the phone down on the bedside table, face down, and looked up and saw him watching her, and went pink.

He didn’t say anything.

He picked up his own phone from the windowsill and opened it and looked at hers. A small blue circle, in a bedroom on Camphor Hill, on the edge of the bed. He looked at it. Then he put his phone down beside his watch and turned round.

She was laughing at him. Silently, with her hand over her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

The phone had rung four times since the July before. Four times in a year, in the drawer by the back door, under the tea towels. A boy from the fish market with a hook through his hand. A woman with a cut her husband had made. A man from the docks who wouldn’t say what had happened. And once, in February, at four in the morning, Ding Jiale, who’d been driving a friend’s car and come off the road, and who’d rung Mok himself and asked for Doctor Ghost by name. He’d had a gash across his scalp. He was training to drive ambulances now. He’d told Elara, on the cellar table, with his eyes shut, that he was going to be the best driver they’d ever had because he knew what it was like in the back.

They’d gone together every time. She operated. He handed her things, and held the light, and didn’t correct her, and it nearly killed him every time, and he went every time.

The rest of the news was the kind that came at the long table on Sundays. Peng ran the gatehouse on the hill again, with a limp, and had married a girl from the fish stall, and sent mandarins every winter. Her uncle wrote from Cold Water Bay on the first of every month, three pages, mostly about the food, and she went to see him at every change of season and came back quiet and then talked all the way home. Her father came to dinner every other Sunday. He sat at the long table in his good coat and asked her things, about the hospital, about the rig, about the cat, and listened to every answer as if he were writing it down.

Mr. Yin had sent his card in September, as always. He was learning to swim.

✦ ✦ ✦

The window was open. The tree filled it.

It was slow. It was always slow after a day like this, when there was nothing to hurry for and nothing waiting in the drawer, and she was warm and soft and still a bit tearful under him, and kept laughing at nothing, at the cat, at the A that fell over. He kissed her and kept kissing her before anything else. He kissed the scar on her wrist, and the zigzag, and the inside of her elbow, and her mouth, and she held his face in both her hands, her right hand and her left, and looked at him in the dark the whole time.

She said his name, not loudly, the way she said it across the kitchen when she wanted the salt.

Afterwards she talked.

She talked him to sleep, the way she did on the nights when neither of them was on call. She lay on her side with her head on his shoulder and told him about the registrar who’d gone pink, and the woman at the market, and how she was going to frame the banana cap, and a moon of Jupiter they’d found that year that was smaller than any of the others, and that she’d decided was hers. Her voice went on and on in the dark, low and quick and warm, three things at a time, and she lost the third one, and found it, and lost it again.

He found her right hand on the sheet. He turned it over and put his thumb on the inside of her wrist, on the pulse, over the scar, where he’d put it the first night five and a half years ago and nearly every night since.

It was steady. It was quick and light and steady, and he lay and felt it under his thumb, and listened to her voice going on above it, and somewhere in the middle of the moon of Jupiter he fell asleep.

chapters.title: The First Time He Saw Her
chapters.desc: At the end of a twenty-six-hour shift he’s sent to look at a young man’s ribs, and a girl in a T-shirt stops him by the lift to ask about her brother’s spleen.
chapters.epigraph: “Left lower ribs. Has anyone looked at his spleen?” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
At twenty to six on a Saturday morning in June, in the twenty-sixth hour of a call that had started on Friday at four in the morning, Wang Xing Yue was asked to go and look at a young man’s ribs.

The medical intern who rang him was apologetic. He’d been apologetic all night, about everything, and Xing Yue had stopped answering the apologies around three.

“He was hit by a van,” said the intern. “On the Docks road. He’s on the sixth floor, for the concussion. He’s got three ribs cracked on the left, and I just thought, with the left side, a surgeon should—”

“Has he had a CT?”

“Yes. Last night.”

“What did it say?”

There was a pause. Papers.

“Ribs. Three, left, undisplaced. No collection. Spleen intact.” The intern stopped. “It says the spleen’s intact.”

“Then why are you ringing a surgeon at twenty to six?”

“I just thought—”

“You thought the report might be wrong, and you’d like me to read it for you,” said Xing Yue. “It isn’t wrong. Read the next one yourself. If you’re worried about him, examine him. If he’s tender over the spleen, if his pressure drops, if his heart rate goes up, ring me. Don’t ring me because a CT frightened you.” He was walking already. He’d been walking for twenty-six hours, and his legs did it on their own. “I’ll come. Because I’m going that way. Not because you rang.”

He took the back stairs from the ninth floor. He always took the stairs on call. The lifts in the tower were slow at that hour, full of porters and breakfast trolleys, and the stairs were empty and cold and you could think in them.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the sixth-floor landing he passed a woman going down.

She was coming fast, two steps at a time, from the door by the linen room, and she nearly went into him on the turn. He stepped back against the rail. She didn’t look at him. She went past with a motorbike helmet in one hand, in a T-shirt and old jeans with oil on the knees, and her face was set and white, the way faces went in the relatives’ room when someone came in to say something.

He saw her arms as she went by. Old burns across both forearms, healed, shiny, in short straight lines. Exhaust burns. He’d seen them on motorbike couriers in the emergency department, years of leaning on hot pipes. And a tattoo, a fish, going up the left one.

Then she was gone, down the stairs, her boots loud on every step and then not.

He stood on the landing for a second. A woman with no jacket and a helmet, coming out by the linen room at six in the morning, from the floor where a young man hit by a van was lying, going out the back.

He didn’t know why he noticed. He noticed everything at the end of a call; it was the only thing that still worked. He went on up the last flight and through the door. He didn’t think about her again until he saw her across a flower shop two years later, at a wedding, standing by a drinks cooler. He never told anyone. Not the nurses, not the family, not the young man in the bed. It wasn’t his to tell.

✦ ✦ ✦

The young man was in a side room on his own, because he was a Lin.

Xing Yue knew that before he’d looked at the chart. Everybody knew the name. The surname on the door, and the quiet of the corridor, and the security guard by the lifts who’d been told something, and the fact that a twenty-three-year-old hit by a van on the Docks road had a room to himself on the sixth floor when there were people on trolleys downstairs.

LIN RAIDEN, said the board. 23.

He was awake. He was lying on his back with his left arm strapped across his chest and his left eye swollen shut, with seven black stitches over the eyebrow, and he was looking at the door when Xing Yue came in, and his good eye went to Xing Yue’s face and then dropped, as if he’d been hoping for someone else.

“Surgical,” said Xing Yue. “About your ribs. Can I look?”

“I’m fine,” said Raiden Lin. He said it in a silly bright voice, the kind people used when they were not. “Totally fine. Look all you like. I’m a picture.”

Xing Yue examined him. The ribs were where the CT said, tender, and the young man made a face that he turned into a joke. He pressed over the left upper belly, under the ribs, carefully, and watched the face, and there was nothing there. Soft. No guarding. Pulse fine. Pressure fine. He looked at the obs chart, at the three o’clock and five o’clock entries in a nurse’s writing, and at the line beside them in different writing, in biro, big and blocky: woke him, knew name and day.

Somebody had sat up with him all night.

He didn’t ask who. There was a plastic chair beside the bed, pulled close, and a sketchbook on the seat with a tyre mark across the back of it. He didn’t touch it.

“You’re fine,” said Xing Yue. “Your spleen’s fine. It’s not a surgical problem. They’ll keep you two nights for your head.”

“Told you,” said Raiden, and shut his eye.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at the lift when the family came.

He heard them before he saw them. A lot of feet, and a man’s low voice, and the lift at the other end of the corridor opening. Then they came round the corner.

A big grey man in a dark coat, heavy and slow, with a face like the side of a building and two men behind him who stopped at the corner and stayed there. Everybody knew that face too. Beside him a young woman in her twenties, cool and sharp, in a dark green dress, walking as if she’d come to sort something out. A thin pale one in pale blue, silent, who looked at everything and said nothing. A young woman at the back with a laptop under her arm and her phone already up.

And in the middle of them, talking, a small one in a T-shirt.

She had her hair in a plastic clip that wasn’t holding it. A lot of hair, long and dark, coming down on one side. A round face. Quick dark eyes. She was talking to the grey man as they came, about the hospital, about the ward, about how sixth floor meant medicine and not surgery, which was good, wasn’t it, Baba, because if it was surgical they’d have put him on nine. She saw the nurse at the station and changed direction without stopping and read the chart over the nurse’s shoulder, upside down, talking the whole time.

Then she looked up and saw him by the lift, in his scrubs, with his badge, and came straight at him.

“Left lower ribs,” she said. “Has anyone looked at his spleen?”

He looked down at her.

“It’s the left ribs, isn’t it,” she said, all in one breath, before he could answer. “Eight, nine and ten, or near there, and the spleen sits right under the left ribs, and I read that it can bleed slowly and look like nothing for hours and then all at once, a delayed rupture, and I just want to know if anyone’s checked, because nobody’s said, and if nobody’s said—”

“CT last night,” said Xing Yue. “It’s fine. I’ve just examined him. We’ll keep an eye.”

She stopped. She breathed out.

“Oh, good,” she said. “Thank you. Sorry.”

And she went past him into the room, already talking, and he heard her through the open door telling her brother off for not looking both ways, and for scaring Baba, and for having a face like a burst plum, and her brother saying Elara, stop, and her not stopping.

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked at her once, properly, through the open door.

She was standing at the end of the bed with her hand on the rail and her hair coming down, telling the young man that he was an idiot and she loved him and he was an idiot, and her face was doing three things at once, cross and frightened and so relieved it was nearly laughing. The grey man had sat down heavily in the plastic chair. The sharp one in green had picked up the sketchbook and was looking at the tyre mark on the back with narrowed eyes. The quiet one stood by the window. The one with the laptop was filming.

He had no word for what happened to him then.

He knew the words for most things. He’d spent twelve years learning them. He knew the word for every part of a person and most of the things that could go wrong with each one. He stood by the lift on the sixth floor in the twenty-sixth hour of a call and looked at a small woman in a T-shirt talking without stopping, and there wasn’t one.

The lift came. He didn’t get in it.

He went to the window at the end of the corridor instead, where you could see over the hospital garden and the roofs to the harbour, and stood there with his hands in the pockets of his scrubs and looked at the sky going from grey to pink over the cranes.

He told himself it was twenty-six hours awake.

He’d seen it in others. Residents at the end of a long call who cried at a kind word, who fell in love with a nurse’s voice on the phone at four in the morning and couldn’t remember it by lunch. It was the brain running on nothing. It was a known thing. It would be gone by the time he’d slept.

He stood at the window until her voice had stopped coming down the corridor, and then a little longer.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went home. He didn’t sleep.

He lay on his bed at Banyan Terrace with the blinds down and the light coming through them in stripes and his eyes shut, and he could hear her. Not the words. The run of it. The way it went on and on and didn’t stop for breath, and went up at the ends of things.

At eleven that night he rang his brother.

An Yu was in the north. He answered on the second ring, and listened, which was what An Yu did, and didn’t laugh, which was also what An Yu did.

“Is there any literature on it?” said Xing Yue.

“On what?”

“First sight. Whether it’s real. Whether there’s a mechanism.”

There was a silence on the line.

“I’ll look,” said his brother.

He sent three papers the next morning, without a word of his own. Two were useless. The third was about prairie voles, and pair-bonding, and what happened in the brains of small animals who chose one other animal and stayed with it for the rest of their lives. Xing Yue read it twice. He didn’t reply.

✦ ✦ ✦

Before he left the hospital that morning, at the end of the call, he’d written one line.

He’d done it standing at the nurses’ station on the ninth floor, on the back of a sheet torn off a prescription pad, while the day team came in. L. Elara — spleen. That was all. He hadn’t known why. He’d folded the sheet in half and put it in his wallet, behind his driving licence, and forgotten it was there.

He found it again in September, when the lists of fourth-years going into their fifth came round to the surgical tutors, and her name was on one of them. Lin Elara. He sat in his office and looked at the name on the list, and then took out his wallet and looked at the sheet.

He didn’t do anything.

She was a student. He taught students. He’d be on her rotation one day, most likely, signing her logbook, and that was a rule he’d never once thought about breaking because he’d never once wanted to. So he did nothing. He put her name out of his mind, and she came back into it at the ends of long nights, and he put her out again.

He didn’t throw the sheet away. He didn’t cross out the line.

He thought, for a year, that it was sleep deprivation, and he was a careful doctor, and he gave it every chance to wear off. It didn’t.

chapters.title: Elara Before the Lins
chapters.desc: On the morning of her wedding, Lin Jian sits at his kitchen table before dawn and remembers the autumn of 2002: a schedule sold to the wrong man, a fire, and a children’s home on Plum Steps.
chapters.epigraph: “I never once asked her to stop talking.” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
He was awake at two. He was always awake before the days that mattered.

The house was dark. He came down the stairs in his socks so as not to wake Ah Sim, who’d wake anyway, and sat at the long table in the kitchen with the light off and the fire out and the eleven chairs pushed in round him. His suit was upstairs on the back of the bedroom door, pressed. Ah Sim had pressed it on Thursday and again last night, and told him not to sit down in it till the car.

It was his only suit. He’d been married in it, and worn it to bury his wife, and stood at the back of four weddings in it. In four hours he’d walk his daughter down a garden path in it, because she’d asked him to.

She’d asked. At this table. Will you walk me? And he’d said if you want, and she’d said I asked, Baba, and the whole table had gone quiet.

He sat in the dark and put his hands flat on the wood, the way he used to put them on a map, and let himself remember it. He didn’t, usually. He’d kept it shut for twenty-five years. This morning it seemed right to open it once, before he put the suit on.

✦ ✦ ✦

The tea house was on the old harbour front, before they knocked it down. A back room upstairs with a fan that didn’t work.

Zuo Hanlin wanted the piers. The old Walled City piers, the ones the lighter boats worked from, out to the ships and back. Most of them were Zuo’s already, or Lin Jian’s, or nobody’s. One small firm held out. Four boats, an office on the quay with a flat above it, a stubborn man who wouldn’t sell. Qu Lighterage.

Lin Jian was thirty-five. He was the most frightening man in the Walled City and he knew it, and he liked it, the way you liked a good coat. He had a house with a red door and two daughters at home and a son away at the farm in the borderlands, and a wife who didn’t ask. He didn’t need the Qu piers. He wanted the two Zuo didn’t.

So he sold Zuo what Zuo needed. The night schedule for the Qu boats, which nights they went out and which they stayed tied up. The name of the old man who watched the quay.

“Only the boats,” said Zuo, and poured him tea.

He believed it. That was how it was done then. You burned a man’s boats and he went away somewhere else and started again. Nobody died of it. He drank the tea and went home.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the night of the eleventh of October he was at the top of the house, at his window, at two in the morning, because he couldn’t sleep.

He saw the glow over the old piers. Orange, low down, behind the roofs. He watched it a while. He told himself it was the boats.

In the morning it was in the paper. Page nine. Four paragraphs.

He read it at this table. He remembered the cup in his hand, and Ah Sim at the stove, and the smell of the rice. Fire at Walled City lighter office kills two. The office and the flat above it. The owner and his wife. The boats were undamaged. Police thought it was deliberate. Nobody had been charged.

The boats were undamaged.

He put the paper down. He didn’t eat. Ah Sim put a bowl in front of him and he didn’t touch it, and she took it away at noon without a word, and that was the first time in his life Ah Sim had looked at him the way she looked at him for the next twenty-five years: as if she were waiting for him to tell her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told his wife a version.

He said a man he’d done business with had died. A fire. He said it was nothing to do with him. She looked at him across the bedroom, and he knew that she didn’t believe him, and he went downstairs.

Three days later Mok told him the rest.

Mok drove him even then. He was young, thinner, and he’d heard it at the noodle stall at the mouth of the alley, from a fireman’s brother. They’d found a child. In the morning, when the fire was out, in the back of the flat, by the washing machine, in a laundry basket under a pile of wet towels. A little girl. Not a mark on her. Asleep.

“Where is she?” said Lin Jian.

“The home on Plum Steps,” said Mok. “No family. They say there’s no family.”

Lin Jian sat in the back of the car and was silent for the rest of the drive.

That night he told his wife all of it. The tea house, the schedule, the watchman’s name, only the boats. He told her in the dark, sitting on the edge of the bed with his back to her. When he’d finished she didn’t say anything for a while. Then she said the thing he’d remembered every day since, in exactly her voice, which was the only thing of hers he could still hear clearly.

That’s the worst thing you’ll ever do. Now the only thing left is to love her more than the others, and never let her see it.

He hadn’t said he’d bring the child home. He hadn’t thought it. She’d thought it for him, the way she thought most things first.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went to Plum Steps the next week.

It was an old house at the top of a long flight of stone steps behind the church, with an iron gate and a yard and a roof that let the rain in. There were buckets in the corridor. He stood in the yard in his good coat and the matron came out and looked at him. She was a small woman with grey hair pulled back and a bunch of keys at her belt, and she knew who he was before he opened his mouth. Everybody did.

He said he’d come about the roof.

She looked at him a while longer. Then she showed him the roof. She showed him the corridor, and the buckets, and the room at the end where the children slept, and a window into the room where they played.

He looked through the window. He did that once.

All these years he’d remembered the window more clearly than anything behind it. The glass, old, with a bubble in it. The paint coming off the frame. He looked through it and then he looked at the paint, and the matron stood beside him and didn’t say anything at all.

He paid for the roof. It was done in a fortnight.

Then he did the papers. He was good at papers, then. He knew which office and which clerk, and what to say and what to leave out, and how a name could go into one end of a building and come out of the other end as a different name, with a stamp on it. It was the kind of thing he’d done for other men’s cargo for fifteen years. He did it for a child. The name Qu went in. It didn’t come out.

He’d been proud of that, once. Not the reason. The doing of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He brought her home on a Saturday, the sixteenth of November.

It was cold, the first cold week. Mok drove him to the bottom of the steps and waited by the car. He went up the long flight on his own, and through the iron gate, and the matron was in the yard with a small bag and a coat, and the child.

He didn’t remember what was said in the yard. He’d tried. It was gone.

He remembered the steps.

She walked down the first flight holding his hand. His hand was enormous and hers was nothing, and she held two of his fingers and walked beside him one step at a time, and she talked. She’d talked since he came through the gate. She talked to him the way you’d talk to anyone, as if he were nobody, as if he were just a man.

At the turn of the steps, below the gate, where the wall cut off the yard, she stopped. She put her arms up.

He picked her up.

That was the one he kept. He’d had it twenty-five years. She weighed nothing. Her coat smelled of the home’s soap, and her hair was coming out of whatever someone had tied it with, and she put one arm round his neck as if she’d done it a hundred times, and went on talking into his collar. All the way down. Every step to the bottom, and across the pavement to the car, where Mok stood with the door open and looked at the ground.

She told him about a bell. On a boat. Her father’s boat had a bell, she said, and you rang it when you came in, so people on the quay knew it was you. She told him how it sounded. She told him twice, in case he hadn’t heard.

He carried her down the steps and listened, and didn’t say a word, and didn’t ask her to stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

His wife gave her the new name that night. He wasn’t in the room. He was in the yard, in the dark, by the back door, because he couldn’t be in the room.

She told him after. Xiaoyue. Little moon. There’s a moon called Elara. A small one. That way she keeps a piece of it.

He’d said yes. It was the first thing about the child he’d been asked.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four Ah Sim came down.

She didn’t turn the light on either. She came across the kitchen in her slippers and put the kettle on and stood by it with her back to him while it boiled, and then she put a cup of tea down on the table beside his hands.

She was eighty-three. She’d been at this stove the morning of the paper. She’d never once asked him, in twenty-five years, and she wasn’t asking now.

“Suit,” said Ah Sim.

He went up and put it on. He did the tie in the mirror on the landing, twice, because the first time his hands weren’t right. When he came down she looked at him from the stove and nodded, and turned away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mok was in the alley with the car at five, the old black Mercedes, with the engine running, under the one streetlight by the noodle stall.

Lin Jian got in the back. Mok pulled out of the alley mouth and turned towards the hill, and neither of them said anything for a while. The city was grey and empty. The harbour went past on the left, and the place where the tea house used to be, which was a car park now.

“She talked all the way down the steps,” said Lin Jian.

“I remember,” said Mok.

They drove. At the lights by the fish market he looked out of the window at nothing.

“I never once asked her to stop talking,” he said. “Not once. In twenty-five years.”

“No,” said Mok.

He looked down at his hands on his knees, in the funeral suit, and thought about the weight of her on the steps. It was the one good thing in it. He’d never told her he carried her. He thought he might, one day. Not today. Today she was going to walk, and he was going to be beside her, because she’d asked.

The car went up the hill towards the hospital in the first light, and he sat in the back and waited for it to stop.

chapters.title: Elara Narrates a Cafeteria Lunch
chapters.desc: Twenty minutes on the mystery meat in the hospital canteen, while the chief resident eats his and the next table watches him listen.
chapters.epigraph: “Twenty minutes on it, and I still don’t know what animal it was.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The canteen at City Hospital was in the basement of the tower, under the pharmacy, and it had no windows, and on Tuesdays it served the meat.

Nobody called it anything else. It was on the board at the counter as Braised Pork in Brown Sauce, and every Tuesday a woman in a hairnet ladled it onto rice from a steel tray, and every Tuesday half the hospital ate it and the other half stood in front of the tray and looked at it, and walked on to the noodles.

Elara stopped in front of it with her tray.

Xing Yue, behind her, saw her stop. She was a student on the emergency department for six weeks, her last rotation before finals, and she’d been on since seven, and she had a smear of something on the sleeve of her white coat that she hadn’t noticed yet. She looked at the brown tray. She leaned closer.

“I’ll have that,” she said to the woman in the hairnet. “Please. A lot of it.”

The woman gave her a lot of it. Xing Yue had the same, because he had it every Tuesday, and they took their trays to a table in the corner by the drinks machine.

Everyone noticed. Everyone had noticed for months. The chief surgical resident, who ate his lunch standing up at the nurses’ station in eleven minutes or not at all, sitting down at a corner table in the canteen at half past one on a Tuesday with a final-year student, and staying there. Two nurses from the burns unit looked round as they passed. A porter slowed down.

He didn’t look at any of them. He sat down opposite her and picked up his chopsticks.

Elara didn’t pick up hers. She picked up her fork, and turned a piece of the meat over on her plate, and looked at the underside of it.

“Right,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She started with the texture.

She pressed the piece flat with the back of her fork and watched it spring back, slowly, the way it would if it had been cooked for hours, or a short time and then reheated more than once, which she thought was more likely. She told him so. She told him what that meant about the kitchen and about Tuesdays. She cut a piece in half and looked at the inside, and said that the grain went the wrong way for pork belly, which it said it was, and the wrong way for shoulder, and that she’d done the pig’s foot in first year and knew what pig looked like on the inside, thank you.

He ate a piece of his.

She stopped. She watched him chew it and swallow it. Her face was like a student watching a consultant drink something out of a specimen pot.

“You just ate it,” she said. “You don’t even know what it is.”

“It’s lunch,” said Xing Yue, and ate another piece.

She looked at him across the table as if he’d told her he didn’t wash his hands. Then she went back to her plate.

✦ ✦ ✦

The colour was next.

She held a piece up on her fork under the canteen’s strip light and turned it. Brown on the outside, from the sauce. Inside, under the brown, it was a sort of grey-pink that she said she’d only ever seen on one other thing, and she wasn’t going to say what, because he was eating. She said the sauce was doing a lot of work. She said the sauce was the hardest-working thing in the building, harder than the emergency department, and that somebody should give it a medal.

At the next table, two of his residents had stopped talking.

He could see them out of the corner of his eye without turning his head. Dr. Rao, from his own team, with his neat notes beside his tray, and Dr. Weng, the intern who’d been three weeks in on the morning of Mr. Yin’s leak and was now seven months in and slightly less frightened. They’d been talking about a rota. They weren’t any more. They were sitting with their chopsticks in the air, not eating, looking at the corner table.

They weren’t looking at her. They were looking at him.

He knew what they were seeing. He knew what he looked like on a ward round, because he’d been told, by Dr. Fei, more than once, and by a resident who’d cried in the sluice. He knew how he looked when someone presented a case badly. And here he was at a corner table with a student explaining the inside of a piece of meat to him with her fork in the air, and he was listening to every word of it, and nodding at the right places, and not looking at his watch.

Rao caught his eye.

“Is it pork, Dr. Wang?” he said. “Do you think?”

Xing Yue looked at him. Not for long.

“Eat your lunch, Dr. Rao,” he said. “You’ve got the drain chart for bed six to rewrite before the two o’clock, and you know why, and if it isn’t done when I get upstairs, you’ll do it again in front of the patient.”

Rao went back to his rice. So did Weng. Neither of them said another word.

Elara, across the table, hadn’t stopped talking at all. She hadn’t noticed. She was on to the fat.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had theories.

She laid them out one at a time, the way she’d lay out the possible causes of a fever on a ward round, from the most likely to the most frightening. It was pork, and the kitchen was simply bad at pork. She rejected that one; the grain was wrong. It was beef, cut against itself and passed off as pork because pork was cheaper to put on the board, which made no sense, because beef cost more.

She rejected that one too. It was goose, until she decided it wasn’t. It was some kind of pressed meat that had been made out of several other meats and was technically no animal at all, only an idea of one, which she liked a lot and kept for a minute, and then rejected, because she said it had a shape, and ideas didn’t.

That left one.

She leaned across the table. She lowered her voice, which for Elara meant it was only audible to the four nearest tables.

“I think,” she said, “it’s the same piece. Every week. I think they make it once, in about 1987, and every Tuesday they heat it up again and put more sauce on it. And we eat the top of it, and they make more sauce. I think it’s been here longer than you have.”

He put his chopsticks down.

He didn’t laugh. He nearly did. He felt it come up and stopped it somewhere behind his teeth, and she saw him stop it, and her whole face lit up with delight.

“You think so too,” she said. “Your mouth went.”

“It’s a terrible theory,” said Xing Yue. “It doesn’t account for the fat.”

She opened her mouth to tell him exactly how it accounted for the fat. He picked his chopsticks up again and ate another piece of the meat, looking at her, and she stopped with her mouth open in pure horror.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d bought a pudding. He always did, on Tuesdays. A small pot of egg custard with caramel on the bottom, from the fridge by the till, which he ate last and slowly and was, as far as he knew, the only thing in his life he’d never told anyone he liked.

It was on his tray, by his elbow, with the spoon on top.

She was back on the fat. She was explaining what happened to fat when you reheated it fifty times over thirty-six years, and how it would look under a microscope, and whether you could date it like a tree. Her hands were going. Her fork was going. And her other hand came across the table without her looking at it, in the middle of the sentence, and picked up his pudding and his spoon.

He watched it go.

She didn’t stop talking. She took the lid off it with her thumb, talking, and put the spoon in, talking, and ate it. All of it. Small spoonfuls, one after another, between sentences, without once looking down at what she was doing, as if it had been hers all along, as if this were simply what happened to a pudding near her.

At the next table Weng made a small sound. Rao kicked him.

Xing Yue didn’t say anything. He let her.

He leaned back in his chair a little, and under the table his knee came to rest against hers. He didn’t move it there on purpose. He found it there. She felt it, he could tell; there was the smallest catch in the middle of a word, between microscope and rings, and then she went on. She didn’t move her knee away. She pressed back against his, once, and left it there.

They sat like that for the rest of lunch.

She finished his pudding. She scraped the caramel off the bottom of the pot with the spoon, talking about tree rings, and put the empty pot back on his tray, exactly where it had been, with the spoon on top. She still didn’t seem to know she’d done it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past two his pager went, and hers a second after, and they stood up together.

She looked down at her plate. Most of the meat was still on it, in pieces, examined from every side.

“Twenty minutes,” she said. “Twenty minutes on it, and I still don’t know what animal it was.”

“Pork,” said Xing Yue. “It says so on the board.”

She looked at him as though he were a lost cause, and picked up her tray.

They went out of the canteen by the back way, the corridor that ran past the kitchen to the service lifts, where it was warm and smelled of rice and nobody went except porters. Halfway down it she stopped him with a hand on his arm.

“I’ve just realised,” she said. “I ate your pudding. All of it. Why didn’t you stop me?”

He looked down at her. She had a little caramel at the corner of her mouth, and her face was pink, and she was trying to look sorry and failing completely.

“You were busy,” he said.

She looked at him. Then she put her tray down on top of a stack of clean ones by the kitchen door and stood up on her toes, took his face in both her hands, and kissed him, there in the warm back corridor by the service lifts, with the canteen’s dishwasher roaring behind the wall.

She tasted of caramel. He held onto her by the back of her white coat and kissed her back, longer than he’d meant to, until a porter came round the corner with a cage of bread and stopped, and looked at the ceiling, and waited.

She let him go. She picked up her tray.

“There,” said Elara. “Now you’ve had some.”

She walked off towards the lifts and the emergency department, humming, with her tray in her hands and her white coat crooked where he’d held it. He stood in the corridor by the kitchen door with the porter and the bread and the taste of his own pudding, and it was a while before he remembered where he was supposed to be going.

chapters.title: Perfect Squares
chapters.desc: On Christmas Eve, a month after the knife, he cuts her dinner into exact squares. She tells him what she thinks of that, and then she makes him do a dumpling.
chapters.epigraph: “Eighths. A dumpling has eight if you try hard enough.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
He cut the pork first.

It was the braised belly Ah Sim made on cold Sundays, which he’d watched her make eleven times from the kitchen doorway in the Walled City before she let him near the pot. He’d made it this afternoon in the flat with the windows steamed up and Elara asleep on the sofa under a blanket, her right arm on a cushion in its splint. It had taken four hours. It had come out nearly right.

He put a piece on the board and cut it into squares.

He did it the way he did everything with a blade: once, clean, no sawing. Across, and across again, and then the other way, until the piece was a neat grid of small even cubes, each one the size you could pick up on a spoon with the wrong hand and not drop. He did the next piece. And the next.

Behind him, at the counter, she was watching.

He could feel her watching. He’d been able to feel it since the day they met, on a ward round, the back of his neck going warm. She was on the high stool in his old grey jumper with the sleeves rolled up over her left hand, and the splint on its cushion on the counter beside her plate, and she hadn’t said anything since he’d started cutting.

That was new, the not saying anything. It had been new for a month. She talked again now, a little, since the Saturday she’d talked for two hours on the sofa about wet towels. But she talked in short runs with long gaps between them, like someone walking on a bad leg, and some of the gaps went on so long that he’d started holding his breath through them without meaning to.

He cut the fish. Squares. He cut the green beans into short lengths that were as near to squares as a green bean could get.

He put the plate in front of her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d looked at it, and said she was going to learn to cut her own food, with her left hand and then her right, and that he was going to hate it.

He’d said yes.

Then she’d reached across with her good hand and taken him by the collar and pulled him down over the counter and kissed him, with the pork going cold between them, and let him go, and picked up her spoon.

That had been five minutes ago. He’d stood there afterwards with his collar crooked, not sure what he’d been told, and she’d eaten three squares of pork and a square of fish one after another with her left hand, carefully, not dropping any, and not looking at him.

Now she put the spoon down.

“Every time,” she said.

He waited.

“Every meal. Every single one since I came home. You stand at that board and you cut everything into squares. Rice cakes. Fish. That omelette on Tuesday. You cut an omelette into squares. You cut a bun. You cut a bun into squares and it fell apart and you put it back together on the plate so it looked like a bun again.” Her voice was going, the way it did now, fast and then stopping. “They’re all the same size. I measured one. With the edge of the spoon. They’re exactly the same.”

“They’re the size that fits on the spoon.”

“I know what size they are.” She looked at the plate. “I can’t do it myself. I know I can’t. I’m not saying cut it into strips. I’m saying they’re perfect. Every one of them’s perfect. You do it like it’s an operation.”

She stopped. The gap went on. He let it.

“It makes me want to throw the plate at you,” said Elara. “And it makes me want to cry. And I don’t know which.”

He didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

The dumplings were the fourth thing.

He’d steamed them last, so they’d be hot, and he brought the basket over and took the lid off, and the steam went up between them. Ah Sim’s pork and chive, folded the way she folded them, twelve pleats, which had taken him two years of Sundays to get to nine.

He put two on her plate. He picked up the knife.

“No,” said Elara.

He stopped.

“Not quarters,” she said. “You were going to do quarters. I watched you do quarters on Sunday. Don’t.” She looked at the dumpling on her plate, and then at him, and there was a gleam at the corners of her eyes that he hadn’t seen since before the alley. “Eighths.”

He looked at the dumpling.

“Eighths,” she said again. “A dumpling has eight if you try hard enough. You can do it. You can do anything. You put my wrist back together on the stones with your belt.”

“Meng put your wrist back together.”

“You kept it on. Eighths.”

He put the dumpling on the board.

It was a ridiculous thing to do. He knew it, and she knew it, and she sat on the stool with her chin on her good hand and watched him do it. He cut it in half, cleanly, so the filling didn’t fall out. Then each half in half again, holding the skin with the flat of the knife so it wouldn’t tear. Then each of those, carefully, on the slant, so each little wedge kept a bit of the pleat and a bit of the filling, and nothing spilled.

Eight. Even. A dumpling in eight pieces on a board, laid out like the face of a clock.

He looked up.

She was laughing. Not much. Not the laugh you could hear down a corridor. Just a breath of it, through her nose, with her hand over her mouth. But it was the first time since November.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood at the board with the knife in his hand and understood something.

He’d thought the squares were for her. That was why he’d done it. She couldn’t hold a knife and a fork, so he’d cut her food. It was practical. It was what you did.

But he’d been doing it for a month, and he’d been doing it perfectly, and he’d been doing it for every meal whether it needed it or not. The bun. The omelette. He’d stood at this board every night and taken more care over cutting a piece of fish than he took over some bowel joins, and he hadn’t once asked himself why.

It was because there was nothing else.

He couldn’t fix the nerve. Nobody could. It would grow back a millimetre a day, or it wouldn’t, and he’d sit in Meng’s clinic and watch her try to move her little finger, and he couldn’t do anything about it. He couldn’t make her talk to her father. He couldn’t make her sleep without the nerve pain waking her at three, or stop her lying on her back in the dark with her eyes open. He couldn’t undo the alley. He couldn’t undo March, when he’d found her name, and held it back.

He could cut a piece of pork into squares. He could do it perfectly. Every square the same, every night, and that was one thing in the whole of this that he could get exactly right.

The squares were for him.

He put the knife down.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d seen it. She was watching his face.

“I’ll hate it,” he said. “When you can do it yourself. You said I would. I will.” He looked at the dumpling in its eight pieces. “I’ll learn not to.”

She didn’t say anything.

Then she picked up a fork from the counter. Not the spoon. A fork, in her left hand, awkwardly, and she held it out to him across the counter.

He took it.

“Go on,” said Elara.

He speared a square of pork off her plate and held it out to her. She leaned forward on the stool and took it off the fork with her mouth, and sat back, and chewed it, looking at him.

He did another. A square of fish. She took that too.

The third time, she didn’t wait for the fork. She reached out with her good hand and took his wrist, and turned it, and took the piece of dumpling straight off his fingers, an eighth with a bit of the pleat on it, and her mouth closed on the tips of his fingers as she did it. Warm. She held his wrist there.

There was sauce on his thumb, from the pork. She looked at it.

Then she kissed it off.

She put her mouth on the pad of his thumb and kissed the sauce away, slowly, and then the side of it, and then the inside of his wrist where she was holding it, and looked up at him over his own hand. Her eyes were wet. She was smiling.

He couldn’t move.

“They’re good squares,” said Elara. “I’ll give you that. They’re the best squares anyone’s ever cut.”

He leaned across the counter, over the plate, over the eight pieces of dumpling going cold, and she let go of his wrist and put her hand on his face instead and pulled him the rest of the way, and kissed him. Slower than the first time that night. Her good hand in his hair. Her splint on its cushion between them, and the steam still coming off the basket, and the city outside the steamed-up windows going on with Christmas without them.

When she let him go she picked up the fork again and held it out.

“More,” she said. “And then I’m going to do one myself, with my left hand, and it’ll be a terrible square, and you’re going to eat it.”

He did. It was terrible. It was the size of three of his and the shape of nothing, and the pork fell off the fork twice before she got it to him.

He ate it, and told her it was perfect, and she knew he was lying, and it was the first lie between them she didn’t mind.

chapters.title: The Cousin Who Wants Emergency Medicine
chapters.desc: Yu Chen comes to Banyan Terrace to ask his mentor about emergency medicine, and about something harder. Elara walks in talking.
chapters.epigraph: “Ask her what she wants. Then do that.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
Yu Chen had been holding the same cup of tea for twenty minutes, and hadn’t drunk any of it.

He sat at one end of the long grey sofa at Banyan Terrace with the cup in both hands on his knee, the way people held things in waiting rooms. He was in a grey jumper with the cuffs pushed up and his hair in his eyes, and he’d come straight from a morning on the wards, final year, with his lanyard still round his neck and a pen in his pocket he’d forgotten to take out. He’d rung on Thursday to ask if he could come on Saturday. He’d never rung to ask before. He’d always just been told when the mentoring meetings were, by email, and turned up on time.

Xing Yue sat in the armchair opposite with his own tea, and drank it, and waited.

“It’s the forms,” said Yu Chen. “For after. They want a first choice by March. For training.”

“I know when they want it.”

“Emergency or surgery.” He looked at the tea. “Everyone thinks surgery. Because of you. Because of the family. They think I’ll do what you did.”

“Do you want to?”

Yu Chen didn’t answer straight away. He was like that. He thought before he spoke, and when he’d thought, he said one thing, and it was usually the right one, and then his ears went red.

“No,” he said. “I like the not knowing. In the emergency department. On a night shift, you don’t know what’s coming through the doors. You’ve got four minutes to work it out. I like that. In theatre you know what you’re doing before you start.” He stopped. “That’s not a criticism.”

“I didn’t take it as one.”

“I just think I’m better when I don’t know.”

Xing Yue looked at his cousin across the room.

He’d been his mentor for three years. He’d watched him in a skills lab, and on a ward, and once, from a corridor, in the emergency department at three in the morning, standing over a cubicle with a drunk man who was trying to hit him, keeping his voice level and his hands open until the man sat down. He’d heard about the night in February when a boy died in resus under Yu Chen’s hands, and he’d watched him come in for his next shift on time and do his job.

“Emergency,” said Xing Yue. “You’re good when you don’t know what’s coming. You don’t panic. And you don’t like being thanked, which helps, because nobody will ever thank you.”

Yu Chen looked up.

“That’s it?”

“That’s it. Put it first on the form. Don’t let anyone talk you out of it, including the family. Including Nainai. Especially Nainai.”

Yu Chen nearly smiled. He looked down at the tea again, and didn’t drink it, and didn’t put it down, and didn’t get up to leave, and Xing Yue understood that the forms hadn’t been what he’d come for.

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone went on the arm of the chair. The registrar on call.

He took it without getting up. A man on 9B with a pressure that had dropped after his evening drugs, and the registrar wanted to know whether to wait and see.

“Wait for what?” said Xing Yue. “For it to drop further, so you can be sure? Go and see him. Give him fluid. Stop his evening drugs. Ring me in an hour with a number, not with a feeling.” He listened. “No. You’re not bothering me. You’d be bothering me if you waited.”

He hung up. Yu Chen was looking at him with an expression he’d seen on residents before. The one they had when they’d just heard him on the phone and were glad it wasn’t them.

“Go on,” said Xing Yue.

Yu Chen turned the cup a quarter turn on his knee.

“How do you look after someone,” he said, “who doesn’t want looking after?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say who, and Xing Yue didn’t ask. He’d seen the two of them across a flower shop a year ago and said nothing, and he’d been saying nothing ever since, and he had no intention of starting now.

“Someone who does things,” said Yu Chen, slowly. “That could hurt her. Not stupid things. Things she’s good at. Things she’s chosen. And she’s—” He stopped and chose another word. “She’s sure. She doesn’t want anyone standing in front of her. She’d be furious if she thought I was trying to. And I lie awake.”

Xing Yue looked at him.

He thought about a hall floor at one in the morning, and a small woman sitting against the shoe rack with her knees up, shaking. That world raised me. I’m not going to stop going when they ring. Don’t ask me to. He thought about a dot on his phone crossing the river on a June afternoon, and not knowing for four hours if she was the one bleeding.

“You can’t,” he said.

Yu Chen’s face fell.

“Not the way you mean.” Xing Yue put his cup down. “You can’t stand in front of her. You can’t make her stop, and if you try, you’ll lose her, and you’ll deserve to. And you can’t stop lying awake. I haven’t found a way. I don’t think there is one.”

“Then what do you—”

The front door opened downstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

They both heard it. Then her voice, coming up the stairs before she did.

“—because if they think I’m doing another weekend of nights on that floor after what happened with the drains, they can think again, and Liao said, he actually said, Dr. Lin, you’re persuasive, go away, which means yes, he always means yes when he says go away—”

She came round the top of the stairs in her scrubs and her cardigan, with her lanyard on and a paper bag from the bakery in one hand and her hair falling out of its clip, and saw them.

She stopped.

Xing Yue knew what she was seeing. Two Wangs, one on the sofa and one in the chair, both sitting up straight, both with the faces of men who’d been talking about something and stopped the second they heard the door.

“Oh,” said Elara.

She looked from one to the other.

“You both look guilty,” she said. “You both look exactly the same kind of guilty. It’s a family face. I’ve never noticed. Yu Chen, you’ve got his face. You’ve got the face he does when I find out he’s bought me something.” She put the bag down on the counter. “Have you eaten? You haven’t eaten. Neither of you. Don’t tell me. There’s a cup of cold tea in your hand, Yu Chen, and it’s full, I can see it from here.”

“I’m fine,” said Yu Chen.

“You’re not. You’re a final-year student on a Saturday. Nobody in final year has eaten since August.” She was already getting plates down. “I’ve got pork buns. Six. And egg tarts. Sit there. Both of you. Don’t talk about whatever it was. I don’t want to know. Eat.”

They ate.

She stood at the counter and ate a pork bun herself, standing up, and told them about the drains on 9B, and about a patient who’d tried to discharge himself in a hospital gown and been found at the bus stop, and about Liao’s sweets, which had changed from lemon to aniseed and nobody knew why. She didn’t ask once what they’d been talking about. She made Yu Chen have a second egg tart. She made him drink a fresh cup of tea, all of it, and watched him do it.

Xing Yue sat in his armchair and watched his cousin’s shoulders come down, a little at a time, while she talked at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked Yu Chen to the door at six.

On the landing, at the top of the stairs, with the door open and Elara behind them in the kitchen singing along to the radio, badly, Yu Chen stopped and turned round.

“You didn’t finish,” he said. “You said I can’t. Then what do I do?”

Xing Yue looked at him.

He thought about the hall floor again. Next time ring me first. I’ll drive. I’ll wait in the car. He thought about sitting in the car outside a checkpoint at the border at two in the morning with the engine off, watching her kneel by a river in a crowd of strangers with her green bag, and not getting out.

“Ask her what she wants,” said Xing Yue. “Then do that.”

Yu Chen didn’t move.

“That’s all?”

“It’s harder than it sounds. You’ll want to do something else every time. Do that anyway.” He held the door. “And when she lets you, go with her. Hold the torch. Drive the car. Wait outside. Don’t make her choose between you and the thing.”

Yu Chen thought about it, the way he did, all the way through, before he said anything. Then he nodded once and went down the stairs, and at the bottom he looked back up, and his ears were red, and he lifted a hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he came back into the kitchen she was waiting for him.

She was leaning on the counter with her arms folded and her lanyard still round her neck and an egg tart in one hand, and she had the face on. The one she had on ward rounds when someone was hiding a result.

“So,” said Elara. “What were you talking about?”

“You,” said Xing Yue.

She looked at him.

“You were not. Liar. You’ve never talked about me to anyone in your life. You’d rather have your teeth out.” She pointed the egg tart at him. “It was about Eliana, wasn’t it. It was. I could see it. He had the face. He had the exact face you had in the lift the week we met, when I’d held your tie, and you looked like you’d been hit by a—”

He reached out and took hold of her lanyard.

The blue cord round her neck, with her hospital badge on the end of it. He took it between his fingers, and she stopped mid-sentence and looked down at his hand, and he pulled. Not hard. Just enough. She came towards him across the kitchen, one step, two, with the cord drawing her in, until she was standing against him with the egg tart held out to one side, looking up.

“That’s cheating,” she said.

He kissed her.

He kissed her to stop her asking, and she knew it, and she let him anyway. She dropped the egg tart on the counter behind her.
