She put both hands flat on his chest and then in his shirt, holding on, and kissed him back, slow and then not slow, with her lanyard still wound round his fingers between them so she couldn’t have gone anywhere if she’d wanted to.

She didn’t want to. She pushed him back against the fridge and kissed his jaw and his mouth again, and the radio went on playing behind them, and she’d forgotten what she’d asked.

She remembered at about eleven, in bed, with her head on his chest.

“It was Eliana,” she said into the dark.

“Go to sleep,” said Xing Yue.

She laughed into his chest, and didn’t ask again, and he lay with his hand in her hair and thought about his cousin lying awake on the other side of a wall in the Walled City, and hoped he’d listened.

chapters.title: Banned From Trivia Night
chapters.desc: The hospital social club bans Elara from the Tuesday quiz after four weeks of her team winning. She appeals, and Xing Yue, on the other side, gets every question wrong.
chapters.epigraph: “Knowing things isn’t cheating. It’s just knowing things.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
The quiz was on Tuesdays, in the staff social club behind City Hospital, a low room at the back of the old boiler house with a bar along one wall and a dartboard nobody had used since the darts went missing in 2019.

Elara came on the ferry. She’d come every Tuesday since February, straight from the surgical floor at Harbourside in her coat over her scrubs, because her old year from medical school had a team, and five of the six were interns at City now, and the sixth was her. They were called Nil By Mouth. After losing the first week, they had won four in a row.

This was mostly because of Elara.

She knew things. She’d always known things. She knew how many moons Jupiter had, and which one she was named after, and the name of every bone in the hand in the order they went. She knew old films her father had watched on the television in the kitchen when she was small, and the capitals of countries nobody had been to, and the year the tram line on the harbour road was built, and what a group of crows was called. She didn’t try to know any of it. It went in and stayed.

On the fifth Tuesday, when Nil By Mouth won by eleven points, a registrar from orthopaedics threw a beer mat at the scoreboard.

On the sixth Tuesday, Mr. Tu from the pathology lab, who ran the quiz and had run it for twenty years, came over to their table before the first round with his clipboard and an expression of deep regret.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I’m so sorry,” said Mr. Tu. “Dr. Lin. I really am. But I’ve had complaints.”

“Complaints,” said Elara.

“Seven. In writing. Two of them in verse.” He looked at his clipboard. “The feeling is that it’s no longer a fair contest. That the other teams are coming for second place. That Nil By Mouth has, and I’m quoting, a ringer from across the harbour.” He lowered the clipboard. “I’m going to have to ask you not to play. For the good of everyone. You’re welcome to come and have a drink. You just can’t answer anything.”

Her team made a noise like a ward when the tea trolley’s late.

Elara stood up.

“I’d like to appeal,” she said.

Mr. Tu blinked. Nobody had ever appealed. He looked at his clipboard as if it might tell him what to do, and it didn’t.

“On what grounds?”

“Knowing things isn’t cheating,” said Elara. “It’s just knowing things. I don’t use my phone. I don’t look anything up. I’ve never once gone to the toilet during a round, which is more than I can say for orthopaedics.” She looked round the room. “If they can prove I’m cheating, ban me. If I’m just better, they should learn some capitals.”

The room went up. Half of it booed. Half of it cheered. The orthopaedic registrar threw another beer mat.

Mr. Tu held up his hand.

“All right,” he said. “All right. An appeal round. Sudden death. Ten questions.” He looked round the room, the way he did when he was choosing a picture round. “Dr. Lin on her own. Against the best table in the room that isn’t hers. If she wins, it proves the complaint, and the ban stands. If she loses, she can play next week.”

“That’s not fair,” said Elara. “If I win, I’m banned for winning.”

“That’s what the complaint is,” said Mr. Tu, not unkindly. “That you win.”

She opened her mouth to argue. Then she looked across the room to see who she’d be playing, and shut it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The best table in the room that wasn’t hers was the consultants’.

There were four of them, on a good Tuesday. Professor Liao, who came for the lemonade and never answered anything. Dr. Fei, who answered everything about television and nothing about anything else. A quiet woman from radiology who knew all the flags. And, since February, at the end of the table with a cup of Pu’er he’d brought from home in a flask because the club only sold builder’s tea, Wang Xing Yue.

He’d started coming in February, the week after she did. He said Fei had made him. Fei said she hadn’t, and that he’d just turned up one Tuesday and sat down, and had come every week since, and never once looked at the quiz sheet, only at the Nil By Mouth table, all evening.

The consultants’ table had come second four weeks running.

Fei stood up and put her hand on his shoulder.

“He’ll do it,” she said. “Wang. You’re up. You’re the only one of us who knows anything.”

He looked at Fei. Then he looked across the room at Elara, standing by her table with her arms folded and her coat still on. Then he got up and went and stood at the front of the room by Mr. Tu’s table, with his tea, and Elara went and stood on the other side, and the whole club went quiet to listen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Tu read the first question.

“How many moons does Jupiter have?”

Elara had her mouth open. It was the easiest question she’d ever been asked. It was practically her name. She looked at Xing Yue to see if he’d go first, and he did.

“Four,” he said.

The room murmured. Elara turned and looked at him.

He didn’t look back. He stood at Mr. Tu’s table with his tea in his hand and his face perfectly calm, the face he had on ward rounds when he was about to take a resident apart.

“Four is wrong,” said Mr. Tu. “Dr. Lin?”

“Ninety-five,” said Elara, slowly. “As of last year. Confirmed ones.”

“Correct.”

The second question was the smallest bone in the human body. Xing Yue said the hamate. Elara said the stapes, and stared at him, because he’d taught first-years for five years and the hamate was the size of a hazelnut.

The third was the capital of Burkina Faso. He said Lagos. The fourth was who had directed Psycho. He said a name Elara had never heard, which might have been a man who’d once delivered his post. The fifth was what a group of crows was called. He said a flock.

“A murder,” said Elara. “It’s a murder. You know it’s a murder. You told me it was a murder in October when we saw them on the hospital roof.”

“Dr. Lin, please address your answers to me,” said Mr. Tu.

He got the sixth wrong. And the seventh, and the eighth. He got them wrong in the same level voice every time, without a flicker, as if he were reading the answers off a card, and every time he said something wrong the room laughed louder, and Fei at the consultants’ table put her head on her arms, and Professor Liao drank his lemonade and looked at the ceiling.

Elara got every one right. She couldn’t not. She stood there with the right answer coming out of her mouth every time, furious, while the man she’d watched read a CT scan at a glance told the whole social club that the longest river in the world was the one that ran past the fish market.

Ten-nil.

“Well,” said Mr. Tu, in the silence afterwards. “I think that’s conclusive.”

The complainants cheered. Her own team groaned. The orthopaedic registrar stood on his chair. Mr. Tu wrote something on his clipboard and shook her hand, and told her she was welcome any Tuesday for a drink and that she would always be, in his view, the finest quiz player he had ever banned.

She looked round for Xing Yue.

He’d gone back to the consultants’ table and was screwing the lid on his flask.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found him in the car park.

It was dark and cold and raining a little, and his car was parked under the one light by the boiler-house wall, and he was standing beside it holding the passenger door open for her, as if he’d known she’d come straight out, which he had.

“You did that on purpose,” said Elara.

He didn’t say anything.

“You got every single one wrong. On purpose. Ten questions. You know the stapes. You know it’s a murder of crows. You told me what Psycho was about at two in the morning when I couldn’t sleep, the whole film, scene by scene, you did the music.” She was standing in the rain with her hair getting wet. “You made it look fair. You made sure I won by ten so nobody could say they’d let me off. You got me banned.”

“Get in the car,” he said. “You’re getting wet.”

She got in the car, because she was. He shut the door and came round and got in the other side.

She turned in her seat and looked at him.

“Why?”

He looked straight ahead through the windscreen, at the rain coming down in the light by the wall.

“You come over on the ferry,” he said. “Every Tuesday. After a day shift at Harbourside. You get here at seven and you play till half past ten and you get the last ferry back, or you come home with me and you’re up at five to get the first one. You’ve been doing it six weeks.” He looked at her. “You fell asleep on the ferry last Tuesday and missed your stop and went round twice. You told me it was funny.”

“It was funny.”

“I wanted Tuesdays back,” said Xing Yue.

She stared at him. She opened her mouth to tell him that this was the single most high-handed thing he’d ever done, and that he’d had no right, and that she’d decide how she spent her own Tuesdays, thank you, and that she’d been enjoying herself—

He leaned across her and pulled her seatbelt down.

She stopped. He drew it across her, slowly, the way he’d tuck in a sheet, and his face was close to hers in the dark of the car, and he said, against her ear, “Jupiter has ninety-five.”

The belt clicked into the buckle.

He kissed her.

He kissed her with one hand still on the buckle and the other on the seat beside her hip, in the car park behind the boiler house, with the rain on the roof. She made a furious sound against his mouth and grabbed his coat in both fists, and didn’t push him away. She pulled him closer. She kissed him back with her wet hair against his face and her heart going and the seatbelt holding her down in the seat, and he didn’t let her up.

“The stapes,” he said, when he lifted his head. “In the middle ear.”

He kissed her again before she could say anything.

“Ouagadougou,” he said, against her jaw.

She laughed into his mouth. She couldn’t help it. He went through all ten. A kiss for every one. Hitchcock, against her throat. A murder of crows, with his hand in her hair. The longest river in the world, which he said properly, and then the length of it, because he couldn’t stop himself, and she pulled him down by his coat and kissed him so he would.

When he’d got to ten he sat back in his own seat.

She sat in hers, with her belt on and her hair wet and her mouth tingling, and looked at him across the dark car.

“I’m still furious,” said Elara. “I’m going to tell everyone you did it. I’m going to tell Mr. Tu.”

“He knows,” said Xing Yue, and started the car. “He asked me to. Last week.”

She stared at him all the way out of the car park. Then she started laughing, and laughed most of the way home, and on Tuesday the week after she was on the sofa at Banyan Terrace at eight o’clock with her feet in his lap and a bowl of noodles, asking him the capitals of countries nobody had ever been to, and he got every one of them right.

chapters.title: Doctor’s Orders: Nap
chapters.desc: After three nights in a row he writes her a prescription for a nap. She complies, loudly, like an operation note, and falls asleep in the middle of a sentence.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m complying. Loudly. Those are different things.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
She came in at a quarter past nine on Sunday morning after her third night in a row, and instead of going to bed she cleaned the kitchen.

He watched her do it from the sofa. She took her shoes off by the door and put them facing out, and washed her hands at the kitchen sink for a full surgical scrub, the way she always did when she came in off a ward. Then she didn’t stop. She wiped the counter. She emptied the dishwasher, which he’d emptied at seven. She took every jar out of the cupboard over the kettle and put them back in a different order, talking, telling him about the night: the man in bed three who’d pulled his drip out twice, the registrar who’d eaten her biscuits, the kettle in the doctors’ room on the seventh floor, which had started making a noise.

“Elara,” he said.

“It’s not a whistle. It’s lower than a whistle. It’s like a moan. Like it’s sad about something. At four in the morning it’s the only sound on the whole floor and I keep thinking it’s a patient.”

“Elara. Go to bed.”

“I’m not tired.” She opened the fridge and looked into it. “I’m past tired. I’ve gone out the other side. If I lie down now I’ll just lie there and think about the kettle.”

He got up.

He went into the study and came back with the prescription pad from his desk, the one he wasn’t supposed to have at home and always did, and his pen, and sat down at the kitchen counter, and wrote on it while she watched him over the top of the fridge door.

He tore the sheet off and held it out to her.

She took it. She read it, which nobody else in the city could have done.

Wang Xing Yue. Patient: Lin Elara. Nap. Ninety minutes. Supine. Now. Signed.

He’d signed it. With the squiggle he signed drug charts with, the one the pharmacists rang her to translate.

She looked at the sheet. She looked at him.

“There’s no dose,” said Elara. “There’s no route. That’s not a real prescription.”

“Supine is the route,” said Xing Yue. “Ninety minutes is the dose. Go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went. She went loudly.

She walked up the stairs in front of him holding the prescription out in front of her like a candle and narrating, in her ward voice, the one she used for dictating operation notes into the little machine at the end of a list.

“Patient climbs stairs,” she said. “Unassisted. Some reluctance. Patient enters bedroom. Patient notes that the bed has not been made since she left it at seven last night, and that this is unlike the consultant, and draws her own conclusions.”

He’d been waiting up. They both knew it. He didn’t say anything.

“Patient removes cardigan,” said Elara, removing it. “Patient removes scrub top. Patient puts on consultant’s grey T-shirt, which is the only acceptable sleeping garment in the building. Patient sits on edge of bed. Patient is complying. Loudly. Those are two different things, and I’d like that noted.”

“Noted,” he said, from the doorway.

“Patient lies down.” She lay down, on her back, on top of the covers, with her arms at her sides and the prescription flat on her chest. “Supine. As instructed. Patient’s pillow is too flat. Patient requests a second pillow.”

He gave her his. She put it under her head without stopping.

“Patient is positioned,” said Elara. “Patient is now going to have a nap. Patient would like the record to show that she is not tired, that this is a waste of a good morning, and that the kettle on the seventh floor is still a problem.”

He pulled the covers out from under her, and put them over her, and drew them up to her chin. He tucked them in down both sides. She watched him do it with her eyes narrowed.

“Patient has been tucked in,” she said. “Against her will.”

“Ninety minutes.”

“Is the consultant staying to observe?”

He took a journal off the bedside table and lay down beside her on top of the covers, in his clothes, with the journal open on his chest.

“Yes,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t read it.

He held it open at a page about bile leaks and looked at the first paragraph, and listened to her. She hadn’t stopped. She’d moved on from the operation note, because it was hard to keep up an operation note lying down, and was telling him about the kettle again. She’d decided the kettle needed a name. She was going through names.

She told him about a kettle her father had in the Walled City when she was small, an old tin one that Ah Sim kept on the back of the stove, which also made a noise, but a happier one, more like a song, and how she’d thought for years that all kettles sang and been disappointed by every kettle since, and how the seventh-floor kettle was the opposite of Ah Sim’s, it was the saddest kettle she’d ever—

She stopped.

He waited for the rest.

It didn’t come. He turned his head on the pillow. She’d gone to sleep in the middle of the word, between one breath and the next, with her mouth a little open and her hand curled on top of the covers over the prescription. All at once, the way she did everything.

He lay there and looked at her.

The saddest kettle she’d ever heard, he thought. And she wants to call it something kind, so it’ll cheer up. He finished the sentence for her in his head, the way he’d heard her finish a hundred of them. He thought she’d probably have called it after a patient. Then he thought she wouldn’t, because she’d say it was bad luck.

He didn’t move. He held the journal open on his chest at the same page and didn’t read it, and listened to her breathing go long and slow.

✦ ✦ ✦

At about twenty minutes in his phone buzzed on the bedside table.

He had it on silent. It buzzed anyway, on the wood, a low rattle. He picked it up before the second one. A registrar on call for the weekend, a boy from Fei’s team, ringing about a man on 9B who wasn’t Xing Yue’s patient.

He got up off the bed without shaking it. He went out onto the landing and pulled the bedroom door to behind him, and answered with his back to it.

“You’re ringing me about a patient on Fei’s list,” he said, low. “On a Sunday. When I’m not on call. Why?”

The registrar started to explain.

“Fei’s on call. Ring Fei. If you’ve rung me because you’re frightened to ring her, that’s the wrong reason, and you know it, and she’ll know it too when I tell her on Monday.” He let the boy get half a sentence further. “Don’t ring this number again today. If you wake anybody in this flat, I’ll have you on nights until the summer.”

He hung up. He turned the phone off altogether, which he never did, and went back in and lay down again beside her without making the bed move.

She hadn’t stirred.

✦ ✦ ✦

She slept two hours, not ninety minutes. He didn’t wake her.

At some point he put the journal down on the floor. At some point he took his glasses off and put them on the bedside table and lay on his side facing her, with the light coming in grey through the slatted blinds. At some point he picked up the pad, which he’d left on the bedside table, and his pen, and wrote a second line under the first, and tore the sheet off again and put it on the pillow beside her face, where she’d see it.

Then he sat up on the edge of the bed with his back to her and put his watch on, and waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

He heard her wake. He heard the covers move and her breathing change, and the crackle of the paper by her face.

He didn’t turn round.

There was a pause. Then a sound, half a laugh and half a groan, muffled, as if she’d put her face back in the pillow. He knew what she’d read. He’d written it in his own writing, under the first line, with the squiggle after it again.

Repeat as needed.

He felt the bed move. She’d sat up. Then she was on her knees on the mattress behind him, and he felt her hands on his shoulders, and her breath, warm, on the back of his neck.

She kissed him there.

Just above his collar. The place at the top of his spine where his hair was cut short. She kissed it slowly, and then the side of his neck, under his ear, and her hands came round from his shoulders to his chest and held on, and she rested her chin on his shoulder with her mouth by his jaw.

“The patient’s read the prescription,” she said in his ear. Her voice was low and rough from sleep. “The patient has some concerns about the second line.”

He didn’t move. He’d stopped breathing.

“The patient wonders,” said Elara, “what else is as needed.”

He turned round.

He took her face in his hands and turned her down onto the bed, onto the pillow, onto the prescription, which crackled under her head, and kissed her. She laughed into it. She pulled the covers back and him in under them with her, the way he’d tucked her in, except the other way, and wrapped her arms round his neck and her legs round his and held on, warm from two hours of sleep, and the light through the blinds came in in stripes across both of them.

It was slow. It was the slowest Sunday he’d ever spent. He kissed her as if they’d been given the whole day by prescription, which they had. She talked at first, of course she talked, she told him the second line was a breach of protocol and she was going to report him to the pharmacy, and then she stopped telling him anything, and said his name instead, into his shoulder, and then not into anything, out loud.

Afterwards she lay on his chest with the crumpled prescription stuck to her cheek.

He peeled it off. He smoothed it flat on his chest and looked at it. Two lines, his writing, a crease through the middle where her head had been.

“I’m keeping that,” said Elara.

“It’s a prescription.”

“It’s mine. It’s got my name on it.” She took it out of his hand. “I’m putting it in the drawer. With the coin and the red packet. In case I need a repeat.”

She did. It was still there, years later, at the back of the bedside drawer in another house, folded in four, the ink gone soft, with a coin and a red packet that said Come home for breakfast. She took it out sometimes after a run of nights and read it, and put it back.

He never wrote her another one. She’d come in after three nights and stand in the hall with her shoes in her hand and say, “I need a repeat,” and he’d put his journal down.

chapters.title: The Machine
chapters.desc: Jinx builds the rig at night in the garage, from calipers and graph paper and a hand she measured at Ev’s kitchen table. Then she doesn’t watch.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t know hands. I know linkages.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
The first afternoon, Jinx traced round it.

She put the graph paper flat on Ev’s kitchen table at Fig Tree Lane and held it down at the corners with a teapot and a jar of salted lemons, and Elara put her right hand on it, palm down, fingers spread as far as they’d go, which wasn’t far. Jinx went round it with a hard pencil. Slowly. In and out of every finger, round the thumb, down the side of the wrist to where the scar started, and stopped there.

Then she got the calipers out.

They were the good ones, the steel ones she used on crankshafts. She measured the first finger at the base, at the middle joint, at the top joint, at the tip. Length between each. Width at each. She wrote the numbers down the side of the finger on the graph paper in small hard figures. Then the next finger.

Elara talked.

She talked the whole time. She told Jinx about Ev’s lemon tree, and Jun Hyuk’s rosemary, and a patient she’d had in 2024 who kept a tortoise in his locker on the ward and how nobody had found out for a week. She told her about the moons of Jupiter. She told her about the little bones in the wrist, all eight of them, by name, in order, because Jinx’s calipers were right next to them. She didn’t stop for breath. Her voice went up and up.

Jinx didn’t look at her face. She looked at the hand.

She knew what the talking was for. She’d sat in her father’s shop at eight years old with a cut across her palm from a sheet of tin and hummed every song on the radio, one after another, as loud as she could, so she wouldn’t cry, and she hadn’t. Elara was doing the same thing. Jinx let her.

When the voice cracked, on the seventh bone of the wrist, Jinx kept measuring. She didn’t look up. She moved the calipers to the next joint and read the number off, out loud, flat, the way she’d read a number off a gauge.

“Fourteen point two.”

Elara stopped. Then she breathed, and said the name of the eighth bone, and went on.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came back every afternoon for a week.

The tall doctor was on the step every time she came up the path. He sat with his elbows on his knees, looking at the lane, and nodded to her, and she nodded back. He never once asked what she was doing. She liked him for that. She’d liked him for it since a flower shop, when he’d come in late and stood beside the cake and looked at Elara as if she were the only thing in the room that was the right way up.

She measured everything. The angle each finger would bend to on its own, with a protractor she’d borrowed from Raiden’s desk. How far it would go if Jinx pushed it, gently, with one finger, until Elara’s face went white and Jinx stopped. How hard the thumb could pinch against the first finger, on a gauge off an old brake line that she’d cleaned up and fitted with a new dial. The answer was almost nothing. She wrote the almost nothing down.

On the last afternoon she rolled up the graph paper and put it inside her jacket.

“What will it be?” said Elara.

“Don’t know yet,” said Jinx. “Something that moves.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She built it at night.

The garage opened at seven and shut at seven, and after that, when the bikes were put away and the shutter was down and Raiden was upstairs drawing, she spread the graph paper on the long bench under the window and looked at it until it told her what it wanted.

She didn’t know hands. She’d said so at Ev’s table. She knew linkages: how a lever moved a rod moved a cam, how a spring pulled back against a load, how you made a thing that did one movement over and over, ten thousand times, without wearing out. A finger was a linkage. Three joints, a set of cables running down the inside, a set running down the back. Somebody had cut the cables and somebody else had tied them back together, and now the cables were stiff and the signal to them was faint, and what they needed was load. Something to pull against. A bit more every week.

So she made them something to pull against.

A forearm rest first, padded, at the height she’d measured, so the hand would hang out over the end of the bench. Then a sling for each finger, on a thin spring, and a rail behind them so the springs could be swapped from soft to stiff. She wound the springs herself on the lathe from piano wire, a dozen of them, each one a bit stiffer than the last.

The pinch gauge, off the brake line, bolted to a little stand.

A pegboard. She drilled it on the pillar drill at two in the morning, row after row, the first row big enough for a broom handle, each row after it smaller, down to the last, where the pins were finer than sewing needles and she had to hold them with tweezers.

Then the wire. She bent it by hand into a long wandering track with no straight bits in it, and put a little ring on a handle round it, and wired them both to a buzzer off a dead alarm clock, so that if the ring touched the wire anywhere, the whole garage would know.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third night Raiden came down the stairs at two with coffee.

He stood at the bottom in his dressing gown with two mugs and looked at the bench. At the frame, and the springs, and the pegboard, and the graph paper with a hand on it, pinned to the wall.

“What is it?” he said.

“Hers,” said Jinx.

He looked at it a second longer. Then he put one mug down by her elbow and went back upstairs with the other one, and didn’t ask again.

He came down every night after that, at two, with coffee. He never asked once. On the fifth night he left a sheet of tracing paper on the bench beside the mug, with a drawing on it of a better way to fix the forearm rest so it wouldn’t creep, and she looked at it, and it was better, and she did it his way.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last thing was the knobs.

Everything on it had to move. The height of the rest. The tension on every spring. The gap on the pinch gauge. The angle of the camera she’d fixed on an arm over a practice pad, so Elara could see on a little screen what her fingers were doing in the places she couldn’t feel them yet.

Jinx sat on the stool at three in the morning with the graph paper and thought about how Elara would make it harder.

Because she would. She’d need to. In a month the soft springs would be too soft and the big pins would be too big, and Elara would need to move everything on one notch, and then another. And she wouldn’t ask. Jinx knew she wouldn’t. She’d seen her face at the table at Fig Tree Lane when the calipers got to the scar. She’d sooner bite through her own lip than ask somebody to make it harder for her because she was getting better.

So nobody would have to.

Jinx went to the drawer and got out a box of knurled steel knobs, the kind with a ridged edge your fingers could grip without slipping, and she fitted one to every single thing on the rig that moved, and set every one of them so it turned exactly a quarter at a time and clicked. A quarter turn. One notch harder. Anybody could do it. You didn’t need to say a word.

She finished at five, on the Friday. She sat on the stool and looked at it.

It looked like something out of a museum of torture. She knew it did. She didn’t care.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first morning was the Saturday.

Elara came in a taxi at a quarter to five, with her coat buttoned wrong, and stood in the doorway of the garage and looked at the bench.

Jinx told her what each part was for, in as few words as she could. Then she said what she’d decided at three in the morning: five, before she opened, and nobody needed to know. And Elara said she didn’t want anyone to know, not her father, not her sisters, not him, and Jinx nodded, because of course, and went to the other end of the garage and got down on her creeper under a bike that didn’t need anything doing to it.

She put the radio on low. She turned her back.

She didn’t watch.

She heard it, though. She couldn’t help hearing it. She heard the springs creak and stop, and the pinch gauge click and not click, and the little pins go down on the bench one after another and roll. She heard the buzzer go. And go. And go again, so many times that she stopped hearing it as a sound and started feeling it in her teeth. She lay on her back under the bike with a spanner in her hand and didn’t do anything with it.

She heard Elara stop breathing properly, about an hour in. A small catch, and then another. Not crying. The thing just before.

Jinx lifted the spanner and dropped it.

On the concrete, from about her own height, so it hit hard and bounced, and went skidding away under the next bike with a noise like a dropped tray. She swore, at nobody, loudly and badly and at length, every word she’d learned in the shop under the flyover, and rolled out on her creeper after it and couldn’t reach it and swore again.

Behind her, at the bench, she heard a sound.

Elara was laughing. Wet and surprised, with her hand over her mouth, laughing at a grown woman lying on a creeper on the floor of her own garage, swearing at nothing.

Jinx got the spanner back. She rolled under the bike again without turning round.

The buzzer went. And went. But the breathing had come back.

At half past five Raiden came down the stairs in his dressing gown with three coffees, put one by Elara’s elbow and one on the floor by Jinx’s boots, and went back up with the third without a word, which for Raiden was a kind of medal.

At seven Elara put her coat on.

“Same time tomorrow,” said Jinx, from under the bike.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, later, when the garage was open and the first customer had been and gone, she went up to the flat for a minute.

Raiden was at his drawing table by the window in a T-shirt, with the light on the paper. He looked up when she came in. He hadn’t once asked about the rig. He’d been good about that all week, better than she’d known he could be.

“All right?” he said.

She stood in the middle of the room. She thought about saying she was fine. She thought about the buzzer, and the catch in Elara’s breathing, and her own hands, which had been shaking a little since five, in a way they never shook on a bike.

She went across the room and sat down on his knee, which she never did, in her overalls, and put her head on his shoulder.

He put the pencil down. He put his arms round her and held on, and didn’t ask, and after a while he put his face in her hair and kissed the top of her head, and she let him, with her eyes shut, until the bell went downstairs.

chapters.title: Xing Yue’s Handwriting
chapters.desc: Nobody can read a word he writes except Elara. Pharmacists ring her to translate, and some of the notes are only for her.
chapters.epigraph: “That says ‘bring milk’. Obviously.” — Elara Lin
chapters.content:
October 2022

The first one was on the pillow.

She woke at three in the afternoon in his bed, with the blinds cutting the sun into stripes on the wall, and the sheet from the prescription pad was beside her face. She held it up to the light. It looked like a heart trace on a bad day. A line that went along and jumped and fell over and got up again.

She read it straight off.

Gone to buy food. Back by half three. You don’t snore. You talk in your sleep. Don’t go home.

It didn’t occur to her until much later that she shouldn’t have been able to. She just could. She’d always been good at bad writing: her father’s, which was all capitals and pressed so hard it went through the paper; Ah Sim’s shopping lists, which were half pictures; the old consultants on her first ward who wrote TCI and NAD and ? and expected you to know what they’d meant. His was worse than any of them. It was the worst she’d ever seen.

She read it again anyway, lying on her back, and laughed into the pillow, and then folded it in four and put it in the pocket of her cardigan, where it stayed for a month, until she moved it to the back of her phone case, where it went soft and grey at the folds and stayed for five years.

✦ ✦ ✦

July 2024

The pharmacist rang on a Sunday at ten past eight in the morning.

Elara was asleep. She’d done a night. She was in their bed at Banyan Terrace with the blinds down and her face in his pillow, because he’d gone in at seven for a list, and her phone rang on the bedside table and she answered it without opening her eyes.

“Dr. Lin? I’m so sorry. It’s Xiong, in pharmacy at City. Dr. Wang said—Dr. Wang’s in theatre, and the nurse said to ring you, she said you’d—” He stopped. “There’s a drug chart on 9B. Bed twelve. I’ve been looking at it for ten minutes.”

“Send me a photo,” said Elara, into the pillow.

He sent it. She opened one eye and looked at it on the screen. A drug chart, his writing, three lines in the space for new drugs, and a signature like a fish hook.

She read it to him. All three lines, the drug and the dose and when, slowly, with her eyes shut again by the end, because once she’d seen it she didn’t need to keep looking.

There was a pause on the line.

“How did you do that?” said Mr. Xiong.

“I don’t know,” said Elara. “I just can.”

“Could you—would you mind if I saved your number?”

She told him he could, and went back to sleep, and forgot about it. By September she had four pharmacists, two ward sisters, a theatre manager and Professor Liao’s secretary saved in her phone under XY translate, and they rang her on her own ward rounds and in the canteen and once, memorably, in the bath. She did it every time. She never once got it wrong.

He found out in October, he told her that night, when a ward sister thanked him for marrying someone useful.

“We’re not married,” he said.

“Well, hurry up,” said the sister. “I need her number for when she’s on leave.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Spring 2025

The fridge at Banyan Terrace had notes on it.

It had always had a list on it, hers, in her round fast writing, with her shopping and her rotas and, since April, a line at the bottom in capitals that said XY’S SECRET — CROSS ABOUT IT, about the hair clip in his glovebox. But in the spring of 2025, with her on nights and him on days and the two of them sometimes not awake in the flat at the same time for a week, his notes started going up beside it.

He stuck them on with the magnet shaped like a fish that Raiden had given them.

One morning she came in at eight off a night and there were four. She stood in front of the fridge in her coat and read them, one after the other.

Bring milk.

Eat something. The soup on the second shelf. Not the yoghurt.

The boiler man comes Tuesday.

I love you.

They all looked exactly the same. Four scraps of prescription pad, four lines of the same bad-day heart trace, falling over and getting up. If anybody else had come into the kitchen, they’d have thought he’d written bring milk four times. They’d have thought it was a man with a lot of feelings about milk.

She stood there in her coat and looked at the fourth one.

He’d never written it before. He’d said it, the night she moved in, in the bath. He’d said it since. He didn’t say it often. He’d never put it on paper, and he’d put it on the fridge, between the boiler man and the milk, in writing nobody else on earth could read, as if it were one more thing that needed doing that week.

She took it off the fridge. She put the fish magnet back on the boiler man.

She brought the milk.

✦ ✦ ✦

Autumn 2026

She never had to explain the margins to anyone. Nobody else ever read them.

That was the point of them, she thought later. That autumn, when she was the ghost three nights a month and the anatomy tutor in the day and he was a man who knew everything and had promised not to ask, he left journals open on the kitchen table at night with a pencil in the gutter, and wrote in the margins under her notes, and she wrote back. A gunshot to the liver. A spleen that tore days after a fall. What would you have used. I’d have shunted first. You told me that two weeks ago. Then rubbed it out.

Anybody could have picked those journals up. Anybody who came into the flat. Eliana came round once and sat at that table with one of them open in front of her for ten minutes and said, it’s a trauma journal, and turned the page.

Eliana couldn’t read his side. Nobody could. To anybody else it was a woman’s pencil notes on a vessel repair, with a heart trace running down beside them. Only Elara could see it was a conversation. Only Elara could see it was the most careful, patient, frightening conversation anyone had ever had with her, and that it went on every night for three months, in the dark, in the gutter of a book, and that he never once wrote the question he wanted to.

✦ ✦ ✦

May 2027

The card came with the frames.

He gave them to her on the path in the hospital garden after the photographs, in the first light, with the night staff drinking their coffee on the grass and Nainai poking Raiden’s arch with her stick. Two frames in brown paper. Her mother’s nursing registration, with the photograph of a young woman in a cap who had Elara’s face. Her father’s boat licence, with a man trying not to laugh.

She’d looked at them and not been able to say anything.

Then she’d opened the card.

It was one line, in the heart-trace writing, across the middle. She’d read it in a second. Everyone was watching her. Raiden was right behind her, looking over her shoulder, and Elowen, and Jinx, and Ev had come to stand at her elbow without anyone seeing her move.

“What does it say?” said Raiden. “I can’t read it. Nobody can read it. Elara. What does it say?”

“No,” said Elara.

She folded the card and put it inside her dress, against her heart, and she didn’t tell any of them, then or at the banquet or ever. Raiden sulked until the soup. Elowen tried twice. Eliana said she’d find out, and Elara said she wouldn’t, because it was on paper, and paper was the one thing Eliana couldn’t get into.

It said: Here is the rest of your name.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later that month

She told him at Camphor Hill, in the long kitchen, a week after the wedding, with the card out on the table between them. She’d taken it out to look at again. She took it out most days.

“It’s the most romantic thing about you,” she said. “You know that? Not the house. Not the ring. Not the loupes, even. That only I can read you.” She turned the card over in her fingers. “Everyone else gets a heart trace. Pharmacists ring me. Your registrars ring me. Your own grandmother sends your letters to me so I can read them back to her over the phone. And when you want to tell me something, you write it down in front of all of them, and none of them can see it.”

He was looking at her across the table. He didn’t say anything.

He reached across and took her right hand, and turned it over.

He had a biro in his shirt pocket. He always did. He took the cap off with his teeth and held her wrist flat on the table, palm up, the scar across the inside of it pale and silver, and wrote on it. Across the scar. Small, in the heart-trace writing, three words that went along and fell over and got up again, while she sat still and felt every letter.

Then he bent his head and blew on it, to dry the ink.

She felt his breath on the inside of her wrist, over the words, warm, and her whole arm went to gooseflesh up to the shoulder. He looked up at her with his mouth still close to her wrist.

She didn’t wait. She put her other hand in his hair and pulled him up across the table, and he came, and kissed her, with the card between them and the biro rolling off onto the floor and her right hand held flat on the table under his so she wouldn’t smudge it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t wash it off for two days.

She showered with her right arm held up out of the water, the way you’d hold a cake over your head in a crowd. She taught the first-years the forearm on the Tuesday morning in a short-sleeved shirt, and halfway through, a boy in the front row put his hand up and asked what was written on her wrist.

She looked down at it. Three words in blue biro across the scar, slightly smudged at one end from the pillow.

“That says bring milk,” said Elara. “Obviously.”

The boy looked at it. The whole front row leaned in to look at it. It looked like a heart trace.

“It doesn’t look like it says that,” said the boy.

“It’s my husband’s writing,” said Elara. “Nobody can read it but me. Flexor carpi radialis. Find it on your own forearm, please, and stop looking at mine.”

It didn’t say bring milk.

It said what the fourth note on the fridge had said, two years before, between the boiler man and the milk. Only now it said it on her, in ink, over the place where he’d held her together on the stones, and when it finally faded off on the Thursday she stood in the bathroom at Camphor Hill and looked at the bare scar, and went downstairs and found him in the study, and held her wrist out, and he got his pen.

chapters.title: The Stitches Competition
chapters.desc: At the trainees’ skills night Elara takes on her husband and his cousin with a pig’s foot each. She wins, and he asks for a rematch at home.
chapters.epigraph: “Best of three. I want it in writing.” — Wang Xing Yue
chapters.content:
The skills night was in the same grey stone building near the courts where she’d done her test, and the same porter was on the door with a list.

He looked at her name on it. He looked at her.

“You’re the one who ran,” he said. “Across the car park. At the tall one.”

“Yes,” said Elara. “Sorry.”

“He’s inside,” said the porter, and ticked her off.

Every surgical trainee who could get off the rota had come, because there was free food. The long room on the ground floor had been set up with tables in rows and a pig’s foot on every table, pale and scrubbed and pinned to a board, with a cut down the middle of each one where somebody from the college had made the wounds that afternoon. There were trays of instruments, and boxes of sutures, and at the front, on a table by himself with a stopwatch and a cup of tea, Mr. Zhai.

He looked up when she came in and his eyebrows went up into his hair.

“Dr. Wang,” he said. “I remember you. The talker.”

“I’m married now,” said Elara. “It’s a different Dr. Wang. Well. It’s the same me. It’s a different name.”

“I know who you married,” said Mr. Zhai, and pointed his stopwatch at the side of the room.

Xing Yue was standing against the wall in his dark coat with his hands in his pockets, looking at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d been asked to judge. City Hospital had sent him, because, Professor Liao had said, he was the only one who’d make the trainees frightened enough to try. He’d stood at the side all evening while they did their knots and their skin closures and their little bowel joins on models, and walked between the tables with his hands behind his back, and stopped at one and said “Again,” in a voice that made a trainee from Harbourside drop her needle holder.

When Xing Yue had moved on, Elara went over and gave her a boiled sweet and told her he’d done the same to her on her first day, and she was married to him, and it got better.

“Does it?” said the trainee.

“No,” said Elara. “But you stop minding.”

Yu Chen was there too, at the back, in a grey jumper with his ears already pink. He’d come because Xing Yue had told him to, and because Eliana wanted a photo. He’d been married four weeks. He kept touching his ring with his thumb when he thought nobody was looking.

At nine o’clock Mr. Zhai stood up with his stopwatch.

“Final round,” he said. “Three volunteers. Ten interrupted stitches each, on a pig’s foot, against the clock. Quality first. Speed second. I’ll judge it myself.” He looked round the room over his glasses, and his eyes came to rest, with great satisfaction, on the side wall. “Dr. Wang. Not that one. The consultant. You’ve spent all evening telling them they’re slow. Come and show them.”

The room went quiet.

Xing Yue didn’t move. Then he took his hands out of his pockets.

“And you,” said Mr. Zhai, pointing the stopwatch at Yu Chen, who went red to the neck. “The cousin. I’ve heard about you. And—” He turned. He looked at Elara.

The room started to laugh before he’d even said it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They put the three tables side by side at the front.

Elara stood at the one on the left. Yu Chen in the middle. Xing Yue on the right, with his coat off and his sleeves rolled up and his glasses on, looking at his pig’s foot as if it were a patient who’d lied about their history.

The trainees crowded round. Someone was filming. Someone else, at the back, was taking bets.

The room was cold. The college was always cold. Elara felt it go into her right hand while Mr. Zhai was explaining the rules, the fingers stiffening, the white coming up from the tips. She didn’t hide it. She put her right hand under her left arm, inside her cardigan, and held it there against her own side, and stood waiting with it tucked in.

A trainee at the front was watching her.

“What are you doing?” she said.

“Warming it,” said Elara. “I had a nerve injury. It goes white in the cold, every time, it always will. If I start with it like this the first three stitches are rubbish.” She held it there, counting. “You’ve got to know what your hands do. Not what you want them to do. What they actually do. In a cold room, at four in the morning, after twelve hours. Then you work with that.”

The trainee looked at Elara’s hand under her arm. A few of the others did too. One of them, a boy from orthopaedics, put his own hands in his armpits, thoughtfully, as if he’d never thought of it.

She took hers out. It was pink. She picked up the needle holder.

“Go,” said Mr. Zhai, and pressed the stopwatch.

✦ ✦ ✦

She talked.

She talked from the first stitch: about the pig’s foot she’d named in first year, and about bananas, and the porter on the door. She talked about Mr. Zhai’s stopwatch, which she said was older than her, and Mr. Zhai said it was older than her mother, and the room laughed, and she was already on stitch four.

Beside her Yu Chen wasn’t talking at all.

He was good. She could see it out of the corner of her eye. Neat, careful, every stitch exactly where it should be and every knot laid down flat, the way someone did it who’d learned in an emergency department where you had to do it right the first time because the patient was going to sit up and leave. He was slow. He knew he was slow. He didn’t hurry. She liked him for it.

On her right, she didn’t look. She knew exactly what he’d be doing. She’d watched him close a thousand times. Every stitch identical, the spacing perfect, the knots so square you could have built a house on them, and silent, his face completely still, his hands moving in that unhurried way that looked slow and wasn’t. He’d be perfect. He’d be perfect on every one.

She was on seven. She was telling the room about the time she’d got lost in the basement at Harbourside and come out in the mortuary.

She was on nine.

“Dr. Wang,” said Mr. Zhai, without looking up from his stopwatch. “Would you mind not talking.”

“Yes,” said Elara, and tied off ten, and put the needle holder down.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Time,” said Mr. Zhai.

He wrote it down. Then he looked up at the right-hand table, where Xing Yue was tying his tenth knot, and wrote that down too, a few seconds later. Then Yu Chen, who finished a little after and put his instruments down neatly side by side and let his breath out.

Mr. Zhai went along the three boards with his glasses on the end of his nose and pressed the skin either side of every stitch with the end of his pen. He turned Xing Yue’s board round under the light and looked at it from the other side.

Then he came back to his table and sat down.

“The consultant’s are perfect,” he said. “I’d expect nothing less, or I’d have reported him. The cousin’s are perfect and slow, which in emergency medicine is the right way round. His wife’s”—he nodded at Elara—“are as good as the consultant’s, or near enough. And she was faster.” He put the stopwatch down. “By a few seconds. While talking about a mortuary.”

He looked at Xing Yue.

“You lost,” said Mr. Zhai. “To your wife. In front of every surgical trainee in the city. On film.”

The room went up.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found her afterwards by the coats.

She was pulling her cardigan on, and grinning, and being congratulated by three trainees from Harbourside and the boy from orthopaedics, who’d kept his hands in his armpits all evening. Yu Chen was by the door on the phone, saying “No, she won,” to somebody, with his ears going.

Xing Yue came through the crowd and stood in front of her.

The trainees took one look at his face and melted away.

She looked up at him.

“Best of three,” said Xing Yue. “I want it in writing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At home he wrote it.

He did it at the long table at Camphor Hill at half past eleven, in his coat still, on a sheet of hospital headed paper from the pad in his bag, while she sat opposite eating cold dumplings from the fridge and watching him with enormous enjoyment.

Rematch. Best of three. Ten interrupted stitches per round. Pig’s foot. Timer: kitchen clock. Judge: none. Loser does the washing up for a month. Neither party to talk during a round.

He looked at the last line. He crossed it out. He wrote, instead: First party may talk.

He signed it. He pushed it across the table to her with the pen, and she signed under him, still chewing, and they both looked at it.

“Where are we going to get pig’s feet at midnight?” said Elara.

He got up and went to the fridge and opened the bottom drawer.

There were three. Wrapped in paper from the market. She stared at them.

“You bought pig’s feet,” she said. “Before. Before you even knew you’d lose.”

“I knew I’d lose,” said Xing Yue.

✦ ✦ ✦

They did it on the long table with the kitchen clock on the windowsill and the window open to the dark garden and the cat watching from the wall.

The first round she won by a stitch. She talked the whole time, about the trainee who’d dropped her needle holder, about Yu Chen’s ears, about Mr. Zhai. He didn’t say a word. He was perfect, and slightly slower than her, exactly as he’d been at the college.

The second round he won. By a stitch. She looked at his board. It was perfect.

The third round, she could tell.

She was on her fifth stitch when she looked up and saw that he wasn’t on his. He was on his third. He had the needle holder in his hand and he was tying a knot, beautifully, and he was tying it slowly, and he wasn’t looking at the pig’s foot at all. He was looking at her.

He was watching her hands. He was watching her face while she talked, and her hands while they worked, and he was tying the slowest knot she’d ever seen him tie, on purpose, so that he’d lose.

She stopped talking.

“You’re doing that on purpose,” said Elara.

He didn’t answer. He kept tying the knot.

She put her needle holder down. She got up and came round the long table, past the clock and the cold dumplings and the signed sheet of paper, and took the needle holder out of his hand in the middle of the knot.

He let her.

She put it down on the board beside his pig’s foot. She took his glasses off and put them on the table. Then she put both her hands on his face, her right one and her left, and kissed him, while he was still sitting in his chair with his hands in the air where the needle holder had been.

He made a sound against her mouth that was nearly a laugh. Then his hands came down, onto her waist, and pulled her into his lap, and he kissed her back. Slow, and then not slow. Her knees were on either side of him on the kitchen chair, and the clock on the windowsill went on without either of them, and the cat on the wall decided to leave.

“You lost on purpose,” she said, against his mouth.

“I lost,” said Xing Yue. “It’s in writing.”

“I want a rematch.”

He stood up, with her still wrapped round him, which made her shriek, and carried her out of the kitchen and down the hall, past her shoes by the door, facing out, and up the stairs, and she laughed all the way up and told him he was going to be doing the washing up for a month, and he said he knew, and didn’t put her down.

The pig’s feet stayed on the kitchen table all night. In the morning there were three boards in a row, ten perfect stitches on the first, ten perfect stitches on the second, and on the third, five of hers and three of his, and a knot, half tied, that he never finished.

She kept the sheet of paper. It went in the drawer with the prescription.
